Hi Ahmer, hope this email finds you well. 
Thank you for your email of March 12, 2025 summarizing the transitional tax issues for tax year 2025. Below, we provide a detailed response on each point. As discussed, we have already shared draft advice with you with respect to depreciation expenses. We encourage you to review that draft advice alongside this email. Our responses here address your four key queries with focused explanations:
1.	Depreciation Treatment for TY 2025: WDV vs. Cost as at June 30, 2024

You’ve asked whether tax depreciation in tax year 2025 should be based on the last written down value (WDV) of assets as of June 30, 2024, or on the original cost, given the shift from Final Tax Regime (FTR) to Normal Tax Regime (NTR). The answer depends on the asset’s prior use under FTR and hinges on interpretations of section 22 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”). In essence, for assets that were used entirely under FTR in prior years, we can argue the opening tax WDV remains at original cost (since no depreciation was ever “allowed” against taxable income), whereas for assets partially used under FTR, there is a question of how the previously disallowed depreciation is treated.

•	Assets 100% used under FTR: 

In the past, these assets generated only FTR income (e.g. export sales) on which no tax depreciation was claimable (FTR did not allow deductions per Section 169(2). Consequently, one position is that their tax WDV on July 1, 2024 should still be the original cost, since the company never actually took any tax depreciation on them. Section 22(5) of the Ordinance defines WDV as cost minus “depreciation deductions allowed… in previous tax years”. Because no depreciation was allowed under FTR (it was explicitly barred by law), those assets have not been depreciated for tax purposes. In other words, depreciation that was never permitted shouldn’t reduce the asset’s WDV. This view finds support in case law: courts have held that only depreciation actually allowed counts, and disallowed depreciation is ignored for computing next year’s WDV. Moreover, the Finance Act 2016 added an explanation to Section 22(5) of the Ordinance deeming depreciation “allowed” during tax-exempt periods, but notably no such deeming was enacted for final-tax periods. This implies that unless income was exempt, unclaimed depreciation is not automatically treated as allowed – supporting a higher WDV in your case.
Nevertheless, tax authorities may take a different stance: They often contend that when an asset was used in FTR business, its depreciation, though not deducted, is deemed allowed for WDV purposes. The rationale (drawn from Section 22(3) and 22(6)) is that an asset used to earn business income but with “another use” (here, a use that didn’t enter normal tax) should be treated as if fully used for business when computing WDV. In practice, past tax return forms have reduced WDV by the full depreciation amount even if a portion was disallowed due to FTR use. There is even Tribunal case law suggesting that under presumptive tax regimes, all expenses, including depreciation, are considered allowed (since the taxpayer paid a fixed tax without accounting for expenses). This view implies the asset’s tax WDV was steadily reduced over the FTR years, despite no deduction being claimed, because the asset was “losing value” and the law did not explicitly freeze depreciation. In short, the tax department could argue that the opening WDV at July 1, 2024 is the cost less all notional depreciation for those years.
Suggested approach: We advise adopting the taxpayer-favorable interpretation that opening WDV equals original cost (less any depreciation actually claimed against non-FTR income). This means for a wholly-FTR asset, virtually full cost remains available for depreciation from tax year 2025 onwards. This approach is supported by a “literal” reading of the term “allowed” in Section 22(5) and by case precedents. It also aligns with the concept that a taxpayer is not obliged to claim depreciation if it yields no benefit. That said, this is an aggressive position. We expect the tax department may challenge it with the contrary arguments noted above. To mitigate risk, we recommend making clear disclosures in the tax computation for TY 2025 if we take this position. For example, we can add a note in the return explaining that no depreciation had been allowed under FTR, hence we are taking cost as the tax WDV. It would also be prudent to submit a formal letter to the tax office articulating this treatment, to preempt any allegation of “omitting” income or filing inaccurate particulars. This transparency can help avoid penal consequences while the position is defended on technical grounds.
In the (conservative) alternative, the company could use the lower WDV per tax records (i.e. cost minus all prior notional depreciation) as the base for tax year 2025 depreciation. This would satisfy the FBR’s likely view and avoid an immediate dispute. The downside is a smaller depreciation deduction going forward (and thus higher taxable income). Note that even under this approach, any depreciation that was disallowed in the FTR years isn’t lost forever – it would effectively be recognized upon disposal of the asset. Section 22(9) of the Ordinance provides that when you sell a depreciable asset, any depreciation that was not allowed in prior years gets factored into the gain/loss calculation. Practically, this means if we accept a reduced WDV now, the “missing” depreciation will reduce any taxable gain (or increase an allowable loss) on a future sale of the asset. In other words, the tax impact is deferred to disposal rather than taken as depreciation. This is a more cautious route if you prefer to avoid controversy in the short term.
•	Assets partially used under FTR in prior years: These are assets that had mixed use – for example, used in export operations (FTR) and local taxable operations (NTR) during the same year. In such cases, historically the company would have claimed depreciation only on the portion of use related to taxable (NTR) income, while the portion allocable to FTR income was not claimed (it was disallowed). The complication is how the tax WDV was computed. Under Section 22(3), when an asset is used “partly in deriving income from business chargeable to tax and partly for another use,” the depreciation deduction is pro-rated. Section 22(6) of the Ordinance then says that for WDV calculation, you treat the asset as if it were used wholly for business (effectively assuming the full year’s depreciation was allowed). As a result, the tax WDV on record as of June 30, 2024 for such an asset may have been reduced by the entire depreciation amount, even though part of that depreciation was never actually claimed (the FTR part was disallowed in the computation). 
Keeping in view of the above, we suggest adopting a consistent stance for both fully and partially FTR-used assets – ideally the more beneficial one of a higher opening WDV (i.e. not reducing WDV for FTR-disallowed depreciation). This gives you a larger depreciation deduction in TY 2025 and beyond, which can help offset the now-taxable export income. It is supported by a fair reading of the law and certain judicial dicta. Notably, one Tribunal case in 2012 (106 Tax 370) dealing with an asset used in both PTR and NTR regimes held that only the portion of depreciation actually allowed should factor into the taxable gain on sale implying that un-allowed depreciation was recognized as such. This adds weight to the argument that un-allowed depreciation is not deemed “allowed” for future purposes. The implications of FA 2016 are in company’s favor here: by introducing a deemed allowance rule only for exempt income (and not for final-tax income), the law tacitly confirms that in other cases (like FTR) there is no automatic deemed allowance. Again, full disclosure of the method in the return is advised to avoid any appearance of concealment. If challenged, an alternate argument is that even if Section 22(6) forced a reduced WDV, the “lost” depreciation would be recouped under Section 22(9) at disposal, so the timing is the only issue.
In conclusion our recommendation is to claim depreciation in TY 2025 on the basis of the assets’ cost minus only actual depreciation allowed in prior normal-tax years. This means effectively using cost as of June 30, 2024, for assets that had only FTR use, and a proportionately adjusted WDV for assets with partial FTR use. This approach is grounded in law (Sections 22(3), 22(5), 22(6) and FA 2016’s amendments) and supported by case law, though it may be viewed as aggressive by the authorities. We will take all necessary steps (disclosures, justifications) to support this position. We trust this clarifies the depreciation treatment for TY 2025, but please let us know if you wish to discuss the risk dynamics further or prefer the conservative approach.
2.	Taxability of Trader Receivables Outstanding as at June 30, 2024
You inquired about how to treat trade receivables that were outstanding as of June 30, 2024, in light of the transition from FTR to NTR. This is a crucial transitional issue because under the FTR (for exports/trading income), tax was essentially on a receipts basis – the 1% withholding on realized export proceeds was the final tax, and income was not recognized on an accrual basis. Now, under NTR (minimum tax regime), income is to be taxed on an accrual basis, with the 1% being merely a minimum tax. The question is what to do with sales made before July 1, 2024 (when FTR was in force) for which payment was not yet received by June 30, 2024. We see three possible treatment options for these outstanding receivables, each with its own consequences:
•	Option 1: Treat Outstanding Receivables as Taxed under FTR (Accrual Back to Prior Periods). Under this approach, the company would effectively accelerate the taxation of those receivables into the FTR period, ensuring they are taxed at the FTR rate (1%) rather than under the new regime. In practice, this could be done by revising the prior year’s tax return(s) to include the outstanding amounts as if they had been received (or by making a special accrual in the final FTR year). For example, if a chunk of sales in June 2024 remain uncollected, we could tax it in the tax year 2025 return to treat those as if realized by June 30, 2024 and pay the 1% final tax on them now. Any tax that does get withheld when the customer actually pays (post-July) would then be claimable as a refund or adjustable against future taxes, to avoid double taxation. Essentially, the company draws a line at June 30, 2024 and clear the slate of all receivables by subjecting them to FTR.
This keeps all income up to the transition date under the old regime, providing consistency. It avoids the complication of bringing pre-July sales into the post-July normal tax computation. The tax rate is the favorable 1%, with no risk of additional tax on these amounts under normal rates. Using a single regime for the cutoff period reduces the chance of disputes, as the FBR will see that we did not “escape” taxation on pre-transition income – the company pays the final tax due on it. In fact, in similar transitions in the past we have seen advice that using one regime per return is cleaner and less contentious.
Nevertheless, this option requires a current cash outflow to pay the tax on receivables that haven’t yet been collected. Essentially, we’d be pre-paying tax on income before cash is in hand. Additionally, when the customer eventually pays and deducts 1% withholding (now as minimum tax), the company would need to ensure that amount is credited or refunded, since the company would have paid final tax on that revenue. That could result in overpaid tax that might only be recovered later as a refund, which ties up some cash in the interim. Despite these downsides, this approach eliminates future uncertainty – those receivables would not factor into the normal tax regime at all.
•	Option 2: Tax Outstanding Receivables under NTR (Normal Tax Regime) when Received. This approach essentially lets the new law take its course: any receipts that come in after July 1, 2024 will be treated as income under the NTR/minimum tax regime. That means in the tax year the money is received, the company will include the corresponding sale revenue in its normal taxable income (even though the sale occurred earlier). The 1% withheld at source upon receipt will be treated as an advance/minimum tax, not full and final. If the normal tax on that income (based on profit margins and corporate tax rates) exceeds 1%, the company will pay the difference. If it’s lower, the 1% acts as minimum tax (no refund of the excess). In effect, the income from those pre-July sales will be taxed as if it were part of the post-July business. This is the default position under FA 2024’s change – exports realized on or after July 1, 2024 are no longer final-taxed, they contribute to taxable income subject to minimum 1% tax.
The big drawback is potentially higher tax cost. Under FTR, those receivables would have effectively only borne 1% tax. Under NTR, depending on your profitability, the effective tax rate on that revenue could be much higher. For example, if those sales have a typical gross profit of 20%, the profit portion will be taxed at the corporate rate (29% for TY2025 plus super tax under section 4C), which is far above 1%. Even with 1% credit, the additional tax could be significant. This option could thus result in an unexpected tax burden on sales that you may have assumed were effectively taxed at 1%. 
3.	Treatment of Fixed Asset Additions during Jul–Dec 2024
You sought confirmation on the “receipt-based rule” for fixed asset additions in July 2024 to December 2024, the documentation needed, and whether these additions are eligible for depreciation. We interpret this as clarifying when an asset is considered acquired for tax purposes (especially in the context of the mid-year transition), and ensuring that any assets purchased in that period are properly accounted for so that you can claim depreciation (and initial allowance, if applicable) at the right time.
First, a bit of context: since your company’s tax year is a special year (not ending in June), the period January 2024 to June 2024 falls into tax year 2025 (which, for the export business, was still under FTR). Under FTR, no depreciation deduction was allowable against export income. However, any assets acquired in this period will form part of your pool of depreciable assets going forward into the NTR period. It’s important to correctly establish their cost basis and acquisition date for future depreciation claims.
“Receipt-based” rule for asset acquisition: In tax practice, an asset is generally considered acquired (for purposes of claiming tax depreciation or initial allowance) when it is available for use and the taxpayer has taken delivery/possession. In other words, simply placing an order or making a partial payment does not qualify – there should be receipt of the asset. We confirm that for any asset additions in Jul–Dec 2024, you should ensure you have documentation that the asset was delivered and installed (or otherwise ready to be used) by December 31, 2024. For example, if machinery was purchased from abroad in October 2024, you should have the bill of lading/goods receipt note showing it arrived by year-end, and ideally a commissioning report showing it became operational. This evidence will support that the asset was “acquired” in Tax Year 2025. Conversely, if an asset was ordered in late 2024 but only delivered in January 2025, it would not count as an addition in TY 2025 for tax purposes – it would be considered acquired in TY 2026.
Why is this important? Because under the tax law, depreciation is allowable from the tax year in which the asset is first put to use (or available for use) and owned by the taxpayer. If an asset is not received by the cutoff date of the tax year, you cannot start depreciating it in that year. Given that TY 2025 for you was largely under FTR, depreciation wasn’t being utilized; however, the company still want to record the correct acquisition date since it affects when initial depreciation allowances apply and how the opening WDV is determined for TY 2026 (the first NTR year).
Documentation to reinforce acquisition and payment: At minimum, maintain the following for each fixed asset addition in Jul–Dec 2024:
•	Vendor Invoice/Purchase Contract – indicating the date of sale/purchase and the asset description.
•	Delivery evidence – this could be a delivery challan, goods received note (GRN), installation certificate, or Bill of Entry for imports, showing the asset arrived at your premises (or was installed and ready to use) on or before Dec 31, 2024.
•	Payment evidence – proof that payment was made (or at least arranged) for the asset. While tax law does not generally require payment to claim depreciation, large unpaid balances could raise questions of whether the sale was finalized. Also, Section 75 of the Ordinance requires payments above certain thresholds to be made through banking channels; ensure compliance to avoid any disallowance issues. If an asset was acquired on credit, it’s still considered acquired as long as you had the asset in possession, but be mindful to pay through proper banking means when due to satisfy the tax rules.
Having this documentation will serve two purposes: (1) It will satisfy auditors or tax department that the asset is genuine and in use, and (2) it will allow the company to substantiate any claims for depreciation or initial allowance at the correct time.
Eligibility of depreciation: Now, for assets acquired in January 2024 to June 2024, can you claim depreciation and if so, when? Since during that half-year your export income was under FTR (no deductions allowed against it), any depreciation on assets used for that FTR income would not have been claimable in tax year 2025. If an asset was partially used for local (taxable) operations in that period, you could claim prorated depreciation for the local-use portion in tax year 2025. In practice, we will have computed the depreciation for the local business as usual. Any portion related to export use was disallowed (not deducted) due to section 67 and 169. This means, for tax purposes, those assets’ WDV at Dec 31, 2024 is effectively their cost (since the depreciation attributable to export use was not allowed). Going into TY 2026 (post-transition), those assets will be part of the depreciation schedule with opening WDV equal to cost (if we take the view discussed in Point 1 that disallowed depreciation doesn’t reduce WDV. Thus, yes, they are fully eligible for normal depreciation from tax year 2026 onward. The company will claim depreciation on them in TY 2026 at the applicable rates.
For completeness, note that if any asset addition in Jul–Dec 2024 was purely for the local segment of your business (taxable), you likely have already claimed half-year depreciation on it in the tax year 2025 return. If that’s the case, its WDV going forward would be cost minus that half-year depreciation. If an asset was for export use, no depreciation was claimed, so WDV remains cost. In either case, from July 1, 2024 onward, all operations are under NTR, so the concept of splitting depreciation by use vanishes and you’ll simply depreciate the remaining WDV going forward.
In summary: All fixed assets acquired in Jul–Dec 2024 will be part of your depreciable assets pool for the normal tax regime. Ensure you have taken receipt of them by year-end 2024 and have the paperwork to prove it. Those assets will qualify for depreciation deduction in the first normal-tax year (tax year 2026 for exports) at their proper opening WDV. We will not lose any depreciation on them – what wasn’t claimable during FTR (January 2024 to June 2024) essentially gets deferred but preserved as part of the asset’s tax base. It is reinforced that the tax computations should attach a schedule reconciling the fixed asset additions and its treatment (no depreciation claimed in tax year 2025 due to FTR but included in opening WDV for TY 2026). This will make it clear to any reviewer how the company we handled the transition.
4.	Initial Allowance Eligibility (Post July 1, 2024)
Lastly, you asked about the eligibility of Initial Allowance on assets in the post-July 1, 2024 period, and how the treatment works after the regime change – specifically, conditions for claiming it and the applicable law/practice. Initial allowance is the one-time depreciation relief allowed under Section 23 of the Ordinance for new assets. To clarify, initial allowance (IA) is distinct from normal annual depreciation: IA is typically 25% of cost for plant and machinery (and 15% for industrial buildings, though IA on buildings was withdrawn a few years back for most cases). It’s allowed in the year the asset is first put to use, provided certain conditions are met.
Key points regarding initial allowance in our context:
•	Post-July 1, 2024 (NTR period) – eligibility: From the point your business income becomes taxable under the normal regime, any new eligible asset you acquire and put to use will qualify for initial allowance in that year. The conditions are: (a) the asset is a depreciable asset (plant, machinery, furniture, building etc. as listed in the Third Schedule), (b) it is used by the taxpayer for the first time in Pakistan in that tax year, and (c) it is ready for use in the business. The asset should not be a used asset previously used by you or acquired from a related party in certain tax-favorable transactions, because those scenarios are usually excluded from IA. In practice, most new machinery purchases will qualify. For example, if you purchase new production equipment in August 2024 and it’s operational in October 2024, and since by tax year 2025 your export income will be taxable, you will be able to claim initial allowance (25% of its cost) in the tax return for TY 2025. In other words, assets first used during FTR years do not retrospectively get initial allowance once you shift to NTR. IA is effectively forfeited on those and going forward you just depreciate them annually (as we discussed above). The law sees IA as a benefit you elect to take in the first year of use; if that year no benefit was claimable (due to FTR) or you chose not to claim it, it doesn’t carry forward. This underscores why planning acquisitions around transitions is important.
Because your FTR period ended June 30, 2024, any asset that was first used between January 1, 2024 and June 30, 2024 (assuming that was all under FTR for exports) did not get an initial allowance. Unfortunately, as noted, we cannot claim it in tax years 2025 or 2026 for those assets. The tax law doesn’t grant “deferred” initial allowance. The initial allowance, like depreciation, was never allowed under FTR, but unlike normal depreciation, you don’t get a later benefit except that your WDV remains higher. The consolation is that the cost remains in the asset’s base, so you depreciate the full cost over time instead of getting a chunk upfront. If there are any major assets in that category, we can discuss if foregoing IA was material – but since it couldn’t be claimed anyway, it’s a moot point now.
In practical terms, for tax year 2026 and onwards, you are eligible to claim initial allowance on all qualifying assets. The company will utilize this to maximize tax relief on new capital investments. For assets acquired prior to the transition that did not get IA, the company will simply depreciate them normally (their base was not eroded by IA since none was claimed). As an aside, if for any strategic reason you wanted not to claim initial allowance (for example, to smooth income or because you anticipate losses), you could choose not to. 
To conclude this point: Post-July 1, 2024, initial allowance becomes available to you again as a tax benefit. The company should ensure all conditions are met to claim it on new assets. The section 23 and past practice support that it’s a one-year, first-use deduction. 
We trust the above addresses your four queries comprehensively. In summary, tax year 2025 is a transitional year with careful considerations for depreciation basis, receivables, and asset additions. The detailed draft advice already shared with you provides further legal analysis, especially for the depreciation question, and we encourage you to review it for a deeper understanding of the rationale. 
Please feel free to reach out with any follow-up questions or if you would like to discuss any of these points in a meeting.

**Subject:** Withholding Tax Exemption & Salary Tax Documentation – Employee in Gilgit-Baltistan

Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing in my capacity as a tax consultant to address your queries regarding: (1) the applicability of withholding income tax on a salary paid to an employee working in Gilgit-Baltistan, and (2) the proper documentation to evidence taxes deducted and deposited for that employee. Please find below a detailed response on each point.

**1. Withholding Tax on Salaries in Gilgit-Baltistan:**  The Gilgit-Baltistan (G-B) region holds a special constitutional status, under which federal taxes (including income tax) have historically not been enforced there. In fact, Pakistani income tax laws are generally **not applicable within Gilgit-Baltistan’s territory**【8†L81-L89】. Multiple government notifications and court decisions (including a 2024 judgment by the G-B Chief Court) have **affirmed that Gilgit-Baltistan is exempt from federal taxes such as income tax**【17†L87-L94】. Practically, this means that if an employee’s salary pertains to services rendered in G-B (and the employee is a G-B resident earning income only in that region), you are **not required to deduct withholding tax** under Section 149 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for that salary. This exemption stems from G-B’s autonomous tax jurisdiction – for example, the **Finance Act, 2018** recognized taxpayers registered with the Gilgit-Baltistan tax authorities by treating them as “filers” in Pakistan【30†L59-L67】, underscoring that those earning income in G-B fall outside FBR’s normal tax ambit. In summary, **salaries paid to employees working exclusively in Gilgit-Baltistan can be paid without federal tax withholding**, **provided** the income is confined to G-B and the employee does not have Pakistan-source income taxable by FBR. It is advisable, however, to maintain proof of the employee’s G-B tax status or any relevant exemption certificate if available, so that you can justify the non-deduction to FBR or any other inquiry in the future.

**2. Documentation of Taxes Deducted & Deposited:**  To keep all stakeholders informed and compliant, it is important to document any taxes that have been withheld from the employee’s salary and deposited to the government treasury. We recommend preparing and providing the following records:

- **Challan Copies (Payment Receipts):**  Provide the client/employee with copies of the tax payment challans (also known as CPR – Computerized Payment Receipts) for the withholdings. Each challan evidences the amount of tax deducted from the employee’s salary and the date it was deposited to the government’s account. These receipts serve as official proof that the tax amounts were indeed remitted to the Federal Board of Revenue (or relevant authority) against the employee’s NTN.

- **Annual Tax Deduction Certificate:**  At the close of the fiscal year, issue an official tax deduction certificate to the employee, detailing the total salary paid during the year and the total income tax withheld from that salary. This certificate is usually provided under Section 164 of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 (read with Rule 42 of the Income Tax Rules) and is commonly given by employers to their staff each year【32†L173-L180】. It stands as a formal record for the employee (and for your client’s files) of the tax deducted and deposited on the employee’s behalf. The employee can use this certificate for their own tax return filing or any audit support, as it verifies that tax on their salary has already been paid at source.

- **Reconciliation Statement:**  Internally, prepare a reconciliation of the total taxes deducted vs. total taxes deposited for this employee’s salary to ensure accuracy. This involves matching the sum of monthly withholding amounts (as per payroll records or monthly withholding statements filed under Section 165 of the Ordinance) with the aggregate amount shown on the deposit challans for the year. By reconciling these figures, you can confirm that the full amount deducted from the employee’s pay has been deposited to the national exchequer. It is good practice to share a summary of this reconciliation with the client/employee – for instance, a brief report showing monthly salary, tax withheld each month, and the challan reference for each payment. This transparency will reassure the employee that no portion of the withheld tax is outstanding or misallocated.

By providing the above documentation, you will **apprise your client (or the concerned employee)** of the exact taxes deducted and deposited against their salary. In essence, the challan copies and the tax deduction certificate act as the employee’s evidence that their salary tax obligations have been fulfilled through withholding. Meanwhile, maintaining the reconciliation and supporting statements in your records will help address any queries from tax authorities and ensure that your company’s reporting obligations are met in full.

Please note that while Gilgit-Baltistan is currently exempt from Pakistan’s income tax regime, tax laws can evolve. It is prudent to stay updated on any changes in legislation or FBR guidelines post-2025 that might affect G-B’s tax-exempt status. If any new notifications require withholding or reporting for G-B salaries, you should comply accordingly. In the absence of such changes, the guidance above remains valid: **no withholding is needed for G-B-sourced salaries**, and all deducted taxes (if any) must be properly deposited and documented with the aforementioned proofs.

I trust that the above explanation satisfactorily addresses your concerns. Should you require any further clarification or assistance with tax compliance matters, please feel free to contact me.

Sincerely,  
**[Your Name]**  
Tax Consultant | [Your Firm Name]

Dear Atiq Sb,

I hope this email finds you well.

We refer to your email dated March 5, 2024, wherein you have sought our opinion on the following matters:

1. Applicability of withholding income tax on salary payments to an employee working in Gilgit-Baltistan (GB); and  
2. Possibility of obtaining a refund of taxes already deducted and deposited for such employee before the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR).

Our detailed response is set out below for your kind consideration:

---

**1. Withholding Tax on Salaries Paid in Gilgit-Baltistan**

Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) enjoys a unique constitutional status under which the enforcement of federal taxes, including income tax, has historically been excluded. This position has been consistently upheld through various governmental notifications and judicial pronouncements, including a recent 2024 judgment by the GB Chief Court.

Accordingly, salaries paid for services rendered exclusively within GB are not subject to withholding tax under section 149 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. This exemption arises from GB’s autonomous tax jurisdiction. Notably, the Finance Act, 2018 recognized this special status by amending the definition of “filer” to include individuals listed on the Active Taxpayers Lists maintained by the Gilgit-Baltistan Council Board of Revenue and the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Council Board of Revenue.

For ease of reference, the relevant extract from Circular No. 03 of 2018 – *Exploration of Important Amendments through the Finance Act, 2018* – is reproduced below:

> “Persons filing their Income Tax returns in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan were being subjected to higher rates of withholding tax applicable to non-filers... In order to facilitate such persons, the definition of a ‘filer’ under section 2(23A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 has been amended through the Finance Act, 2018. Consequently, individuals appearing on the Active Taxpayers Lists maintained by the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Council Board of Revenue and the Gilgit-Baltistan Council Board of Revenue shall also be treated as filers under the Ordinance…”

In light of the foregoing, where an employee is engaged exclusively for services in GB, no deduction of withholding tax on salary is required. However, it is strongly recommended to maintain contemporaneous documentation evidencing that the employment services were rendered within GB (such as employment contracts, deployment letters, timesheets, or other relevant records), to substantiate the non-deduction position before any tax authority or inquiry in the future.

---

**2. Refund of Taxes Already Deducted and Deposited**

With respect to taxes already deducted and deposited with FBR in relation to the concerned employee, please note that once taxes have been deposited, the employer cannot directly recover the same.

The only available recourse is for the employee to file an income tax return with FBR, correctly disclosing the exempt nature of the salary income, and simultaneously submit a refund application under section 170 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. The processing and issuance of any refund will then be subject to FBR’s scrutiny and procedures.

---

We trust that the foregoing adequately addresses your queries. Should you require any further clarification or assistance on this matter or any other tax compliance matters, please do not hesitate to reach out.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Designation]  
[Your Firm Name]

# Tax Treatment of OUP Pakistan’s Digital Platforms (ORB, My E-Mate, Oxford Extend)

## Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Goods vs. Services Classification

Under the Income Tax Ordinance 2001, withholding tax on payments differs for goods and for services. **Section 153(1)** requires every prescribed payer to deduct tax when making payments: **Clause (a)** covers payments for the *sale of goods*, while **Clause (b)** covers payments for the *rendering of services*【37†L8268-L8276】. The applicable withholding rates (specified in the First Schedule of the Ordinance) are substantially lower for goods than for services. For example, payments to a resident company for the sale of goods are typically subject to ~4% withholding (for active taxpayers), whereas services rendered by a company attract ~8% withholding【37†L8268-L8276】. These taxes on goods/services are usually treated as a **minimum tax** on the recipient (except certain manufacturers and listed companies for goods)【50†L1-L4】.

**Definition of “goods”:** The Ordinance defines *“goods”* in **Section 2(19)** in line with general commercial usage. Although the exact text of Section 2(19) is not quoted here, it is interpreted consistently with the Sales Tax Act and Sale of Goods Act definitions. Under **Section 2(12) of the Sales Tax Act 1990**, *“goods”* include *“every kind of movable property other than actionable claims, money, stocks, shares and securities”*【32†L1-L4】. Similarly, the Constitution (Article 260(1)) defines goods to include all materials, commodities, and articles【45†L84-L92】. Intangible digital products (like online access rights) do **not** fall neatly into “movable property” or “materials/commodities.” Conversely, *“services”* are broadly defined (in provincial laws and by FBR) as anything which is **not** goods – including facilities, amenities or advantages provided for consideration【29†L1-L4】. In essence, if a transaction doesn’t involve supplying tangible movable property, it is treated as a service for tax purposes.

**Digital goods vs. services – guidance:** Pakistani tax authorities and courts have grappled with the goods/services distinction in various contexts. The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has indicated that to determine the nature of a supply, one touchstone is whether it can be classified under a tariff code as a good; if not, it is a service【45†L91-L99】. For instance, FBR proposed using the Pakistan Customs Tariff to decide if something is a “good” – anything not identifiable as such would fall under “services”【45†L91-L98】. Several court rulings (e.g. on electricity, gas, and aviation charges) underscore the importance of the goods/services distinction for tax jurisdiction【31†L125-L133】. In the absence of explicit local case law on digital platforms, the likely position is that **online digital platforms are services**, not goods, since they provide access to content/functionalities (an “advantage”) rather than a transfer of tangible property. There is no physical commodity changing hands – the subscriber obtains a service (access to an e-learning system), not ownership of a chattel. Therefore, payments to Oxford University Press Pakistan (OUP SMC) for Oxford Reading Buddy, My E-Mate or Oxford Extend should be treated as payments for services under Section 153(1)(b), *not* for sale of goods.

*Income Tax withholding implications:* Classifying these platform subscriptions as services means withholding tax under Section 153 will be at the service rate. OUP (as a resident company) would have **8%** deducted by corporate customers on payments (if OUP is an active taxpayer; 16% if not on the Active Taxpayers List), whereas if the same receipts were treated as goods, the withholding would only be ~4%【37†L8271-L8279】. This distinction is significant: the higher service withholding is also treated as a **minimum tax** on OUP’s income (i.e. even if net profits are lower, 8% of gross receipts is the floor tax)【50†L1-L4】. OUP would prefer the lower goods rate; however, misclassifying a clear service as “goods” could be challenged by tax authorities. Notably, “IT services” and “IT-enabled services” enjoy a concessionary 4% withholding rate (for filers) under recent law【47†L603-L610】, but those terms are defined for *exported* services and specific registered entities. Unless OUP’s platforms qualify as **IT-enabled services** as per Section 2 of the Ordinance (which requires registration with bodies like PSEB for exports), the general services rate applies. In summary, for income tax purposes **the digital platforms are services**, subject to withholding under Section 153(1)(b). OUP must account for the higher advance tax on receipts, though this will be adjustable against its final tax liability (or minimum tax if applicable).

## Sales Tax Act, 1990 – Federal Sales Tax on Goods

Sales tax in Pakistan is bifurcated: the Federation (FBR) taxes **goods** under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, while provinces tax **services** under their respective statutes. Determining whether OUP’s digital platforms are “goods” or “services” is therefore crucial to identify which tax (federal or provincial) applies.

**Definition of goods (Sales Tax Act):** As noted, *“goods”* are defined in Section 2(12) of the Sales Tax Act as *“every kind of movable property other than actionable claims, money, stocks, shares and securities”*【32†L1-L4】. This is an inclusive definition focusing on tangible movables. Traditionally, this has been interpreted to cover physical articles, merchandise, and even electricity (the law was amended to include electricity explicitly as goods)【45†L85-L92】. Intangible products, rights, or digital content are **not** expressly mentioned in the definition of goods. In practice, if something cannot be touched or moved physically, it is generally not treated as a “good” for sales tax. An access code or online subscription is a **chose in action** (a right to access), not a tangible article. It does not fall under any Pakistan Customs tariff code for goods either (there is no HS code for a purely online service). Consistent with FBR’s guidance, anything not classifiable as a good in the customs tariff would be deemed a service【45†L91-L98】. Therefore, **digital platform access is not a “good” under the Sales Tax Act**.

**Taxability of digital access codes:** If OUP sells a physical product (for example, a printed card or USB with an access key), one might argue there is a tangible component. However, tax authorities look at the *substance* of the transaction. The value in an Oxford Reading Buddy or My E-Mate subscription lies in the service/content, not the paper or token delivering a code. Thus, even if an access code is printed on paper, FBR would likely treat the sale as a supply of **intangible content (service)** rather than of the paper itself. There is presently no explicit FBR ruling on e-learning subscriptions, but by analogy, **software delivered electronically** has been treated as a service in many cases (whereas software on a CD could be a good). The National Tax Council has deliberated that ambiguous cases should be clarified via unanimous definitions, and suggested that what doesn’t fall under “goods” by the classical definition be taxed as services【45†L85-L94】【45†L99-L107】. 

**Exemption for books (Sixth Schedule):** Importantly, **printed books and educational textbooks are exempt from sales tax on goods** under the Sixth Schedule to the 1990 Act. Specifically, (old Serial No. 53, now consolidated around Serial 32 after Finance Act 2022) covers *“Newsprint, newspapers, journals, periodicals, books (excluding directories, brochures and leaflets)”* as tax-exempt items【4†L28-L36】. Educational textbooks are thus zero-rated or exempt from federal GST【4†L28-L33】. OUP’s core business – physical books – falls in this exempt category. However, **digital materials are not “books” within the meaning of this exemption**. The Sixth Schedule ties exemptions to specific HS codes (e.g. 4901.9100 covers printed books)【4†L30-L33】, which do not encompass digital content. A subscription or e-book (PDF/online) has no tariff code, and the exemption for “books” is not drafted to include electronic/digital publications. In fact, recent tax reforms explicitly narrowed the book exemption to *“newsprint and educational textbooks”* only (excluding anything not in printed form)【0†L1-L4】【0†L7-L13】. Therefore, **sales of access to OUP’s digital platforms cannot enjoy the book exemption** in the Sixth Schedule – that exemption applies only to tangible books. If the digital platforms were mistakenly treated as “goods,” they would be unclassified taxable goods (standard 18% GST) with no explicit exemption – but since we conclude they are services, the federal sales tax on goods does not levy on them at all. 

**Conclusion – federal sales tax:** Oxford Reading Buddy, My E-Mate and Oxford Extend **do not constitute “goods”** under the Sales Tax Act 1990. OUP’s revenue from these platforms is not subject to the federal GST regime (which covers goods) except possibly any ancillary supply of physical media. Instead, the **provincial sales tax on services** (discussed next) is the relevant regime. OUP should be cautious not to bundle the digital access in a way that could mistakenly be seen as part of the book supply – the safer approach is to separately identify and invoice the digital service to keep the book exemption intact for the book component.

## Provincial Sales Tax on Services – Treatment of Digital Education Platforms

Since OUP’s digital platforms are services, they fall under provincial sales tax jurisdiction. Each province (and the Islamabad Capital Territory via Federal ordinance) has its own sales tax on services law, but there is broad similarity in structure. We analyze each relevant jurisdiction:

- **Sindh – Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SSTSA):** Sindh taxes services listed in the Second Schedule of the Act, at generally **15%** standard rate (recently increased from 13% to 15% from July 2024)【13†L7-L15】. The Act defines *“taxable service”* as any service listed in the Schedule, provided by a registered person in Sindh, in the course of an economic activity. Critically, the law was amended to adopt a **broad definition of “service”**: *“service means anything which is not goods”* (Clause 2(79) as amended, analogous to Section 2(aaa) of KP Act)【29†L1-L4】. Thus, Sindh will view OUP’s digital platform subscriptions as services by default. We must identify the category they fall under. Likely, these platforms come under **“Information technology (IT) services” or “digital/online services.”** Sindh’s schedule does not explicitly use the term “e-learning,” but it taxes *“software or IT-based system development consultants”* and related IT services. In practice, the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) has treated various online services as taxable under the IT/technical services heading. In a recent SRB special procedure, *“IT services include cloud-based streaming services”*【11†L1-L4】 – indicating that streaming or online access platforms are considered *IT services* for SST purposes. By analogy, an educational digital platform is an IT-enabled service (hosting and providing access to educational content online). Therefore, Oxford Reading Buddy, My E-Mate, Oxford Extend would be taxable in Sindh, presumably under the IT services category (historically tariff code 9832.0000 in Sindh’s schedule). The **applicable Sindh SST rate** would be 15%. Sindh has in the past offered reduced rates on certain services via notifications (e.g. IT services at 5% or 3% without input tax credit, per SRB Notification 3-4/8/2013)【17†L43-L50】, but those are subject to conditions. As of 2025, no specific exemption for educational digital services exists in Sindh. (Notably, *education services provided by formal educational institutions were proposed to be taxed at 15% in Budget 2024*【17†L53-L62】【17†L57-L65】, though with possible concessions for nonprofit schools; however, OUP’s platforms are not delivered by schools themselves but by a publisher, and do not fall under “education services” by an institution). Thus, OUP should charge Sindh sales tax on any platform subscriptions provided to customers in Sindh (or if the service is initiated from Sindh to unregistered recipients elsewhere, SRB may still assert jurisdiction).

- **Punjab – Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012 (PSTSA):** Punjab’s law similarly taxes services listed in the Second Schedule, with a **standard 16%** rate【13†L7-L15】. - **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa – KPK Finance Act, 2013 & KPK Sales Tax on Services Act, 2022:** Khyber Pakhtunkhwa initially followed the 2013 Act, but in 2022 it enacted an updated Sales Tax on Services Act to harmonize with other provinces【28†L937-L946】. ## Bundled Transactions: Physical Books + Digital Access Codes

OUP often packages digital access with textbooks (for instance, a textbook comes with a code for Oxford Extend or My E-Mate). This raises the question of **composite vs. multiple supplies** in sales tax. Pakistani tax law does not explicitly define composite supplies in the manner some VAT systems (e.g. EU or Malaysia) do, but the principle can be inferred. Essentially, if an **exempt good** (a book) is sold along with a **taxable service** (digital access), the tax authorities will seek to tax the portion attributable to the service. 

- **Composite supply** refers to a situation where goods and services are supplied together as a single indivisible package for one price, and one element is the principal supply. If Pakistan had a uniform GST, one might tax the whole bundle at the rate of the principal element. However, in Pakistan’s split system, a composite supply crossing the goods/services divide is problematic – federal and provincial jurisdictions are different. There is no straightforward rule saying one part “absorbs” the other for tax; instead, each authority may claim its portion.

- **Multiple (mixed) supply** would mean treating the book and the digital access as two separate supplies, each with its own tax treatment (book exempt, digital service taxable). This is the more prudent approach under our system. In practice, FBR and the provincial authorities expect a **reasonable allocation of the bundle price** to each component. If OUP sells a textbook + ORB access code as a single bundle price, it should internally allocate a value to the book and to the code. The book portion would be exempt (Sixth Schedule) and the digital portion would attract provincial sales tax. OUP can do this by specifying separate line items or a split of value on the invoice. 

If no allocation is made, there is a risk of **double taxation or dispute**. For example, the Sindh Revenue Board could argue the entire bundle is a “service” (since it includes a service element) and try to tax the full price, while FBR would deny exemption on a book sold with a paid online component unless separated. There have been analogous situations: e.g., restaurant services involve supply of food (goods) and dining service; to avoid both federal and provincial taxes on restaurant bills, an arrangement was reached to treat it wholly as a provincial service (with FBR zero-rating the food)【31†L125-L133】. But such clear arrangements exist only via specific notifications (e.g., FBR has at times notified cooked food for consumption on premises as exempt to let provinces tax it). In the case of books with digital access, no explicit notification exists. Thus, the safest course is **treating it as a mixed supply** – the book is a separate (exempt) good, the digital access a separate service.

In a bundled sale, **withholding tax** implications also arise: Payment for a combined supply that includes goods and services might theoretically be subject to both 153(1)(a) and 153(1)(b) portions. In practice, if invoiced separately, the buyer would deduct 4% on the book price and 8% on the digital service fee. If not separated, many withholding agents would err on the side of treating the whole as services (higher rate) to avoid short deduction. This again incentivizes clear separation.

**Recommendation:** OUP should **unbundle composite offerings** of books + digital. If a single price is advertised (e.g. Rs. 1,000 for textbook plus online access), the invoice should specify, say, Rs. 900 for the book (exempt under Sixth Schedule) and Rs. 100 for the digital service (plus applicable provincial sales tax, e.g. 13% Sindh or 5% Punjab on that portion). This allocation should be based on fair value (perhaps the standalone price of the digital access if sold separately). By doing so, OUP will correctly apply exemptions and taxes: no federal sales tax on the book portion【4†L28-L36】, and provincial sales tax on the digital portion. It will also simplify withholding tax treatment (distinct payment for goods vs services). If OUP fails to segregate, it could face disputes or have to defensively charge service tax on the full bundle (which would make its educational products more expensive).

In summary, **bundled transactions must be treated as multiple supplies** for Pakistani tax purposes. The digital platform element **cannot piggyback on the book’s tax-exempt status**. Provincial tax authorities will expect their share from the digital component. Sensibly allocating the price between the two components and complying with respective tax rules will ensure OUP remains compliant and avoids future tax controversies over its innovative blended learning products.

| **Oxford Reading Buddy**  | Digital reading platform (online service – not a tangible good) | Treated as **Service** under Section 153(1)(b). Withholding on payments to OUP by customers at **8%** (for company payer to company payee, if OUP is ATL) or 10% (if payer is individual/AOP) of gross amount【37†L8268-L8276】. This is a minimum tax on OUP. *Not* eligible for lower “goods” rate, since ORB isn’t sale of goods. | **Provincial Sales Tax on Services** applies (no federal GST on goods). Classified as an **IT/digital service**. <br>– **Sindh SRB:** Taxable at 15%【13†L7-L15】 (standard), under IT services category (e.g. online information/database access).【11†L1-L4】<br>– **Punjab PRA:** Taxable at 16%, however qualifies as software/IT service – eligible for **5% reduced rate** without input tax credit【21†L49-L58】.<br>– **KPK KPRA:** Taxable at 15% standard; likely eligible for **5% (or 3%)** under IT services incentive【21†L49-L58】.<br>– **Balochistan BRA:** Taxable at 15% (no special reduction announced).<br>*Exemption:* Not exempt as “books”. Sixth Schedule book exemption does **not** cover digital subscriptions【4†L28-L36】. |
| **My E-Mate**       | Online e-learning platform with e-books and resources (service) | Treated as **Service** (Section 153(1)(b)). Withholding tax ~**8%** on payments to OUP (company rate)【37†L8268-L8276】. If schools (companies/AOPs) pay OUP, they must deduct this at source. This WHT is adjustable against OUP’s tax; if OUP qualifies as an IT service exporter, it might avail 4% WHT, but for domestic sales it’s standard service rate. | **Provincial Service Tax applies:** My E-Mate provides access to e-books and learning tools, falling under IT/online services. <br>– **Sindh:** 15% SST on IT services. (If My E-Mate is billed along with textbooks, only the digital portion is taxable).<br>– **Punjab:** 16% PST, or 5% under reduced rate for IT services【21†L49-L58】. My E-Mate’s provision of e-books likely counts as an IT-enabled service (akin to digital library), so PRA’s 5% should apply if conditions met.<br>– **KP:** 15% or reduced ~5% for IT services as per KPRA’s schedule. <br>– **Balochistan:** 15% under BRA.<br>*No general exemptions.* If part of a textbook bundle, separate the e-service value to tax it; the print book remains exempt. |
| **Oxford Extend**   | Digital teaching/learning support platform (service) | Treated as **Service** for withholding. Subject to Section 153(1)(b) – WHT @ **8%** (companies) on payments【37†L8268-L8276】. Schools or institutions paying license fees for Oxford Extend must deduct this tax. (If OUP invoices a composite package of textbooks + Extend access, the portion for Extend is service fee for WHT). | **Provincial Service Tax applies:** <br>– **Sindh:** 15% SST. Oxford Extend (being an online platform for teachers/students) is an IT service. No education-specific exemption in Sindh (education institutions’ own fees had an exemption threshold, but that doesn’t cover a vendor’s platform) – so standard rate or any SRB notification rate (3% if no inputs) would apply.【17†L43-L50】<br>– **Punjab:** 16% or concessionary 5% as IT service. Oxford Extend likely falls under *“information technology enabled services”* (which Punjab defines to include databases, online content etc.), hence the reduced 5% tax is applicable【21†L49-L58】. <br>– **KP:** 15% (with potential reduction to 5% under KP’s IT services incentives). <br>– **Balochistan:** 15% standard PST.<br>*Note:* Oxford Extend often accompanies textbooks – ensure to invoice digital access separately. The **book component is exempt【4†L28-L36】**, the Extend platform fee is taxable. |

**Sources:**

- Income Tax Ordinance 2001, Section 153(1)(a)&(b) – differential WHT on goods vs services【37†L8268-L8276】. Definition of “goods” (movable property) and “services” (everything not goods) per tax laws【32†L1-L4】【29†L1-L4】.  
- Sales Tax Act 1990, Section 2(12) – *“goods”* defined as movable property (excludes intangibles)【32†L1-L4】. Sixth Schedule, Table-1 – exempts printed books/newspapers (not digital content)【4†L28-L36】.  
- Provincial sales tax statutes (Sindh 2011, Punjab 2012, KP 2022, Balochistan 2015): Classification of IT and digital services. *Standard tax rates:* Punjab 16%, Sindh/KP/Balochistan 15%【13†L7-L15】. Reduced rate for software/IT services in Punjab/KP (5%)【21†L49-L58】; SRB inclusion of online streaming in “IT services”【11†L1-L4】.  
- National Tax Council discussions on goods vs services definitions【45†L85-L94】【45†L91-L99】 and need for harmonization.

Please only read the content below.

Mr. Samiullah Siddiqui						                        January 7, 2025
Finance Director 
Oxford University Press Pakistan (SMC-Pvt) Limited				   DTA 000
Plot 38, Sector 15
Korangi Industrial Area
Karachi


Dear Sir 


INCOME TAX AND SALES TAX IMPLICATIONS: DIGITAL PRODUCTS


We refer to the e-mails dated July 31, 2024, and January 3, 2025, and the discussions held with our Partner Muhammad Shaheryar Khan in the context of the ‘e-product’ offered by Oxford University Press Pakistan (SMC-Pvt) Limited [OUP SMC]. A brief understanding of the products is given in the ensuing paragraphs: 

(i)	The Oxford Reading Buddy (ORB) platform, developed by Oxford University Press (OUP), serves a global audience. It provides associates, including OUP SMC, with access to a shared publishing platform and personalized lockers, enabling them to manage digital publications independently while benefiting from global resources. The platform supports the seamless flow of rights, money, and data between associates and the central system. OUP SMC is authorized to enter sub-rights licenses for distributing electronic rights. Customers purchase digital content via access tokens, and OUP SMC manage the financial transactions, ensuring revenue flows back to the central platform. Platform usage fees cover access to global content and locker maintenance, striking a balance between branch autonomy and global integration.

(ii)	The My E-Mate platform, powered by Magicbox, operates as a third-party digital reader, facilitating content distribution for OUP associates at both local and global levels. Authors grant electronic rights to OUP, which licenses these rights to associates for further distribution. The platform supports flexible access through school subscriptions or access codes and ensures online and offline availability via secure, encrypted apps. An annual licensing fee funds platform operations, enabling the smooth transfer of rights, revenue, and data. 

(iii)	The Oxford Extend platform serves as a comprehensive learning and content management system (LMS/CMS), designed for schools to access educational materials through subscriptions. E-books, licensed by OUP in collaboration with authors, are uploaded to the platform and made accessible via secure apps for both online and offline use, ensuring uninterrupted access even without internet connectivity. Schools subscribe to the platform and e-books, generating revenue through royalties on branch net receipts and service charges for access and maintenance. Additionally, schools pay annual fees for platform updates and ongoing support. Oxford Extend ensures smooth integration through robust onboarding and training programs, allowing schools to maximize its potential. 
2.	Our opinion has been sought on the implications of income tax and sales tax on the above products of the OUP SMC. The issues, we consider, that need to be resolved are: 

(i)	The appropriate classification of sales related to ORB for income tax withholding purposes needs to be addressed, specifically whether these sales qualify as "products" subject to 5% withholding tax or as "services" subject to 9% withholding tax. 

(iv)	For Oxford My E-mate, requires advice on the income tax and sales tax implications of the two distinct sales models. In the B2B model, where subscriptions are sold directly to schools, clarification is sought on the applicable withholding tax rates and the treatment of digital subscriptions under federal and provincial sales tax frameworks. In the B2C model, where access codes are bundled with physical book sales, guidance is needed on the tax implications of such bundled transactions.

Understood.

In that case, **here’s what I will do** instead:  
✅ I will still prepare a **detailed, well-structured professional advice**  
✅ Based on a **deep understanding** of the statutes you listed (the laws I know and apply up to date)  
✅ **Cite sections and schedules properly** from Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, Sales Tax Act, 1990, and the four provincial laws  
✅ Use **standard interpretations** and **FBR/SRB/PRA/BRA/KPRA positions** (general practice)

- "Goods" under ITO means tangible items — typically physical products.
- ORB involves **online access to digital content**, maintained and updated via a platform. Customers purchase **access rights** (tokens) rather than a tangible product.

**Conclusion:**  
- ORB access constitutes a **service** — specifically, the **provision of digital learning services**.
- Accordingly, withholding under **Section 153(1)(b)** should apply at the **service rate** (currently 8% for filers, 9% for non-filers).

# Legal Advisory: Sales Tax Treatment of Lubricant Sales in Drum Packaging (Third Schedule STA 1990)

## Background and Issue  
You have inquired about whether the sale of lubricants in drum packaging (bulk B2B sales, e.g. to fleet operators or transporters) can be treated as outside the scope of the Third Schedule of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (Pakistan). The Third Schedule generally subjects specified goods to sales tax based on their **retail price (Maximum Retail Price or MRP)**. We address: (1) the definition and scope of the Third Schedule’s MRP-based regime; (2) its application to lubricants sold in *retail* versus *bulk* form; (3) relevant precedent or guidance (FBR notifications, circulars, case law) on this distinction; and (4) potential risks or counterarguments if authorities challenge treating drum sales as outside the Third Schedule.

## Third Schedule – MRP-Based Sales Tax Regime  
**Statutory Scope:** The Third Schedule of the STA 1990 lists goods on which sales tax is charged **at the retail price** (inclusive of all duties/taxes other than sales tax) rather than on the transaction value. Under Section 3(2)(a) of the Act, **“taxable supplies… of goods specified in the Third Schedule shall be charged to tax at [17%/18%] of the retail price”**, and the manufacturer or importer must **print the retail price and amount of sales tax on each article or package**【22†L203-L212】. In other words, for Third Schedule items, the manufacturer pays sales tax as if the product is sold to the end-consumer at MRP, capturing the entire supply chain’s value in one go. 

**“Retail Price” Definition:** The law defines *“retail price”* (for Third Schedule purposes) as *“the price fixed by the manufacturer or importer… inclusive of all duties, charges and taxes (other than sales tax) at which a particular brand or variety of an article should be sold to the general body of consumers”*【20†L33-L40】. This makes clear that the MRP-based regime is oriented toward **consumer sales** – i.e. the price at which goods are ultimately sold to consumers (general public) is the tax base. The highest such price is used if multiple prices are fixed【20†L35-L40】. 

**Goods Covered:** The Third Schedule (as updated) includes many consumer goods – for example, household appliances, batteries, tires, auto parts, **lubricating oils and vehicular fluids (when sold in retail packs)**, packaged foods, etc【43†L24-L32】【43†L39-L43】. The presence of consumer-packaged goods in this list underlines that it targets retail trade. Notably, the law permits the government to add or remove items from the Third Schedule via notification【22†L211-L215】, allowing policy adjustments for specific goods.

## Application to Lubricants – Retail Packs vs. Bulk Drums  
**Lubricants in Third Schedule:** Lubricating oils (and similar vehicular fluids like brake or transmission fluids) were brought into the Third Schedule via Finance Act 2019. The relevant entry covers *“Lubricating oils, brake fluids, transmission fluid, and other vehicular fluids **sold in retail packing**.”*【43†L28-L33】. Therefore, when such oils are sold in typical **retail packaging** (e.g. small bottles, cans, or pails intended for consumer/aftermarket retail sale with an MRP), the sales tax must be charged on the MRP printed on that pack. Manufacturers/importers of these retail packs are required to print the price and charge 17%/18% GST on that price to all buyers, irrespective of the actual lower transaction price to distributors, etc., and then pass on the tax to the government【22†L203-L212】.

**Bulk Sales in Drums:** The question arises whether lubricants sold in **bulk drums (e.g. 50L, 210L barrels)** to business customers fall outside this Third Schedule (MRP) regime. The **statutory wording** is important – it limits the Third Schedule treatment to lubricants **“sold in retail packing.”** A drum container intended for B2B sale/use is generally **not a “retail pack”** in the ordinary sense. Such drums are typically sold to industrial or commercial buyers (e.g. transport companies, service stations, fleet operators) rather than to the general consumer market. They usually **do not carry a printed retail price** because they are not meant to be placed on a retail shelf for direct sale to individual consumers. This suggests that **bulk drum sales should not meet the Third Schedule criteria**, since the law specifically targets retail-packaged goods.

**Legislative Intent:** The inclusion of the qualifier “sold in retail packing” for lubricants implies that only **consumer-pack** lubricants (e.g. 1-litre engine oil bottles, 4-litre cans, etc.) are meant to be taxed on MRP. By contrast, bulk lubricants used for commercial purposes would logically be taxed under the **normal regime (value/transaction-based)** rather than MRP. Indeed, the Third Schedule entries for other automotive goods reinforce this retail vs. wholesale distinction. For example, *storage batteries* and *tyres* are listed in the Third Schedule, but explicitly **“excluding those sold to automotive manufacturers or assemblers”*【43†L31-L35】 (i.e. excluding bulk OEM sales). Likewise, auto-parts are included only if in retail packing and **not when sold to assemblers**【43†L39-L43】. This shows the law carves out sales that are **business-to-business (B2B) supply chain transactions** as opposed to retail consumer sales. By analogy, lubricant drums sold to fleet operators or commercial resellers are **bulk B2B transactions** not aimed at retail consumers, and thus arguably **outside the scope of the Third Schedule’s MRP requirement**. They would be subject to ordinary GST on the actual sale value (invoice price).

**Conclusion on Scope:** Based on the above, **lubricant sales in drum packaging can reasonably be treated as outside the Third Schedule**, since the Third Schedule mandates MRP-based taxation only for lubricants *“sold in retail packing.”* The absence of an MRP on drum packaging and the commercial nature of such sales support this classification. The manufacturer in such cases would charge standard sales tax (e.g. 18%) on the actual selling price of the drum (net invoice value) rather than on any notional retail price.

## Precedents, FBR Guidance, or Case Law  
**FBR Notifications/Circulars:** To date, there is **no specific publicly-known FBR ruling or circular** explicitly on lubricants distinguishing retail vs. bulk packaging for sales tax. The Finance Act 2019 changes that added lubricants to Third Schedule were explained generally in budget briefings. It was understood that lubricant manufacturers must charge MRP-based tax on their **consumer packs** going forward【27†L28-L36】. There was no indication that genuine bulk sales to industry would be subject to MRP; the law’s wording itself provides the guideline by restricting to “retail packing.” 

We note by analogy that the Federal Board of Revenue has recognized *packaging/market segment distinctions* for other products in tax policy. For example, until recently, certain **“bulk sales of edible products under brand names or trademarks”** were exempt from sales tax, with only retail packed goods being taxed – an exemption that was **removed in Budget 2023** to curb abuse【39†L243-L251】. The existence (and subsequent removal) of that exemption highlights that authorities have historically treated **bulk wholesale sales differently from retail sales** for tax purposes. In the case of lubricants, however, no special exemption was needed – the law simply never brought bulk drums into the Third Schedule in the first place.

**Case Law:** There appears to be *little to no reported litigation* specifically on whether bulk-pack goods should be excluded from Third Schedule if the law’s language implies such exclusion. This is likely because the statute is fairly clear when it uses qualifiers like “sold in retail packing” or “excluding those sold to manufacturers.” Courts, in principle, would give effect to these words. The absence of an explicit court case on lubricants suggests the industry norm aligns with the plain reading: i.e. companies charge MRP-based tax on small retail packs, whereas drums or bulk B2B supplies are transacted on value. 

That said, general principles from case law on tax statutes would apply: tax laws are to be strictly interpreted. If a good doesn’t unambiguously fall within the higher tax regime (MRP/Third Schedule), the benefit of doubt typically goes to the taxpayer. Thus, if challenged, one would argue that **the government intentionally used “sold in retail packing” to limit the Third Schedule’s reach**, and it could have included bulk sales explicitly if it so desired (as it did by adding/excluding other categories).

## Risks and Counterarguments  
While the legal footing for excluding drum sales from the Third Schedule is solid, it is prudent to consider potential **risks or counterarguments** the tax authorities might raise:

- **Substance Over Form Argument:** The authorities might argue that the *economic substance* of the sale (lubricant for vehicular use) is the same, whether sold in 5-liter cans or 200-liter drums, and that the Third Schedule intention is to tax such oils at the stage of manufacturer on the full retail value to capture revenue. They could view the **packaging distinction as a loophole** if they suspect drums are being used to circumvent MRP-tax on what eventually becomes retail consumption. Essentially, they may claim that these bulk sales ultimately trickle down to end-users (e.g. a fleet operator consuming the oil in vehicles is the end consumer, or a drum buyer could resell oil in loose form to smaller customers). However, this argument would have to override clear statutory language – which is difficult in a tax context. The law’s literal wording supports the taxpayer: only **retail-packed lubricants** are in the Third Schedule【43†L28-L33】. Unless and until the FBR amends the Schedule to include bulk lubricants, a court or tribunal would likely uphold the literal interpretation.

- **Anti-Avoidance Concern:** If a pattern emerges industry-wide where what used to be sold in consumer packs shifts to drum sales purely to avoid MRP-based tax, the FBR could view it as **tax avoidance**. The immediate risk is FBR auditors challenging specific transactions: e.g. issuing a show-cause notice asserting that drums were effectively supplied to unregistered retailers or final consumers and should have borne MRP tax. They might attempt to re-characterize those supplies as Third Schedule sales and demand the difference (tax on full retail value minus tax already paid on invoice value). This could entail substantial tax exposure and potential penalties/surcharges for “short payment” of tax. However, the success of such an audit stance would depend on facts (were the drums truly for bulk business use vs. a disguised retail supply chain) and on the adjudicating authority’s view of the law’s scope.

- **Comparative Treatment / Industry Norms:** Another practical risk is if **industry practice is split** or unclear. If some lube oil manufacturers (perhaps conservatively or due to FBR pressure) are charging MRP-based tax even on drum sales, the FBR may question others who do not. It’s worth confirming the prevalent practice and any informal guidance. Consistency with industry practice and prior FBR acceptance strengthens your position. Conversely, deviating from what FBR expects (if, say, they believe all branded lubricant sales should be on MRP) can invite scrutiny.

- **Future Changes:** The government could respond by changing the law or issuing a clarification. For instance, the FBR could issue a notification to explicitly **include bulk lubricant sales in the Third Schedule** (they have the power under Section 3(2)(a) proviso to include or exclude items【22†L211-L215】). This risk is prospective – it wouldn’t retroactively undermine the current treatment, but it would affect future sales. The 2023 removal of bulk-sale exemptions in other sectors【39†L243-L251】 suggests a policy trend of **narrowing such carve-outs**. Thus, one should monitor budgetary changes or FBR circulars for any sign that bulk lubricants might be brought into the MRP regime or that the definition of “retail packing” could be broadened or clarified unfavorably.

## Recommendations and Mitigation  
**Document the Classification:** If you proceed with treating drum-pack lubricant sales as outside the Third Schedule, maintain clear documentation supporting this position. Ensure that **drum packages do not carry any MRP** and are labeled for bulk/industrial use. Your sales records and marketing materials should consistently treat these as B2B wholesale supplies. This helps demonstrate that in form and substance these were never intended as retail consumer sales, buttressing the “not retail packing” argument.

**Customer Profile:** Whenever possible, sell drums to registered businesses (with GST registration) who will either consume the product in business operations or resell it with proper invoicing. For example, sales to fleet operators for their own use, or to sub-distributors who will invoice onward sales (even if not on MRP, at least charging standard sales tax on value). If drums are sold to any party that is essentially an end consumer but unregistered (e.g. a very large farmer or unregistered industrial end-user), that scenario might raise the question of whether it was effectively a retail sale. Keeping the buyer profile in the **commercial sector** reduces the risk of being seen as a retail channel.

**Monitor FBR Guidance:** Stay alert to any **FBR general orders, rulings, or clarifications** on this issue. In case of uncertainty, a proactive approach could be to seek an **advance ruling or written clarification from the FBR** on the status of bulk lubricant sales. While not always guaranteed, an affirmative response would give you protection. Even a budget commentary or FBR’s official **Sales Tax General Order (STGO)** explaining the 2019 Third Schedule changes could be useful if it implicitly acknowledges the “retail packing” limitation (for example, FBR’s notes on Finance Act 2019 clearly listed lubricants *sold in retail packing* as Third Schedule items【42†L4080-L4088】, indicating that’s the condition for MRP tax).

**Potential Litigation Readiness:** Be prepared to defend your position legally if challenged. The key points in defense would be the **literal statutory language** and the **legislative intent** as evidenced by the wording and structure of the Third Schedule (as discussed above). Citing the explicit text of the Third Schedule and any analogous treatment of other products (like batteries/tyres and the now-removed bulk food exemption) would form a strong basis. If necessary, courts would likely examine the ordinary meaning of “retail packing” – which in common parlance and commercial practice would exclude 210L drums sold business-to-business. Obtaining an expert tax legal opinion now (in addition to this advisory) could also bolster your file for any future dispute.

## Conclusion  
In summary, **lubricants sold in bulk drum packaging can be legitimately classified outside the Third Schedule’s MRP-based regime** under the Sales Tax Act 1990. The law restricts Third Schedule treatment to lubricants *“sold in retail packing,”* implying that purely B2B bulk transactions should be taxed on actual transaction value, not on a deemed retail price【43†L28-L33】. This interpretation is supported by the text of the Schedule and analogous provisions for other goods. 

However, there are **practical risks**: tax authorities may question this classification if they perceive revenue leakage or avoidance. It is crucial to implement the position carefully – limit such sales to genuine bulk channels, keep robust documentation, and comply with standard GST invoicing on those sales. Additionally, remain vigilant for any changes in law or FBR stance. So long as the law remains as is, you have a defensible position grounded in statute. Should the FBR formally challenge it, you would be prepared to argue that the Third Schedule simply does not extend to your drum-pack lubricant sales, using the clear language of the Act and any relevant interpretations to support your case【20†L33-L40】【43†L28-L35】.
