Tax Advisory – Applicability of Section 236A to K-Electric’s Internal Vehicle Sale
Background
K-Electric Limited (the “Company”) plans to dispose of used company vehicles through an internal sealed-bid process limited to its own employees. These vehicles, being vacated due to employee resignations or promotions, will be offered on an “as is, where is” basis. All interested K-Electric employees may submit confidential sealed bids, with the highest bidder for each vehicle winning the sale (Terms and Conditions.docx) (Terms and Conditions.docx). The question arises whether this internal sealed-bid sale constitutes a “sale by public auction” under Section 236A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, thereby triggering advance tax withholding obligations. This advisory examines the scope and intent of Section 236A, analyzes the nature of the proposed sale, and assesses K-Electric’s withholding tax responsibilities.
Overview of Section 236A – Scope and Intent
Section 236A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 imposes an advance tax at the time of sale by auction. In essence, the law requires any person conducting a sale of property or goods by way of auction (including a tender process) to collect a withholding tax from the buyer at the time of sale. The relevant text of Section 236A states:
“Any person making sale by public auction or auction by a tender, of any property or goods (including property or goods confiscated or attached... belonging to or not belonging to the Government, local Government, any authority, a company, … or any other authority) shall collect advance tax, computed on the basis of the sale price of such property, from the person to whom such property or goods are being sold.” (Advance tax on sale through auction)
In simpler terms, whenever a sale is conducted through a bidding process (auction) – whether an open outcry public auction or a sealed-bid auction by tender – the seller (or the person managing the auction) must withhold a certain percentage of the sale price from the buyer as advance income tax and deposit it to the government. The current prescribed rate under Section 236A is 10% of the gross sale price for movable property/goods (for income tax filers, higher for non-filers) (Advance tax on sale through auction). This collected amount is adjustable against the purchaser’s final tax liability for the year (10 percent WHT through auctions: FBR compiling database of courts - Business Recorder). (For auctions of immovable property, a reduced rate of 5% applies as per the proviso to Section 236A (Advance tax on sale through auction), but that is not relevant to vehicle sales.)
Legislative Intent: Section 236A was introduced to ensure the documentation of auction transactions and to capture tax at source on such sales. Auctions often involve open market value determinations; by withholding a percentage from the buyer, the tax authorities can bring those transactions into the tax net and obtain advance tax revenue (10 percent WHT through auctions: FBR compiling database of courts - Business Recorder). The provision’s scope is deliberately broad – covering auctions of assets whether owned by government or private entities (explicitly including a “company” in its ambit) (Advance tax on sale through auction). An explanation added via Finance Act 2020 further clarified that even certain renewals (e.g. of licenses originally auctioned) and installment payments fall under “sale by public auction or auction by tender,” evidencing the legislature’s intent to capture all forms of auction-based sales in the tax net () (). In sum, Section 236A’s intent is to impose an advance withholding tax on any sale carried out through a competitive bidding process.
Key Terms – “Auction” and “Public Auction”: In understanding Section 236A, it is vital to interpret what constitutes an “auction” (particularly a “public auction” or an auction “by tender”). Generally, an auction is a mode of sale where would-be buyers competitively bid, and the item is sold to the highest bidder. This can be done via live bidding or by submitting written bids (tenders). A “public auction” typically means an auction open to the general public, ensuring open competition. As defined in case law, “public auction means a public sale at which each bidder may offer increasing bids, and the item is sold to the highest bidder. This involves the auction being held in public, all members of the public having a right to attend, with competitive bidding for the item.” (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice). The emphasis is on the openness of the sale to any interested member of the public and transparent, competitive bidding.
By contrast, an “auction by tender” refers to an auction conducted through a sealed bidding process (a tender). Instead of live outcry, buyers submit secret bids by a deadline, and the seller then selects the highest or most favorable bid (What Is an Auction? Definition, How It Works, and Its Types). This is a common method for asset disposals by governments or companies. Notably, Section 236A’s wording includes “auction by a tender” alongside public auctions, indicating that a sealed-bid tender process is treated as a form of auction for tax purposes (Advance tax on sale through auction). In other words, the law does not confine itself only to traditional open-outcry auctions – it also covers sales by tender, which are essentially “silent” auctions.
Does the Sealed-Bid Mechanism Constitute an Auction or Public Auction?
Sealed-Bid Process as an Auction: The internal sale mechanism K-Electric is using – inviting sealed bids from multiple employees and selling to the highest bidder – is, in substance, an auction. It is a competitive bidding process (albeit a silent one) designed to yield the best price. This aligns with the concept of an “auction by tender”, where bidders submit written bids and the highest bid wins (What Is an Auction? Definition, How It Works, and Its Types). The Income Tax Ordinance explicitly brings “auction by tender” within the ambit of Section 236A, so purely from the standpoint of the sale method, a sealed-bid sale is an auction. Each interested employee is effectively a bidder, and the company will award the vehicle to the top bidder – a process functionally identical to an auction scenario (only without an auctioneer’s hammer).
However, the critical distinction here is the audience and openness of the bidding. Unlike a typical public auction, K-Electric’s tender is not open to the public at large – it is an internal tender open only to the company’s employees (Terms and Conditions.docx) (Terms and Conditions.docx). This raises the question: Does a closed, internal bidding process qualify as a “public auction” under Section 236A? The term “public auction” inherently implies general public participation. In the classic definition (Secretary of State v. Sunderji, Privy Council 1938), a public auction is one held “in public” with “all members of the public having a right to attend” and bid, ensuring broad competition (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice). K-Electric’s sealed bid sale deviates from this – participation is restricted to K-Electric employees only, and outsiders cannot attend or bid. In effect, it is a closed auction or a private tender.
“Public Auction” vs. Private/Closed Auction: Given the above, the sealed-bid sale does not meet the ordinary meaning of a “public” auction, since it is not open to all interested buyers, only to a defined internal group. It is more akin to a private sale with a competitive element – the competition is limited to employees (perhaps as a perk or internal policy to offer used assets to staff) rather than opened up to the public marketplace. This nuance is important in interpreting Section 236A. The statute’s language “sale by public auction or auction by tender” (Advance tax on sale through auction) suggests the auctions contemplated are those where broad participation is expected (either through a public bidding event or a tender process typically advertised to potential bidders). Nothing in Section 236A explicitly addresses a scenario of a non-public, internal auction.
On one hand, the inclusion of “auction by tender” in the law could imply that any competitive bidding process, even a sealed tender, triggers Section 236A. The law does not add the qualifier “public” before “tender.” In many cases, tenders for disposal of assets (e.g. by government agencies) are indeed publicly advertised, but the statute’s phrasing could cover private tenders as well. In strict legal theory, if multiple bidders are solicited and the sale is awarded to the highest bidder, it is an auction form — regardless of whether the bidder pool is the general public or a subset (such as employees). Thus, one view is that the K-Electric sealed bid sale does constitute an “auction by tender” under Section 236A’s scope, because it is a sale via competitive bidding.
On the other hand, a strong argument can be made that the spirit and intent of “sale by public auction” in Section 236A presume an open market event. The use of the word “public” before “auction” signals that Parliament was targeting auctions open to public participation. The law was introduced to capture tax from auctions that are generally accessible – for example, auctions of government property, court auctions, or corporate asset auctions where any interested party can bid. In K-Electric’s case, the sale is not advertised publicly and is limited to employees (an invited class of bidders). This could be characterized as a private arrangement (essentially an employee-only offer) rather than a public auction.
In summary, the sealed-bid mechanism is unquestionably an “auction” in the broad sense, but it is not a “public auction” due to its limited pool of bidders. Whether Section 236A applies hinges on whether the law is interpreted to cover all auctions/tenders or only those of a public nature. We now turn to how the law treats the person conducting such a sale.
Is K-Electric a “Person Making Sale by Public Auction” in this Case?
Section 236A places the withholding obligation on “any person making sale by public auction or auction by tender” (Advance tax on sale through auction). Typically, this would include:
•	Auctioneers or organizers of auctions (for example, a government department auctioning licenses, or a company auctioning scrap through a bidding process), and
•	Sellers themselves if they directly conduct the auction of their property.
In this scenario, K-Electric is the owner of the vehicles and is itself conducting the bidding process (through its Procurement/Disposal Committee) for sale to employees (Terms and Conditions.docx). There is no external auctioneer; K-Electric effectively steps into the role of the auction-conductor. If the sale is deemed to fall under Section 236A, K-Electric would be the “person making the sale by auction” and thus the withholding agent responsible for collecting the advance tax from the buyers (employees). The law explicitly covers auctions by “a company” (Advance tax on sale through auction), which would encompass K-Electric if it is conducting an auction-type sale.
However, this hinges on the characterization of the sale as a “sale by public auction or auction by tender” under the law. If we conclude (as our analysis leans) that this internal sale is not truly a “public auction”, then K-Electric would not be considered a person making a sale by public auction. Instead, K-Electric would simply be a seller in a private sale transaction. In that case, Section 236A would not be triggered, and K-Electric would have no obligation under that section.
In essence:
•	If Section 236A is applicable (i.e. the sale is treated as an auction/tender under the law), K-Electric is the withholding agent and must fulfill the tax collection duty.
•	If Section 236A is not applicable (i.e. the sale is viewed as a private/internal sale not falling within “public auction or tender”), K-Electric is not acting as an auction conductor in the statutory sense and thus has no withholding obligation under that section.
Withholding Tax Obligations Under Section 236A
Assuming for a moment that Section 236A did apply to this sale, what would K-Electric’s obligations be? Under the Ordinance, K-Electric would be required to:
•	Collect advance income tax at 10% of the gross sale price of each vehicle from the winning bidder (employee) at the time of receiving the sale price (Advance tax on sale through auction). For example, if a car is sold to the highest-bidding employee for PKR 1,000,000, K-Electric must collect an additional PKR 100,000 as advance tax. The payment by the employee would effectively be PKR 1,100,000 (PKR 1,000,000 to K-Electric for the car, and PKR 100,000 which K-Electric withholds for FBR).
•	Deposit the collected tax to the government (FBR) in the prescribed manner (usually under the relevant tax challan code for Section 236A) within the due timeframe. Failure to collect/deposit could expose K-Electric to withholding agent liability and possible default surcharges/penalties ().
•	Issue the employee a certificate of tax collected (so the employee can claim this 10% as advance tax paid on their behalf for tax credit in their own tax return). The tax is adjustable against the employee’s tax liability for the tax year (Advance tax on sale through auction) (it is not a final tax on the employee, except in special cases like auctioned toll manufacturing rights which are a final tax by subsection (3)).
It is important to note that this tax is borne by the purchaser (employee), not by K-Electric. Section 236A envisions the bidder effectively paying the extra 10% as part of the transaction cost. In practice, many auction organizers announce in their bid terms that the successful bidder will be liable to pay the advance income tax in addition to the bid price () () – meaning if Section 236A applied, K-Electric would likely recover it from the employee along with the sale price.
Impact if Not Applicable: If our conclusion is that Section 236A does not apply to this internal sale, then no such tax needs to be collected by K-Electric from the employee bidders under this section. The transactions would proceed with the employees simply paying the agreed bid price for the vehicle (and the usual motor vehicle transfer fees to excise etc., but no 10% income tax via the company). K-Electric would then have no withholding reporting requirement for these sales in its monthly statements under Section 236A.
It is worth mentioning that even if Section 236A does not apply, employees are not entirely outside the tax net – for instance, the Excise & Taxation Department will collect advance tax at the time of transfer of vehicle registration (under Section 231B of the Ordinance) but those are separate provisions and apply irrespective of sale method. Section 236A is specifically about the mode of sale (auction).
Analysis Supporting Non-Applicability of Section 236A
After careful review, we conclude that Section 236A should not be deemed applicable to K-Electric’s proposed sealed-bid vehicle sale to employees, on the balance of legal interpretation. The reasoning is detailed below:
•	Not a “Public” Auction in Substance: The sale in question lacks the fundamental characteristic of a “public auction,” namely openness to the general public. As defined in jurisprudence, a public auction is one to which all members of the public have access as bidders (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice). Here, K-Electric has confined the bidding to its employees only, via an internal invitation (Terms and Conditions.docx). No external or general bidders are permitted (in fact, the bid documents require a company employee ID for participation) (Terms and Conditions.docx). This is essentially a closed tender. Because Section 236A repeatedly uses the term “public auction,” it implies the auctions contemplated are those accessible by the public at large. A transaction that is not open to the public should fall outside the scope of what is meant by “sale by public auction” in the statute.
•	Legislative Wording and Intent: When Section 236A was introduced in 2009, the language used was solely “sale by public auction” (Manufacturers are entitled to tax credit of 2.5 percent: Finance Act, 2009 released - Business Recorder). The intent was clearly to tax sales made in open auction forums. The later insertion of “or auction by a tender” broadened the form of auction covered, but did not explicitly remove the “public” element from the equation (ORDER SHEET). We interpret this as the legislature aiming to cover both traditional open-outcry auctions and sealed-bid auctions, provided they are public in nature (i.e. the tender is publicly advertised or generally accessible). In other words, the law targets the method of sale (auction vs. private negotiation), assuming an auction inherently implies multiple potential bidders invited on an open basis. K-Electric’s method, while competitive, is an in-house process not in line with the typical auction sale the law envisioned. It is reasonable to argue that a private sale — even if using a bidding mechanism — was not the mischief Section 236A aimed to address. The mischief was unreported income from auctions; an internal sale to an employee is more akin to an asset transfer within a closed group and less likely to suffer the same tax evasion concerns as a public auction would.
•	No Public Advertisement or Auction Formalities: In practice, sales by public auction involve public notices/advertisements, auctioneers, bidding in presence of competitors, etc. (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice). None of these hallmarks are present in the current case. The process was communicated internally within the company and will be executed by a committee, not an auction house. The format is more like an employee privilege or internal disposal procedure. Tax law should not be stretched to cover this scenario when its language (“public auction”) does not naturally extend here. Any ambiguity in defining “auction” vs “private sale” should be resolved in favor of the taxpayer – it is a well-settled principle that charging or penal provisions in tax law are to be interpreted strictly, and if the law does not clearly bring a transaction within its ambit, the doubt is decided against imposing the levy. Here, the doubt revolves around whether an employee-only tender is within Section 236A; given the ambiguity, the interpretation that imposes no new withholding obligation on the company is preferable and defensible.
•	Absence of FBR Clarification to the Contrary: We are not aware of any specific FBR circular or official clarification that addresses the status of internal auctions or sales to employees under Section 236A. The FBR’s enforcement guidance has focused on obvious auction scenarios (e.g. auctions by courts, government agencies, etc.) (10 percent WHT through auctions: FBR compiling database of courts - Business Recorder). Nowhere has it been indicated that a limited-group sale like this must be treated as a public auction for withholding purposes. In the absence of direct guidance, one must rely on the statutory language and general principles. Those, as discussed, tilt towards treating this sale as outside the ambit of Section 236A.
•	Supporting Case Law Analogy: While no court case directly on point (i.e. deciding the applicability of Section 236A to a private company’s employee-only auction) has been reported, the courts have consistently underscored what “public auction” entails. The Privy Council definition from Sunderji (adopted in later cases) stresses universal accessibility and open competition (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice). Similarly, in Vishal Builders vs. DDA (ILR 1977 Delhi), it was reiterated that “public auction means it is being held in public, all members of the public having a right to attend” (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice). By applying these definitions, K-Electric’s sealed bid process would not qualify as a public auction. It is a closed competition. Therefore, in a purposive sense, Section 236A should not be invoked. If challenged, K-Electric can argue that “sale by public auction” in the law requires the sale process to be open to the public, which was not the case here (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice).
•	Distinction from Open Tender Sales: It is useful to contrast this with a scenario where K-Electric (or any company) disposes of assets via a tender open to outside bidders. In that case, clearly Section 236A would apply – for instance, if the Company advertised in newspapers for sealed bids from the general market for these vehicles, it would be conducting a sale by tender to the public and would have to collect the 10% tax (). The only distinguishing factor in our case is the limited circle of bidders (employees). That difference – in our view – is legally significant enough to take the transaction out of Section 236A’s “public auction” domain. The sale remains a private/internal arrangement, not a marketplace auction.
Taking all these points together, we find substantial grounds to conclude Section 236A is not applicable to the proposed internal sale. K-Electric can justifiably take the position that it is not required to withhold 10% advance tax on these vehicle sales under Section 236A, since the sales are not being made by way of a public auction or public tender. They are disposals to employees under a company policy, using a competitive bidding to ensure fairness and transparency internally – a scenario outside the contemplation of the auction tax provision.
Conclusion and Recommendation
Conclusion: Based on the analysis of Section 236A’s language, intent, and relevant interpretations, the internal sealed-bid sale of used vehicles to K-Electric employees should fall outside the scope of “sale by public auction” as meant in the Income Tax Ordinance. The process, while auction-like, is a closed tender limited to employees and thus not a “public auction or auction by tender” in the statutory sense. Consequently, K-Electric would not be classified as a person conducting a sale by public auction in this context, and no advance tax under Section 236A needs to be collected from the employee-buyers.
Recommendation: We advise that K-Electric document the nature of this sale (e.g. internal circulars, the invitation terms to employees (Terms and Conditions.docx)) to substantiate that it was an internal disposal and not an open auction. This will be useful in justifying why Section 236A was considered inapplicable, should FBR inquire. The Company should be prepared to explain that the sale was a one-time benefit offer to employees rather than a public bidding process. Given FBR’s general vigilance on auction tax compliance (10 percent WHT through auctions: FBR compiling database of courts - Business Recorder), a prudent measure would be to retain a record of this legal position (perhaps even seek a formal ruling from FBR, if absolute certainty is desired).
Nonetheless, under prevailing law and interpretations, K-Electric is on solid ground to not deduct 10% advance tax on these employee vehicle sales, for the reasons outlined above. The Company should communicate to winning employee bidders that no Section 236A tax is being charged on these transactions (unlike in a public auction where bidders pay an extra 10%). We reiterate that this conclusion hinges on the closed nature of the bidding – if any aspect of the sale were opened to external bidders or public advertisement, the conclusion would differ.
In summary, Section 236A is not applicable to K-Electric’s internal sealed-bid vehicle sale to employees, and thus the Company has no withholding obligation under that section for these sales, based on our analysis of the law’s scope, intent, and the specific facts at hand. This position is supported by the ordinary meaning of “public auction” in legal parlance (Public Auction: Definition. – Mystery of Law and Justice) and the principle of strict interpretation of tax statutes in favor of the taxpayer where any ambiguity exists. K-Electric can proceed with the sale without the additional complication of Section 236A advance tax, barring any contrary directive from tax authorities.

**Taxability of Dividend Income Received by a Holding Company Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**

Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, dividend income received by a holding company is generally taxable in accordance with Section 5, which prescribes the taxation of dividends at the rates specified in Division III of Part I of the First Schedule. For most corporate entities, this rate is 15%, unless a specific exemption or reduced rate applies. However, where such dividend income is received from a wholly owned subsidiary within a group structure that has validly opted for group taxation under Section 59AA, an exemption from tax may be available under Clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance. This exemption is contingent upon the group maintaining 100% ownership throughout the tax year and formally electing to be assessed under the group taxation regime. In such a case, the dividend income received by the holding company is not subject to corporate tax.

It is important to distinguish this from the group relief regime under Section 59B, which permits the surrender of tax losses between companies within the same group. While Section 59B facilitates intra-group tax efficiency, it does not provide any exemption for dividend income. Accordingly, unless the specific conditions of Clause 103A are met, dividend income received by a holding company will remain taxable, and the tax deducted at source under Section 150 will be available for adjustment against the company’s tax liability.

Furthermore, even where dividend income constitutes the sole source of income for a holding company, the entity remains subject to corporate tax compliance obligations, including the filing of an income tax return. Where the dividend income qualifies for exemption under Clause 103A, no tax liability would arise; however, compliance with filing requirements may still be necessary. It is also relevant to note that dividend income is generally excluded from the scope of minimum tax under Section 113, as it does not fall within the definition of turnover.

In conclusion, dividend income received by a holding company from its wholly owned subsidiary is not subject to corporate tax, provided the conditions for group taxation under Section 59AA are met and the exemption under Clause 103A is applicable. In all other cases, such income will be taxable at the applicable rate, subject to adjustment for tax withheld at the time of distribution.

Under the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, the taxability of dividend income received by a **holding company**—particularly in the context of **group taxation under Section 59AA** or **group relief under Section 59B**—is subject to specific provisions, exemptions, and rates, as outlined below:

---

### **1. General Taxability of Dividend Income (Section 5):**

- **Section 5(1)** provides that dividend income is subject to **tax at the rates specified in Division III of Part I of the First Schedule**.
- As per **Division III**, the **rate of tax** on dividends varies depending on the nature of the company distributing the dividend (e.g., mutual funds, REITs, inter-corporate dividends).
- **For ordinary companies**, the rate is generally **15%**, unless a reduced rate or exemption applies.

---

### **2. Exemption for Inter-Corporate Dividend Income – Holding/Subsidiary Scenario:**

Under **Clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule**, **dividend income received by a company** from its **wholly owned subsidiary** is **exempt from tax**, provided:

- Both the **recipient and the paying company** are part of the **same group structure**, and
- They **opt for group taxation under Section 59AA**, and
- The group is **wholly owned**, i.e., 100% ownership (direct or indirect) is maintained throughout the tax year.

Hence, **if the holding company receives dividends from a wholly owned subsidiary under a valid group taxation arrangement**, the **dividend income is exempt from tax**.

---

### **3. Dividend Income under Group Relief (Section 59B):**

- Section 59B relates to **group relief**, whereby one company in a group can **surrender its tax losses** to another profitable company within the group.
- **Dividend income received by a holding company does not directly benefit from group relief**, unless the dividend-paying entity's profits are indirectly affected by the surrender of losses.
- **Group relief does not itself create an exemption for dividend income.**

---

### **4. Where Exemption Is Not Available:**

If the conditions of **Clause 103A** are **not met** (e.g., due to less than 100% ownership, absence of a group taxation option under Section 59AA, or a lapse in the continuity of ownership), then:

- Dividend income will be taxable in the hands of the holding company at the applicable rates (generally **15%**).
- However, **tax withheld under Section 150** at the time of payment will be **adjustable against the tax liability** of the holding company.

---

### **5. Holding Company Having Only Dividend Income – Corporate Tax:**

- Even if the **only income** of a holding company is **dividend income**, it is **not exempt from corporate tax filing obligations**.
- However, **if dividend income is exempt under Clause 103A**, then **no tax liability arises**, though filing may still be required.
- If the dividend is **not exempt**, the company will be subject to tax at the **prescribed rate** and may not incur minimum tax under **Section 113**, depending on facts (as dividend income is generally excluded from turnover for Section 113 purposes).

---

### **Conclusion:**

- **Corporate tax is not applicable on dividend income** received by a **holding company from its wholly owned subsidiary**, provided the **group taxation regime under Section 59AA** is validly elected and maintained.
- **In other cases**, the **dividend income is taxable at the rate of 15%** (unless a specific rate or exemption applies).
- **Filing obligations** and **withholding adjustments** will apply accordingly.

# 1. **Irrevocable Group Taxation Option under Section 59AA**  
Under Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, Section 59AA allows a 100% owned group of companies (holding and subsidiaries) to opt for taxation as “one fiscal unit,” but this choice is explicitly **irrevocable**【4†L51-L58】. In practice, this means the decision is not limited to a single year – once group taxation is elected, it continues for the duration of the group structure (as long as 100% ownership and other conditions are maintained). The law requires all companies in the group to file a declaration of irrevocable option with the tax authorities in the first quarter of the tax year *for which* the option is exercised【2†L159-L167】. Because the option is irrevocable, the group cannot freely switch back to separate filings in later years. Only a structural change (e.g. a subsidiary leaving the group) would end the consolidated treatment, and even then the tax rules specify that if a subsidiary is divested, the group taxation ceases in the year of disposal (with no partial year benefit)【2†L189-L194】. In summary, the Section 59AA option, once taken, binds the group to a consolidated tax filing for all subsequent years of that group’s existence – it is not a year-by-year election.

# 2. **Unbundling a Company – Treatment of Business vs. Depreciation Losses**  
When unbundling a company (such as splitting an integrated utility like K-Electric into separate generation, transmission, and distribution entities), Pakistan’s tax law does **not** provide a mechanism to arbitrarily split existing tax losses between the new entities. Tax losses “belong” to the legal entity that incurred them and generally remain with that entity unless a specific tax provision permits their transfer【26†L285-L292】. In an unbundling via a Scheme of Arrangement (approved by court/SECP), typically one company transfers assets/business to a newly formed company. In such cases, the acquiring company does not inherit the transferor’s accumulated tax losses – those remain with the original company【25†L1238-L1243】. This means “business losses” and “unabsorbed depreciation” from the pre-unbundling period stay with the original entity and cannot be allocated to the new spun-off companies by default. For example, if prior to unbundling the parent had large tax losses due to depreciation on its assets, after transferring those assets to a new subsidiary the **parent** would still carry forward those tax depreciation losses, while the new subsidiary would start with a fresh tax depreciation basis on the received assets. Pakistani tax law does allow **merger/amalgamation** scenarios where losses can transfer (under continuity of ownership/business conditions), but a de-merger or asset spinoff does not automatically allow loss transfer. In short, you cannot segregate “depreciation losses” to follow the assets unless a specific amalgamation provision is invoked. The original company will retain its brought-forward losses (including any unabsorbed depreciation), subject to normal carryforward rules (unabsorbed depreciation can be carried indefinitely under current law【28†L159-L166】). The new unbundled entities will not receive a portion of the parent’s prior losses – they will only carry forward losses *they themselves* incur after the unbundling.

# 3. **Group Relief (Section 59B) and Supply-Segment Losses in Unbundling**  
Section 59B of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 provides for **group relief**, allowing a holding or subsidiary company to surrender its **current year** assessed business loss to another group company. In the context of unbundling (e.g. separating a “Supply” or distribution business into a subsidiary), any losses incurred by that supply/distribution entity can potentially be surrendered to other group companies *if all Section 59B conditions are met*. Notably, **only assessed losses of the current tax year** are eligible – this excludes capital losses and excludes any brought-forward losses from prior years【12†L151-L159】. Key conditions under Section 59B include: (a) the shareholding threshold – the holding company must directly own ≥55% of the subsidiary (if listed) or ≥75% (if unlisted)【12†L155-L163】; (b) the companies must be locally incorporated and designated for group relief; (c) the surrendering company should not be engaged in *trading* activities (a pure trading company cannot avail group relief)【13†L169-L177】; (d) the same business must continue for at least three years in the subsidiary, and the shareholding must be maintained for five years – if the holding sells shares dropping ownership below the threshold within 5 years, the previously claimed relief is recaptured and taxed【12†L165-L168】. Also, a subsidiary can only surrender losses for up to three consecutive years, after which any unutilized losses revert to its own carryforward pool【13†L181-L189】. From an unbundling perspective, this means if, say, the newly unbundled “Supply Co.” incurs losses (e.g. due to distribution costs), those losses (excluding any prior losses before group formation) could be surrendered to the parent or sister companies like a generation or transmission company – provided the ownership structure (post-unbundling) satisfies the above thresholds and corporate governance requirements. The **supply-related losses** would then offset the taxable profits of another group entity (for example, a profitable generation company), effectively yielding group-level tax savings. It’s crucial to ensure the arrangement doesn’t violate the restriction on “business of trading” – however, distribution of electricity is typically treated as a service/utility, not a trading of goods, so it should qualify for group relief. In summary, supply/distribution losses can be surrendered under Section 59B subject to conditions: the group must have the requisite ownership linkage, only current-year business losses (no carryforwards) are surrendered, and the companies must abide by the 5-year continuity rule and other stipulations【12†L161-L168】【13†L169-L177】. When planning an unbundling, one must consider that any losses existing **prior** to group formation cannot be shared (they stay with the company that earned them), and ensure that using group relief will not be clawed back by a change in ownership or business activity in subsequent years.

# 4. **Examples of Listed Companies with Carryforward Tax Losses**  
There are numerous Pakistani listed companies that have accumulated tax losses carried forward on their books. One notable example is **K-Electric Ltd** (formerly Karachi Electric Supply Company). K-Electric reported very large assessed tax losses during the late 2000s when it was incurring substantial losses. For instance, as of March 31, 2008, the company’s assessed tax losses were about Rs 73.179 billion【36†L1-L4】, and by the end of the next year (June 30, 2009) had grown to Rs 85.476 billion, reaching approximately Rs 99.204 billion by a subsequent period【36†L9-L12】. These carryforward losses were disclosed in its financial statements and could be used to offset future taxable profits (subject to the time limits for business loss carryforward and indefinite carryforward for depreciation allowances). Another example is **Hascol Petroleum Ltd**, a listed oil marketing company that suffered heavy losses in recent years. Hascol’s tax filings for Tax Year 2020, for example, declared a taxable loss of approximately **Rs 24.78 billion**, on which it paid only minimum tax and even claimed a refund due to overpaid taxes【40†L1-L7】. This indicates a significant carryforward tax loss available on Hascol’s books (the company’s financial statements also show unrecognized deferred tax assets corresponding to tens of billions of rupees of tax losses in recent years). Aside from these, companies in sectors like aviation and energy often carry tax losses; for instance, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) and certain independent power producers have historically had carryforward losses due to initial year losses or accelerated depreciation. The key point is that such carryforward tax losses are disclosed in financial statement notes (often labeled as “assessed tax losses” or deferred tax asset notes) for investor awareness. The above examples (**K-Electric** with tens of billions in brought-forward losses, and **Hascol Petroleum** with ~Rs25 billion loss in TY2020) illustrate the scale of carryforward losses held by Pakistani companies【36†L1-L4】【40†L1-L7】.

# 5. **Accounting Treatment of Tax Depreciation (EY’s 50% Rule Guidance)**  
The Finance Act, 2018 introduced a significant change in how companies can utilize brought-forward depreciation for tax purposes. Previously, unabsorbed tax depreciation could be used fully to offset taxable income (and any remainder carried forward indefinitely). The 2018 amendment placed a cap: in any given tax year, **brought-forward depreciation losses can only offset up to 50% of that year’s “business income”**, with the remainder carried forward【28†L159-L166】 (an exception was made for smaller taxable incomes up to Rs 10 million). In effect, this ensures that at least half of a company’s taxable profit in a year will be subject to tax if the company has prior depreciation pools. The advisory from EY that “the full amount of brought-forward tax depreciation and 50% of the current year’s depreciation” should be adjusted in the tax charge calculation is rooted in this law change. The rationale is to reflect, in the company’s tax provision and deferred tax accounting, the portion of depreciation that **cannot** shield income in the current year. In practice, tax accountants following EY’s guidance would disallow (add back) 100% of any brought-forward depreciation during the tax computation (since at most only half of current-year profit can be covered by it), and also disallow 50% of the current year’s depreciation charge. This approach effectively ensures that only 50% of the current year’s depreciation is reducing the current taxable income, with the rest being carried forward. The reasoning is that if a company has substantial depreciation, only a portion will be immediately effective in reducing taxes (the rest becomes a deferred tax asset for future years). By adjusting the full brought-forward and half of current depreciation, the accounting profit is aligned to a more realistic taxable profit under the new rules – preventing the company from under-providing current tax. Put another way, this method anticipates that at least half of the depreciation (whether from prior years or current year) will not be utilizable against this year’s profits due to the 50% limitation, and thus treats that portion as a deferred expense. This yields a more conservative and accurate current tax expense in the financial statements. It also means companies with large depreciation pools will now pay some income tax even if they have hefty depreciation available, since only half of the year’s profit can be sheltered【28†L159-L166】. The EY-advised treatment ensures compliance with this rule and avoids overstatement of deferred tax assets that might take many years to realize.

# 6. **Service Tax on Transmission/Distribution under SSTSA 2011 & BSTSA 2015 (and CAPEX Input Tax)**  
Yes – under provincial law, *transmission and distribution of electric power* are considered taxable services in provinces like Sindh and Balochistan. The Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (and similar Balochistan Act, 2015) charge sales tax on services such as “electric power transmission services” (classified under tariff code 9854.0000)【48†L1-L8】. In an unbundling scenario, the newly formed Transmission Company and Distribution Company would each be providing provincially-taxable services: the transmission of electricity (wheeling power over lines), and possibly the distribution/supply service to end consumers (though the sale of electricity units themselves is treated as a supply of goods for federal sales tax). Sindh and Balochistan have included these in their taxable service schedules – for example, a Sindh-registered entity providing power transmission is subject to Sindh sales tax (the standard SST rate has been around 13% in recent years, now 15% as of 2023). 

**Input Tax on CAPEX vs. Output Tax:** One challenge is that the *input* sales tax on capital equipment (e.g. transformers, transmission towers, etc.) is federal VAT (under the Sales Tax Act, 1990) typically at a higher rate (e.g. 17% GST on goods, now 18% in 2023) than the applicable provincial service tax rate (e.g. 13%). This rate mismatch can result in excess input tax. In principle, a service provider registered with SRB/BRA can claim input tax credits for sales tax paid on inputs (including goods) used in providing the service, **but only to the extent allowed by provincial law and inter-government arrangements**. Historically, there has been no automatic refund mechanism for excess input VAT incurred by service providers, and provinces often disallow or limit input tax adjustment on goods. In practice, **only the portion of input tax equivalent to the provincial output tax is effectively utilizable**, and any excess tends to be unrecoverable (disallowed or carried forward without refund). For example, if a Sindh Transco pays 17% GST on a new transmission line but can only charge 13% SST on its service, it will accumulate more input tax than output tax. The common approach is that the *differential portion* (the 4% excess in this example) cannot be claimed and becomes a cost to the business. The provincial statutes and rules support proportionate adjustments: input tax credit is generally restricted if the input relates to taxable activity with a lower tax incidence. In essence, the company would claim credit up to the amount of SST due, and any remaining input tax would either be disallowed or carried forward in hopes of future output tax generation (but since the rate difference is structural, the excess may never be realized). **Therefore, typically only the equivalent of 13% out of the 17% input tax can be adjusted**, leaving ~4% as a permanent cost unless some special adjustment mechanism exists. As a result, CAPEX-related input tax for transmission/distribution businesses must be carefully treated: the **full 17%** GST on capital goods is not freely creditable against provincial tax. Either the *entire* federal input tax is disallowed by the province (if no cross-credit agreement is in place), or at best the firm gets credit for the portion equal to its SST output and the remainder sits as unusable excess. Companies in the power sector have raised this concern in various forums, as it leads to cascading tax. This issue was one reason behind efforts to harmonize sales tax between federation and provinces. (Notably, as of 2023 the standard SST rate has increased to 15%【50†L25-L29】, narrowing the gap but not eliminating it.) In summary, transmission and distribution services are taxable by Sindh/Balochistan, and because the **provincial output tax is lower than the input tax on capital purchases, the excess input VAT is effectively not recoverable** – essentially the differential portion is disallowed. Businesses typically treat that disallowed portion of input tax as part of the capital expenditure cost. Until a refund or adjustment mechanism is developed between FBR and the provinces, firms should plan for only partial input tax credit on their CAPEX under these regimes.

# 7. **NTDC and Provincial Service Tax on Transmission – Application and Dispute**  
The National Transmission & Despatch Company (NTDC), which transmits electricity across provinces, historically did **not charge or pay provincial sales tax** (Sindh Revenue Board or Balochistan Revenue Authority) on its transmission services, relying on legal arguments to contest the applicability. NTDC’s position has been that its activities were already subject to federal sales tax as part of the electricity supply chain, and thus not separately taxable as a provincial service. In fact, until recently the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) was charging 17% GST on the full value of electricity delivered to distribution companies – a value that implicitly included the transmission and distribution components【56†L59-L67】. Electricity is defined as “goods” for federal sales tax purposes, so the entire billing (generation + transmission + distribution) fell under federal jurisdiction. NTDC argued that the “service” element of transmitting electricity could not be carved out for provincial taxation without causing double taxation or jurisdictional conflict. Essentially, NTDC and the DISCOs viewed the transmission charge as part of the cost of supplying electricity (a federally taxed supply of goods) rather than a separate service rendered in Sindh or Balochistan. 

**Legal Grounds Cited by NTDC:** One argument has been constitutional: that sales tax on services falls to provinces, but in this case electricity transmission was inseparable from the good (electric power) being delivered, which falls under federal sales tax on goods. NTDC also pointed out the lack of clear mechanism to segregate the value of the “service” from the electricity price on which FBR was already collecting GST【56†L77-L85】. Moreover, the service is of an inter-provincial nature – power may originate in one province and terminate in another – which raised questions of which province’s tax applies (until “place of supply” rules were agreed, there was risk of multiple provinces claiming the tax). NTDC likely leveraged these uncertainties, and litigation ensued between NTDC and provincial authorities (Sindh SRB in particular issued notices for SST on transmission charges). While contesting SRB’s jurisdiction, NTDC essentially refrained from paying SST, awaiting a policy resolution via the National Tax Council or Council of Common Interests. The company’s stance was bolstered by the fact that provincial authorities themselves recognized the overlap – in 2019 the provincial revenue boards jointly acknowledged that FBR was collecting 17% on what was a mix of goods and services in the power sector, and they sought to “segregate” the portion attributable to services【56†L59-L67】【56†L77-L85】. This indicates that even provinces knew the law was grey on this point, which NTDC used to justify not charging provincial tax. 

**Current Status – Harmonization:** This long-standing dispute was effectively resolved in 2023. Through Finance Act, 2023, the federal government **amended the law to formally transfer sales tax on “production, transmission, and distribution of electricity” to the provinces**【54†L148-L157】【54†L161-L168】. A consensus declaration between the center and provinces agreed that electric power transmission would be treated as a service taxable by provinces from July 1, 2023【54†L161-L168】. In other words, the legal ambiguity has been removed: going forward, NTDC’s transmission services are squarely under provincial sales tax (with the value of the service to be excluded from federal GST on electricity). This also came with place-of-provision rules to split tax for inter-provincial transmissions【48†L7-L15】. Prior to this change, NTDC did not levy SRB/BRA tax and defended that stance by arguing lack of provincial jurisdiction and pointing to the comprehensive federal GST already being paid on the overall electricity supply. Now, however, NTDC is expected to comply with provincial tax for its services (charging the applicable SST to its customers like K-Electric or DISCOS in Sindh/Balochistan). In summary, **NTDC initially resisted SRB/BRA service tax**, contending that its transmission fees were part of a federally-taxed good (electricity) and that provincial taxation would amount to double taxation or unconstitutional overlap. This led to legal disputes and an eventual policy solution. With the 2023 amendments, the law is clear that provinces have the right to tax the transmission service, so NTDC will have to apply provincial sales tax going forward – but its past stance was grounded in the ambiguity that existed before harmonization【56†L59-L67】【56†L77-L85】.

Thanks for confirming the jurisdiction. I’ll now dive into the specific Pakistani tax and service tax provisions, including Section 59AA and 59B of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, and applicable laws under the Sindh and Balochistan service tax regimes. I’ll also look into listed companies with carryforward losses for financial statement references.

I’ll get back to you shortly with detailed answers and analysis for each question.

Please improve it more below and try to incorporate references from the Income Tax Rules, 2002, especially Rule 231D for yearly compliance requirement: 

1.	Irrevocable Group Taxation Option under Section 59AA
Under section 59AA of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] allows a 100% owned group of companies (holding and subsidiaries) to opt for taxation as “one fiscal unit,” but this choice is explicitly irrevocable. In practice, this means the decision is not limited to a single year – once group taxation is elected, it continues for the duration of the group structure (as long as 100% ownership and other conditions are maintained). The law requires all companies in the group to file a declaration of irrevocable option with the tax authorities in the first quarter of the tax year for which the option is exercised. Because the option is irrevocable, the group cannot freely switch back to separate filings in later years. Only a structural change (e.g. a subsidiary leaving the group) would end the consolidated treatment, and even then the tax rules specify that if a subsidiary is divested, the group taxation ceases in the year of disposal (with no partial year benefit). In summary, the section 59AA of the Ordinance option, once taken, binds the group to a consolidated tax filing for all subsequent years of that group’s existence – it is not a year-by-year election.
2.	Unbundling a Company – Treatment of Business vs. Depreciation Losses
When unbundling a company (such as splitting an integrated utility like K-Electric into separate generation, transmission, and distribution entities), Ordinance does not provide a mechanism to arbitrarily split existing tax losses between the new entities. Tax losses “belong” to the legal entity that incurred them and generally remain with that entity unless a specific tax provision permits their transfer. In an unbundling via a Scheme of Arrangement (approved by court/SECP), typically one company transfers assets/business to a newly formed company. In such cases, the acquiring company does not inherit the transferor’s accumulated tax losses, those remain with the original company. This means “business losses” and “unabsorbed depreciation” from the pre-unbundling period stay with the original entity and cannot be allocated to the new spun-off companies by default. For example, if prior to unbundling the parent had large tax losses due to depreciation on its assets, after transferring those assets to a new subsidiary the parent would still carry forward those tax depreciation losses, while the new subsidiary would start with a fresh tax depreciation basis on the received assets. Ordinance does allow merger/amalgamation scenarios where losses can transfer (under continuity of ownership/business conditions), but a de-merger or asset spinoff does not automatically allow loss transfer. In short, you cannot segregate “depreciation losses” to follow the assets unless a specific amalgamation provision is invoked. The original company will retain its brought-forward losses (including any unabsorbed depreciation), subject to normal carryforward rules (unabsorbed depreciation can be carried indefinitely under current law. The new unbundled entities will not receive a portion of the parent’s prior losses – they will only carry forward losses they themselves incur after the unbundling.
3.	Group Relief (Section 59B) and Supply-Segment Losses in Unbundling
Section 59B of the Ordinance provides for group relief, allowing a holding or subsidiary company to surrender its current year assessed business loss to another group company. In the context of unbundling (e.g. separating a “Supply” or distribution business into a subsidiary), any losses incurred by that supply/distribution entity can potentially be surrendered to other group companies if all section 59B conditions are met. Notably, only assessed losses of the current tax year are eligible, this excludes capital losses and excludes any brought-forward losses from prior years. Key conditions under section 59B include: (a) the shareholding threshold – the holding company must directly own ≥55% of the subsidiary (if listed) or ≥75% (if unlisted); (b) the companies must be locally incorporated and designated for group relief; (c) the surrendering company should not be engaged in trading activities (a pure trading company cannot avail group relief); (d) the same business must continue for at least three years in the subsidiary, and the shareholding must be maintained for five years – if the holding sells shares dropping ownership below the threshold within 5 years, the previously claimed relief is recaptured and taxed. Also, a subsidiary can only surrender losses for up to three consecutive years, after which any unutilized losses revert to its own carryforward pool. From an unbundling perspective, this means if, say, the newly unbundled “Supply Co.” incurs losses (e.g. due to distribution costs), those losses (excluding any prior losses before group formation) could be surrendered to the parent or sister companies like a generation or transmission company – provided the ownership structure (post-unbundling) satisfies the above thresholds and corporate governance requirements. The supply-related losses would then offset the taxable profits of another group entity (for example, a profitable generation company), effectively yielding group-level tax savings. It’s crucial to ensure the arrangement doesn’t violate the restriction on “business of trading” – however, distribution of electricity is typically treated as a service/utility, not a trading of goods, so it should qualify for group relief. In summary, supply/distribution losses can be surrendered under Section 59B subject to conditions: the group must have the requisite ownership linkage, only current-year business losses (no carryforwards) are surrendered, and the companies must abide by the 5-year continuity rule and other stipulations. When planning an unbundling, one must consider that any losses existing prior to group formation cannot be shared (they stay with the company that earned them), and ensure that using group relief will not be clawed back by a change in ownership or business activity in subsequent years.
4.	Examples of Listed Companies with Carryforward Tax Losses
For example, is Hascol Petroleum Ltd, a listed oil marketing company that suffered heavy losses in recent years. Hascol’s tax filings for Tax Year 2020, for example, declared a taxable loss of approximately Rs 24.78 billion, on which it paid only minimum tax and even claimed a refund due to overpaid taxes. This indicates a significant carryforward tax loss available on Hascol’s books (the company’s financial statements also show unrecognized deferred tax assets corresponding to tens of billions of rupees of tax losses in recent years). Aside from these, companies in sectors like aviation and energy often carry tax losses; for instance, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) and certain independent power producers have historically had carryforward losses due to initial year losses or accelerated depreciation. The key point is that such carryforward tax losses are disclosed in financial statement notes (often labeled as “assessed tax losses” or deferred tax asset notes) for investor awareness. 
5.	Accounting Treatment of Tax Depreciation (50% Rule Guidance)
The Finance Act, 2018 introduced a significant change in how companies can utilize brought-forward depreciation for tax purposes. Previously, unabsorbed tax depreciation could be used fully to offset taxable income (and any remainder carried forward indefinitely). The 2018 amendment placed a cap: in any given tax year, brought-forward depreciation losses can only offset up to 50% of that year’s “business income”, with the remainder carried forward (an exception was made for smaller taxable incomes up to Rs 10 million). In effect, this ensures that at least half of a company’s taxable profit in a year will be subject to tax if the company has prior depreciation pools. The advisory from EY that “the full amount of brought-forward tax depreciation and 50% of the current year’s depreciation” should be adjusted in the tax charge calculation is rooted in this law change. The rationale is to reflect, in the company’s tax provision and deferred tax accounting, the portion of depreciation that cannot shield income in the current year. In practice, tax accountants following EY’s guidance would disallow (add back) 100% of any brought-forward depreciation during the tax computation (since at most only half of current-year profit can be covered by it), and also disallow 50% of the current year’s depreciation charge. This approach effectively ensures that only 50% of the current year’s depreciation is reducing the current taxable income, with the rest being carried forward. The reasoning is that if a company has substantial depreciation, only a portion will be immediately effective in reducing taxes (the rest becomes a deferred tax asset for future years). By adjusting the full brought-forward and half of current depreciation, the accounting profit is aligned to a more realistic taxable profit under the new rules, preventing the company from under-providing current tax. Put another way, this method anticipates that at least half of the depreciation (whether from prior years or current year) will not be utilizable against this year’s profits due to the 50% limitation, and thus treats that portion as a deferred expense. This yields a more conservative and accurate current tax expense in the financial statements. It also means companies with large depreciation pools will now pay some income tax even if they have hefty depreciation available, since only half of the year’s profit can be sheltered. The EY-advised treatment ensures compliance with this rule and avoids overstatement of deferred tax assets that might take many years to realize.
6.	Service Tax on Transmission/Distribution under SSTSA 2011 & BSTSA 2015 (and CAPEX Input Tax)
Under provincial law, transmission and distribution of electric power are considered taxable services in provinces like Sindh and Balochistan. The Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (and similar Balochistan Act, 2015) charge sales tax on services such as “electric power transmission services” (classified under tariff code 9854.0000). In an unbundling scenario, the newly formed Transmission Company and Distribution Company would each be providing provincially-taxable services: the transmission of electricity (wheeling power over lines), and possibly the distribution/supply service to end consumers (though the sale of electricity units themselves is treated as a supply of goods for federal sales tax). Sindh and Balochistan have included these in their taxable service schedules – for example, a Sindh-registered entity providing power transmission is subject to Sindh sales tax (the standard SST rate has been around 13% in recent years, now 15% as of 2023).

7.	NTDC and Provincial Service Tax on Transmission – Application and Dispute
The National Transmission & Despatch Company (NTDC), which transmits electricity across provinces, historically did not charge or pay provincial sales tax (Sindh Revenue Board or Balochistan Revenue Authority) on its transmission services, relying on legal arguments to contest the applicability. In fact, until recently the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) was charging 17% GST on the full value of electricity delivered to distribution companies – a value that implicitly included the transmission and distribution components. Electricity is defined as “goods” for federal sales tax purposes, so the entire billing (generation + transmission + distribution) fell under federal jurisdiction. NTDC argued that the “service” element of transmitting electricity could not be carved out for provincial taxation without causing double taxation or jurisdictional conflict. Essentially, NTDC and the DISCOs viewed the transmission charge as part of the cost of supplying electricity (a federally taxed supply of goods) rather than a separate service rendered in Sindh or Balochistan.
One argument has been constitutional: that sales tax on services falls to provinces, but in this case electricity transmission was inseparable from the good (electric power) being delivered, which falls under federal sales tax on goods. NTDC also pointed out the lack of clear mechanism to segregate the value of the “service” from the electricity price on which FBR was already collecting GST. Moreover, the service is of an inter-provincial nature – power may originate in one province and terminate in another – which raised questions of which province’s tax applies (until “place of supply” rules were agreed, there was risk of multiple provinces claiming the tax). NTDC likely leveraged these uncertainties, and litigation ensued between NTDC and provincial authorities (Sindh SRB in particular issued notices for SST on transmission charges). While contesting SRB’s jurisdiction, NTDC essentially refrained from paying SST, awaiting a policy resolution via the National Tax Council or Council of Common Interests. The company’s stance was bolstered by the fact that provincial authorities themselves recognized the overlap – in 2019 the provincial revenue boards jointly acknowledged that FBR was collecting 17% on what was a mix of goods and services in the power sector, and they sought to “segregate” the portion attributable to services. This long-standing dispute was effectively resolved in 2023. Through Finance Act, 2023, the federal government amended the law to formally transfer sales tax on “production, transmission, and distribution of electricity” to the provinces. A consensus declaration between the center and provinces agreed that electric power transmission would be treated as a service taxable by provinces from July 1, 2023. In other words, the legal ambiguity has been removed: going forward, NTDC’s transmission services are squarely under provincial sales tax (with the value of the service to be excluded from federal GST on electricity). This also came with place-of-provision rules to split tax for inter-provincial transmissions. Prior to this change, NTDC did not levy SRB/BRA tax and defended that stance by arguing lack of provincial jurisdiction and pointing to the comprehensive federal GST already being paid on the overall electricity supply. Now, however, NTDC is expected to comply with provincial tax for its services (charging the applicable SST to its customers like K-Electric or DISCOS in Sindh/Balochistan). In summary, NTDC initially resisted SRB/BRA service tax, contending that its transmission fees were part of a federally-taxed good (electricity) and that provincial taxation would amount to double taxation or unconstitutional overlap. This led to legal disputes and an eventual policy solution. With the 2023 amendments, the law is clear that provinces have the right to tax the transmission service, so NTDC will have to apply provincial sales tax going forward – but its past stance was grounded in the ambiguity that existed before harmonization.
