The provincial authorities have tried to resolve such issues through coordination – typically the rule is that the province where the service **originates (where the provider is registered)** charges the tax. In our example, the Karachi entity would charge Sindh sales tax (13%) on its invoice to the Quetta entity, and the Quetta entity, if it is also registered in Balochistan, might not additionally pay Balochistan tax but it might not get credit for the Sindh tax either (since cross-provincial input tax credit is not straightforward). This increases the cost of inter-company service transactions. 

During restructurings, companies often centralize certain functions (like a shared service center for HR, IT, finance). The shared service center will likely need to charge a service fee to other group entities, which triggers provincial sales tax. **Sindh and Balochistan Sales Tax Acts** cover a wide range of services – from consultancy, franchising, management services, to warehousing, transportation, etc. If, for instance, a demerged **GenCo and Disco** (to revisit the K-Electric scenario) have a service agreement – say the Disco provides customer support services to the GenCo – that service could be taxable. Similarly, if the holding company provides use of a brand name or “franchise” to its subsidiaries, provincial sales tax on franchise fees (which Sindh taxes at 13%) would apply. In Balochistan, services like **“technical, scientific and engineering services”** or **“management consulting”** are taxable under the 2015 Act, so intra-group technical service fees are caught. 

Therefore, after unbundling, **compliance** with provincial tax laws is essential: each entity must obtain the required sales tax registration in each province where it has a taxable service activity. For example, a company headquartered in Sindh that also provides services in Balochistan may need a registration (or at least file for withholding agent status) with the Balochistan Revenue Authority. Also, inter-company agreements should factor in the additional cost of sales tax – some groups choose to gross-up or adjust transfer prices accordingly. It may be possible to **avoid formal service charges** by structuring certain cost sharing arrangements (which, if done carefully and without a profit element, might not be seen as taxable services). However, tax authorities are generally vigilant against treating what are effectively services as mere reimbursements. 

In summary, **Sindh and Balochistan sales tax laws** will apply to services exchanged post-restructuring just as they would for any third-party transactions. Corporate groups should ensure they **map out all inter-company services** (management fees, royalties, IT support, logistics, etc.) and check the schedules of the Sindh and Balochistan Sales Tax Acts to see if those services are taxable. If yes, they should implement invoicing and tax remittance accordingly to avoid penalties. The provincial authorities have become quite active in auditing entities for uncharged services tax (for example, the Sindh Revenue Board might ask if a company is receiving services from any related party and whether tax is being paid). Thus, tax planning for unbundling isn’t complete without addressing the **indirect tax** aspect – it can significantly impact the cost structure and require new compliance capabilities in the newly formed entities.  

**7. Depreciation Limitation (50% in First/Last Year) and Accounting Impact**  Another important technical point in Pakistani tax law is the treatment of **depreciation in the year of acquisition and disposal** of assets, which has seen changes in recent Finance Acts and has implications for accounting (deferred tax). Historically, prior to Tax Year 2021, the tax law allowed a **full year’s depreciation in the year an asset was acquired** (no matter if it was acquired early or late in the year) and **no depreciation in the year of disposal**【8†L228-L236】【8†L230-L238】. This all-or-nothing approach was simple but could lead to mismatches with accounting depreciation (which is prorated to the actual period of use) and potential tax planning quirks (e.g. rushing purchases just before year-end to get a full year’s deduction). 

**Change by Finance Act 2020:** Effective Tax Year 2021 (for assets put to use on or after 1 July 2020), a proviso to Section 22 was inserted to **restrict first-year depreciation to 50%** of the normal amount if the asset is acquired in that year, and conversely to allow **50% depreciation in the year of disposal**【8†L233-L241】【8†L234-L242】. In essence, the tax code moved to a **half-year depreciation rule**, whereby in the first year of use you get half of what you otherwise would, and in the final year (disposal year) you get the other half (instead of none). This mirrors common practice in many jurisdictions (often called the half-year convention). The rationale was to **apportion depreciation more evenly** and prevent taxpayers from getting a full deduction for maybe just a few days’ use of an asset. For example, if a company bought machinery in June 2021 (with tax year July–June), under old rules it could depreciate the full rate (say 15% of cost) for that one month of use; the new rule limits that first-year claim to half (7.5%). Likewise, if it sells an asset in the middle of a year, previously it would lose the deduction entirely for that year, but now it can still claim half of the normal full-year rate in the disposal year. 

**Change by Finance Act 2022:** After two years, this policy was reversed. The Finance Act, 2022 removed the half-year restriction going forward. From 1 July 2022, the law reverted to allowing **100% of the depreciation in the acquisition year** (and correspondingly, back to **0% in the disposal year**)【48†L25-L33】【48†L35-L40】. The “rationalization” was likely in response to feedback that the half-year rule added complexity and did not significantly impact long-term tax revenue (since it only deferred part of the deduction to a later year). A tax handbook confirms: *“From July 1, 2022, 100% depreciation will be allowed in the year of purchase”*【48†L35-L40】, effectively eliminating the 50% first-year limit for assets bought after that date. (Note: Assets acquired during the period July 2020 – June 2022 were subject to the half-year rule; those rules would still govern their depreciation until disposal. The 2022 change is not retroactive but going forward.) 

**Accounting and Deferred Tax Treatment:** These changes required careful accounting consideration under IAS 12 *Income Taxes*. The half-year rule introduced in 2020 led to **temporary differences** between book and tax depreciation. Financial accounting depreciation (under IAS 16) is typically calculated on a pro-rata basis over the asset’s useful life. For instance, if an asset with a 10-year life is acquired on the first day of Year 1, the company would depreciate ~10% of its cost in that first year (full year’s worth). Tax, under the half-year rule, would only allow 50% of the normal depreciation (which might be, say, 10%/2 = 5% if tax also uses straight-line, or if tax uses reducing balance, 50% of that figure). This means in Year 1, **taxable income is higher than accounting income** (because tax depreciation expense is lower) – creating a **deductible temporary difference** (more depreciation will be available in future relative to accounting). A deferred tax asset arises in Year 1 for the tax effect of the depreciation disallowed (since the company will get that deduction in the final year of asset use/disposal). Conversely, in the asset’s last year of use, tax will allow 50% depreciation even though accounting will have perhaps taken depreciation up to the point of sale (or if the asset is fully depreciated in books by that time, accounting expense might be zero while tax has 50% left to deduct). In that final period, taxable income is lower than accounting income (tax deduction with no book expense), reversing the temporary difference (using up the deferred tax asset). The net effect over the asset’s life is nil (both book and tax end up depreciating 100% of cost), but the timing differs, which is the hallmark of a temporary difference. Companies needed to account for this starting 2020. For example, upon purchase of a significant asset, they would calculate the difference between book depreciation (prorated for months of use) and tax depreciation (either full or half depending on purchase date) and recognize a deferred tax entry. If the asset was bought early in the year, book dep > tax dep (DTA created). If bought very late in the year, interestingly, tax dep (always 50% of full-year rate) might exceed book dep (which could be, say, only 1 month’s worth ~8.3% of annual) – in that scenario, taxable income is actually lower than accounting income in Year 1 (due to relatively higher tax depreciation), creating a **taxable temporary difference** and a deferred tax liability. The half-year rule thus required asset-by-asset (or class-by-class) scheduling to get deferred taxes right. Many firms disclosed that the change had a one-time impact on their deferred tax balances when it was enacted. 

When the rule was **reverted in 2022**, there was again an effect: assets acquired from July 2022 onward get full depreciation in first year, so no new temporary difference on those. However, what about assets acquired under the old rule but not yet disposed by 2022? The law did not explicitly address transitional treatment for those. Likely, those assets will continue under the regime they were acquired in (meaning they’ll still get 50% in disposal year later). If so, the deferred tax recorded for those will run its course. New purchases won’t have that particular timing issue (though normal differences between accounting useful life and tax depreciation rates still cause temporary differences). 

From a **financial reporting perspective**, companies had to adapt their deferred tax calculations at each Finance Act change. For example, when Finance Act 2020 was enacted, any asset on books that was expected to be bought or sold in the future would be affected – strictly speaking, IAS 12 would require recognizing the deferred tax impact of the change in tax law in the period of enactment. Similarly, Finance Act 2022’s change might have led to a release of some deferred tax (if companies anticipated half-year deductions for future purchases, those expectations would be updated). In practice, since the half-year rule mostly defers or accelerates deductions within a few years, the deferred tax impacts were not extremely large relative to asset cost, but they are noteworthy for compliance with accounting standards. The **Institute of Chartered Accountants of Pakistan (ICAP)** issued guidelines (Technical Release) when the half-year rule was introduced and withdrawn, to ensure consistent accounting by companies for minimum tax, depreciation changes, etc.【34†L510-L518】 (the Hascol financials excerpt, for instance, references adoption of *IAS 12 Revised 2012* and ICAP’s interpretation on accounting for minimum taxes and final taxes, which is related). 

In summary, the **50% depreciation limitation** was in effect for two tax years and required companies to carry deferred tax assets or liabilities to reflect the timing difference it created. Now, with full depreciation in the first year reinstated (and none in the last year), the system has reverted to its prior state, simplifying the alignment: companies can once again get a full year’s tax depreciation which more closely aligns with what most would take in accounting (assuming they use full year depreciation if acquired at period start). There will still be differences if an asset is acquired part-way through the year (because accounting will pro-rate whereas tax will still give a full year if any use in that year), but that difference is now *permanent* in nature (extra tax depreciation that accounting never took is like a permanent tax benefit, not reversing later since disposal year has no deduction for tax). Actually, to clarify: under current law, if an asset is used even for one day in the year of purchase, tax gives a full year deduction, which is *more* than accounting’s prorated expense – this creates a **permanent difference** (affecting the effective tax rate in that year) rather than a temporary difference, because tax won’t “claw back” that extra half-year when sold (since no tax depreciation in disposal year, but by the time of disposal the book value might also be different). Companies thus now may experience a favorable permanent difference (lower taxable income) in acquisition year and an unfavorable permanent difference (higher taxable income) in disposal year. Permanent differences don’t give rise to deferred tax, but they do affect the current tax charge in those periods. During the half-year rule period, those were converted to timing differences (lower deduction now, but extra deduction later). 

From a **planning perspective**, the reinstatement of full-first-year depreciation in Finance Act 2022 may encourage capital investment timing near year-end to accelerate deductions (since one can effectively get a “bonus” depreciation for part-year ownership). The Finance Act 2023 did not significantly adjust depreciation rules further (it focused more on other areas like taxation of income, PIA losses, etc.), so the 2022 regime stands as of 2025. Corporate tax and finance professionals should ensure that their fixed asset register aligns with the current tax law: assets bought in FY2021 or FY2022 had that 50% limit – track those for half depreciation in disposal year – whereas assets from FY2023 onward don’t. All these differences must be communicated to the accounting team for proper deferred tax computation. In disclosures, if material, companies should describe any impact of these Finance Acts on their tax expense. For example, a company might state: *“During the year, the Company’s tax charge was reduced by the reinstatement of full-year depreciation on additions, as per Finance Act 2022, resulting in a lower current tax and corresponding higher effective tax rate reconciliation item for depreciation (permanent difference).”* Alternatively, if still utilizing assets under the old regime: *“The Company has recognized a deferred tax asset of Rs. X million on account of depreciation timing differences arising from the half-year depreciation provisions applicable to certain additions in prior years【8†L233-L241】.”* 

In conclusion, the 50% depreciation rule was a temporary measure that required close attention but has now been **“undone”**. The episode underscores the need for tax departments to stay abreast of Finance Act changes and to coordinate with financial reporting teams. Something as technical as depreciation timing can have ripple effects on tax provisioning and compliance. The Finance Act 2018 had not introduced this rule – it came in 2020 and went out in 2022 – illustrating how quickly tax law can evolve. By maintaining a dialogue between tax advisors and accountants, companies can ensure that such changes are properly implemented in both their tax filings and their books (with deferred tax capturing any timing impacts).【8†L233-L241】【48†L35-L40】 

**Sources:** Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Sections 59AA, 59B, 57, 97A; Income Tax Rules, 2002 – Rule 231D【54†L188-L196】【23†L231-L239】; Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011; Balochistan Sales Tax on Services Act, 2015【50†L37-L44】; Finance Act, 2018 & 2022 (relevant provisions); Finance Act, 2023 (Section 57(2C) for PIA)【38†L407-L414】; Company financial reports and tax commentaries【34†L510-L518】【8†L233-L241】.

**1. Irrevocable Group Taxation under Section 59AA and Rule 231D**

Section 59AA of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 permits 100% owned groups (holding and subsidiaries) to be taxed as a single fiscal unit. This option is irrevocable — once exercised, it remains valid for as long as the group structure (with full ownership) is maintained. The group cannot revert to separate taxation unless structural changes occur (e.g. divestment of a subsidiary), in which case group taxation ends in the year of disposal with no partial-year benefit.

Rule 231D of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 outlines the procedure. All group companies must jointly submit a declaration of irrevocable option within the first quarter of the tax year, signed by their CEOs and supported by SECP certificates confirming compliance with corporate governance. Once approved, the holding company files a consolidated return annually, attaching audited financials of all members. However, subsidiaries must still file their own returns for record purposes and notify the Commissioner annually of continued inclusion in the group. They must also independently submit withholding statements.

Non-compliance with procedural requirements under Rule 231D (e.g. late filing, unmatched year-ends, or missing SECP certifications) can invalidate group taxation. Thus, while the option is irrevocable, ongoing annual compliance is critical to retain the consolidated status.

---

**2. Unbundling: Business vs. Depreciation Losses**

In unbundling scenarios (e.g. K-Electric’s separation into Generation, Transmission, and Distribution companies), tax losses — including unabsorbed depreciation — remain with the original legal entity unless explicitly transferrable under law. A demerger or asset transfer via court-approved Scheme of Arrangement does not automatically allow the receiving entity to inherit these losses. As per current law, only amalgamations under specific conditions permit loss transfer.

Thus, business and depreciation losses incurred pre-unbundling continue with the parent entity. The newly formed entities begin with a fresh tax base, and cannot inherit the parent’s accumulated tax losses.

---

**3. Group Relief (Section 59B) and Supply Segment Losses**

Section 59B allows surrender of current-year business losses to another group company if: (a) shareholding is ≥55% (listed) or ≥75% (unlisted); (b) companies are locally incorporated and designated for group relief; (c) losses are not capital or brought-forward; (d) the same business continues for three years, and shareholding is retained for five years.

In unbundling, a newly created entity (e.g., a Distribution Co.) may surrender its current-year business loss to a group company (e.g., a Generation Co.), subject to the above conditions. Prior-period losses cannot be surrendered. Additionally, trading entities are excluded, but electricity distribution is typically treated as a utility service — qualifying for group relief. Losses surrendered are capped at three years, after which unutilized amounts revert to the originating entity.

---

**4. Example: Listed Companies with Carryforward Losses**

Hascol Petroleum Ltd serves as an example, having reported losses of ~Rs 24.78 billion in Tax Year 2020. Such losses are reflected as deferred tax assets in financials and disclosed in notes as “assessed tax losses.” Similar losses are common in capital-intensive sectors like aviation and energy (e.g. PIA, IPPs) due to initial operating deficits or accelerated depreciation.

---

**5. Tax Depreciation: 50% Utilization Rule**

The Finance Act, 2018 introduced a cap on utilizing brought-forward depreciation: only up to 50% of current year’s business income can be offset, with excess carried forward. EY’s guidance reflects this: tax computations disallow 100% of brought-forward depreciation and 50% of current-year depreciation to align with the statutory limit. This conservative accounting ensures accurate tax provisioning and recognition of deferred tax assets, acknowledging that large depreciation pools cannot fully shield profits under the revised regime.

---

**6. SST/BST on Transmission and Distribution; CAPEX Input Tax Limitations**

Under the Sindh and Balochistan Sales Tax laws (SSTSA 2011, BSTSA 2015), transmission and distribution are taxable services (Tariff Code 9854.0000). Post-unbundling, transmission and distribution companies must charge and deposit provincial SST/BST (currently 15%).

Input tax on CAPEX (typically 18% under the Sales Tax Act, 1990) creates a mismatch with the lower provincial output tax (15%), resulting in excess input tax that is not refundable or adjustable. Provinces allow input adjustment only up to the extent of output tax; any differential (e.g., 3%) is typically disallowed and treated as a cost. Without a harmonized credit/refund mechanism between FBR and provincial authorities, CAPEX-related VAT becomes partially non-recoverable.

---

**7. NTDC and SST on Transmission: Legal Dispute and Resolution**

NTDC initially contested SRB/BRA jurisdiction over transmission services, arguing these were part of the federally taxed “supply of electricity” (a good under federal GST law) and not separately taxable services. Additionally, inter-provincial nature of NTDC’s operations raised ambiguity over the place of taxation.

This ambiguity was resolved via the Finance Act, 2023, wherein the federal and provincial governments agreed to transfer taxation of transmission services to provinces effective July 1, 2023. NTDC is now obligated to charge provincial SST on transmission, but its prior stance — backed by legal uncertainty and federal GST coverage — was arguably valid until the harmonization.

1.	Irrevocable Group Taxation Option under Section 59AA
Under section 59AA of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] allows a 100% owned group of companies (holding and subsidiaries) to opt for taxation as “one fiscal unit,” but this choice is explicitly irrevocable. In practice, this means the decision is not limited to a single year – once group taxation is elected, it continues for the duration of the group structure (as long as 100% ownership and other conditions are maintained). The law requires all companies in the group to file a declaration of irrevocable option with the tax authorities in the first quarter of the tax year for which the option is exercised. Because the option is irrevocable, the group cannot freely switch back to separate filings in later years. Only a structural change (e.g. a subsidiary leaving the group) would end the consolidated treatment, and even then the tax rules specify that if a subsidiary is divested, the group taxation ceases in the year of disposal (with no partial year benefit). In summary, the section 59AA of the Ordinance option, once taken, binds the group to a consolidated tax filing for all subsequent years of that group’s existence – it is not a year-by-year election.
The mechanics of exercising the group taxation option are prescribed by Rule 231D. Each company in the 100% group (the holding and each subsidiary) must jointly file an application to the Commissioner declaring their irrevocable option to be taxed as one unit. This application is due within the first quarter of the first tax year for which group taxation is sought. It must be signed by the CEOs of the holding and subsidiary companies and should include details like their NTNs and corporate registration numbers. Additionally, every group company must furnish a certificate from the SECP confirming compliance with the Code of Corporate Governance. Once approved, the holding company files the consolidated tax return on behalf of the group for each tax year, attaching audited financial statements of all group members. This consolidated return computes tax as if the holding and subs were one business. Importantly, while the group option is one-time and irrevocable, certain annual compliance requirements still apply: each subsidiary must continue to file its own return (in its jurisdiction) marked for record purposes, along with a copy of the group taxation application, to show that its income is included in the group return and thus not separately taxable. Each subsidiary must also notify the holding company’s Commissioner each year that it remains part of the group taxation arrangement. Moreover, all companies in the group must file independent withholding tax statements for any taxes they deduct as agents (e.g. on salaries, payments). In essence, the holding company handles the primary tax filing and payment for the consolidated income, but subsidiaries still have reporting duties to ensure transparency and facilitate audits. If any condition of group taxation ceases (for instance, a subsidiary is divested or leaves the 100% group), Rule 231D specifies that the group taxation will not apply for the year of that exit. The companies would then revert to separate taxation going forward. Compliance with Rule 231D is critical failure to meet the procedural requirements (timely application, SECP certification, matching year-ends, etc.) can invalidate the group taxation status for that year. In summary, while Section 59AA provides the framework, Rule 231D is the roadmap for implementation, ensuring that the irrevocable option is properly executed and that each year’s filings reflect the ongoing unified taxation status. The option is irrevocable in that companies cannot arbitrarily opt out later; however, they must annually comply with filing the consolidated return and related notifications to maintain the one-unit treatment.

2.	Unbundling a Company – Treatment of Business vs. Depreciation Losses
When unbundling a company (such as splitting an integrated utility like K-Electric into separate generation, transmission, and distribution entities), Ordinance does not provide a mechanism to arbitrarily split existing tax losses between the new entities. Tax losses “belong” to the legal entity that incurred them and generally remain with that entity unless a specific tax provision permits their transfer. In an unbundling via a Scheme of Arrangement (approved by court/SECP), typically one company transfers assets/business to a newly formed company. In such cases, the acquiring company does not inherit the transferor’s accumulated tax losses, those remain with the original company. This means “business losses” and “unabsorbed depreciation” from the pre-unbundling period stay with the original entity and cannot be allocated to the new spun-off companies by default. For example, if prior to unbundling the parent had large tax losses due to depreciation on its assets, after transferring those assets to a new subsidiary the parent would still carry forward those tax depreciation losses, while the new subsidiary would start with a fresh tax depreciation basis on the received assets. Ordinance does allow merger/amalgamation scenarios where losses can transfer (under continuity of ownership/business conditions), but a de-merger or asset spinoff does not automatically allow loss transfer. In short, you cannot segregate “depreciation losses” to follow the assets unless a specific amalgamation provision is invoked. The original company will retain its brought-forward losses (including any unabsorbed depreciation), subject to normal carryforward rules (unabsorbed depreciation can be carried indefinitely under current law. The new unbundled entities will not receive a portion of the parent’s prior losses – they will only carry forward losses they themselves incur after the unbundling.
3.	Group Relief (Section 59B) and Supply-Segment Losses in Unbundling
Section 59B of the Ordinance provides for group relief, allowing a holding or subsidiary company to surrender its current year assessed business loss to another group company. In the context of unbundling (e.g. separating a “Supply” or distribution business into a subsidiary), any losses incurred by that supply/distribution entity can potentially be surrendered to other group companies if all section 59B conditions are met. Notably, only assessed losses of the current tax year are eligible, this excludes capital losses and excludes any brought-forward losses from prior years. Key conditions under section 59B include: (a) the shareholding threshold – the holding company must directly own ≥55% of the subsidiary (if listed) or ≥75% (if unlisted); (b) the companies must be locally incorporated and designated for group relief; (c) the surrendering company should not be engaged in trading activities (a pure trading company cannot avail group relief); (d) the same business must continue for at least three years in the subsidiary, and the shareholding must be maintained for five years – if the holding sells shares dropping ownership below the threshold within 5 years, the previously claimed relief is recaptured and taxed. Also, a subsidiary can only surrender losses for up to three consecutive years, after which any unutilized losses revert to its own carryforward pool. From an unbundling perspective, this means if, say, the newly unbundled “Supply Co.” incurs losses (e.g. due to distribution costs), those losses (excluding any prior losses before group formation) could be surrendered to the parent or sister companies like a generation or transmission company – provided the ownership structure (post-unbundling) satisfies the above thresholds and corporate governance requirements. The supply-related losses would then offset the taxable profits of another group entity (for example, a profitable generation company), effectively yielding group-level tax savings. It’s crucial to ensure the arrangement doesn’t violate the restriction on “business of trading” – however, distribution of electricity is typically treated as a service/utility, not a trading of goods, so it should qualify for group relief. In summary, supply/distribution losses can be surrendered under Section 59B subject to conditions: the group must have the requisite ownership linkage, only current-year business losses (no carryforwards) are surrendered, and the companies must abide by the 5-year continuity rule and other stipulations. When planning an unbundling, one must consider that any losses existing prior to group formation cannot be shared (they stay with the company that earned them), and ensure that using group relief will not be clawed back by a change in ownership or business activity in subsequent years.
4.	Examples of Listed Companies with Carryforward Tax Losses
For example, is Hascol Petroleum Ltd, a listed oil marketing company that suffered heavy losses in recent years. Hascol’s tax filings for Tax Year 2020, for example, declared a taxable loss of approximately Rs 24.78 billion, on which it paid only minimum tax and even claimed a refund due to overpaid taxes. This indicates a significant carryforward tax loss available on Hascol’s books (the company’s financial statements also show unrecognized deferred tax assets corresponding to tens of billions of rupees of tax losses in recent years). Aside from these, companies in sectors like aviation and energy often carry tax losses; for instance, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) and certain independent power producers have historically had carryforward losses due to initial year losses or accelerated depreciation. The key point is that such carryforward tax losses are disclosed in financial statement notes (often labeled as “assessed tax losses” or deferred tax asset notes) for investor awareness. 
5.	Accounting Treatment of Tax Depreciation (50% Rule Guidance)
The Finance Act, 2018 introduced a significant change in how companies can utilize brought-forward depreciation for tax purposes. Previously, unabsorbed tax depreciation could be used fully to offset taxable income (and any remainder carried forward indefinitely). The 2018 amendment placed a cap: in any given tax year, brought-forward depreciation losses can only offset up to 50% of that year’s “business income”, with the remainder carried forward (an exception was made for smaller taxable incomes up to Rs 10 million). In effect, this ensures that at least half of a company’s taxable profit in a year will be subject to tax if the company has prior depreciation pools. The advisory from EY that “the full amount of brought-forward tax depreciation and 50% of the current year’s depreciation” should be adjusted in the tax charge calculation is rooted in this law change. The rationale is to reflect, in the company’s tax provision and deferred tax accounting, the portion of depreciation that cannot shield income in the current year. In practice, tax accountants following EY’s guidance would disallow (add back) 100% of any brought-forward depreciation during the tax computation (since at most only half of current-year profit can be covered by it), and also disallow 50% of the current year’s depreciation charge. This approach effectively ensures that only 50% of the current year’s depreciation is reducing the current taxable income, with the rest being carried forward. The reasoning is that if a company has substantial depreciation, only a portion will be immediately effective in reducing taxes (the rest becomes a deferred tax asset for future years). By adjusting the full brought-forward and half of current depreciation, the accounting profit is aligned to a more realistic taxable profit under the new rules, preventing the company from under-providing current tax. Put another way, this method anticipates that at least half of the depreciation (whether from prior years or current year) will not be utilizable against this year’s profits due to the 50% limitation, and thus treats that portion as a deferred expense. This yields a more conservative and accurate current tax expense in the financial statements. It also means companies with large depreciation pools will now pay some income tax even if they have hefty depreciation available, since only half of the year’s profit can be sheltered. The EY-advised treatment ensures compliance with this rule and avoids overstatement of deferred tax assets that might take many years to realize.
6.	Service Tax on Transmission/Distribution under SSTSA 2011 & BSTSA 2015 (and CAPEX Input Tax)
Under provincial law, transmission and distribution of electric power are considered taxable services in provinces like Sindh and Balochistan. The Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (and similar Balochistan Act, 2015) charge sales tax on services such as “electric power transmission services” (classified under tariff code 9854.0000). In an unbundling scenario, the newly formed Transmission Company and Distribution Company would each be providing provincially-taxable services: the transmission of electricity (wheeling power over lines), and possibly the distribution/supply service to end consumers (though the sale of electricity units themselves is treated as a supply of goods for federal sales tax). Sindh and Balochistan have included these in their taxable service schedules – for example, a Sindh-registered entity providing power transmission is subject to Sindh sales tax (the standard SST rate has been around 13% in recent years, now 15% as of 2023).
Input Tax on CAPEX vs. Output Tax: One challenge is that the input sales tax on capital equipment (e.g. transformers, transmission towers, etc.) is under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 typically at a higher rate (e.g. 17% on goods, now 18% in 2023) than the applicable provincial service tax rate (e.g. 15% in SRB). This rate mismatch can result in excess input tax. In principle, a service provider registered with SRB/BRA can claim input tax credits for sales tax paid on inputs (including goods) used in providing the service, but only to the extent allowed by provincial law and inter-government arrangements. Historically, there has been no automatic refund mechanism for excess input incurred by service providers, and provinces often disallow or limit input tax adjustment on goods. In practice, only the portion of input tax equivalent to the provincial output tax is effectively utilizable, and any excess tends to be disallowed. For example, if a Sindh Transco pays 18% GST on a new transmission line but can only charge 15% SST on its service, it will accumulate more input tax than output tax. The common approach is that the differential portion (the 3% excess in this example) cannot be claimed and becomes a cost to the business. The provincial statutes and rules support proportionate adjustments: input tax credit is generally restricted if the input relates to taxable activity with a lower tax incidence. In essence, the company would claim credit up to the amount of SST due, and any remaining input tax would be disallowed. Therefore, typically only the equivalent of 15% out of the 18% input tax can be adjusted, leaving 3% as a permanent cost unless some special adjustment mechanism exists. As a result, CAPEX-related input tax for transmission/distribution businesses must be carefully treated: the full 18% GST on capital goods is not freely creditable against provincial tax. Either the entire federal input tax is disallowed by the province (if no cross-credit agreement is in place), or at best the firm gets credit for the portion equal to its SST output and the remainder sits as unusable excess. Companies in the power sector have raised this concern in various forums, as it leads to cascading tax. This issue was one reason behind efforts to harmonize sales tax between federation and provinces. (Notably, as of 2023 the standard SST rate has increased to 15%, narrowing the gap but not eliminating it.) In summary, transmission and distribution services are taxable by Sindh/Balochistan, and because the provincial output tax is lower than the input tax on capital purchases, the excess input VAT is effectively not recoverable essentially the differential portion is disallowed. Businesses typically treat that disallowed portion of input tax as part of the capital expenditure cost. Until a refund or adjustment mechanism is developed between FBR and the provinces, firms should plan for only partial input tax credit on their CAPEX under these regimes.
7.	NTDC and Provincial Service Tax on Transmission – Application and Dispute
The National Transmission & Despatch Company (NTDC), which transmits electricity across provinces, historically did not charge or pay provincial sales tax (Sindh Revenue Board or Balochistan Revenue Authority) on its transmission services, relying on legal arguments to contest the applicability. NTDC’s position has been that its activities were already subject to federal sales tax as part of the electricity supply chain, and thus not separately taxable as a provincial service. In fact, until recently the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) was charging 17% GST on the full value of electricity delivered to distribution companies – a value that implicitly included the transmission and distribution components. Electricity is defined as “goods” for federal sales tax purposes, so the entire billing (generation + transmission + distribution) fell under federal jurisdiction. NTDC argued that the “service” element of transmitting electricity could not be carved out for provincial taxation without causing double taxation or jurisdictional conflict. Essentially, NTDC and the DISCOs viewed the transmission charge as part of the cost of supplying electricity (a federally taxed supply of goods) rather than a separate service rendered in Sindh or Balochistan.
One argument has been constitutional: that sales tax on services falls to provinces, but in this case electricity transmission was inseparable from the good (electric power) being delivered, which falls under federal sales tax on goods. NTDC also pointed out the lack of clear mechanism to segregate the value of the “service” from the electricity price on which FBR was already collecting GST. Moreover, the service is of an inter-provincial nature – power may originate in one province and terminate in another – which raised questions of which province’s tax applies (until “place of supply” rules were agreed, there was risk of multiple provinces claiming the tax). NTDC likely leveraged these uncertainties, and litigation ensued between NTDC and provincial authorities (Sindh SRB in particular issued notices for SST on transmission charges). While contesting SRB’s jurisdiction, NTDC essentially refrained from paying SST, awaiting a policy resolution via the National Tax Council or Council of Common Interests. The company’s stance was bolstered by the fact that provincial authorities themselves recognized the overlap – in 2019 the provincial revenue boards jointly acknowledged that FBR was collecting 17% on what was a mix of goods and services in the power sector, and they sought to “segregate” the portion attributable to services. This indicates that even provinces knew the law was grey on this point, which NTDC used to justify not charging provincial tax.
This long-standing dispute was effectively resolved in 2023. Through Finance Act, 2023, the federal government amended the law to formally transfer sales tax on “production, transmission, and distribution of electricity” to the provinces. A consensus declaration between the center and provinces agreed that electric power transmission would be treated as a service taxable by provinces from July 1, 2023. In other words, the legal ambiguity has been removed: going forward, NTDC’s transmission services are squarely under provincial sales tax (with the value of the service to be excluded from federal GST on electricity). This also came with place-of-provision rules to split tax for inter-provincial transmissions. Prior to this change, NTDC did not levy SRB/BRA tax and defended that stance by arguing lack of provincial jurisdiction and pointing to the comprehensive federal GST already being paid on the overall electricity supply. Now, however, NTDC is expected to comply with provincial tax for its services (charging the applicable SST to its customers like K-Electric or DISCOS in Sindh/Balochistan). In summary, NTDC initially resisted SRB/BRA service tax, contending that its transmission fees were part of a federally-taxed good (electricity) and that provincial taxation would amount to double taxation or unconstitutional overlap. This led to legal disputes and an eventual policy solution. With the 2023 amendments, the law is clear that provinces have the right to tax the transmission service, so NTDC will have to apply provincial sales tax going forward – but its past stance was grounded in the ambiguity that existed before harmonization.

- Exclusion of capital or prior-year losses.
- Prohibition on relief for pure trading companies.
- Mandatory business continuity for 3 years and shareholding retention for 5 years (failing which, the relief is clawed back).

In an unbundling scenario, a newly formed supply/distribution company can surrender current year losses (e.g., due to high operating costs) to a profitable group entity (e.g., generation company), provided post-unbundling conditions of Section 59B are met. Note that only losses incurred after group formation are eligible for surrender.

---

### 4. **Examples of Listed Companies with Tax Losses**

Listed entities like Hascol Petroleum Ltd. illustrate the carryforward of significant tax losses. For instance, Hascol reported losses exceeding Rs. 24 billion in Tax Year 2020, leading to minimal tax liability and deferred tax assets. Other examples include Pakistan International Airlines and certain IPPs, where early-stage losses or high depreciation resulted in large deferred tax balances. Such disclosures appear in financial statements under “assessed tax losses” or “deferred tax asset” notes.

---

### 5. **Accounting for Tax Depreciation – 50% Limitation**

The Finance Act, 2018 introduced a cap where only 50% of business income can be offset using brought-forward depreciation (except where income is below Rs. 10 million). As a result, companies with large depreciation pools will pay tax on at least half their income annually.

EY’s advisory recommends:
- Disallowing 100% of brought-forward depreciation.
- Disallowing 50% of current-year depreciation.

This ensures alignment with tax law and avoids overstating deferred tax assets. Only 50% of current depreciation is utilized, with the rest carried forward. This treatment provides a conservative estimate of tax expense in financial statements, especially for capital-intensive companies.

---

### 6. **Provincial Sales Tax on Transmission/Distribution & CAPEX Input Tax Issues**

Under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 and the Balochistan Act, 2015, electric power transmission and distribution are taxable services (Tariff Code: 9854.0000). In unbundled structures, the transmission and distribution entities are separately registered and liable to provincial sales tax (currently 15% in Sindh as of 2023).

**CAPEX Input Tax Challenge:**  
Capital equipment (e.g., towers, transformers) typically bears 18% federal GST, whereas the output SST is lower (e.g., 15%). Provinces generally allow input adjustment only to the extent of output liability. The excess (e.g., 3%) is often disallowed and becomes part of the asset’s cost unless a cross-credit mechanism is available. This creates a structural tax leakage and limits input adjustment on capital expenditure.

---

### 7. **NTDC and the Evolution of Provincial Sales Tax Jurisdiction**

NTDC historically resisted charging provincial SST, arguing that electricity is a federally-taxed “good,” and transmission is an inseparable component. The ambiguity stemmed from dual taxation concerns, inter-provincial supply complications, and the absence of place-of-supply rules.

This dispute persisted until the Finance Act, 2023, which clarified that “transmission and distribution of electricity” are provincially taxable services effective July 1, 2023. NTDC is now required to apply SST on its services and exclude these values from federal GST. Prior resistance was based on legal grey areas that have since been resolved through federal-provincial consensus.

On behalf of ENI Pakistan, we hereby submit our detailed response and the requested information regarding taxable services alleged to have been received from ENI S.p.A., ENI Servizi S.p.A., and ENI International Resources Limited (collectively, “the service providers”) during the years 2017 and 2018. We appreciate the opportunity to explain our position, and we remain committed to full cooperation in this matter.  

## Summary of Services and Reimbursements (2017–2018)  

As directed, the following table provides the name of each service provider, a description of the services, and the value of services **received** and **paid** during the periods Jan–Dec 2017 and Jan–Dec 2018, respectively. All amounts are stated in PKR (Pakistani Rupees):

| **Total** |                                      |                                          | **400,000,000** | **400,000,000** | **425,000,000** | **425,000,000** |

**Explanation of the Above Services:** The services from the above group entities principally consisted of:  

- **ENI S.p.A.:** Provision of technical assistance and managerial support to ENI Pakistan’s oil and gas operations under a Technical Services Agreement. This included expert advice, project management support, and other technical guidance.  
- **ENI Servizi S.p.A.:** Provision of various administrative and support services (such as information technology support, procurement coordination, and other back-office services) under a Service Agreement.  
- **ENI International Resources Ltd (EIRL):** Secondment of skilled expatriate personnel to ENI Pakistan and related human resource support. The personnel seconded through EIRL worked exclusively for ENI Pakistan’s projects, and EIRL billed ENI Pakistan for their actual payroll cost and associated benefits.  

**Reimbursements at Actual Cost (No Profit Element):** All the above payments made by ENI Pakistan to the service providers were **pure reimbursements of actual costs** incurred by those entities on behalf of ENI Pakistan. Critically, **no mark-up, profit, or service fee** was charged by ENI S.p.A., ENI Servizi, or EIRL on these transactions. This is confirmed by the inter-company agreements governing these services, which explicitly stipulate that only actual costs will be charged without any profit or duplication of charges. For instance, the service agreement between ENI Pakistan and ENI S.p.A. provides that ENI S.p.A. shall charge **“only the actual costs incurred”** for the support services, with no element of profit. Similar clauses exist in the agreements with ENI Servizi and EIRL, ensuring that ENI Pakistan only reimburses expenses **at cost**. We have enclosed copies of the relevant agreements for your ready reference, highlighting the clauses confirming the **“at cost”** reimbursement structure. Furthermore, we are providing certificates from our external auditors (M/s Ernst & Young) for the years 2017 and 2018, which certify that all payments made to these related companies were at actual cost, with no profit element or double-charging. These measures substantiate that the nature of the transactions was **intragroup cost sharing** rather than the procurement of taxable services from third-party vendors.  

## Legal Position and Justification under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011  

ENI Pakistan respectfully submits that the above-described reimbursements do **not constitute taxable services** under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“the Act”), for the reasons explained below. We base this position on the relevant provisions of the Act, which distinguish genuine service fees from mere expense reimbursements:  

1. **No “Consideration” for a Service – Only Expense Recovery:** Section 5(1)(a) of the Act defines the *“value of a taxable service”* as **“the consideration in money… which the person providing a service receives from the recipient of the service”**, excluding the amount of sales tax【25†L399-L402】. In other words, sales tax is levied on the **consideration** (i.e. the service fee or charge) that a service provider charges for rendering a service. In the present case, ENI Pakistan paid **no consideration for any service**, since the inter-company charges were strictly limited to reimbursing actual expenditures. The foreign affiliates did not **receive any payment for their own benefit** – they merely recovered costs spent on our behalf. There was no element of profit or value-add charged to ENI Pakistan. Accordingly, the *“value of the taxable service”* in these transactions is effectively zero, because the payments were not in the nature of a fee for services but purely a **pass-through of costs**. Taxing such pass-through cost reimbursements would stretch the meaning of “consideration” beyond the intent of the law. Simply put, without a genuine service fee or mark-up, there is no taxable *“service”* value upon which sales tax can be levied. This interpretation is consistent with the scheme of the Act, which is to tax the provision of services **for a consideration** – not to tax the reimbursement of expenses.  

2. **Reimbursed Expenses Are Not Taxable Services:** It is a well-established principle (and supported by case law) that **only the net service charges or fee are subject to sales tax, and any reimbursed expenditures incurred on behalf of the service recipient should not form part of the taxable base**. The Sindh High Court has affirmed that under the Act, **“only the quantum and value of [the] service… is taxable… and not the amount being reimbursed by the service recipient.”**【23†L799-L804】 In other words, amounts which are simply paid back to reimburse costs are **outside the scope of SST**, as they do not represent payment for a service. In our case, since the invoices from ENI S.p.A., ENI Servizi, and EIRL consisted solely of **reimbursable cost components** (e.g. employee salaries, travel costs, and shared administrative overheads at actuals) and **no part of the invoice was a fee or profit**, those reimbursed cost components are not taxable. The taxable value, if any, would only be an actual *service fee* element – and here there was none. We draw attention to the fact that many of the costs reimbursed (particularly under EIRL’s invoices) were in the nature of **employee salaries and benefits** for personnel working for ENI Pakistan. Had those individuals been direct employees of ENI Pakistan, their services to the Company would fall outside the definition of “economic activity” (being services of an employee to an employer, per Section 4(3)(a) of the Act) and thus not be taxable【12†L392-L399】. Simply routing these employment costs through an affiliate (for administrative convenience) should not transmogrify them into taxable services. The substance remains that ENI Pakistan bore its own staff costs – which is not a taxable service. The law should not impose sales tax on such **pure reimbursements of employee costs**, especially in the absence of any independent service provider’s profit.  

3. **No Taxable “Economic Activity” by Group Companies in Providing Support:** The Act generally envisages an “economic activity” (Section 4) whereby a person engages in providing services **on a commercial basis**. In the present intragroup arrangements, the foreign affiliates were **not carrying on a business of providing services to customers in Sindh**; rather, they were fulfilling internal group obligations without any profit motive. While ENI S.p.A., ENI Servizi, and EIRL undoubtedly provided assistance to ENI Pakistan, they did so **as part of the ENI corporate group’s internal cost-sharing and support framework**, not as outsiders pursuing profit. We acknowledge that an activity may qualify as an economic activity even if not for profit, **if** it is carried on in a business-like manner (Section 4(1)(a))【12†L383-L392】. However, it is our respectful view that these support arrangements were **incidental to ENI’s main business operations** and were not akin to services marketed or offered to unrelated clients. The absence of any profit element strongly indicates that these arrangements were not in the nature of a service **industry or trade**, but rather inter-company collaborative efforts. Therefore, treating these cost reimbursements as if they were normal taxable service transactions would be inconsistent with the intent of the SST law, which targets **services provided in a commercial context for consideration**.  

4. **Relevant Provisions of the Act and Second Schedule:** We have also examined the Second Schedule of the Act (taxable services tariff) to identify any entries that might cover the subject transactions. The services rendered by the group companies to ENI Pakistan could ostensibly be classified under categories like “management consulting” or “business support services” if they were provided by a third-party firm for a fee. However, given the **at-cost nature** of these inter-company charges, we submit that they do not squarely fit into the taxable service categories in a typical sense. Even if one were to argue a category applies, the **taxable value** would still only be the **consideration actually charged** for the service, per Section 5 of the Act – which, as explained, was nil beyond reimbursement of expenses. We also note that there have been no charges for any franchising, license fees or other royalty-like services from these entities; the entirety of the transactions was limited to operational support cost sharing.  

In light of the above points, ENI Pakistan maintains that the amounts paid to ENI S.p.A., ENI Servizi S.p.A., and ENI International Resources Ltd. during 2017 and 2018 are **outside the purview of Sindh sales tax on services**. Levying SST on these amounts would effectively amount to taxing our **own internal costs**, which the law does not intend. This position is firmly supported by the language of the statute (sections cited above) and judicial interpretation thereof, as well as fundamental principles of VAT/Sales Tax which distinguish between payments for services vs. reimbursements. We therefore respectfully request that the honorable SRB kindly **drop the proceedings** initiated under the Show Cause Notice.  

## Conclusion and Prayer  

**Enclosures & Evidence:** In support of our above submission, we enclose herewith the following documents for your kind consideration:  

- **Copies of Agreements** between ENI Pakistan Limited and each of the three service providers (ENI S.p.A., ENI Servizi S.p.A., and ENI International Resources Ltd.), duly highlighting the clauses that stipulate charging on an actual cost (no-profit) basis.  
- **Auditor’s Certificates** issued by M/s Ernst & Young for the years 2017 and 2018, verifying that all inter-company payments made to the above entities were reimbursements of actual expenses, containing no profit or mark-up and no duplicated charges.  

We kindly urge you to review the enclosed agreements and certificates, which corroborate the factual stance that ENI Pakistan was only bearing its share of costs. We are confident that the evidence will affirm that **no taxable services were received** in the sense contemplated by the Act.  

**Cooperation and Further Assistance:** ENI Pakistan Limited reiterates its commitment to fully cooperate with the Sindh Revenue Board. Should your good office require any additional information, explanation, or documentation, we stand ready to promptly provide the same. Our team (and our tax advisors A.F. Ferguson & Co.) will also be present at the scheduled hearing on March 4, 2025 to elaborate on this written reply and address any queries. We appreciate the opportunities given to explain our position, and we trust that our submissions will be given due consideration.  

**Prayer:** In view of the facts explained and the legal provisions discussed above, we respectfully pray that the learned Deputy Commissioner kindly **vacate the Show Cause Notice dated September 20, 2019**, without any adverse action, as the subject transactions are not chargeable to Sindh sales tax. We request that this reply along with the enclosures be made part of the record of the case, and that the matter be decided on the basis of the presented facts and evidence which clearly support ENI Pakistan’s stance. We are optimistic that upon review, the honorable SRB will acknowledge the bona fide nature of these reimbursements and conclude this proceeding accordingly in a just and fair manner.  

Thank you for your consideration of our submission. We remain at your disposal for any further clarification.  

Yours sincerely,  

for **ENI Pakistan Limited**  

*(Authorized Signatory)*  

**Enclosures:** As above (List of Agreements and Auditor Certificates)

# Taxability of Intra-Group Services under Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011

## Overview of Intra-Group Agreements  
ENI Pakistan Limited (“ENI Pakistan”) has entered into intra-group agreements with its affiliates for sharing of personnel and support functions. These include: 

- **Secondment Agreement (Eni SpA & Eni International Resources Ltd.)** – An agreement for secondment of Eni personnel within the group. Under this arrangement, expatriate employees remain on the payroll of the seconding company (Eni International Resources Ltd.) and are assigned to work for another group entity. The receiving entity reimburses **all costs** related to the seconded employees (salaries, allowances, taxes, etc.) to the seconding company, **with no mark-up or profit**【22†L129-L137】. The seconded staff legally remain employees of the seconding affiliate, not ENI Pakistan. 

- **Service Agreement (Eni Servizi S.p.A. & ENI Pakistan)** – An agreement for **international travel, accommodation, and related support services** provided by Eni Servizi (a group service company) to ENI Pakistan. ENI Pakistan pays only the **actual expenses** incurred by Eni Servizi in providing these services, on a **full cost reimbursement basis with no profit element**【27†L274-L277】. This means Eni Servizi simply passes through the travel and lodging costs of ENI Pakistan’s personnel, without any added margin. 

- **Service Agreement (Eni S.p.A. & ENI Pakistan)** – An agreement under which Eni S.p.A. provides **specialist and business support services** (such as technical expertise, coordination, and other back-office support) to ENI Pakistan. Charges under this agreement are strictly limited to the **actual costs incurred by Eni S.p.A.** in rendering the support, **excluding any profit or mark-up**【17†L228-L234】. An auditor’s certificate confirms that the fees charged to ENI Pakistan comprise only allocable actual costs (with no duplication or profit)【17†L228-L234】. 

Collectively, these contracts demonstrate that ENI Pakistan’s intercompany transactions are **intra-group cost-sharing arrangements**. Each affiliate recovers only the expenses it incurred on ENI Pakistan’s behalf, and **none of the agreements involve a commercial profit**. In essence, ENI Pakistan is bearing its portion of joint costs (for personnel and support services) rather than paying for a service in the open market. 

## Absence of Taxable **“Service”** – No Independent Economic Activity (Section 4)  
Under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SSTSA 2011), the sales tax is levied on services **provided in the course of an economic activity** in Sindh. The affiliated companies in these agreements are not engaged in any **independent commercial service business** in Sindh – their activities are **incidental to the internal operations** of the Eni corporate group【30†L190-L197】. The support functions and secondments are not offered to third parties in the open market; they exist solely to allocate resources within the Eni group. Hence, the fundamental requirement of a **“taxable economic activity”** under Section 4 of SSTSA 2011 is not satisfied【30†L190-L197】. Simply put, internal cost allocations do not amount to a taxable **economic enterprise** rendering services to consumers – it is merely the group managing its own affairs. 

Notably, Section 4(3)(a) of the Act expressly **excludes employer-employee services** from the ambit of taxable services. Had the expatriate staff under the Secondment Agreement been directly employed by ENI Pakistan, their services to ENI Pakistan (their employer) would unquestionably fall **outside the sales tax net** by virtue of Section 4(3)(a)【30†L197-L200】. Structuring their deployment through an affiliate (Eni International Resources Ltd.) does not alter this substantive reality. The seconded individuals work under ENI Pakistan’s direction as part of its organization, and the arrangement remains, in substance, an HR allocation rather than a **service provision** by one independent entity to another. Taxing such an arrangement would elevate form over substance. It would effectively mean taxing a company for utilizing its own human resources, which **“would amount to taxing one’s own costs”**, a result **contrary to settled tax principles**【30†L203-L210】.

Moreover, **intra-group cost allocations** like these lack the profit motive characteristic of economic activities. The affiliated service providers are **not earning revenue** in a business sense; they are simply **recouping shared costs**. This absence of any commercial gain further indicates that these transactions are **not taxable services**, but rather internal transfers. As a matter of law and policy, sales tax targets activities where value is added in exchange for consideration – not pure reimbursements within a corporate family.

## No Consideration or Value Addition for Services (Section 5)  
Section 5 of SSTSA 2011 imposes tax on the **“value of a taxable service”**, which is generally the **consideration paid** for the service. In the present case, there is **no separate consideration** paid for any service – only the **reimbursement of actual costs**. The payments from ENI Pakistan to its affiliates do not contain any element of profit, margin, or value-added component that could be characterized as the “price” of a service. The **absence of a markup or service fee** confirms that these arrangements were not intended as revenue-generating services at all, but rather **cost settlements**【30†L185-L193】. 

Critically, the charges billed to ENI Pakistan represent **only the cost of inputs** (e.g. salaries, travel expenses) that ENI Pakistan would otherwise have borne directly. In other words, ENI Pakistan is ultimately paying for its **own expenses**, channeled through group companies for administrative convenience. Such pass-through costs **do not constitute “consideration for a service”** in the sense of Section 5(1)(a) of the Act【30†L185-L193】. There is no bargained-for **service fee** being paid; there is only a reimbursement of expense. Taxing these amounts would effectively mean taxing expenditures that **do not correspond to any service value**, leading to inequitable double taxation (the expenses might already be subject to income tax or other levies in the hands of the employees or vendors, for example). 

Pakistan’s superior courts have affirmed that **sales tax on services cannot be levied on components of a transaction that are mere reimbursements and not part of the actual service value**. The Hon’ble **Supreme Court of Pakistan**, in a recent judgment, analyzed the **“gross amount charged”** for services under SSTSA and held that reimbursed expenses (such as salaries paid to seconded or outsourced staff) are **not part of the taxable value of the service**【25†L224-L232】【25†L235-L243】. The Court clarified that those reimbursed costs are **borne by the service recipient** and **do not form part of the service provider’s economic activity or the consideration for the service**【25†L224-L232】. Section 5’s concept of taxable value is thus limited to the **true consideration for the service itself**, nothing more. Any amounts representing costs **recovered on behalf of the recipient** lie outside the scope of tax. The Supreme Court further emphasized that while invoices might include reimbursable items for transparency, such items **“have no nexus with the service or its value”**, and their inclusion in billing **“does not warrant taxation on the total invoiced amount”**【30†L227-L235】【30†L239-L247】. Only the portion of the invoice representing the **service’s intrinsic value** is subject to sales tax, and **“the quantum [of tax] is charged for the service alone, nothing more and nothing less”**【30†L227-L235】. 

In ENI Pakistan’s case, there is **no separate service fee** at all – the **entire invoiced amount is reimbursement**. According to the Supreme Court’s reasoning, this means there is no taxable value on which to levy sales tax, since the **“gross amount charged” is not consideration for a service**【25†L224-L232】. The **Sindh High Court** has reached the same conclusion in **IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt) Ltd. v. Province of Sindh (2022 PTD 576)**, where it was held that only the **value of the service rendered** can be taxed under the SSTSA, and not any reimbursed cost component that might be billed along with the service【26†L274-L280】. The High Court stressed that reading SSTSA’s charging and valuation provisions together, the tax cannot be imposed on elements of a transaction that fall outside the **essence of the service**【26†L274-L280】. This judicial guidance squarely applies here – the **essence** of ENI’s intercompany arrangements is cost sharing, not service provision for consideration.

## Persuasive Legal Position and Conclusion  
In light of the above, it is **respectfully submitted** that the amounts transacted under the cited intercompany agreements fall **outside the charging scope of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**. The arrangements are **intra-group reimbursements** of actual costs with **no profit element**, lacking the hallmarks of a taxable service (no independent business activity, and no true consideration for service). Taxing these internal cost allocations would effectively amount to taxing the company’s **own operational expenses**, which finds no support in the law or precedent【30†L203-L210】. Both the **Supreme Court of Pakistan** and the **Sindh High Court** have affirmed that such reimbursements are **not subject to sales tax**【25†L235-L243】【26†L274-L280】. 

Therefore, the services outlined in the three agreements – when properly characterized – do not constitute **taxable services** under Section 4, nor do the intercompany payments constitute **consideration for any service** under Section 5 of SSTSA 2011. These transactions are merely a mechanism to allocate costs within the Eni corporate group, with **no value addition** or profit earned by the service-providing affiliates. We urge that the Sindh Revenue Board recognize the true nature of these arrangements and conclude that **Sindh sales tax is not applicable** on these intra-group reimbursements. This position is firmly grounded in the contract terms, the intent of the law, and the consistent view of superior courts in Pakistan. 

**\[All of the above is submitted for the kind consideration of the Sindh Revenue Board, in support of ENI Pakistan’s stance that the impugned transactions are not taxable under the SSTSA 2011.\]**【30†L190-L197】【25†L235-L243】

More Refined below: 

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the selection of our client for audit under section 177 of the Ordinance is procedurally defective for want of the mandatory Board approval under Clause 105A of Part-IV, Second Schedule, Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Under Clause 105A, the Commissioner must obtain the Board’s prior written approval before initiating an audit under section 177 of the Ordinance. In the present case no valid approval of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has been obtained in compliance with this requirement. Indeed, as the Appellate Tribunal held in Sprint Oil & Gas Services bearing ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025, the legislature has “with clear intent, mandated that the Commissioner directly seek approval from the Board”. Any deviation from the Clause 105A procedure vitiates the entire audit process.
Legal Provisions
Clause 105A of Part IV of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance provides that no person shall be selected for audit under section 177 of the Ordinance unless the Commissioner first obtains prior written approval of the FBR specifying the person, tax year, and grounds for audit. The Federal Board is empowered under the FBR Act and rules to delegate powers, but such delegation must comply with legal mandates (Section 8, FBR Act, 2007). As recently affirmed by the Appellate Tribunal, these provisions impose a strict procedure: the Commissioner must personally seek and obtain Board approval for each audit. The Tribunal stressed that Clause 105A “requires the Commissioner to directly seek approval from the Board”, and does not authorize processing the request through an intermediary.
In the instant case, the Clause 105A requirement has not been complied with. Although Annexure A shows the Commissioner’s request and a Board response, the form of the approval is procedurally flawed. The Board’s letter is addressed to the Chief Commissioner, LTO Karachi (Annexure A), rather than directly to the Commissioner as mandated by Clause 105A. In Sprint Oil, the Tribunal pointed out this very defect: the impugned Board approval “was issued to the Chief Commissioner Inland Revenue…rather than to the Commissioner, as required by the aforementioned clause”. This procedural irregularity parallels the present case. As in Sprint Oil, the approval in our client’s case was communicated through the Chief Commissioner, adding an impermissible administrative layer. This violates Clause 105A’s clear mandate and creates an “administrative bottleneck” that the law did not intend.
Furthermore, the Appellate Tribunal observed that the approval granted by the FBR Member under Clause 105A in Sprint Oil “is not in compliance with the law”. By parity of reasoning, the purported approval in this case (see Annexure A) cannot cure the defect. In short, the Clause 105A approval procedure was neither properly sought nor properly granted. Consequently, the notice under section 177 of the Ordinance issued to our client is ultra vires: it rests on no valid statutory authority.
This position is squarely supported by the recent ATIR decision in Sprint Oil & Gas Services bearing ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025. The Tribunal’s operating findings are instructive: it held that Clause 105A’s requirement of “directly seeking approval from the Board” must be strictly followed. The Tribunal noted that involving the Chief Commissioner “introduces an additional administrative layer” not sanctioned by law. Citing these failures, the Tribunal conclusively ruled that the audit proceedings were invalid. It explicitly declared the impugned approval “not in compliance with the law” and the subsequent tax order “illegal, void ab initio, and without jurisdiction”. In Sprint Oil, therefore, all actions taken under the flawed Clause 105A approval were quashed.
Our client’s case is governed by the same principles. We respectfully submit that the Tribunal’s reasoning applies in identical fashion here. The Approval letter in Annexure A suffers from the precise defects identified in Sprint Oil. As a result, pursuant to the Tribunal’s holding, the Section 177 notice (and any resulting assessment or demand) is rendered null and void. We refer to the enclosed decision in Sprint Oil & Gas Services for further detail; key paragraphs have been extracted above with references 
Conclusion
In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the Notice under Section 177 for Tax Year 2019 is untenable. K-Electric’s selection for audit was made without valid Board approval as required by Clause 105A. This deficiency is fatal: the Appellate Tribunal has made clear that any audit initiated without strict compliance with Clause 105A is ultra vires. Since the statutory procedure was not followed, the Notice (and any purported tax demand thereunder) is without lawful authority. The approval purportedly granted by the FBR is itself “not in compliance with the law”, and the proceedings built upon it are “illegal, void ab initio, and without jurisdiction”. In light of these authoritative pronouncements, the Notice must be set aside.
