Please read the below and prepare a concluding paragraph: 

At the outset, we respectfully submit that the entire audit selection and approval process leading to this notice is vitiated by fundamental legal defects. In particular, as established in the recent Honorable Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Islamabad [ATIR] decision in case of M/s Sprint Oil & Gas Services bearing ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025, none of the steps taken by the FBR Board or its officers complied with the law. Each defect, discussed below, renders the purported approval and consequent proceedings void ab initio.
ILLEGALITY OF APPROVAL UNDER CLAUSE 105A
Clause 105A of Part IV, Second Schedule to the Ordinance sets out a special audit-selection procedure requiring formal sanction of the FBR Board. In the present case, the Member (IR-Ops), FBR purported to approve of our client’s audit outside the mandated process. The ATIR in Sprint Oil expressly held that an approval by the Member under Clause 105A “is not in compliance with the law”. The ATIR further noted that Clause 105A “stipulates that the Commissioner must directly seek approval from the Board”, meaning no alternative procedure (such as Member-signoff) is permissible. Here the Member (IR-Ops) never obtained the Board’s direct sanction as required. By Sprint Oil’s reasoning, any Clause-105A approval obtained in this manner is legally null and void.
INVALID BOARD “MEETING” UNDER SECTION 3(7) OF THE FBR ACT, 2007
The FBR Act, 2007 prescribes the procedure for Board meetings. Although the Board purported to approve this audit by circulation of a memo, the ATIR held that a “meeting held by the Board under section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007, exceeded the authority” granted by the statute. In other words, conducting a “meeting” by circulation (without a proper quorum or formal meeting) is not sanctioned by the Act or rules. Consequently, the so-called Board decision in this manner was itself unauthorized. Any action taken via that irregular meeting (including approval of our client’s audit) is therefore of no legal effect, having been made outside the scope of Section 3(7).
LACK OF FORMAL DELEGATION TO THE MEMBER (IR-OPS)
Independently, there was no valid delegation of Board powers to the Member (IR-Ops) for Clause-105A approvals. Section 8 of the FBR Act read with Rule 3(1) of the FBR Rules, 2007 mandates that any delegation of the Board’s functions must be formally notified by the Board. In Sprint Oil, the ATIR emphasized that the Board never issued any such delegation notification. It pointed out that “the power delegated by the Board to the Member had not been formally notified, as required under section 8 of the FBR Act, 2007, in conjunction with rule 3(1)”. In the absence of a formal notification, the Member (IR-Ops) had no lawful authority to act as Board. Thus, even setting aside Clause 105A, the Member’s attempt to approve the audit is void for want of any delegated jurisdiction.
ULTRA VIRES EXPANSION BY RULES 3(3) AND 3(4)
The Board may not rely on Rule 3(3) or 3(4) of the FBR Rules to cure these defects. Those provisions allow a member (e.g. the Chairman) to act pending formal delegation, but Sprint Oil held that they “conflict with section 9 of the FBR Act” and “improperly broaden its scope”. Section 9 merely preserves the validity of Board actions despite technical defects (such as vacancies) it does not confer any new substantive powers on individual members. Allowing Rules 3(3) or (4) to sidestep the delegation requirement would unlawfully expand the Act. The ATIR therefore ruled that Rules 3(3) and (4) are ultra vires Section 9 and cannot impart authority where none exists. In short, no reliance can be placed on these rules to justify the Member’s actions in our case.
INVALIDITY OF SUBSEQUENT PROCEEDINGS
Each of the above flaws was found in Sprint Oil to be fatal. The ATIR concluded that because the Board’s initial approval was “flawed”, “all subsequent actions taken, including the issuance of the contested order under section 121… were automatically rendered invalid”. The ATIR ultimately declared the impugned order “illegal, void from the beginning (ab-initio), and without jurisdiction”. By parity of reasoning, the Notice under section 177 issued to our client (and any resulting assessment under section 121) must also be regarded as void ab initio. The entire audit process here rests on the very same defective foundation that Sprint Oil struck down. As a matter of law, a notice predicated on an invalid selection cannot stand. In fact, the Business Recorder and Customs Today reports of Sprint Oil emphasize that all subsequent proceedings are rendered invalid. Accordingly, the impugned Notice and any downstream action are a nullity. For the sake of brevity, the operating paragraphs of aforesaid decision as under: 
“By respectfully following the above judgment, the impugned order dated 13.11.2024 is annulled.

14. CONCLUSION OF THE ABOVE APPEALS

I. The approval granted by the learned Member (IR-Ops), FBR, under clause (105A) of Part-IV of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance is not in compliance with the law.

ii. Furthermore, the meeting held by the Board under section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007, exceeds the authority granted by the FBR Act, 2007, and the rules formulated under it.

iii. Additionally, the power delegated by the Board to the Member (IROps) has not been formally notified by the Board as required by section 8 of the FBR Act, 2007, in conjunction with rule 3(1) of the
FBR Rules, 2007.

iv. Moreover, sub-rules (3) and (4) of rule 3 of the FBR Rules, 2007, conflict with section 9 of the FBR Act, 2007. These rules improperly broaden the scope of section 9, which contradicts the established
legal principle that rules cannot extend the scope of statutory provisions.

v. As a result, since the approval granted by the Board under Clause (105A) is flawed, the subsequent actions taken, including the issuance of the impugned ex-parte order under section 121 of the Ordinance, are automatically rendered invalid.”
(emphasis is our)

Please read the attached notice and prepare a detailed response on behalf of our client (K-Electric Limited) on account of the audit under Clause 105A. For your ready reference, please find the attached recent order of similar fact in favor of the taxpayer and board approval in our client case.

K-Electric Limited  
KE House, 39-B Sunset Boulevard, Phase-II, DHA, Karachi  

Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  
Large Taxpayer Office, Karachi  

**Subject:** Reply to Notice under Section 177 for Tax Year 2019  

Respected Sir,  

This is in reference to the Notice under section 177 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”) dated [___] for Tax Year 2019 addressed to K-Electric Limited.  We respectfully submit that the entire audit selection and approval process leading to this notice is vitiated by fundamental legal defects.  In particular, as established in the recent ATIR Islamabad decision _M/s Sprint Oil & Gas Services_ (ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025), none of the steps taken by the FBR Board or its officers complied with the law.  Each defect, discussed below, renders the purported approval and consequent proceedings void ab initio.  

## Illegality of Approval under Clause 105A  
Clause 105A of Part IV, Second Schedule to the Ordinance (inserted by the Finance Act, 2022) sets out a special audit-selection procedure requiring formal sanction of the FBR Board.  In the present case, the Member (IR-Ops), FBR purported to approve K-Electric’s audit outside the mandated process.  The Appellate Tribunal in Sprint Oil expressly held that an approval by the Member under Clause 105A “is not in compliance with the law”【14†L106-L108】.  The tribunal further noted that Clause 105A “stipulates that the Commissioner must directly seek approval from the Board”【14†L124-L126】, meaning no alternative procedure (such as Member-signoff) is permissible.  Here the Member (IR-Ops) never obtained the Board’s direct sanction as required.  By Sprint Oil’s reasoning, any Clause-105A approval obtained in this manner is legally null and void.  

## Invalid Board “Meeting” under Section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007  
The FBR Act, 2007 prescribes the procedure for Board meetings.  Although the Board purported to approve this audit by circulation of a memo, the ATIR held that a “meeting held by the Board under section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007, exceeded the authority” granted by the statute【14†L109-L110】.  In other words, conducting a “meeting” by circulation (without a proper quorum or formal meeting) is not sanctioned by the Act or rules.  Consequently, the so-called Board decision in this manner was itself unauthorized.  Any action taken via that irregular meeting (including approval of K-Electric’s audit) is therefore of no legal effect, having been made outside the scope of Section 3(7).  

## Lack of Formal Delegation to the Member (IR-Ops)  
Independently, there was no valid delegation of Board powers to the Member (IR-Ops) for Clause-105A approvals.  Section 8 of the FBR Act – read with Rule 3(1) of the FBR Rules, 2007 – mandates that any delegation of the Board’s functions must be formally notified by the Board.  In Sprint Oil, the tribunal emphasized that the Board never issued any such delegation notification.  It pointed out that “the power delegated by the Board to the Member had not been formally notified… as required under section 8 of the FBR Act, 2007, in conjunction with rule 3(1)”【14†L112-L113】.  In the absence of a formal notification, the Member (IR-Ops) had no lawful authority to act as Board.  Thus, even setting aside Clause 105A, the Member’s attempt to approve the audit is void for want of any delegated jurisdiction.  

## Ultra Vires Expansion by Rules 3(3) and 3(4)  
The Board may not rely on Rule 3(3) or 3(4) of the FBR Rules to cure these defects.  Those provisions allow a member (e.g. the Chairman) to act pending formal delegation, but Sprint Oil held that they “conflict with section 9 of the FBR Act” and “improperly broaden[] its scope”【14†L114-L116】.  Section 9 merely preserves the validity of Board actions despite technical defects (such as vacancies) – it does *not* confer any new substantive powers on individual members.  Allowing Rules 3(3) or (4) to sidestep the delegation requirement would unlawfully expand the Act.  The ATIR therefore ruled that Rules 3(3) and (4) are ultra vires Section 9 and cannot impart authority where none exists【14†L114-L116】.  In short, no reliance can be placed on these rules to justify the Member’s actions in our case.  

## Invalidity of Subsequent Proceedings  
Each of the above flaws was found in Sprint Oil to be fatal.  The tribunal concluded that because the Board’s initial approval was “flawed”, “all subsequent actions taken, including the issuance of the contested order under section 121… were automatically rendered invalid”【14†L120-L123】.  The ATIR ultimately declared the impugned order “illegal, void from the beginning (ab-initio), and without jurisdiction”【14†L129-L130】.  By parity of reasoning, the Notice under section 177 issued to K-Electric (and any resulting assessment under section 121) must also be regarded as void ab initio.  The entire audit process here rests on the very same defective foundation that Sprint Oil struck down.  As a matter of law, a notice predicated on an invalid selection cannot stand.  In fact, the Business Recorder and Customs Today reports of Sprint Oil emphasize that **all subsequent proceedings** are rendered invalid【14†L120-L123】.  Accordingly, the impugned Notice and any downstream action are a nullity.  

## Prayer  
In view of the foregoing, K-Electric Limited respectfully prays that the Notice under section 177 (Tax Year 2019) and any proceedings emanating therefrom be declared null and void ab initio, and be set aside.  We trust that you will kindly rescind this notice and take note of the established law in Sprint Oil.  

Yours faithfully,  

**For K-Electric Limited**

# Reply to Section 177 Notice (Tax Year 2019)

## Introduction  
K-Electric Limited respectfully submits this reply to the Section 177 notice issued by the Large Taxpayers’ Office, Karachi, for Tax Year 2019. It is respectfully submitted that the selection of K-Electric for audit under Section 177 is procedurally defective for want of the mandatory Board approval under **Clause 105A of Part-IV, Second Schedule, Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**. Under Clause 105A, the Commissioner must obtain the Board’s prior written approval before initiating an audit under Section 177. In the present case no valid approval of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has been obtained in compliance with this requirement【4†L52-L60】【16†L85-L89】. Indeed, as the Appellate Tribunal held in *Sprint Oil & Gas Services* (ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025), the legislature has “with clear intent, mandated that the Commissioner directly seek approval from the Board”【8†L104-L110】. Any deviation from the Clause 105A procedure vitiates the entire audit process. 

## Background  
For Tax Year 2019, the Commissioner, Large Taxpayers’ Office, Karachi, sought the FBR’s approval to select K-Electric for audit. A correspondence from the Commissioner to the Board (dated ___202X) and the Board’s response (dated ___202X) are annexed hereto as **Annexure A**. The Board’s letter (Member, Inland Revenue (Operations)) ostensibly grants approval under Clause 105A (refer Annexure A). However, that approval was conveyed via the Chief Commissioner, LTO Karachi, and not directly to the Commissioner as the law requires. Thereafter, LTO Karachi issued the Section 177 notice (TY 2019) to K-Electric. This reply explains why that notice is without lawful authority.  

## Legal Provisions  
Clause 105A of Part IV of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 provides that no person shall be selected for audit under Section 177 unless the Commissioner first obtains prior written approval of the FBR specifying the person, tax year, and grounds for audit. The Federal Board is empowered under the FBR Act and rules to delegate powers, but such delegation must comply with legal mandates (Section 8, FBR Act, 2007). As recently affirmed by the Appellate Tribunal, these provisions impose a strict procedure: the Commissioner must **personally** seek and obtain Board approval for each audit. The Tribunal stressed that Clause 105A “requires the Commissioner to directly seek approval from the Board”【16†L85-L89】, and does *not* authorize processing the request through an intermediary.  

## Application to the Present Case  
In the present case, the Clause 105A requirement has not been complied with. Although Annexure A shows the Commissioner’s request and a Board response, the form of the approval is procedurally flawed. The Board’s letter is addressed to the **Chief Commissioner, LTO Karachi** (Annexure A), rather than directly to the Commissioner as mandated by Clause 105A. In *Sprint Oil*, the Tribunal pointed out this very defect: the impugned Board approval “was issued to the Chief Commissioner Inland Revenue…rather than to the Commissioner, as required by the aforementioned clause”【12†L233-L238】. This procedural irregularity parallels the present case. As in *Sprint Oil*, the approval in K-Electric’s case was communicated through the Chief Commissioner, adding an impermissible administrative layer. This violates Clause 105A’s clear mandate and creates an “administrative bottleneck” that the law did not intend【4†L52-L60】【12†L233-L238】.  

Furthermore, the Appellate Tribunal observed that the approval granted by the FBR Member under Clause 105A in *Sprint Oil* “is not in compliance with the law”【12†L178-L182】. By parity of reasoning, the purported approval in this case (see Annexure A) cannot cure the defect. In short, the Clause 105A approval procedure was neither properly sought nor properly granted. Consequently, the Section 177 notice issued to K-Electric is ultra vires: it rests on no valid statutory authority.  

## Reliance on Precedent  
This position is squarely supported by the recent ATIR decision in *Sprint Oil & Gas Services* (ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025) (Annexure B). The Tribunal’s operating findings are instructive: it held that Clause 105A’s requirement of “directly [seeking] approval from the Board” must be strictly followed【16†L85-L89】. The Tribunal noted that involving the Chief Commissioner “introduces an additional administrative layer” not sanctioned by law【4†L52-L60】. Citing these failures, the Tribunal conclusively ruled that the audit proceedings were invalid. It explicitly declared the impugned approval “not in compliance with the law”【12†L178-L182】 and the subsequent tax order “illegal, void ab initio, and without jurisdiction”【16†L85-L89】. In *Sprint Oil*, therefore, all actions taken under the flawed Clause 105A approval were quashed.  

K-Electric’s case is governed by the same principles. We respectfully submit that the Tribunal’s reasoning applies in identical fashion here. The Approval letter in Annexure A suffers from the precise defects identified in *Sprint Oil*. As a result, pursuant to the Tribunal’s holding, the Section 177 notice (and any resulting assessment or demand) is rendered null and void. We refer to the enclosed decision in *Sprint Oil & Gas Services* for further detail; key paragraphs have been extracted above with references【16†L85-L89】【12†L178-L182】.  

## Conclusion  
In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the Notice under Section 177 for Tax Year 2019 is untenable. K-Electric’s selection for audit was made without valid Board approval as required by Clause 105A. This deficiency is fatal: the Appellate Tribunal has made clear that any audit initiated without strict compliance with Clause 105A is ultra vires. Since the statutory procedure was not followed, the Notice (and any purported tax demand thereunder) is without lawful authority. The approval purportedly granted by the FBR is itself “not in compliance with the law”【12†L178-L182】, and the proceedings built upon it are “illegal, void ab initio, and without jurisdiction”【16†L85-L89】. In light of these authoritative pronouncements, the Notice must be set aside.  

## Prayer  
In light of the foregoing, K-Electric Limited most respectfully prays that:

---

**Conclusion**  

In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the Notice issued under Section 177 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, is legally unsustainable and void ab initio. The audit selection process, including the purported approval under Clause 105A, suffers from multiple incurable legal defects, each of which independently vitiates the proceedings. As conclusively determined by the Honorable Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue in the case of *M/s Sprint Oil & Gas Services* (ITA Nos. 1993/IB/2024 & 95/IB/2025), the approval granted by the Member (IR-Ops) was not in accordance with law; the so-called Board meeting conducted via circulation violated Section 3(7) of the FBR Act, 2007; no formal delegation under Section 8 read with Rule 3(1) of the FBR Rules was ever made; and the reliance on Rules 3(3) and 3(4) to circumvent statutory requirements was ultra vires the FBR Act. Consequently, the Tribunal declared that all subsequent actions, including assessment orders, were automatically rendered invalid.  
   
Applying the same binding principles to the present case, it follows that the Notice under Section 177 issued to our client is without lawful authority, and any proceedings emanating therefrom, including any future assessment under Section 121, are null and void. We, therefore, most respectfully request that the Notice under Section 177 for Tax Year 2019, along with any consequential proceedings, be withdrawn forthwith in the interest of justice and adherence to the rule of law.  

---

On April 16, 2025, well before the prescribed deadline for submission of the relevant records, UEPL duly filed a formal request seeking an extension of time until May 2, 2025. This request was made in good faith and in strict compliance with the Board’s established procedures. **Despite this pending request, the Board issued the SCN within the same month**, thereby effectively depriving UEPL of a fair and sufficient opportunity to respond and to furnish the requisite documentation before any adverse action could be taken.

We respectfully submit that the issuance of the SCN in these circumstances is **premature and unjustified** under the applicable legal framework. It is a well-established principle of natural justice that a taxpayer must be afforded a meaningful opportunity to comply before any penal measures are imposed. Issuing a Show Cause Notice while an extension request is still under consideration contravenes this fundamental tenet of due process. We humbly submit that such action is contrary to both the letter and spirit of the law and to established administrative practice.

Furthermore, we wish to highlight that UEPL’s record of compliance is exemplary. As noted above, we have consistently ranked among the top five withholding agents, and our financial and withholding tax records are subject to regular audit and scrutiny. At all times, UEPL has promptly submitted withholding tax returns and remitted payments as required. In light of this impeccable compliance history, the triggering of a penalty notice in the present scenario is unexpected and inequitable.

2nd Floor, Shaheen Complex, M. R. Kiyani Road

**Subject:**  Reply to Show Cause Notice No. SRB-COM-II/WHT/DC-24/2024-25/569305 dated April 9, 2025 (Alleged Non-Production of Records)

Respected Madam,

## Factual Background and Extension Request  
We refer to your Show Cause Notice dated April 9, 2025 (Ref. No. SRB-COM-II/WHT/DC-24/2024-25/569305) directing United Energy Pakistan Limited (UEPL) to furnish copies of the audited financial statements for the years ended December 31, 2023 and December 31, 2024 by April 16, 2025. In compliance with this notice and in light of the volume of records requested, we acted promptly. Specifically, our office submitted a formal request on April 16, 2025 — the prescribed deadline — seeking an extension of time until May 2, 2025 to furnish the demanded information. We emphasize that this request was made well before the deadline, underscoring our proactive approach and good faith in addressing your requirement.

## Violation of Natural Justice  
Despite our timely extension request, the Show Cause Notice was issued within the same month and a hearing has been scheduled for April 28, 2025. This compressed timeline leaves UEPL with no meaningful opportunity to prepare or present its case. Issuing the SCN on April 9 and requiring a reply within seven days — immediately followed by a hearing only a few weeks later — effectively deprives the taxpayer of reasonable time to respond.  Such a course of action falls short of the fundamental principles of natural justice, which mandate that a taxpayer be afforded adequate time to be heard and to comply with the notice.  In effect, the principle of *audi alteram partem* (the right to be heard) is compromised when a notice and hearing are scheduled in such close proximity, especially given that our extension request is still pending.

## UEPL’s Consistent Compliance Record  
It is pertinent to note that UEPL has maintained an exemplary record of compliance with all SRB regulations.  Our company has consistently provided requested information in a timely manner and has fully met its withholding and other tax obligations.  For several consecutive tax years, UEPL has been among the top five registered withholding agents of the Sindh Revenue Board.  This unblemished compliance history underscores our commitment to transparency and cooperation with the tax authorities.  We note that any delay in producing the specified records has been solely due to the diligence required to ensure accuracy and completeness, not any disregard for the Board’s directive.

## Premature and Unjustified Issuance of the SCN  
In light of the foregoing, we respectfully submit that the Show Cause Notice was issued prematurely and without sufficient justification.  The SCN contemplates the imposition of a penalty under Section 43 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 for an alleged contravention of Section 27 (production of records) read with the relevant withholding rules.  However, the imposition of any penalty for non-production of records should only be considered after affording the taxpayer a fair opportunity to comply.  Since UEPL has already sought additional time to provide the records in question, the imposition of a penalty at this juncture is unwarranted.

## Request for Relief and Continued Cooperation  
In view of the above, we respectfully request that the Show Cause Notice be withdrawn or held in abeyance pending the outcome of our extension request.  Granting the requested extension until May 2, 2025 will enable UEPL to gather and furnish the audited accounts as demanded in the notice.  We reiterate our commitment to full cooperation and assure you that the necessary documents will be submitted within the extended timeframe.  If the Board proceeds with the hearing as scheduled, we will attend to present our position and provide any clarifications. We reserve the right to appear in person or through our duly authorized representative at the hearing on April 28, 2025, should the matter proceed to that stage.

UEPL values its relationship with the Sindh Revenue Board and remains fully committed to compliance with all statutory obligations.  In light of our impeccable compliance history and the circumstances presented above, we trust that your office will reconsider the necessity of this SCN and grant the relief requested.  We look forward to a favorable resolution of this matter.

Thank you for your attention to this response.  We remain at your disposal for any further information or clarification.

Yours faithfully,

Syed Hasan Baqar Naqvi  
Senior Manager, Legal & Taxation  
United Energy Pakistan Limited  
17th Floor, The Sky Tower – East Wing, Dolmen City, Clifton, Karachi

# Tax Treatment of Royalty Waiver (McDonald’s & SIZA Foods)

Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (PIT Ordinance), the waiver of McDonald’s royalty receivable by SIZA Foods is treated as business income in 2024.  Since SIZA Foods is a company, it must account for business income on an accrual basis【25†L2232-L2234】.  The waived royalty (Rs 2.4 billion) represents a previously deductible expense that was never paid.  Section 34(5) of the Ordinance provides that if an expenditure deduction was allowed and the liability is not discharged within three years, “the unpaid amount of the liability shall be chargeable to tax under the head ‘Income from Business’”【12†L2278-L2284】.  In other words, the entire Rs 2.4 billion is included in SIZA’s 2024 business income.  (This is consistent with section 18(1)(a), which taxes “the profits and gains of any business”【23†L1591-L1594】.) 

### Offset Against 2024 Losses (Section 56)  
Once the royalty waiver is included as business income, the 2024 operating loss of Rs 1.5 billion can be set off against it.  Section 56(1) of the Ordinance allows a loss under any head to be offset against income under any other head for the same year【19†L2787-L2792】.  In practice, SIZA’s Rs 1.5 billion loss offsets Rs 1.5 billion of the royalty income, leaving a net taxable profit of Rs 915 million (as reported).  Thus, the reversal of prior-year royalties does not stand alone as a separate deduction; it is simply treated as income that is first absorbed by the current-year loss.  After this set-off, the remaining profit (Rs 915 million) is subject to tax for 2024.  

### Carry-Forward of Losses (Section 57)  
If any taxable profit remains after the current-year set-off, SIZA may then use its earlier carry-forward losses against that profit.  Section 57 of the Ordinance governs business loss carry-forward: any portion of a business loss not fully set off in its year of origin can be carried forward to offset future business income【21†L2807-L2814】.  In SIZA’s case, after offsetting the 2024 loss, the remaining Rs 915 million of income can be reduced by any available carry-forward losses from prior years (subject to the six-year carry-forward limit in section 57(2)【21†L2814-L2818】).  In other words, any profit remaining after absorbing the waiver and the 2024 loss will be eligible for further offset against SIZA’s unutilized losses (within the statutory limit).  

### Conclusion  
In summary, the Rs 2.4 billion royalty waiver is treated as business income in 2024 under sections 18 and 34.  That income is fully offset by the Rs 1.5 billion 2024 loss in accordance with section 56【19†L2787-L2792】, leaving Rs 915 million of taxable profit. Tax Treatment of Royalty Waiver (McDonald’s & Siza Foods)
The waived royalty of Rs 2.4 billion represents a previously deductible expense that was never paid. According to section 34(5) of the Ordinance provides that if an expenditure deduction was allowed and the liability is not discharged within three years, “the unpaid amount of the liability shall be chargeable to tax under the head ‘Income from Business’”. Consequently, it is also requested check whether the aforesaid were already offered for tax under section 34(5) of the Ordinance, if the aforesaid amount or part already been officer then residual amount should be included in the business income. This is consistent with section 18(1)(a), which taxes “the profits and gains of any business”. 
Once the royalty waiver is included as business income, the 2024 operating loss of Rs 1.5 billion can be set off against it. Section 56(1) of the Ordinance allows a loss under any head to be offset against income under any other head for the same year. In practice, Rs 1.5 billion loss offsets Rs 1.5 billion of the royalty income, leaving a net taxable profit of Rs 915 million as per understanding given to us. Thus, the reversal of prior-year royalties does not stand alone as a separate deduction; it is simply treated as income that is first absorbed by the current-year loss. After this set-off, the remaining profit Rs 915 million is subject to tax for 2024.
If any taxable profit remains after the current-year set-off, Siza Foods may then use its earlier carry-forward losses against that profit. Section 57 of the Ordinance governs business loss carry-forward: any portion of a business loss not fully set off in its year of origin can be carried forward to offset future business income. In SIZA’s case, after offsetting the 2024 loss, the remaining Rs 915 million of income can be reduced by any available carry-forward losses from prior years (subject to the six-year carry-forward limit in section 57(2). In other words, any profit remaining after absorbing the waiver and the 2024 loss will be eligible for further offset against Siza Foods’s unutilized losses (within the statutory limit).
Conclusion
In summary, the Rs 2.4 billion royalty waiver is treated as business income in 2024 under sections 18 and 34. That income is fully offset by the Rs 1.5 billion 2024 loss in accordance with section 56, leaving Rs 915 million of taxable profit. Any of this remaining profit may then be set off against prior-year carry-forward business losses under section 57 (subject to the six-year carry-forward rule. **Subject: Tax Treatment of Royalty Waiver - SIZA Foods (Tax Year 2024)**

Dear Iftikhar,

I hope you are doing well.

In response to your query regarding the tax treatment of the royalty waiver granted by McDonald’s Corporation to SIZA Foods, we would like to provide our views based on the provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 ("the Ordinance").

**Tax Treatment of Royalty Waiver**

The waived royalty amounting to Rs 2.4 billion represents a previously deductible expense that was never discharged. Under section 34(5) of the Ordinance, if an expenditure deduction has been claimed and the corresponding liability is not paid within three years, the unpaid liability is deemed to be income chargeable to tax under the head "Income from Business." 

Accordingly, it is advisable to confirm whether the aforesaid royalty liability or any portion thereof had already been offered for tax in prior years under section 34(5) of the Ordinance. In case any amount was previously taxed, only the residual portion should now be included as business income. This approach aligns with the provisions of section 18(1)(a) of the Ordinance, which subjects to tax the "profits and gains of any business."

Once the royalty waiver is included in business income for tax year 2024, the operating loss of Rs 1.5 billion incurred during the year can be set off against this income. Section 56(1) of the Ordinance permits a loss under any head to be set off against income under any other head for the same tax year. Practically, the Rs 1.5 billion loss would offset an equivalent amount of the royalty income, leaving a net taxable profit of Rs 915 million, as per the details shared.

Thus, the reversal of the prior years’ royalty does not qualify as a separate deduction; rather, it forms part of taxable business income and is absorbed first by the current year’s operational loss. The remaining profit of Rs 915 million becomes taxable for tax year 2024.

**Set-off Against Carry-Forward Losses**

If any taxable income remains after setting off current year losses, SIZA Foods may adjust such profit against its available brought forward business losses. Section 57 of the Ordinance governs the carry-forward of business losses, allowing unutilized losses to be adjusted against future business income, subject to the six-year limitation period prescribed under section 57(2).

Therefore, after absorbing the 2024 loss, the remaining profit of Rs 915 million can be further reduced by any available brought-forward losses, subject to compliance with the statutory time limit and conditions outlined in the Ordinance.

**Conclusion**

In summary, the royalty waiver of Rs 2.4 billion should be treated as business income in tax year 2024 under sections 18 and 34 of the Ordinance. This income will first be offset against the current year’s operating loss of Rs 1.5 billion under section 56, leaving a residual taxable profit of Rs 915 million. Subsequently, the remaining taxable income can be adjusted against any available carry-forward business losses in accordance with section 57, subject to the prescribed conditions.

# Advisory: Finance Act 2024 – Income Tax & SST Implications for OUP Pakistan

**To:** OUP Pakistan (Client)  
**Date:** April 28, 2025  

Dear Sir/Madam,

This advisory updates our prior guidance in light of the Sindh Finance Act, 2024 amendments.  Most importantly, Sections 4 and 5 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act (SST Act) have been revised, with significant impact on how employee services and reimbursed costs are taxed.  Key changes include:  

- **“Economic Activity” expanded (SST §4):** Only services by employees in a *direct* employer‐employee relationship remain excluded【18†L3202-L3208】【36†L515-L523】.  All other employee services (e.g. seconded staff, outsourced manpower) are now treated as taxable economic activity.  
- **“Consideration” broadened (SST §5):** The term “consideration” now expressly **includes reimbursable expenditures or costs** charged by a service provider【18†L3229-L3238】【36†L529-L537】.  In practice, pass-through costs (travel, salaries, etc.) that a vendor or affiliate bills are deemed part of the service fee for SST.  
- **Rate increase to 15%:** Note that the standard SST rate has been raised from 13% to **15%**【12†L3463-L3470】【28†L501-L504】, in line with other provinces.  
- **Judicial precedents superseded:**  Prior case law (IMS Health Pakistan, Sindh HC 2022 PTD 576 and related Supreme Court guidance) held that reimbursed employee costs and outsourced-salary recharges were *not* SST-taxable【18†L3222-L3226】【42†L748-L752】.  The new legislation directly contravenes that position. Going forward, the law requires SST on the full invoiced amount (services plus costs), regardless of those decisions. 

Below we explain each change, its effect on OUP’s IT service models (internal vs external), and our recommendations on withholding tax and sales tax compliance.  

## Extension of “Economic Activity” (SST §4)  
**Prior law:**  Under the SST Act, employee services to *their own employer* were excluded from taxable economic activity. This meant that when an employer paid its own staff, that payment lay outside the SST net.  

**Amendment:**  The Finance Act 2024 narrows this exclusion. Now **only** services by employees who have a **direct contractual relationship** with the employer are exempt【18†L3202-L3208】【36†L515-L523】.  In other words, if an employer “details” or “second[s]” an employee to work for someone else (including a related company or affiliate), those services are **taxable** as part of the employer’s economic activity【18†L3213-L3220】【36†L521-L527】.  Tax commentary confirms this change was intended to “enlarge the scope of economic activity for human resource service providers”【18†L3220-L3226】. 

- *Example:*  If OUP Pakistan’s employee provides IT support to OUP India or another affiliate (and OUP India pays OUP Pakistan back), that recharge is now within SST’s scope, unless the employee is on OUP Pakistan’s payroll under a direct contract. The entire amount billed (including salaries) is SST‑taxable.  
- *Internal IT services:*  Under our prior advice, such intra-group recharges might have been treated as non-taxable personnel costs. Now, **all intra-company billings for employee services** should be treated as taxable services (subject to SST at 15%)【18†L3202-L3208】【42†L741-L744】.  

## Definition of “Consideration” (SST §5)  
**Prior law and case law:**  Historically, SST was levied on the service *fee*, excluding any pure reimbursements (out-of-pocket expenses).  In IMS Health (2022 PTD 576) and a related Supreme Court ruling, courts held that reimbursed expenses (e.g. an employee’s travel, supplies, or salary costs paid on behalf of a client) did **not** constitute “consideration” for SST【18†L3222-L3226】【42†L748-L752】. 

**Amendment:**  The Finance Act now **codifies** that “consideration” includes *any reimbursable expenditure or cost* incurred and charged by the service provider【18†L3229-L3238】【36†L529-L537】.  In effect, the statutory definition of a taxable service’s value covers both the fee and any costs passed through.  Official commentary notes that, apart from prescribed exceptions, SST will apply to the gross amount (fee **plus** reimbursed costs) paid for the service【18†L3229-L3238】. 

- *Impact:*  OUP Pakistan must now treat reimbursements as part of the taxable base.  For example, if OUP Pakistan bills an affiliate for IT support and also recovers travel costs or third-party software charges, those reimbursements must be included in the SST calculation at 15%. The same applies to invoices from external vendors – any cost markup or pass-through items on the vendor’s invoice form part of the service value.  

## Implications for IT Services Invoicing  
These changes have immediate consequences for OUP’s IT service models:  

- **Internal IT services (intra-group):**  Under the “direct relationship” rule, any **secondment or outsourcing of personnel to affiliates or other parties** means SST now applies. For instance, if OUP Pakistan’s IT staff work for Oxford University Press (UK) or another affiliate, the recharged salaries and related costs are taxable.  OUP Pakistan should therefore **charge 15% SST on the full intra-company invoice** (service fee plus reimbursed expenses).  If OUP Pakistan is the *recipient* of such services from abroad, it must effectively “self-charge” SST on those imported services (including reimbursable costs) at 15%.  This is a reversal of earlier treatment.  

- **External IT services (third-party vendors):**  For local or foreign contractors, SST was already chargeable on fees. The amendment means that **any pass-through costs** on a vendor’s invoice must also be treated as SST-includable.  For example, if OUP Pakistan engages a Pakistani IT firm and reimburses its out-of-pocket costs, those reimbursements will now attract SST just like the vendor’s service fee.  If the vendor is foreign, OUP Pakistan must self-assess Sindh SST on the entire payment, including any costs billed, at 15%.  

- **Income Tax Withholding:**  Under the Income Tax Ordinance, OUP Pakistan must withhold tax on service payments to others (typically 15% to a nonresident service provider, subject to treaty relief, and various rates for resident contractors).  Because the SST amendments bring reimbursements into the service fee base, **the amount subject to withholding tax likewise increases**.  Absent guidance, it would be prudent to withhold on the full invoice amount (fee plus reimbursed costs) to avoid under-deduction.  For intra-group charges (e.g. payments to a UK affiliate), this means a higher withholding liability unless costs are invoiced separately.  

## Case Law vs. Amendments (IMS Health, etc.)  
Our prior advice relied on IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt) Ltd. v. Commissioner (Sindh) 2022 PTD 576 (and related appeals), which held that outsourced-employee salaries and pure cost-reimbursements fall outside SST.  These cases effectively limited “economic activity” to direct employment and excluded expenses from “consideration”【18†L3222-L3226】【42†L748-L752】.  The new law, however, **overrides** that approach:  

- The amended Section 4 now **treats detailed/engaged employees as economic activity** for the employer【18†L3213-L3220】【36†L521-L527】. This negates the IMS holding on outsourced manpower.  
- The amended Section 5 explicitly **adds reimbursements to consideration**【18†L3229-L3238】【36†L529-L537】. This nullifies the prior rule that expenses weren’t SST-able.  

In summary, while IMS Health (and a subsequent Supreme Court ruling favoring taxpayers【42†L733-L740】) governed SST treatment before July 2024, the Finance Act now dictates that all such charges are taxable going forward.  Until/unless courts strike down these amendments, OUP Pakistan must assume the new statutory definitions prevail.  

## Recommendations: Withholding Tax and SST Compliance  
Given these changes, we recommend the following actions:  

- **Revise Invoicing Practices:**  Ensure all intra-company and vendor invoices itemize services and reimbursed costs.  Explicitly apply 15% Sindh SST on the total amount (service fee + reimbursements) where required.  Update accounting templates so that every recharge includes SST on cost pass-throughs.  

- **Segregate Costs if Possible:**  To the extent costs can be billed or documented separately (with no mark-up), consider issuing separate invoices for pure reimbursements.  This can help substantiate the nature of those amounts and minimize SST confusion (even though the law treats them as taxable).  

- **Withholding on Full Amount:**  For payments to nonresident affiliates or vendors, withhold tax on the **gross service payment** including any reimbursed expenses.  (Without segregation, the entire invoice is “consideration”【18†L3229-L3238】.)  Confirm any applicable tax treaty rates to reduce double-taxation.  Locally, apply the standard WHT rates on the full billing as well.  

- **Review Contract Terms:**  Update service contracts with affiliates and vendors to reflect that reimbursements will attract SST.  For intra-group arrangements, consider whether a “direct contract” structure might still exempt certain services (limited to truly direct employees).  

- **Document Everything:**  Maintain clear records that reimbursed costs are bona fide expenses.  Even though SST is now applied, this documentation may be useful if disputing tax points or claiming input credits.  

- **Monitor Legal Developments:**  The amendments are expected to take effect from the July 2024 tax period.  It is possible that taxpayers or the courts may challenge the retroactive inclusion of reimbursements, but until such challenges succeed, compliance with the new law is the prudent approach.  

In conclusion, the Finance Act 2024 has significantly tightened SST on services and expenses.  OUP Pakistan should update its tax treatment of service recharges and cost recoveries accordingly.  Please contact us if you need assistance implementing these changes or for further interpretation of specific transactions.  

Sincerely,  

**[Tax Advisory Team]**  

**Sources:** Sindh Finance Act, 2024 (Sections 4–5); PwC and KPMG tax commentaries【18†L3202-L3208】【18†L3229-L3238】【36†L515-L523】【36†L529-L537】; EY tax alert (July 2024)【42†L733-L740】【42†L748-L756】; IMS Health Pakistan (2022 PTD 576).

Change in Law through Finance Act, 2024: 

SINDH SALES TAX ON SERVICES

EXTENDING THE SCOPE OF THE TERM ‘ECONOMIC ACTIVITY’
[Section 4]

Currently, the activities of an employee providing services in that capacity to an employer are excluded from the scope of the term ‘economic activity’. Now only those services of employee will be excluded from economic activity that are provided by employees with whom the employer is in ‘direct’ relationship under a contract of employment.

The Sindh Sales Tax on Services (Amendment) Act, 2021 amended the scope of "Economic Activity" to bring into ambit of Sindh Sales Tax such amounts received by the employees from their employers which are in the nature of ‘fee’ or ‘commission’. The Sindh Finance Act, 2024 (SFA) has further extended the scope of the term ‘economic activity’ to cover such activities of an employee, as detailed or engaged by the employer, that are performed for a person other than the employer in connection with or in the course or furtherance of business of the employer.

It appears that this amendment has aimed to enlarge the scope of economic activity for human resource 
service providers. This will, however, be viewed in the light of judgements of superior appellate fora wherein it is held that cost of employees, being of reimbursable nature, incurred and charged by such service provider cannot be held subject to SST.

DEFINING THE TERM ‘CONSIDERATION’ 
[Section 5]

In the context of ‘value of a taxable service’ for chargeability of SST, the FA 2024 has defined the terms ‘consideration’ and ‘consideration in money’ to mean the gross amount charged by the service provider for the taxable services including any amount that is payable for the services and, except in certain circumstances and subject to certain conditions, ‘consideration’ or ‘consideration in money’ has also included any amount of reimbursable expenditure or cost incurred by the service provider and charged in the course of provision of a service.

This amendment will be viewed in the light of judgements of higher appellate forum wherein it is held that reimbursable expenditure or cost incurred and charged by the service provider cannot be held subject to SST.

# Advisory: Sindh Sales Tax (SST) Amendments and Withholding – Finance Act 2024

## Executive Summary  
The Sindh Finance Act 2024 has significantly expanded the scope of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services (SST) Act.  Most notably, **Section 4** (definition of “economic activity”) has been widened to include services of an employee who, at the employer’s request, works for a third party in the course of the employer’s business【23†L3215-L3218】.  Equally important, **Section 5** (value of taxable services) now defines “consideration” broadly to include **all** amounts charged by the service provider – explicitly covering reimbursable expenditures or costs incurred in providing the service (subject to conditions)【23†L3230-L3238】.  In effect, expenses previously treated as outside SST must now be included in the taxable base unless specifically excluded by forthcoming rules. 

For OUP Pakistan, this means that **cost reimbursements** (e.g. travel, materials, or other out-of-pocket costs) which were historically carved out of SST will generally be treated as part of the service consideration and subject to SST at the new 15% rate【34†L3464-L3471】【23†L3230-L3238】.  This change runs counter to earlier case law (notably *IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd v. Commissioner-II, SRB* 2022 PTD 576), which held that pure reimbursed expenses were not part of taxable service value【28†L263-L268】.  Until detailed SRB rules are issued, we advise treating reimbursements as taxable.  Accordingly, invoices and internal charge models should be restructured to clearly separate fees from pass-through costs.  

On the income tax side, payments to foreign affiliates for IT services remain subject to 15% withholding tax on the fee component (plus any applicable surcharges)【30†L67-L70】. Reimbursements of actual costs can generally be excluded from WHT if documented separately, but if lumped together on an invoice they may inadvertently increase the tax base.  We recommend updating contracts and invoices so that **service fees** and **cost-reimbursements** are invoiced distinctly.  

**Key points:** Under the new law SST at 15% applies to the full invoice amount unless a reimbursement falls under a prescribed exemption【23†L3230-L3238】.  The traditional reliance on *IMS Health* (2022) is now limited, since that decision excluded reimbursements as non-taxable【28†L263-L268】.  Until SRB issues clarification, OUP should assume SST on expense pass-throughs.  Withholding tax on cross-border service fees remains 15% (subject to any treaty relief)【30†L67-L70】, so financial models must reflect the tax on the net service fee only.

## Amendments to the Sindh SST Act, 2011

### Section 4 – “Economic Activity” (expanded scope)  
Previously, “economic activity” under Section 4 of the SST Act excluded a service provided by an employee to their employer (i.e. routine employment services were not taxed).  The 2024 amendments tighten this exclusion.  Now **only** services rendered by an employee under a direct contract of employment to that employer are excluded【23†L3215-L3218】.  In practical terms, if OUP Pakistan “seconds” or details an employee to work for another party (even a related party) as part of OUP’s business, those services are deemed the employer’s economic activity and subject to SST.  The Finance Act inserts a proviso expressly stating that when an employee is detailed or engaged by the employer to perform activities *for a person other than the employer*, in connection with the employer’s business, those activities count as the employer’s economic activity【23†L3215-L3218】. 

*Implications:* If OUP Pakistan sends personnel to provide services to external parties (for example, an employee supporting a related publishing affiliate or a contractor at a client’s site), those services will now fall squarely within SST’s ambit.  OUP should review any such arrangements.  In many cases, the employee will be on OUP’s payroll, and the income remains in OUP’s accounts; under the amendment, the entire amount charged (even if collected from a third-party client) must be treated as OUP’s consideration for SST purposes.  We recommend verifying that OUP’s service contracts or intercompany agreements reflect this change.  If OUP has not been registering or charging SST on such seconded-employee services, this amendment could require registration and collection of SST going forward.

### Section 5 – “Consideration” (including reimbursements)  
Most critically, the Finance Act adds a detailed definition of **“consideration”** (and “consideration in money”) in Section 5.  The amended text makes it clear that the taxable value of a service is the *gross amount charged* for that service, and *includes* (i) any amount payable for the services and (ii) **any amount of reimbursable expenditure or cost** incurred by the service provider and charged to the customer, except where specifically exempted by rule【23†L3230-L3238】.  In other words, reimbursements that were previously treated as “passed-through” costs (not part of service value) are now expressly considered part of the service consideration, subject to any conditions prescribed. 

Concretely, this means OUP Pakistan *must assume* that all cost components invoiced to a recipient (travel costs, training materials, third-party charges, etc.) form part of the SST base.  SST at the standard rate (now 15%) should be applied on the **entire invoice** amount unless and until the SRB issues rules excluding certain reimbursements.  The law itself does not delineate those exceptions yet; it merely authorizes the SRB to prescribe “such circumstances and conditions” for treating some reimbursements differently【23†L3230-L3238】.  In practice, OUP cannot rely on any immunity for reimbursements without clear guidance. 

*Comparison with case law:* This amendment directly contradicts the jurisprudence of *IMS Health Pakistan* (Sindh High Court, 2022) and *Sami Pharmaceuticals* (2021).  In *IMS Health*, the High Court held that a business support services provider could “disintegrate” its invoices into service fees and pass-through costs, and only the net service fee (the actual consideration) was taxable【28†L263-L268】.  The Court noted that “Proviso to Section 5(1)(a) supports the disintegration of the invoice component i.e. service value and other value which is reimbursable”【28†L263-L268】, and cited *Sami Pharmaceuticals* to the effect that “only the value of service…is taxable and not the amount being reimbursed”【28†L263-L268】.  Under the current law, however, those reimbursements are now part of the “gross amount charged” and thus *prima facie* subject to SST【23†L3230-L3238】.  We anticipate that OUP cannot invoke *IMS Health* to exclude reimbursements; the statute now overrides that position.  (Until SRB issues clarifying rules, any persuasive weight of *IMS* is limited.  OUP should prepare to treat cost recoveries as SST-bearing income.)

## Impact on IT Services Invoicing and Cost-Recovery Models

The above changes affect how OUP structures both **internal** (intra-group or cost-sharing) and **external** (third-party) IT service arrangements:

- **Internal/Related-Party IT Services:** If OUP Pakistan obtains IT support from a related non-resident (e.g. OUP UK or another affiliate), it should segregate the charges into (a) the genuine service fee (e.g. license charges, technical support fees) and (b) reimbursed costs (e.g. travel, hardware, training expenses).  Under current practice, many inter-company IT arrangements bill a cost-recovery component.  Going forward, OUP must assume that *both* components will be treated as SST consideration if the provider is located in Sindh.  If the foreign affiliate invoices an all-in lump sum, OUP should treat the entire invoice as subject to SST – although in practice SST only applies to services rendered within Sindh (services imported from abroad might fall under FBR’s jurisdiction instead, see below).  Regardless, it will be important for accounting clarity to **break out expense reimbursements** on invoices.  That way, once the SRB prescribes any exemptions, OUP can more easily apply them.  

- **External IT Services (Pakistan-based providers):** If OUP pays an independent local IT vendor, that vendor will charge 15% SST on its invoice (because SST now covers reimbursements【23†L3230-L3238】).  OUP, as the recipient, does not “add” SST (that is the vendor’s obligation), but OUP should verify that reimbursements are listed on the vendor’s invoice and note that SST has been applied to the full amount.  If OUP pays any SST-registered vendor, it should also check whether OUP is a **withholding agent** under the Sindh SST rules (as amended on June 29, 2024【32†L12-L22】).  For example, certain sectors require the purchaser to withhold a portion of the vendor’s tax.  While the rules are complex, the safe practice is to withhold any SST that should have been collected – especially if the vendor’s invoice suggests reduced or zero tax on reimbursed elements.  (In the absence of a specific exemption, the presumption is that reimbursements are taxable consideration【23†L3230-L3238】.)

- **Export of Services:** If OUP Pakistan exports services (e.g. provides services to a client outside Sindh or outside Pakistan), those are generally outside Sindh’s levy.  In that case, the SST amendment is less relevant.  However, if OUP bills a foreign client and includes reimbursements, it should consider whether any Pakistan SST (provincial or federal) is triggered.  Under the SST Act, services used or consumed outside Sindh might not be taxable, but OUP should confirm the facts in each case.  For domestic transactions, treat reimbursements as taxable until told otherwise.

## Interaction with Case Law

**Previous Reliance on *IMS Health*:** Prior advice to OUP likely cited *IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Commissioner-II, SRB* (Sindh High Court, 2022 PTD 576) for the proposition that reimbursed expenses are not part of SST.  *IMS Health* emphasized that only the “value of the service” (the agreed consideration for the service) is taxed, whereas reimbursed costs could be excluded【28†L263-L268】.  In light of the 2024 amendments, that reliance must be adjusted.  The Finance Act has effectively nullified *IMS Health* on this point by statute: it now deems reimbursed costs to be part of “consideration” unless exempted.  In practical terms, OUP should not count on *IMS Health* to avoid SST on any invoiced reimbursement.  

**Future Outlook:** It is possible the SRB may issue regulations carving out some expenses (e.g. actual airfares, hotel costs) from SST, as is done in some other jurisdictions.  Indeed, KPMG’s analysis notes the new provision is “subject to such conditions as may be prescribed”【18†L531-L539】.  However, no such rules have been issued yet (as of this writing), and courts may rule on this change in due course.  We recommend tracking any SRB notifications on permissible exclusions.  In the meantime, OUP should assume reimbursements are SST-inclusive.  If SRB later exempts certain reimbursements, OUP may adjust retrospectively via amended returns (subject to limitation periods).

## Withholding Tax (Income Tax) Implications

Under the Income Tax Ordinance, payments for technical or consultancy services to non-residents are subject to withholding tax at 15%【30†L67-L70】.  This remains unchanged.  For example, if OUP Pakistan receives IT support (or pays for computer software development, training, etc.) from a parent company or foreign vendor with no Pakistan tax presence, OUP must withhold 15% (plus applicable education cess/surcharge) on the **service fee** portion of the payment【30†L67-L70】.  (If a tax treaty applies, the treaty rate may reduce this obligation, but in the absence of treaty relief OUP should apply 15%.)  It is crucial to distinguish the fee from reimbursed costs when calculating WHT: reimbursements (true out-of-pocket expenses) are generally not subject to income tax or withholding, since they are not “income” to the service provider.  Thus, if the invoice is itemized, with separate lines for service fee and travel/hotel cost, WHT should be applied only to the fee.  If the invoice is **lumped together**, we recommend revising the payment terms to avoid confusion.  

**Example:** OUP Pakistan pays $10,000 to an overseas affiliate for IT services and $2,000 reimbursement of expenses.  Only $10,000 is the fee subject to 15% WHT ($1,500 WHT).  The $2,000 reimbursement, if properly documented, would be passed on net.  If instead a single $12,000 invoice is issued, OUP might withhold $1,800 (15% of $12,000) unless it disaggregates the costs.  The revised SST law would treat the $2,000 as part of the SST base, but it is *not* income and should not be counted in the WHT calculation.  We advise structuring invoices to avoid over-withholding or tax disputes.

## SST Application on Service Fees and Reimbursements

For **services provided by OUP Pakistan** (e.g. training, publishing support, etc.), the SST Act (2011) as amended now requires SST at 15% on all charges, including costs.  If OUP issues an invoice for services (and passes through costs), SST should be applied on the gross amount – that is, the total of the service fee plus any reimbursed expenditures【23†L3230-L3238】.  For local services, the new standard rate of SST is 15%【34†L3464-L3471】, so the SST liability has risen from 13% (prior law) to 15%.  For any cross-charges to related parties within Sindh, SST should similarly be applied to the entire consideration.  

If OUP pays local service providers, it should verify that those vendors have correctly charged 15% SST on their invoices.  While normally the vendor remits SST, OUP should confirm that reimbursements on their bills are included in the tax base, consistent with the amendment.  Additionally, OUP should be aware of the Sindh SST withholding rules (Special Procedure Rules 2014).  Certain transactions (e.g. hiring contractors, service agents, etc.) require the purchaser to withhold a portion of the vendor’s SST and deposit it with the SRB.  The June 29, 2024 notifications have amended the definition of “withholding agent”【32†L12-L22】; OUP should assess whether it qualifies as a withholding agent for any services it procures and comply accordingly.

## Recommendations and Next Steps

1. **Invoice and Contract Review:** Amend OUP’s service contracts and invoicing templates to clearly separate **service fees** and **pass-through costs**.  Ensure every invoice line item is marked as either taxable fee or reimbursable cost.  This will help apply SST and WHT correctly and support any future tax challenges.  

2. **Apply SST to Full Invoice Amount (for now):** Treat all reimbursements as part of consideration subject to SST at 15%【23†L3230-L3238】.  Adjust accounting systems so that SST is calculated on the grand total of services plus recoveries, unless specific exemptions are later provided.  Keep detailed records of expenses in case an exemption is later claimed.  

3. **Withholding Tax Compliance:** For payments to foreign service providers, withhold income tax at 15% on the service fee component【30†L67-L70】.  Obtain tax residency certificates if seeking treaty relief.  Exclude expenses from WHT by contracting for separate reimbursement (and documenting actual costs).  

4. **Registration and Documentation:** If not already registered under the SST Act, ensure OUP is registered if it provides taxable services.  Maintain thorough documentation (invoices, contracts, expense receipts) to substantiate any distinction between fees and reimbursements.  

5. **Monitor SRB Notifications:** Watch for SRB Rules/Notifications implementing the “conditions” for excluding reimbursements.  If the SRB exempts certain costs (e.g. travel) in the rules, apply those going forward.  If no such rules appear, continue to assume reimbursements are taxable.  Consider seeking SRB guidance or clarifications if the tax liability is substantial.  

6. **Legal & Tax Strategy:** Given that the *IMS Health* precedent is effectively superseded, OUP should update its internal tax positions.  Any prior advice based on *IMS* should be reconsidered.  If a large volume of transactions is involved, conduct a gap analysis or a one-time calculation of SST on past reimbursements to estimate potential exposure (taking into account any statutory waiver or limitation periods).  

7. **Coordination with Group Entities:** Communicate these changes to OUP’s global affiliates.  Ensure that inter-company billing (especially for IT or shared services) aligns with the new Pakistani tax rules.  For example, if OUP UK charges OUP Pakistan for services, it should either separate expense items or confirm how they should be treated under Pakistan’s SST law.  

By taking these steps, OUP Pakistan can minimize risk and ensure compliance with the amended tax regime.  In summary, the Finance Act 2024 requires a more conservative approach: **charge SST on reimbursements and withhold tax on fees**.  Once the regulatory picture becomes clearer, OUP can fine-tune its practices. 

**Sources:** Amendments from Sindh Finance Act 2024 (Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011)【23†L3215-L3218】【23†L3230-L3238】; SST rate (2024 Finance Act)【34†L3464-L3471】; IMS Health (2022 PTD 576, SHC)【28†L263-L268】; Federal WHT rates (KPMG Pakistan)【30†L67-L70】.

**Subject: Advisory Note: Impact of Finance Act 2024 on Sindh Sales Tax and Income Tax Withholding**

Dear Atiq Sb,  

I hope this message finds you well.  

Further to your request, we have carefully reviewed the amendments introduced through the Sindh Finance Act, 2024, and have prepared a detailed advisory note analyzing their implications on Sindh Sales Tax (SST) and income tax withholding obligations for OUP Pakistan. A copy of the advisory note is attached herewith for your ready reference.  

The Finance Act 2024 introduces substantial changes to the Sindh Sales Tax regime, most notably through the expansion of the definition of “economic activity” under Section 4 and the redefinition of “consideration” under Section 5 of the SST Act. Under the revised provisions, the scope of taxable services has been materially broadened to include not only services rendered by an employee under secondment arrangements but also all reimbursed expenses associated with the provision of services, unless specifically excluded by future notifications or rules to be issued by the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB). This represents a significant shift from the previously established judicial position, particularly the Sindh High Court's ruling in IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt.) Limited (2022 PTD 576), which permitted exclusion of pure cost reimbursements from the taxable base.  

For OUP Pakistan, the practical consequence of these amendments is that any cost reimbursements, such as travel, training, or third-party charges, which were historically treated as non-taxable pass-through costs, must now be included in the taxable value of services for SST purposes. In the absence of specific exclusions notified by the SRB to date, the conservative and compliant approach would be to treat the full invoiced amount, inclusive of reimbursed expenses, as subject to SST at the newly prescribed standard rate of 15%. Furthermore, care must be taken in structuring future invoicing arrangements to separately disclose the service fee and reimbursable costs to ensure transparent tax treatment and to facilitate any future adjustments should exemptions later be announced by the SRB.  

In relation to income tax withholding, the withholding tax regime under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 remains largely unchanged, and payments for cross-border services continue to attract withholding tax at the rate of 15% on the service fee component, subject to any applicable treaty relief. It is important to emphasize that reimbursed costs should not be subject to income tax withholding, provided that such reimbursements are clearly identified and substantiated with appropriate documentation. Invoices combining service fees and reimbursements without clear disaggregation could inadvertently expose OUP Pakistan to withholding tax on the gross amount, thereby increasing the effective tax burden. Accordingly, it is recommended to ensure proper segregation of invoiced elements at the time of contracting and invoicing.  

We are also aware that some taxpayers have recently challenged the legislative amendment regarding the inclusion of reimbursed expenses within the definition of consideration for taxable services before the Sindh High Court. While the outcome of such proceedings remains pending, it is advisable that OUP Pakistan consult with its legal counsel to evaluate the merits of the pending challenges, assess the potential legal risks and opportunities, and determine whether a similar course of action would be appropriate given the specific nature and materiality of OUP Pakistan’s transactions. It would be prudent to understand the possible implications of any favorable or adverse rulings on the business’s tax position before finalizing a definitive strategy in this respect.  

Given the substantive impact of these legislative changes, it is crucial that OUP Pakistan revises its internal practices to ensure full compliance. This would involve reviewing and amending existing service agreements, revising invoicing templates to separately identify taxable service fees and reimbursed costs, applying SST at 15% on the full invoiced amount (including reimbursed expenses) until notified otherwise, and ensuring that withholding tax is correctly applied only to the taxable service fee component. Further, it would be prudent to closely monitor any future SRB notifications that may specify conditions or carve-outs for the exclusion of certain reimbursements from the scope of taxable consideration.  

We recommend that immediate steps be taken to review current intercompany and third-party arrangements, assess the tax implications under the revised law, and update the internal compliance framework accordingly. We also remain available to assist in implementing these changes, reviewing specific contracts, revising invoice templates, or conducting a broader compliance assessment to ensure that OUP Pakistan remains fully aligned with the amended legal requirements.  

Should you require any further clarification or wish to discuss the attached advisory note in detail, please do not hesitate to contact us. We would be pleased to extend our assistance in navigating the implications of these important changes.  

Best regards,  
Zuhair Ahmed Minhas  
Senior Manager – Tax & Legal Advisory (TLS)  
A.F. Ferguson & Co. (a member firm of PwC Network)
