Advisory: Sindh Sales Tax (SST) Amendments and Withholding – Finance Act 2024
Executive Summary
The Sindh Finance Act 2024 has significantly expanded the scope of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services (SST) Act. Most notably, Section 4 (definition of “economic activity”) has been widened to include services of an employee who, at the employer’s request, works for a third party in the course of the employer’s business. Equally important, Section 5 (value of taxable services) now defines “consideration” broadly to include all amounts charged by the service provider – explicitly covering reimbursable expenditures or costs incurred in providing the service (subject to conditions). In effect, expenses previously treated as outside SST must now be included in the taxable base unless specifically excluded by forthcoming rules.
For OUP Pakistan, this means that cost reimbursements (e.g. travel, materials, or other out-of-pocket costs) which were historically carved out of SST will generally be treated as part of the service consideration and subject to SST at the new 15% rate. This change runs counter to earlier case law (notably IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd v. Commissioner-II, SRB 2022 PTD 576), which held that pure reimbursed expenses were not part of taxable service value. Until detailed SRB rules are issued, we advise treating reimbursements as taxable. Accordingly, invoices and internal charge models should be restructured to clearly separate fees from pass-through costs.
On the income tax side, payments to foreign affiliates for IT services remain subject to 15% withholding tax on the fee component (plus any applicable surcharges). Reimbursements of actual costs can generally be excluded from WHT if documented separately, but if lumped together on an invoice they may inadvertently increase the tax base. We recommend updating contracts and invoices so that service fees and cost-reimbursements are invoiced distinctly.
Key points: Under the new law SST at 15% applies to the full invoice amount unless a reimbursement falls under a prescribed exemption. The traditional reliance on IMS Health (2022) is now limited, since that decision excluded reimbursements as non-taxable. Until SRB issues clarification, OUP should assume SST on expense pass-throughs. Withholding tax on cross-border service fees remains 15% (subject to any treaty relief), so financial models must reflect the tax on the net service fee only.
Amendments to the Sindh SST Act, 2011
Section 4 – “Economic Activity” (expanded scope)
Previously, “economic activity” under Section 4 of the SST Act excluded a service provided by an employee to their employer (i.e. routine employment services were not taxed). The 2024 amendments tighten this exclusion. Now only services rendered by an employee under a direct contract of employment to that employer are excluded. In practical terms, if OUP Pakistan “seconds” or details an employee to work for another party (even a related party) as part of OUP’s business, those services are deemed the employer’s economic activity and subject to SST. The Finance Act inserts a proviso expressly stating that when an employee is detailed or engaged by the employer to perform activities for a person other than the employer, in connection with the employer’s business, those activities count as the employer’s economic activity.
Implications: If OUP Pakistan sends personnel to provide services to external parties (for example, an employee supporting a related publishing affiliate or a contractor at a client’s site), those services will now fall squarely within SST’s ambit. OUP should review any such arrangements. In many cases, the employee will be on OUP’s payroll, and the income remains in OUP’s accounts; under the amendment, the entire amount charged (even if collected from a third-party client) must be treated as OUP’s consideration for SST purposes. We recommend verifying that OUP’s service contracts or intercompany agreements reflect this change. If OUP has not been registering or charging SST on such seconded-employee services, this amendment could require registration and collection of SST going forward.
Section 5 – “Consideration” (including reimbursements)
Most critically, the Finance Act adds a detailed definition of “consideration” (and “consideration in money”) in Section 5. The amended text makes it clear that the taxable value of a service is the gross amount charged for that service, and includes (i) any amount payable for the services and (ii) any amount of reimbursable expenditure or cost incurred by the service provider and charged to the customer, except where specifically exempted by rule. In other words, reimbursements that were previously treated as “passed-through” costs (not part of service value) are now expressly considered part of the service consideration, subject to any conditions prescribed.
Concretely, this means OUP Pakistan must assume that all cost components invoiced to a recipient (travel costs, training materials, third-party charges, etc.) form part of the SST base. SST at the standard rate (now 15%) should be applied on the entire invoice amount unless and until the SRB issues rules excluding certain reimbursements. The law itself does not delineate those exceptions yet; it merely authorizes the SRB to prescribe “such circumstances and conditions” for treating some reimbursements differently. In practice, OUP cannot rely on any immunity for reimbursements without clear guidance.
Comparison with case law: This amendment directly contradicts the jurisprudence of IMS Health Pakistan (Sindh High Court, 2022) and Sami Pharmaceuticals (2021). In IMS Health, the High Court held that a business support services provider could “disintegrate” its invoices into service fees and pass-through costs, and only the net service fee (the actual consideration) was taxable. The Court noted that “Proviso to Section 5(1)(a) supports the disintegration of the invoice component i.e. service value and other value which is reimbursable”, and cited Sami Pharmaceuticals to the effect that “only the value of service…is taxable and not the amount being reimbursed”. Under the current law, however, those reimbursements are now part of the “gross amount charged” and thus prima facie subject to SST. We anticipate that OUP cannot invoke IMS Health to exclude reimbursements; the statute now overrides that position. (Until SRB issues clarifying rules, any persuasive weight of IMS is limited. OUP should prepare to treat cost recoveries as SST-bearing income.)
Impact on IT Services Invoicing and Cost-Recovery Models
The above changes affect how OUP structures both internal (intra-group or cost-sharing) and external (third-party) IT service arrangements:
•	Internal/Related-Party IT Services: If OUP Pakistan obtains IT support from a related non-resident (e.g. OUP UK or another affiliate), it should segregate the charges into (a) the genuine service fee (e.g. license charges, technical support fees) and (b) reimbursed costs (e.g. travel, hardware, training expenses). Under current practice, many inter-company IT arrangements bill a cost-recovery component. Going forward, OUP must assume that both components will be treated as SST consideration if the provider is located in Sindh. If the foreign affiliate invoices an all-in lump sum, OUP should treat the entire invoice as subject to SST – although in practice SST only applies to services rendered within Sindh (services imported from abroad might fall under FBR’s jurisdiction instead, see below). Regardless, it will be important for accounting clarity to break out expense reimbursements on invoices. That way, once the SRB prescribes any exemptions, OUP can more easily apply them.
•	External IT Services (Pakistan-based providers): If OUP pays an independent local IT vendor, that vendor will charge 15% SST on its invoice (because SST now covers reimbursements. OUP, as the recipient, does not “add” SST (that is the vendor’s obligation), but OUP should verify that reimbursements are listed on the vendor’s invoice and note that SST has been applied to the full amount. If OUP pays any SST-registered vendor, it should also check whether OUP is a withholding agent under the Sindh SST rules (as amended on June 29, 2024. For example, certain sectors require the purchaser to withhold a portion of the vendor’s tax. While the rules are complex, the safe practice is to withhold any SST that should have been collected – especially if the vendor’s invoice suggests reduced or zero tax on reimbursed elements. (In the absence of a specific exemption, the presumption is that reimbursements are taxable consideration. 
•	Export of Services: If OUP Pakistan exports services (e.g. provides services to a client outside Sindh or outside Pakistan), those are generally outside Sindh’s levy. In that case, the SST amendment is less relevant. However, if OUP bills a foreign client and includes reimbursements, it should consider whether any Pakistan SST (provincial or federal) is triggered. Under the SST Act, services used or consumed outside Sindh might not be taxable, but OUP should confirm the facts in each case. For domestic transactions, treat reimbursements as taxable until told otherwise.
Interaction with Case Law
Previous Reliance on IMS Health: Prior advice to OUP likely cited IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Commissioner-II, SRB (Sindh High Court, 2022 PTD 576) for the proposition that reimbursed expenses are not part of SST. IMS Health emphasized that only the “value of the service” (the agreed consideration for the service) is taxed, whereas reimbursed costs could be excluded. In light of the 2024 amendments, that reliance must be adjusted. The Finance Act has effectively nullified IMS Health on this point by statute: it now deems reimbursed costs to be part of “consideration” unless exempted. In practical terms, OUP should not count on IMS Health to avoid SST on any invoiced reimbursement.
Future Outlook: It is possible the SRB may issue regulations carving out some expenses (e.g. actual airfares, hotel costs) from SST, as is done in some other jurisdictions. Indeed, KPMG’s analysis notes the new provision is “subject to such conditions as may be prescribed”. However, no such rules have been issued yet (as of this writing), and courts may rule on this change in due course. We recommend tracking any SRB notifications on permissible exclusions. In the meantime, OUP should assume reimbursements are SST-inclusive. If SRB later exempts certain reimbursements, OUP may adjust retrospectively via amended returns (subject to limitation periods).
Withholding Tax (Income Tax) Implications
Under the Income Tax Ordinance, payments for technical or consultancy services to non-residents are subject to withholding tax at 15%. This remains unchanged. For example, if OUP Pakistan receives IT support (or pays for computer software development, training, etc.) from a parent company or foreign vendor with no Pakistan tax presence, OUP must withhold 15% (plus applicable education cess/surcharge) on the service fee portion of the payment. (If a tax treaty applies, the treaty rate may reduce this obligation, but in the absence of treaty relief OUP should apply 15%.) It is crucial to distinguish the fee from reimbursed costs when calculating WHT: reimbursements (true out-of-pocket expenses) are generally not subject to income tax or withholding, since they are not “income” to the service provider. Thus, if the invoice is itemized, with separate lines for service fee and travel/hotel cost, WHT should be applied only to the fee. If the invoice is lumped together, we recommend revising the payment terms to avoid confusion.
Example: OUP Pakistan pays $10,000 to an overseas affiliate for IT services and $2,000 reimbursement of expenses. Only $10,000 is the fee subject to 15% WHT ($1,500 WHT). The $2,000 reimbursement, if properly documented, would be passed on net. If instead a single $12,000 invoice is issued, OUP might withhold $1,800 (15% of $12,000) unless it disaggregates the costs. The revised SST law would treat the $2,000 as part of the SST base, but it is not income and should not be counted in the WHT calculation. We advise structuring invoices to avoid over-withholding or tax disputes.
SST Application on Service Fees and Reimbursements
For services provided by OUP Pakistan (e.g. training, publishing support, etc.), the SST Act (2011) as amended now requires SST at 15% on all charges, including costs. If OUP issues an invoice for services (and passes through costs), SST should be applied on the gross amount – that is, the total of the service fee plus any reimbursed expenditures. For local services, the new standard rate of SST is 15% (, so the SST liability has risen from 13% (prior law) to 15%. For any cross-charges to related parties within Sindh, SST should similarly be applied to the entire consideration.
If OUP pays local service providers, it should verify that those vendors have correctly charged 15% SST on their invoices. While normally the vendor remits SST, OUP should confirm that reimbursements on their bills are included in the tax base, consistent with the amendment. Additionally, OUP should be aware of the Sindh SST withholding rules (Special Procedure Rules 2014). Certain transactions (e.g. hiring contractors, service agents, etc.) require the purchaser to withhold a portion of the vendor’s SST and deposit it with the SRB. The June 29, 2024 notifications have amended the definition of “withholding agent; OUP should assess whether it qualifies as a withholding agent for any services it procures and comply accordingly.
Recommendations and Next Steps
1.	Invoice and Contract Review: Amend OUP’s service contracts and invoicing templates to clearly separate service fees and pass-through costs. Ensure every invoice line item is marked as either taxable fee or reimbursable cost. This will help apply SST and WHT correctly and support any future tax challenges.
2.	Apply SST to Full Invoice Amount (for now): Treat all reimbursements as part of consideration subject to SST at 15%. Adjust accounting systems so that SST is calculated on the grand total of services plus recoveries, unless specific exemptions are later provided. Keep detailed records of expenses in case an exemption is later claimed.
3.	Withholding Tax Compliance: For payments to foreign service providers, withhold income tax at 15% on the service fee component. Obtain tax residency certificates if seeking treaty relief. Exclude expenses from WHT by contracting for separate reimbursement (and documenting actual costs).
4.	Registration and Documentation: If not already registered under the SST Act, ensure OUP is registered if it provides taxable services. Maintain thorough documentation (invoices, contracts, expense receipts) to substantiate any distinction between fees and reimbursements.
5.	Monitor SRB Notifications: Watch for SRB Rules/Notifications implementing the “conditions” for excluding reimbursements. If the SRB exempts certain costs (e.g. travel) in the rules, apply those going forward. If no such rules appear, continue to assume reimbursements are taxable. Consider seeking SRB guidance or clarifications if the tax liability is substantial.
6.	Legal & Tax Strategy: Given that the IMS Health precedent is effectively superseded, OUP should update its internal tax positions. Any prior advice based on IMS should be reconsidered. If a large volume of transactions is involved, conduct a gap analysis or a one-time calculation of SST on past reimbursements to estimate potential exposure (taking into account any statutory waiver or limitation periods).
7.	Coordination with Group Entities: Communicate these changes to OUP’s global affiliates. Ensure that inter-company billing (especially for IT or shared services) aligns with the new Pakistani tax rules. For example, if OUP UK charges OUP Pakistan for services, it should either separate expense items or confirm how they should be treated under Pakistan’s SST law.
By taking these steps, OUP Pakistan can minimize risk and ensure compliance with the amended tax regime. In summary, the Finance Act 2024 requires a more conservative approach: charge SST on reimbursements and withhold tax on fees. Once the regulatory picture becomes clearer, OUP can fine-tune its practices.

Under the revised provisions, the scope of taxable services has been materially broadened to include not only services rendered by an employee under secondment arrangements but also all reimbursed expenses associated with the provision of services, unless specifically excluded by future notifications or rules to be issued by the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB). This represents a significant shift from the previously established judicial position, particularly the Sindh High Court's ruling in IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt.) Limited (2022 PTD 576), which permitted exclusion of pure cost reimbursements from the taxable base.  

For OUP Pakistan, the practical consequence of these amendments is that any cost reimbursements, such as travel, training, or third-party charges, which were historically treated as non-taxable pass-through costs, must now be included in the taxable value of services for SST purposes. In the absence of specific exclusions notified by the SRB to date, the conservative and compliant approach would be to treat the full invoiced amount, inclusive of reimbursed expenses, as subject to SST at the newly prescribed standard rate of 15%. Furthermore, care must be taken in structuring future invoicing arrangements to separately disclose the service fee and reimbursable costs to ensure transparent tax treatment and to facilitate any future adjustments should exemptions later be announced by the SRB.  

In relation to income tax withholding, the withholding tax regime under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 remains largely unchanged, and payments for cross-border services continue to attract withholding tax at the rate of 15% on the service fee component, subject to any applicable treaty relief. It is important to emphasize that reimbursed costs should not be subject to income tax withholding, provided that such reimbursements are clearly identified and substantiated with appropriate documentation. Invoices combining service fees and reimbursements without clear disaggregation could inadvertently expose OUP Pakistan to withholding tax on the gross amount, thereby increasing the effective tax burden. Accordingly, it is recommended to ensure proper segregation of invoiced elements at the time of contracting and invoicing.  

Given the substantive impact of these legislative changes, it is crucial that OUP Pakistan revises its internal practices to ensure full compliance. This would involve reviewing and amending existing service agreements, revising invoicing templates to separately identify taxable service fees and reimbursed costs, applying SST at 15% on the full invoiced amount (including reimbursed expenses) until notified otherwise, and ensuring that withholding tax is correctly applied only to the taxable service fee component. Further, it would be prudent to closely monitor any future SRB notifications that may specify conditions or carve-outs for the exclusion of certain reimbursements from the scope of taxable consideration.  

We recommend that immediate steps be taken to review current intercompany and third-party arrangements, assess the tax implications under the revised law, and update the internal compliance framework accordingly. 2.	APPLICABILITY OF SECTION 4C FROM TAX YEAR 2023 ONWARDS

2.1	At the outset, we would like to inform you that it is respectfully submitted that the Honorable Sindh High Court, in its judgment dated February 15, 2023, in Constitutional Petition No. D-727 of 2023 (along with reliance on the earlier decision in Shell Pakistan Limited v. Federation of Pakistan & Others – C.P. No. D-5842 of 2022), has conclusively held that the levy of super tax under section 4C of the Ordinance, shall only be applicable from tax year 2023 and onwards. In unequivocal terms, the Court declared:

“Sections 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 is read to reflect that the levy shall be applicable from the tax year 2023.”
(emphasis is our)

2.2	This binding pronouncement clarifies that section 4C of the Ordinance cannot be enforced for tax year 2022. The Honorable Court based this conclusion on the principle that fiscal statutes imposing a tax must be construed prospectively unless expressly stated otherwise. Importantly, the Court found no legislative intent to retrospectively apply section 4C to tax year 2022, thus safeguarding taxpayers' vested rights and expectations for periods already closed.

2.3	Accordingly, any attempt by your good office to impose super tax under section 4C of the Ordinance in our client’s for tax year 2022 is contrary to the express ruling of the Honorable Sindh High Court, and therefore without lawful authority.

The said subsidy was claimed as exempt under Clause 102A of Part I of the Second Schedule. The amended order wrongly omitted this exemption and thus added the entire subsidy to taxable income.

3.2	In this respect, we would inform you that the amended order relies on a recent Sindh High Court judgment. # K-Electric Limited – Reply to Notice for Recovery of Super Tax (Section 4C) – Tax Year 2022  

**To:** Mr. Umair Malik, Assistant/Deputy Commissioner (IR), Zone VI – Range B – Unit 03, LTO Karachi  
**Subject:** Reply to Notice for Recovery of Super Tax under Section 4C for Tax Year 2022 – K-Electric Limited  

**Dear Mr. Malik,**

## Introduction  
We refer to your Notice dated 10-04-2025 (Subject: Payment of Super Tax on High Persons u/s 4C for TY2022)【3†L115-L123】. K-Electric duly filed its income tax return for the year ended 30-Jun-2022 (Tax Year 2022). The original return showed a substantial taxable loss, reflecting the Company’s actual financial results. However, the Commissioner issued an amended assessment u/s 122(5A) on 31-10-2024, which “amended [K-Electric’s] income… to Rs. 25,699,440,644/- before adjustment of brought forward losses”【3†L115-L123】. It was on this (erroneously increased) income base that the Notice was premised.  

## Facts of the Case  
In K-Electric’s original return for TY2022, a taxable loss of Rs. 161,010,650,356 was declared (and initially accepted by the department). The amended assessment, by contrast, treated K-Electric as having positive income of Rs. 25,699,440,644【3†L115-L123】. This change arose entirely because the assessment order disallowed the exemption on the Federal Tariff Differential Subsidy. The Tariff Differential Subsidy (a Federal grant to cover reduced tariffs) was claimed as exempt under **Clause 102A of Part I of the Second Schedule**. The amended order wrongly omitted this exemption and thus added the entire subsidy to taxable income.  

## Legal Error in Citing Sindh High Court Decision  
We note that the amended order relies on a recent Sindh High Court judgment. However, that SHC decision dealt *only* with whether tariff subsidies are includible in turnover for minimum tax (Section 113)【35†L68-L74】. It did **not** address Clause 102A or the exemption of the subsidy from tax. Nor did it overrule the long-standing exemption. In fact, the clause 102A exemption remains in full force: as KPMG observes, “Clause (102A) provid[es] exemption in respect of a subsidy granted by the Federal Government…”【31†L3133-L3141】. The Finance Act 2022 did not omit this exemption, so the Tariff Differential Subsidy is statutorily exempt from tax. Moreover, in prior years (e.g. TY2016 and TY2018–2021) the department itself allowed K-Electric to apply this subsidy exemption in the assessments. In light of these factors, denying the exemption in the TY2022 assessment is legally unsound. In particular, the SHC’s cited case did not pertain to Clause 102A, so reliance on that authority to override the exemption is misplaced. 

## Appeal Filed – Proceedings Should Be Abated  
For completeness, we note that K-Electric has filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR) on November 29, 2024 (DT No. 2073 of 2024) against the impugned assessment. Pursuant to long-standing practice, recovery proceedings under Section 4C should be held in abeyance while the appeal is pending. In any event, the Islamabad High Court’s recent ruling in *Fauji Fertilizer Co. Ltd. v. FBR* expressly held that Section 4C will **not** apply to tax years ending on or before 30 June 2022【41†L2079-L2081】. In practical terms, this means Super Tax cannot be levied on any “transactions or events past and closed on or before 30th June 2022”【41†L2079-L2081】. Because K-Electric’s tax year 2022 closed on 30 June 2022, Section 4C (as read down by the Court) has no application to it. Accordingly, the super tax Notice should be withdrawn outright, or at least stayed pending the outcome of the appeal. 

## Section 4C Computation Error  
The Notice’s computation takes the entire amended income of Rs. 25,699,440,644 as “Taxable Income as per 4C(2)(ii)” and imposes 4% super tax thereon【3†L133-L140】. This computation is fundamentally flawed. Under Section 4C(2)(ii), the “income” subject to super tax must allow all ordinary deductions that are available under the Income Tax Ordinance. The Islamabad High Court in *Fauji Fertilizer* explicitly held that Section 4C must be “read down” to allow deduction of all **brought-forward business losses and unabsorbed depreciation/amortization allowances**【41†L2071-L2078】. In other words, after including the subsidy but *before* levying super tax, K-Electric should be permitted to offset its carried-forward losses and depreciation/amortization (amounting to the originally filed loss of Rs. 161 billion). When those lawful deductions are applied, the remaining “total income for the purpose of 4C” becomes zero. Thus the entire income base of Rs. 25.699 billion is effectively eliminated by losses/depreciation, leaving **no balance subject to super tax**. In short, on a correct reading of the law and facts, the Super Tax computation collapses to zero liability【3†L133-L140】【41†L2071-L2078】. 

## Protective Grounds: Rectification Application  
As a protective measure (in case any doubt remains), K-Electric has already filed a rectification application under Section 221 of the Ordinance (dated 14-02-2025) to correct the obvious errors in the impugned order. That application highlights two key issues: (i) valid tax refunds of **Rs. 1,823,806,394** (under Section 170(4)) were wrongly omitted【45†L79-L82】, and (ii) K-Electric has an additional **withholding tax credit of Rs. 26,570,612** (the impugned order allowed only Rs. 192,652 instead of Rs. 26,763,264)【45†L56-L64】. If these corrections are made, any purported tax demand (including super tax) evaporates. We accordingly incorporate by reference the rectification filing and renew our request therein that the assessment be amended. 

## Prayer  
In view of the foregoing, we respectfully request that the Assistant Commissioner finalize that no Super Tax is due for TY2022 and **withdraw the super tax recovery proceedings under Section 4C**. We trust that our appeal (DT 2073/2024) and the legal issues raised will be given due consideration, and that the demand will be dropped as untenable. 

## Reliefs Requested  
1. Hold the Super Tax notice in abeyance pending the resolution of K-Electric’s appeal (DT 2073 of 2024).  
2. Recognize that Clause 102A exempts the Tariff Differential Subsidy, and rectify the assessment to allow that exemption.  
3. Recompute the income for Section 4C purposes by deducting all brought-forward losses, depreciation and amortization per the IHC’s *Fauji* judgment【41†L2071-L2078】.  
4. Confirm that, after these adjustments, no Super Tax is payable for TY2022 and discontinue/dismiss the recovery proceedings.  

We appreciate your attention to this matter and remain available to provide any further information.  

**Yours faithfully,**  

For **K-Electric Limited**  

Director – Taxation (Authorized Representative)  

Cc: Mr. Pervez Musani, Director Taxation, K-Electric Limited  

**Attachments:** Copy of relevant returns, amended order, and Section 221 rectification application.  

**Sources:** Applicable law and case law as cited above (further details available on request).

No. D-5842 of 2022), has conclusively held that **the levy of super tax under Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, shall only be applicable from Tax Year 2023 onwards**【30†source】. In unequivocal terms, the Court declared:  

> “Sections 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 is read to reflect that the levy shall be applicable from the tax year 2023.”【30†source】

This binding pronouncement clarifies that Section 4C cannot be enforced for Tax Year 2022. The Honorable Court based this conclusion on the principle that fiscal statutes imposing a tax must be construed prospectively unless expressly stated otherwise. Importantly, the Court found no legislative intent to retrospectively apply Section 4C to Tax Year 2022, thus safeguarding taxpayers' vested rights and expectations for periods already closed.  

Accordingly, any attempt by the department to impose super tax under Section 4C on K-Electric Limited for Tax Year 2022 is **contrary to the express ruling of the Honorable Sindh High Court**, and therefore without lawful authority. This provides an additional, independent ground for the withdrawal of the impugned notice issued for recovery of super tax for the said year.

---

It will make your final letter even more seamless and forceful.

parts:
# K-Electric Limited – Reply to Section 4C Notice (Tax Year 2022)

**Factual Background:**  In its 2022 income tax return K-Electric Limited declared a **taxable loss of Rs. 161,010,650,356**.  By an amended assessment u/s 122(5A) dated 31-10-2024, this was suddenly revised to a **taxable income of Rs. 25,699,440,644**.  The only change driving this massive swing was the **disallowance of the tariff differential subsidy amounting to Rs. 172,686,588,000**, which had been claimed exempt under Clause 102A of the First Schedule.  Notably, Clause 102A relief for the same tariff subsidy was consistently granted by the Department in prior years (Tax Years 2016 and 2018–2021).  The current disallowance thus flies in the face of both the statutory exemption and past departmental practice. 

**Erroneous Disallowance of Clause 102A Exemption:**  The tariff differential subsidy is expressly exempt under Clause 102A of the First Schedule to the Ordinance.  There is no lawful basis to deprive K-Electric of this exemption.  The assessment officer’s invocation of a purported Sindh High Court decision to justify the disallowance is unfounded – the cited judgment does not concern the Clause 102A exemption for tariff subsidies.  In short, denying the Rs. 172.686588 billion subsidy is legally unsupportable. 

**Inapplicability of Cited Sindh High Court Ruling:**  The Sindh High Court decision relied upon by the department is irrelevant to the exemption issue.  That decision did not address tariff differential subsidies or Clause 102A and therefore cannot override the clear wording of the statute or the consistent prior practice of allowing the exemption.  In the absence of any valid legal basis, the Clause 102A exemption must stand as claimed. 

**Appeal Before Appellate Tribunal:**  K-Electric has already filed an appeal (ATIR Reference DT-2073 dated 29-11-2024) against the impugned amended assessment.  In view of this pending appeal, it would be premature and improper to press recovery of any alleged tax until the appeal is adjudicated.  We therefore request that all recovery proceedings under Section 4C be kept in abeyance pending the outcome of the ATIR appeal. 

## Section 4C: Islamabad High Court’s *Fauji Fertilizer* Judgment

The Islamabad High Court in *Fauji Fertilizer Co. Ltd.* (W.P. 4027/2022) has squarely addressed the computation of **“income” under Section 4C**.  The IHC held that Section 4C (as introduced by Finance Act 2022) must be “read down” so as to exclude certain items from the super-tax base【4†L47-L54】.  In particular, the Court ruled that **all incomes taxed under the Final Tax Regime are to be excluded** and, importantly, any **brought-forward depreciation allowances, brought-forward business losses, and brought-forward amortization** must be “severed” from the income calculation【4†L47-L54】.  In the Court’s words:

> “[Section] 4C ... shall be read down in calculating the income taxable to super tax so as to: (a) exclude all classes of income ... the tax on which is final ...; and (b) sever the exclusions of brought forward depreciation, brought forward business losses, and brought forward amortization allowances available to the taxpayers under the other extant provisions of the Ordinance”【4†L47-L54】. 

This means that **when computing the chargeable income for Section 4C, one must deduct (and not include) any carried-forward losses, depreciation or amortization**.  Thus, despite the gross “income” figure shown in the amended assessment, the net income for Section 4C purposes must first be reduced by K-Electric’s accumulated losses and allowances. 

## No Super Tax Payable for K-Electric

Applying the above principle, K-Electric’s entire assessed income of Rs. 25.699 billion is more than absorbed by the pre-existing losses and amortizations carried forward from prior years.  After applying these deductions (which the *Fauji* judgment deems mandatory), the net income subject to super tax is effectively **zero**.  In practical terms, no “chargeable income” remains upon which Section 4C can operate.  Consequently, **no super tax is payable** by K-Electric for Tax Year 2022.  The shortfall of Rs. 1,027,977,626 shown in the notice simply does not arise once the brought-forward losses and allowances are properly accounted.  Any contrary calculation (as in the notice) contradicts the IHC’s ruling and the statutory scheme.

## Rectification Application and Additional Adjustments

Without prejudice to the above, we further note that K-Electric filed a rectification application under Section 221 (dated 14-02-2025) to correct clerical errors in the assessment.  This filing highlights additional tax credits and refund adjustments totaling **Rs. 1,823,806,394** (from under-credited withholding taxes and other refunds).  These additional amounts completely offset any tax that could have been claimed.  Even on the assessment’s own terms (ignoring the Section 4C issue), the rectified computation yields no outstanding liability.  In short, when all credits and adjustments are considered, there is no balance due. 

## Conclusion and Prayer

In light of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the demand for Super Tax under Section 4C is wholly unwarranted.  The exemption under Clause 102A was improperly denied, the cited Sindh High Court case is irrelevant, an appeal is pending, and the Islamabad High Court’s *Fauji Fertilizer* decision dictates that all carried-forward losses and allowances must be deducted from the 4C income【4†L47-L54】.  On these grounds (and considering the rectification adjustments), **no super tax is due from K-Electric**.  We therefore request that the recovery proceedings against K-Electric Limited be dropped forthwith.  

 

**[Authorized Signatory]**  
K-Electric Limited  

**Cc:** File; Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (for information)

**Subject: Response to Notice under Section 111(1) for Tax Year 2024**  

Dear Sir,  

I refer to the notice issued under Section 111(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, requiring an explanation regarding the foreign remittance of approximately Rs. 30,000,000 declared in my wealth statement for the Tax Year 2024.

At the outset, I would like to respectfully submit that I am a non-resident Pakistani, residing and employed in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for several years. During the relevant tax year, I transferred an aggregate amount of approximately Rs. 30,000,000 from my overseas personal bank account to my Roshan Digital Account (RDA) maintained in Pakistan with Meezan Bank Limited (Account No. 0104840517, IBAN: PK57MEZN0000250104840517, Digital Branch 0025).

It is emphasized that the foreign remittances represent personal savings accumulated from my lawful earnings abroad, and the remittances were made directly from my own foreign bank account to my own Pakistani bank account. These are purely inward transfers of existing foreign assets, without any element of taxable income, gain, or profit generated in Pakistan. Accordingly, the remittances are **outside the purview of taxable income under Pakistani law**, as they do not represent any Pakistan-source income or any accretion to wealth taxable within the country.

For your ready reference, I enclose herewith a **Foreign Remittance Certificate** issued by Meezan Bank Limited. The certificate endorses that the foreign remittances were duly received in my RDA during the period from July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024 under my name and CNIC, confirming the authenticity and source of the remitted funds.

In view of the foregoing factual position, it is respectfully submitted that the foreign remittances disclosed in my wealth statement are legitimate personal transfers of funds from abroad, duly supported by bank documentation, and fall entirely outside the scope of income chargeable to tax under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. There is thus no cause for addition or amendment to my tax return in this respect.

I trust the above explanation, along with the attached documentary evidence, addresses the concerns raised in your notice. It is, therefore, humbly requested that the proceedings initiated under Section 111(1) may be **dropped**, and no adverse inference may be drawn.

Should you require any further information or clarification, I remain available and committed to fully cooperating with your esteemed office.

Subject: Advisory on Deferral of Employee Payments for Non-Resident Employees

Dear Walid,

I hope you are doing well.

Further to our discussion, we understand that certain employees of UEP have been assigned overseas and, for the fiscal tax year July 2025 to June 2026, will qualify as non-residents under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 ("the Ordinance"). You have sought our advice regarding the possibility of deferring certain payments (such as Leave Encashment, Variable Pay Plan (VPP), etc.) until after July 2025 to align with their non-resident status and mitigate tax deduction.

In this regard, it is important to note that under Section 12 of the Ordinance, salary income is taxable on a cash basis, meaning, it becomes chargeable to tax at the time of actual receipt by the employee, irrespective of when it was earned or accrued. Therefore, in principle, if payments are deferred and made during the fiscal period of July 2025 to June 2026, when the employees are non-resident, the amounts should fall outside the scope of withholding tax, provided the employees continue to satisfy the non-residency criteria (i.e., remaining outside Pakistan for more than 183 days during the relevant tax year).

While deferral of payments to a period of non-residency aligns with the statutory framework, we must caution that Section 110 of the Ordinance grants the Commissioner the authority to re-characterize such deferred payments. Specifically, where it appears that salary payments relating to an earlier period have been deliberately postponed obtaining a tax advantage, the Commissioner may treat such payments as having been made, and taxable in the earlier tax year to which the services rendered pertain. In such an event, the income could be subjected to tax notwithstanding its later actual receipt.

To mitigate this risk, it is critical that employees (and UEP) can establish with plausible reasons that the payments relate to the period of non-residency, rather than being compensation for services rendered during their period of residency. Clear internal documentation linking the payments to services performed after their foreign assignment would strengthen this position. In the absence of a credible explanation, the Commissioner may seek to assess the amounts either in the earlier tax period or in the actual period to which the employment services relate.

In view of the above, while payment of salary is chargeable to tax on the cash basis, it must be carefully managed to avoid exposure under anti-avoidance provisions, where payment of salary is being deferred. We recommend maintaining appropriate documentation and communication with the employees to preserve the integrity of the intended tax treatment.

Hope the above comments serve your purpose. In case of any confusion, please do not hesitate to contact us

Best regards,

parts:
Certainly. Below is a more detailed and formal legal paragraph addressed to the tax department, incorporating references from the Islamabad High Court, Lahore High Court, and Sindh High Court on the non-retrospective applicability of super tax under section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001:

---

It is respectfully submitted that the levy of super tax under section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, as introduced through the Finance Act, 2022, is applicable only from tax year 2023 onwards and does not apply retrospectively to tax year 2022. This position is now conclusively settled by various High Courts across Pakistan. Most notably, the Hon’ble Islamabad High Court in its detailed judgment dated 30 June 2023 in Writ Petition No. 4027 of 2022 and connected matters, has categorically held that the retrospective application of section 4C to tax year 2022 violates the doctrine of past and closed transactions and infringes upon vested rights of taxpayers. The Court emphasized that the right of a taxpayer to retain earnings is a natural and fundamental right which cannot be curtailed by a retroactive tax unless expressly and unambiguously legislated. Given that section 4C was introduced on 1 July 2022—after the close of tax year 2022 on 30 June 2022—the Court held that any attempt to levy super tax for tax year 2022 was ultra vires and without lawful authority. The Court concluded that the provision would only apply prospectively from tax year 2023【6†IHC Super Tax Judgment】.

In a similar vein, the Hon’ble Sindh High Court in Constitutional Petition No. D-5842 of 2022 (Shell Pakistan Limited & Others v. Federation of Pakistan & Others), while deciding a batch of connected petitions, unequivocally held that the super tax under section 4C shall be read as applicable from tax year 2023 onwards. The Court noted that applying section 4C to income years that had already concluded before its enactment would be tantamount to retrospective taxation without express legislative intent, thereby violating the principle of legal certainty and fairness. This finding was subsequently upheld to the extent of interim relief by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, which allowed partial encashment of securities only to the extent of 4%, pending final adjudication【8†Sindh High Court】.

While the Hon’ble Lahore High Court initially took a contrary view in ICA No. 48745 of 2023 (decided on 16 May 2024), wherein the learned Single Judge upheld the retrospective application of section 4C to tax year 2022, this view now stands overridden by the binding and reasoned pronouncements of the Islamabad and Sindh High Courts. It may be further submitted that the Lahore High Court’s analysis did not sufficiently address the constitutional bar on retrospectively impairing vested rights or the doctrine of past and closed transactions, both of which were central to the judgments delivered by the other High Courts【7†20240516 LHC2738 No retrospectvie application】.

In view of the above authoritative pronouncements, it is respectfully requested that no demand of super tax under section 4C be raised for tax year 2022, as the provision is constitutionally and legally applicable only from tax year 2023 and onwards.

---

3.3 THE CONTEXT FOR SUPER TAX AND ENCROACHMENT OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS ............................................................. 20 
3.4 EX-ANTE CERTAINTY OF TAX ......................................................................................................................................................... 23 
3.5 WINDFALL PROFITS OF HIGH EARNING PERSONS ...................................................................................................................... 24

5 CONCLUSION AND ORDERS ....................................................................................................................................... 33 

  



 

 
Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 

-4- 

 

1 PREFACE  

1.1 THE PETITIONS 

1.1.1 The petitioners in the writ petitions listed in the Annex to this judgment are 

aggrieved by the levy of „super tax‟ imposed under § 4C of the Income Tax 

Ordinance 2001 (the Ordinance), and some of them have also received and 

impugned notices from the Commissioner demanding super tax.  There are 

grounds common to all petitioners, and there are grounds specific to some 

petitioners only. 

1.1.2 I cannot think of a better summation of the mood that pervaded the submissions 

of the learned counsels for the petitioners, with its grim pall hung over the court 

room, than the following sentence from Palkhiwala
1
: 

 …[A]s long there are absurd revenue targets, outrageous tax 
demands will continue. 

The revenue would have none of that, its submissions rooted in and sustained 

throughout by the appeal to that mantra-absolute, the supreme will of the 

Parliament, to impose taxes on anything under the sun it wishes to categorise as 

income, and on the precedents of three High Courts affirming that principle in 

the (almost) identical super tax levied earlier under § 4B of the Ordinance.   

1.1.3 There are but some differences between §4C and §4B, not just in the 

circumstances, but the Court was informed, also in the submissions that were 

being advanced before this Court that were not made in the cases heard under 

§4B, and this submission is borne out on a review of those 3 cases.  This will 

become clear during the course of this judgment.  

1.2 SECTION 4C 

1.2.1 Section 4C, inserted vide Finance Act 2022, expressed to become effective on 

01.07.2022, reads as follows: 

4C. Super tax on high earning persons.--(1) A super tax shall be 
imposed for tax year 2022 and onwards at the rates specified in 
Division IIB of Part I of the First Schedule, on income of every 
person: 

Provided that this section shall not apply to a banking company for 
tax year 2022. 

(2) For the purposes of this section, “income” shall be the sum of 
the following:-- 

(i) profit on debt, dividend, capital gains, brokerage and commission; 

(ii) taxable income (other than brought forward depreciation and 
brought forward business losses) under section 9 of the Ordinance, 
excluding amounts specified in clause (i); 

(iii) imputable income as defined in clause (28A) of section 2 
excluding amounts specified in clause (i); and 

                                              
1
 Kanga & Palkhivala‟s The Law and Practice of Income Tax, Eleventh Edition 



 

 
Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 

-5- 

 
(iv) income computed, other than brought forward depreciation, 
brought forward amortization and brought forward business losses 
under Fourth, Fifth and Seventh Schedules. 

(3) The tax payable under sub-section (1) shall be paid, collected and 
deposited on the date and in the manner as specified in sub-section 
(1) of section 137 and all provisions of Chapter X of the Ordinance 
shall apply. 

(4) Where the tax is not paid by a person liable to pay it, the 
Commissioner shall by an order in writing, determine the tax 
payable, and shall serve upon the person, a notice of demand 
specifying the tax payable and within the time specified under 
section 137 of the Ordinance. 

(5) Where the tax is not paid by a person liable to pay it, the 
Commissioner shall recover the tax payable under sub-section (1) 
and the provisions of Part IV, X, XI and XII of Chapter X and Part 
I of Chapter XI of the Ordinance shall, so far as may be, apply to 
the collection of tax as these apply to the collection of tax under the 
Ordinance. 

(6) The Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules 
for carrying out the purposes of this section. 

1.3 COMMON GROUNDS AND INDUSTRY SPECIFIC GROUNDS 

1.3.1 This judgment deals separately with grounds common to all petitioners and with 

grounds specific to certain industries, interleaved with the heading of 

fundamental rights.   

1.3.2 The submissions touching fundamental rights, though common to all, are not 

dealt with under the common grounds heading, but under a separate heading, 

due to the emphasis in counsels‟ submissions for these to be addressed so that 

they remain available explicitly for consideration by the Supreme Court in 

appeal.  The question of fundamental rights would not have been gone into due 

to the principle that Constitutional questions are not to be gone into if the lis can 

be disposed of on other points
2
, had it not been the case that some petitioners do 

not qualify for the industry specific additional grounds for the challenge to §4C.  

These grounds are therefore examined, and to the extent agreed with, their 

benefit cannot be withheld from the industry-specific petitioners who succeed on 

grounds specific to their industries.  The need to write this judgment with 

chapters specific to certain industries arose due to the grounds of challenge 

specific to those industries and not common with the other petitioners. 

2 COMMONS GROUNDS 

2.1 RETROSPECTIVE LEGISLATION TAKING AWAY VESTED RIGHTS 

2.1.1 Ms. Hamid, valiantly leading the respondents‟ case (though appearing for respondent 

no.3, the Commissioner Large Tax Payers‟ Unit), cited numerous judgments (the list it 

                                              
2
 LDA vs Imrana Tiwana (2015 SCMR 1739) 



 

 
Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 

-6- 

 

seemed would never end) for her submission that the Parliament can legislate 

retroactively
3
 to take away vested rights, a brief précis of which is given below: 

i. A statute is to be deemed to be retrospective, if it takes away 
or impairs any vested right acquired under existing laws, or 
creates a new obligation, or imposes a new duty, or attaches a 
new disability in respect of transactions or considerations 
already past and closed.4 

ii. It may be mentioned that by now, it is well-settled 
proposition of law obtaining in Pakistan that if an exemption 
from payment of excise duty or any other tax, has been 
granted for a specified period on certain conditions and if a 
person fulfills those conditions, he acquires a vested right … 
but he can be denied his vested right by a legislative 
provision, like section 31-A, which has been incorporated in 
the Customs Act in 1988. 5 

iii. …It is agreed on all hands that the well settled principles of 
interpretation of statutes are that vested rights cannot be 
taken away save by express words or necessary intendment… 
Therefore, vested rights can be taken away by such a 
legislation and it cannot be struck down on that ground…6 

iv. No doubt the Legislature is competent to give retrospective 
effect to an Act and can take away the vested right of the 
parties… while construing a legislation which has been given 
retrospective effect and interferes with the vested rights of 
the parties, the words used therein must be construed strictly 
and no case should be allowed to fall within the letter and 
spirit of Act which is not covered by the plain language of the 
legislation…7 

2.1.2 Paragraphs from several other judgments
8
 were also cited out of context lifting 

sentences out of those paragraphs as if they were statutory provisions on 

retrospectivity, but those paragraphs cannot be read out of the factual context 

before the respective courts, for the context determined the observations on 

                                              
3
 We‟d skip the finer distinction between retrospective and rectroactive legislation as it is not material for 

this judgment.  The two expressions are used interchangeably here. 
4
  Mehreen Zaibun Nisa versus Land Commissioner, Multan (PLD 1975 SC 397)  

5
 Messrs Army Welfare Sugar Mills Limited and others versus Federation of Pakistan and others (1992 

SCMR 1652) 
6
 Molasses Trading and Export Private Limited versus Federation of Pakistan and others (1993 SCMR 

1905) 
7  

Muhammad Hussain and others versus Muhammad and others (2000 SCMR 367) 
8
  i. Messrs Haider Automobile Limited versus Pakistan (PLD 1969 SC 623); 

ii. Zaman Cement Company Private Limited versus Central Board of Revenue and others 

(2002 SCMR 312); 

iii. Pakistan through Ministry of Finance Economic Affairs and another versus Fecto Belarus 

Tractors Limited (PLD 2002 SC 208); 

iv. Haji Dossa Limited Karachi versus Province of Punjab through Collector, Sahiwal and 

others (1973 SCMR 124); 

v. Sardar Sher Bahadur Khan and others versus Election Commission of Pakistan through 

Secretary, Election Commission, Islamabad and others (PLD 2018 SC 97); 

vi. Mst. Sarwar Jan and others versus Mukhtar Ahmad and others (PLD 2012 SC 217); 

vii. Zila Council Jehlum through District Coordination Officer versus Messrs Pakistan 

Tobacco Company Limited and others (PLD 2016 SC 398); 

viii. Government of Pakistan and another versus Messrs Mardan Industries Limited and 

another (1988 SCMR 410). 



 

 
Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 

-7- 

 

retrospectivity as applicable to those cases
9
.  And several of those judgments 

related to laws other than taxation.   

2.1.3 Parliament „taking away vested rights by retrospective legislation‟ implies that 

those rights vested in the first place by some legislative act, or by grant of an 

exemption (such as in Molasses
10

), or like legislative or executive act, by which 

non-existent rights were created and vested in the citizens.  This principle has no 

application where a natural right existed, not dependent on any beneficence of 

the legislature or the executive, that could be taken away, if at all, 

retrospectively.  The right of a citizen to earn and keep the fruits of its labour is 

an inherent natural and a fundamental right, that does not depend on any 

legislative or executive act.  This right is only subject to such laws on taxation 

by which the citizen pays a part of his earnings to the State by way of tax.   

When that right is curtailed by any legislation, it can only be prospective and 

never retroactive for not being a right vested by legislation in the first place. 

This critical distinction was entirely lost while citing all the judgments on the 

competence of the legislature to pass retroactive legislation taking away vested 

rights. 

2.2 PAST & CLOSED TRANSACTIONS 

2.2.1 Ms Hamid citing a copious number of citations for the Parliament‟s unfettered 

power to impose retrospective legislation by clear language was really quite 

unnecessary.  That rule was never in question by the petitioners as a primary 

premise to start with.  But that rule exists in parallel with, and does so without 

dissonance, with two exceptions, namely, that retrospective (or any) legislation 

cannot override fundamental rights, nor can override rights acquired under 

transactions past and closed or, preferably, rights acquired under „facts and 

events that have already occurred‟
11

.  It is quite pointless to ask that the former 

rule alone be applied, and its exceptions ignored.  The petitioners accept the rule, 

and rest their case on its exceptions.  It is therefore not necessary to visit any 

further the citations by Ms. Hamid affirming the rule.  Mr. Salman Akram Raja 

for the petitioners in several petitions summarized it well that the rule of past 

and closed transactions was unique to our jurisprudence, though Mr. Sukhera 

demonstrated later that it was not, and I add that this is a jurisprudential 

landmark to be proud of, and not, as Ms. Hamid would have us believe, to be 

apologetic about as if it were an inadvertent incongruity with the rule.  This 

exception to the rule was consciously laid down by the Supreme Court and then 

followed consistently.  Its coordinate principles in other jurisdictions are 

                                              
9
 A case is only an authority for what it actually decides and cannot be quoted for a proposition that may 

seem to follow logically from it: Trustees of Port of Karachi vs Muhammad Saleem (1994 SCMR 2213) 
10

 Molasses Trading and Export Private Limited versus Federation of Pakistan and others (1993 SCMR 

1905) 
11

 Province of East Pakistan vs Sharafatullah (PLD 1970 SC 514) 



 

 
Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 

-8- 

 

arbitrariness, unreasonableness, and unexpected liability
12

.  It is a good 

exception.  It must stay.  

2.2.2 Mr. Salman Akram Raja led the submissions on this ground, and his submissions 

were adopted largely by most of the other counsels.  Though Mr. Raja‟s 

submissions were confined to his clients‟ cases, who were allowed a special tax 

year under § 74 of the Ordinance ending on 31
st
 December, other learned 

counsels for the petitioners following normal tax years urged that the same 

principles applied for their clients also.   But given that Mr. Raja‟s petition for 

Fauji Foundation was the first one, and the rest followed suit, it is appropriate 

that his client‟s past and closed transactions be summarised to illustrate, for the 

other petitioners have argued closure of their respective tax affairs for their tax 

accounting years in similar fashion. 

2.2.3 He began by recounting that Fauji Foundation closed its tax accounts on 31
st
 

December 2021.  Super tax was levied on 01.07.2022 for the tax year 2022 and 

onwards, latching on to tax year 2022 for Fauji Foundation, which, for the 

purposes of chargeability of income to tax, closed on 31.12.2021.  Between 

31.12.2021 and 30.06.2022, several transactions were undertaken by his clients 

without super tax being visible on the horizon.  He challenged super tax for 

being charged on „events that had already occurred‟ or „transactions past and 

closed‟, and relied on Molasses to urge that super tax could not be levied for the 

tax year 2022 in any event.  He made these submissions without prejudice to his 

additional submissions that the levy of super tax was violative of the 

fundamental rights under Articles 18, 23 and 24 of the Constitution.  While 

responding to Ms. Hamid‟s stance of the complete freedom of the Parliament to 

impose taxation retroactively, he asked rhetorically, but quite pertinently, what 

would the Courts of this country do if this freedom of the Parliament was 

translated into legislating that Fauji Foundation would pay another tax on their 

income, say, for the year 2000?  He has a point.  

2.2.4 The facts and events already occurred were readily identified by him with 

reference to the audited financials.  He added that Fauji was under statutory 

obligations fastened by the Companies Act, 2017 to finalise its audited accounts 

and lay them for approval in an annual general meeting, which was duly done.  

He cited the following provisions of the Companies Act with reference to 

actions completed by Fauji: 

i) § 132 – the annual general meeting (AGM) was to be held 
no later than 30.04.2022; 

ii) § 134 – the audited accounts were to be laid before the 
AGM; 

iii) § 223, 225 – the financial statements were to be approved, 
with taxation to be expressly stated; 

                                              
12

 See Blodgett vs Holden, infra 



 

 
Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 

-9- 

 
iv) § 241 – as dividends could be paid only out of profits, the 

financial statements had to state the final profitability 
figure, which in turn depended materially on the post-tax 
profits and such reservations from profit for 
reinvestments that were finally locked in the audited 
financial statements approved in the AGM. 

Based on the finalised audited accounts, the company declared and paid 

dividends at 46.5% of post-tax profits, in the sum of Rs. 5.9 billion.  The 

payment of dividend and other financial commitments made these past and 

closed transactions.  If Fauji had known super tax to be payable, its profitability 

would have been lower with post-tax profits, and dividends would either not 

have been paid or would have been in a lesser sum.  He added that the taxation 

liability was a material item in Fauji‟s financial statements, with an immediate 

and direct impact on its share prices for being a listed company.  

2.2.5 Ms. Hamid, replied both orally and in writing that restatement of audited 

accounts was a normal business incident, and it was customary for taxpayers to 

restate their accounts for a number of reasons, including as a result of revised 

assessments, either on the tax payer‟s own volition, or as a result of amended 

assessments by the tax department.   

2.2.6 Mr. Raja responded by saying that para 7 of Ms. Hamid‟s reply resting on her 

submission noted above was based on a false analogy of reopening of 

assessments, for that entailed some error in arriving at the final tax liability, and 

never the question of chargeability to a new tax.  The reopening of assessments 

could be the result of a computational dispute, a dispute on the allowable 

expenses, exemptions, or the like, but never on the very question whether a new 

tax, not existent at the time the accounts were finalised, was chargeable.  He did 

not take issue with the broader proposition of Parliament‟s power to pass 

retrospective legislation, but only with its power to tax transactions past and 

closed.   

2.2.7 Other petitioners with a special tax year complained in a similar vein.  For 

instance, the trustees of Askari Bank Provident Fund approved and finalized 

their financial statements on 04.02.2022, disbursing circa Rs.508 million, and 

permanent withdrawals of circa Rs.82 million, with the remaining amounts 

credited to the accounts of 6330 employees of the bank.  These transactions, per 

Mr. Adnan Haider for the petitioner funds, were irreversible transactions 

undertaken on the basis of the funds‟ tax liability for the special tax year ending 

on 31.12.2021, in reliance on the exemption from tax that was valid and 

subsisting by the end of its special tax year, and therefore a matter past and 

closed, which could not be disturbed by retrospective application of super tax 

imposed on 01.07.2022.   



 

 
Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 

-10- 

 

2.2.8 Mr. Sukhera appearing for other petitioners cited Blodgett vs Holden
13

 to submit 

that the doctrine of past and closed transactions was not unique to Pakistan.   In 

Blodgett, the United States Supreme Court declared §319 of the Revenue Act 

1924 unconstitutional insofar as it levied a tax on transfer of property made prior 

to the date of enforcement of §319. The Revenue Act was passed on 2 June 1924 

and levied a tax on gifts made „during the calendar year 1924‟.  Blodgett 

challenged the exaction of tax on gifts made by him in January 1924.  The US 

Supreme Court set the following question for it to answer: “whether Congress 

had the power to impose a charge upon the donor because of gifts fully 

consummated before such provisions came before it?”  The law report records 

the per curiam opinion of 6 judges of the Court, with 5 concurring with the 

opinion of Mr. Justice Reynolds, who held as follows: 

As to the gifts which Blodgett made during January 1924, we think 
the challenged enactment is arbitrary and for that reason invalid.  It 
seems wholly unreasonable that one who, in entire faith and without the 
slightest premonition of such consequence, makes absolute 
disposition of his property by gifts should thereafter be required to 
pay a charge for so doing.  (emphasis supplied) 

Mr. Justice Holmes added his additional note, which, in material part, reads as 

follows: 

…I think it tolerably plain that the Act should be read as referring 
only to transactions taking place after it was passed, when to 
disregard the rule would be to impose unexpected liability that if 
known might have induced those concerned to avoid it and use their 
money in other ways. 

 

The US Supreme Court found retrospective taxation of consummated 

transactions „arbitrary‟ and „wholly unreasonable‟ for imposing an „unexpected 

liability‟ retrospectively, and therefore invalid under the due process doctrine in 

the American constitution.   

2.2.9 Before we find the answer to this controversy, we need to address the point in 

time when the liability to tax crystallises, for it is the pivotal question in terms of 

the doctrine of past and closed transactions for our purposes. 

2.3
The file is too long and its contents have been truncated.

ORDER SHEET 

IN THE HIGH COURT OF SINDH AT KARACHI 
CP D 5842 of 2022 

___________________________________________________________ 
DATE                      ORDER WITH SIGNATURE OF JUDGE 

___________________________________________________________ 

 
Disposed of matter 
 

1. For order on CMA No.5298/2023 
2. For order on CMA No.5299/2023 

 

24.02.2023  
 

Mr. Ovais Ali Shah & Mr. Ahmed Hussain Advocates for the 
petitioners 
Dr. Shahnawaz Memon, advocate for respondent  
Ms. Fozia Muhammad Murad advocate for respondent 

********** 

1. Urgent application is granted. 

2. Through this application the Commissioner, Inland Revenue, Large 

Tax Payer’s Officer (LTO) seeks discharge of sureties in favor of the 

department furnished before the Nazir of this Court pursuant to ad-interim 

orders passed by this Court. Learned counsel for Respondent places 

reliance on order dated 16.02.2023 passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court 

in C.P.3825 and 3909 of 2022, 126-K to 131-K, 167-K to 193-K of 2023 

(Federation of Pakistan through Chairman Federal Board of Revenue, 

Islamabad vs. Shell Pakistan Limited Karachi & others, and requests 

that in view of the above order, the sureties furnished in matters decided 

by a common judgment be discharged in favor of the Department 

accordingly. 

 Heard and perused the record. It appears that the tax-payers had 

challenged the provisions of Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 

2001, through which Super Tax was levied vide Finance Act, 2022, and by 

way of ad-interim orders passed on various dates in all petitions 

respectively, the amount of Super Tax as may be payable was secured 

before the Nazir of this Court. Thereafter all such petitions were clubbed 

and were decided together vide a common short order dated 22.12.2022 

followed by reasons / judgment dated 13.01.2023, whereby, the petitions 

were though allowed on certain terms; however, the said order / judgment 

was suspended for a period of 60 days. The said judgment was impugned 

in the above case and the Hon’ble Supreme Court has passed an order on 

16.02.2023 which reads as under: - 



CP D 5842 of 2022 

 

Page 2 of 3 
 

 

 
“Learned counsels for the petitioner have pointed out that the Tax Year 2022 for 
which the impugned Super Tax under Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 
2001 ("Ordinance") has been imposed starts from 01.07.2021 until 30.06.2022. In 
the present case, the respondents being high earning taxpayers with incomes 
greater or equal to Rs.300 million claim that they do not fall within the purview of 
Super Tax for two reasons. Firstly, because their accounting year ended on 
31.12.2021 prior to the close of Tax Year 2022 on 30.06.2022. Therefore, the 
impugned Super Tax was being demanded by the petitioner with retrospective 
effect. We are not persuaded by the arguments at this stage because according to 
the learned counsel for the petitioner, the accounting year of the respondents ends 
during the course of Tax Year 2022 to which the provisions of Section 4C 
are lawfully applicable.  
 
2. Pursuant to the second reason, it is held by the impugned judgment that 
the Super Tax is discriminatory. The rates of Super Tax under Section 4C ibid are 
specified in Division II B, Part I of the First Schedule to the Ordinance. However, 
the First Proviso to the Division II B charges income earners of more than Rs.300 
million falling within the category of certain specified industries to a higher rate of 
tax at 10%. Otherwise the rate of tax is 4% for such earners in other industries or 
businesses. The learned High Court has found in favour of the respondents on that 
score on the ground of discrimination. The learned counsel for the petitioner 
submits that the said argument cannot form the basis of altogether striking down 
the impugned Super Tax because implicitly the respondents' argument accepts 
liability to taxation at the rate of 4%. However, he is not able to explain to us the 
justification for charging super tax at a higher rate for industries specified in the 
first proviso. We grant him time to prepare his case on that point.  
 
3. Issue notice to the respondents in all petitions. The learned counsels for the 
respondents who are represented before the Court accept notice.  

4. Insofar as the interim relief is concerned, the as respondents which are liable to 
pay Super Tax at the rate of 10% under the proviso shall deposit the same within 
one week at the rate of 4% which is applicable to assessee industries earning 
income exceeding Rs.300 million provided in Division II B ibid but falling outside 
the proviso thereto. In the event that the respondents have furnished bank 
guarantees on the direction of the High Court then the same shall be en-cashed by 
the petitioner to the extent of 4% tax. Relist in the week commencing 13th March, 
2023”  

 From perusal of the aforesaid order, it appears that insofar as the 

tax-payers who do not fall within the first proviso to Division II-B of Part-I of 

the First Schedule (i.e. who are liable to pay 10% super tax) are 

concerned, have to pay and discharge their liability of Super Tax in full to 

be calculated as per table thereof (between 1% to 4%). To this, Mr. Ovais 

Ali Shah, who has affected appearance for some of the petitioners submits 

that it is not so; rather the order is only applicable to those persons who 

fall within the proviso, being liable to 10% Super Tax and not the rest. He 

has also argued that the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court is an interim 

order and not an order in rem, whereas, Para 1 of the order is not 

applicable to any of the cases as the judgment of this Court was not based 

on the grounds so recorded in the order. However, with respect, we do not 

agree as apparently all such tax-payers case has been discussed in the 

first Para as above, and they are required to pay Super Tax in full. 

Whereas, the tax-payers who fall within the Proviso ibid, and were 



CP D 5842 of 2022 

 

Page 3 of 3 
 

required to pay 10% Super Tax, are for the present purposes required to 

discharge their liability to the extent of 4%. Further this has to be done in 

respect of all tax-payers by way of encashment of securities in favor of the 

department to the extent of 4%. As to the same being an interim order, we 

may observe that matters were decided by way of a common judgment in 

the leading petition bearing CP No.5842 of 2022, whereas, the judgment 

was suspended and in the interregnum, department has approached the 

Hon’ble Supreme Court and to the extent of securities (all sorts) lying with 

the Nazir of this Court, it stands modified; hence, these objections are 

overruled.  

In view of the above facts and circumstances, this application is 

allowed by directing the Nazir of this Court to discharge all sureties 

furnished in the petitions as listed in the schedule to our order / judgment 

dated 22.12.2022 passed in CP D-5842 of 2022 and all connected matters 

to the extent of 1% to 4%, as the case may be, pertaining to Super Tax in 

favor of the respective respondents in all these petitions immediately. The 

concerned Commissioners / Respondents shall approach Nazir’s office for 

assistance and compliance. The application stands allowed / disposed of 

in the above terms. 

 

 

   J U D G E 
 

     J U D G E   

Amjad/PA

History of super tax: 

11. Ms. Asma Hamid, Advocate for FBR collated an 

executive summary of the brief history of super tax which 

may be set out below in order to lend actuality to the analysis: 

1. Tax on income in addition to income tax is 

commonly termed, inter alia, as “super tax”. Amongst the 

earliest enactments that introduced the levy of super tax in 

the Indian sub-continent was the Super Tax Act of 1917. 

Thereafter, the Legislative Council of India enacted the 

Super Tax Act of 1920 which repealed the Super Tax Act of 

1917. It may be noted that till this period, the impost of tax 

in addition to income tax (i.e., super tax) was being made 

through separate legislative enactments until the 

Legislative council of India, on the recommendations of 

All-Indian Income Tax Committee, consolidated income tax 

and tax in addition to income tax (ie., super tax) in the 

Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. Even though the Income Tax 

Act, 1922 dealt with both income tax and super tax, it still 

maintained the distinction and identities of the two 

categories of taxes, and designated a separate chapter for 

super tax, i.e., chapter IX of the Indian Income Tax Act, 

1922 which contained a distinct charging provision, and 



 ICA No.48745 of 2023 8 

 

specified the definition of income and the exemptions 

applicable with respect to the computation of super tax. In 

other words, Chapter IX of the Indian Income Tax Act, 

1922 was a self contained chapter dealing with the charge, 

assessment, collection, and recovery of super tax. It is also 

worth noting that even though the Indian Income Tax Act 

1922 defined super tax as tax in addition to income tax, it 

did not include the same within income tax; the legislature, 

in its wisdom, clearly kept the separate identity of super tax 

maintained.  

2. After its independence, the Islamic Republic of 

Pakistan adopted, as is, the Income Tax Act of 1922 as its 

code on direct taxation. However, from time to time, 

through parliamentary enactments and Ordinances, the 

charges levied, definitions, and computation and recovery 

methods were amended. Thereafter, the Income Tax Act of 

1992 was repealed by the Income Tax Ordinance 1979 

which, with respect to the levy of super tax, adopted a 

similar scheme and maintained the super tax’s distinct and 

self contained identity. Thereafter, the promulgation of the 

Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 repealed the Income Tax 

Ordinance, 1979. Super Tax was reintroduced in the 2001 

Ordinance through the Finance Act, 2015, by adding 

section 4B (super tax for rehabilitation of Temporarily 

Displaced Persons) that imposed a super tax on certain 

persons with retroactive effect on tax year 2015. It is 

important to note that in March 2011, a surcharge of 

income tax was initially added by section 4A through the 

Income Tax (Amendment) Ordinance 2011 dated 

16.03.2011 and then 30.05.2011 and finally omitted by 

Finance Act 2014. It was a tax that was an additional 

charge/amount in addition to the due income tax that 

increased the amount of income tax, however, it was not a 

distinct category of tax in the same nature as, super tax. It 

may be noted, however, that although the nomenclature is 

different, a surcharge or surtax has in common with super 

tax, the quality of being in addition to a charge of normal 

tax/increasing the amount of tax liability. It is pertinent to 

note the levy of surcharge by section 4A was challenged by 

petitioner who was a special tax year taxpayer on the 

ground that as its tax year 2011 had ended prior to the 

passing of the Ordinance through which the surcharge was 

levied, therefore it was not liable to pay. The Hon’ble Sindh 

High Court dismissed the petition, holding that a special 

tax year use did not in any way, entitle a taxpayer allowed 

to use the same, to evade tax; the judgment was assailed in 

the Hon’ble Supreme Court where it remained intact, hence 

attained finality. 

3. It must be noted that section 4B of the Income Tax

of Pakistan unanimously upheld its vires and the appeal
