# Tax Advisory on Mauritius Tax Implications for UEPL’s Branch Income

## 1. Mauritius Taxation of Branch Profits  
As a Mauritius tax resident (GBC-licensed) company, UEPL is generally taxable on its worldwide income【51†L24-L26】.  This means profits of the Pakistan and Iraq branches (as foreign permanent establishments) must be included in UEPL’s Mauritius tax base.  The standard corporate tax rate is 15% on chargeable income【51†L24-L26】.  However, under Mauritius’s revised tax regime effective from 2019, UEPL may qualify for an **80% partial exemption** on foreign‑source income if substance requirements are met.  Notably, “profit attributable to a permanent establishment which a resident company has in a foreign country” is expressly eligible for this 80% exemption【25†L378-L386】.  In practical terms, if UEPL claims this exemption on branch profits, 80% of those profits would be exempt and only 20% would be taxed at 15% (effectively a 3% rate on the full amount)【25†L378-L386】【23†L379-L387】.  (Certain conditions must be satisfied under Financial Services Commission guidelines to claim the exemption.) 

Alternatively, UEPL could choose *not* to claim the 80% exemption, in which case the full 15% Mauritius tax would apply to branch profits.  In that scenario, UEPL can instead utilize Mauritius’s foreign‑tax‑credit regime【30†L67-L72】.  As explained below, a foreign tax credit could offset much or all of the Mauritius tax on those foreign profits if higher foreign taxes have already been paid.

## 2. Foreign Tax Credits and Exemptions in Mauritius  
Mauritian tax law provides **unilateral foreign tax credits** for taxes paid on foreign income, subject to a limitation that the credit cannot exceed Mauritius tax on the same income【30†L67-L72】【21†L575-L583】.  In practice, UEPL can credit Pakistani or Iraqi taxes paid on branch profits against its Mauritius tax liability on that same income, up to the Mauritius tax amount【12†L1041-L1045】【30†L67-L72】.  For example, if Pakistan has already imposed 29–35% tax on branch profits, the full 15% Mauritius tax could be covered by that credit, potentially resulting in no net Mauritian tax (subject to documentation of the foreign tax).  Similarly, if Iraq taxed branch profits (Iraq’s corporate tax rate is around 15%), that tax can be credited against Mauritius tax up to the same limit.

**Important:** UEPL cannot simultaneously claim both the 80% exemption and a foreign tax credit on the same income【30†L67-L72】.  If the 80% exemption is applied to the branch profits (as foreign PE income), Mauritius disallows any credit for foreign tax on that exempted portion【30†L67-L72】.  Thus, UEPL must elect between the exemption regime or the credit regime for each class of income.  In the credits scenario, UEPL would report the full foreign income and claim credit for Pakistani/Iraqi taxes paid【30†L67-L72】.  In the exemption scenario, UEPL reports the foreign income but only pays 3% effective tax (20% of profits at 15%), and no credit is claimed on that income【30†L67-L72】.

## 3. Double‑Taxation Relief under DTAAs  

**Mauritius–Pakistan DTAA:** A comprehensive tax treaty exists between Mauritius and Pakistan (effective 1994, as modified by the MLI) that addresses double taxation of income.  Under Article 7, profits of a Mauritius enterprise are taxable only in Mauritius unless it carries on business in Pakistan through a permanent establishment; in that case Pakistan may tax only the profit attributable to the Pakistan PE【32†L415-L423】.  In UEPL’s case, the Pakistan branch (PE) profits can be taxed in Pakistan, while any remaining UEPL profits not attributable to that branch would be taxed only in Mauritius.  

For relief, Article 23 provides that Mauritius shall give credit for Pakistan tax: **“where a resident of Mauritius derives income from Pakistan, the amount of tax on that income payable in Pakistan … shall be allowed as a credit against the Mauritius tax imposed on that resident”**, limited to the Mauritius tax on that income【12†L1041-L1045】.  (In simpler terms, Mauritius will mitigate double taxation by allowing UEPL to offset Pakistani tax paid on the branch income against its Mauritius tax on that same income, up to 15%.)  This mirrors the domestic credit rule discussed above but is grounded in the DTAA.

The DTAA also limits withholding taxes on remittances from Pakistan to Mauritius.  For instance, dividends paid by a Pakistani company to UEPL (Mauritius resident) are subject to a maximum 10% withholding (if UEPL is beneficial owner)【38†L574-L581】.  Interest and royalties from Pakistan to UEPL are similarly capped at 10% and 12.5%, respectively【54†L629-L636】【40†L699-L706】.  (These reduced rates apply in lieu of Pakistan’s domestic withholding rates.)  These provisions reduce source‑country tax on passive incomes so that Mauritius’s credit or exemption mechanism can more fully offset the lower treaty tax.

**Mauritius–Iraq:** There is no tax treaty between Mauritius and Iraq (the Mauritius Revenue Authority’s treaty list does not include Iraq).  Therefore, UEPL cannot obtain treaty relief for income from the Iraq branch.  Iraqi branch profits and any Iraqi withholding taxes (if applicable) must be relieved under Mauritius’s domestic law only.  In practice, UEPL would treat Iraqi taxes paid as foreign taxes eligible for the unilateral foreign tax credit in Mauritius【30†L67-L72】.  Any standard Iraqi branch taxation (corporate income tax, withholding, etc.) remains fully creditable against Mauritius tax (subject to the usual limitation).  No DTAA exemption or reduced rate is available in the Iraq case.

## 4. Penalties, Interest and Other Consequences of Amending Returns  
If UEPL amends past Mauritius returns to include previously omitted branch income, several late‑filing and late‑payment sanctions can apply.  Per MRA guidelines, an amended return is deemed to be “submitted” on its actual submission date, and the company will owe late‑filing penalties from the original due date onward【44†L87-L94】.  Specifically, Mauritius imposes a penalty of MUR 2,000 per month (or part-month) of delay, up to MUR 20,000 per return【44†L87-L94】【45†L40-L47】.  In addition, any additional tax arising on the amended return must be paid with a **late-payment penalty of 5% of the tax due** plus interest at 0.5% per month on the unpaid tax【45†L50-L58】.  In summary, UEPL should anticipate: 

- **Late-filing penalty:** MUR 2,000 per month (max MUR 20,000) on each amended return beyond its due date【44†L87-L94】【45†L40-L47】.  
- **Late-payment penalty:** 5% of the additional tax owed on the amended return【45†L50-L58】.  
- **Interest:** 0.5% per month on the unpaid tax balance until paid【45†L50-L58】.  

These charges can add material cost to the tax adjustment.  (For reference, amended returns for tax years up to 2019–20 can still be filed under current MRA e‑filing rules【44†L98-L101】.)  On the upside, Mauritius has recently reintroduced a **Tax Arrears Settlement Scheme (TASS)**: if UEPL registers by 31 Dec 2024 and pays any revised tax liability by 31 Mar 2025, penalties and interest on outstanding income tax may be waived entirely【48†L584-L592】.  Participation in TASS could eliminate these additional levies on the amended returns, provided UEPL meets the filing and payment deadlines.  

Aside from financial charges, submitting amended returns may increase the chance of an MRA audit (the MRA notes that amending returns can trigger review, albeit not automatically【44†L98-L104】). UEPL should ensure that all required documentation (branch accounts, tax assessments, intercompany agreements, etc.) is in order to substantiate the amended figures.

## Proposed Timeline  
We suggest the following timetable to deliver comprehensive advice:  

- **Week 1:** Kick-off meeting and data collection. Obtain relevant documents (financials, tax filings, branch details).  
- **Weeks 2–3:** Legal and technical analysis. Review Mauritius tax law (Income Tax Act, GBC regime) and DTA provisions; analyze Pakistan and Iraq tax treatment; compute illustrative tax outcomes.  
- **Week 4:** Drafting and review. Prepare the advisory report and meet internally for quality check; finalize and deliver written advice to UEPL.  

This schedule assumes prompt delivery of required information.  Revisions or additional client questions may extend the timeline modestly.

## Fee Estimate  
We estimate that this engagement will require approximately 30–40 professional hours of mixed seniority (tax partner, senior manager, and associate time), including research, analysis, and report drafting.  Based on our standard rates, we propose a fixed fee of **MUR 300,000 (approximately USD 7,500)** for the project.  This fee covers all work described above.  (Travel or extraordinary disbursements, if any, would be billed separately.)  We would bill upon engagement and deliverables as agreed.  

## Information & Documentation Required  
To perform our analysis and draft the advice, we will need the following materials from UEPL:  

- **Mauritius tax returns and financial statements** for the years in question (including any FSC‐mandated GBC filings).  
- **Pakistan branch financial statements and tax filings**, showing profit calculations and taxes paid (including any withholding tax certificates or assessments).  
- **Iraq branch financial statements and tax filings**, with details of profits and taxes (and any basis of taxation under Iraqi law).  
- **Details of foreign taxes paid or withheld**, including copies of payment vouchers, assessments, or withholding tax certificates from Pakistan and Iraq.  
- **Corporate documentation**, including UEPL’s Certificate of Incorporation, Financial Services Commission (GBC) license or authorization, and Fiscal Tax Residence Certificate if held.  
- **Legal structure and agreements**, such as branch establishment agreements or intercompany service agreements, to confirm the nature of branch operations.  
- **Any prior tax correspondence** with MRA or the Pakistan/Iraq tax authorities relating to these branches.  

Having complete information will ensure our advice is accurate and tailored to UEPL’s circumstances.  We appreciate the opportunity to assist UEPL and look forward to guiding you through the Mauritius tax implications of including your Pakistan and Iraq branch incomes.  

**Sources:** Mauritius tax residency rules and income determination【51†L24-L26】; Mauritius partial exemption regime【25†L378-L386】; Mauritius foreign tax credit rules【30†L67-L72】; Mauritius–Pakistan DTAA (Business Profits and Double Taxation Relief articles)【32†L415-L423】【12†L1041-L1045】; DTAA withholding tax provisions【38†L574-L581】【54†L629-L636】【40†L699-L706】; Mauritius Amendment of Return rules【44†L87-L94】; Mauritius penalty & interest rules【45†L40-L47】【45†L50-L58】; Mauritius Budget 2024 (TASS waiver)【48†L584-L592】.

# Tax Analysis for UEPL Branch Income (Pakistan & Iraq)

Dear Mr. Walid,

Thank you for your inquiries. Below please find our analysis of the Mauritian tax treatment of UEPL’s branch profits and related issues. We address each of your points in turn.

## Income Tax Exposure in Mauritius  
- **Mauritian taxation:** As a Mauritius resident GBC (GBL) company, UEPL is subject to tax on its worldwide income at a flat 15% rate【22†L376-L384】.  Any profits from branches in Pakistan or Iraq are foreign‐source income in Mauritius.  Thus, if these profits are declared, Mauritius would initially tax them at 15% of net profit.  
- **80% partial exemption:** However, Mauritius law provides an **80% exemption** on the profits attributable to a foreign permanent establishment of a resident company (subject to the Mauritian substance requirements)【30†L378-L385】【24†L378-L385】.  In practice this means only 20% of the branch profit is taxed at 15% (effective tax 3%).  This exemption only applies if UEPL meets the FSC’s substance conditions【24†L378-L385】.  If UEPL does not meet those conditions, the full 15% tax would apply to the entire branch profit.  

## Foreign Tax Credits and Exemptions (Pakistan & Iraq)  
- **General credit rule:** Mauritius generally allows a credit for foreign income tax paid on foreign-source income【34†L573-L582】.  Under Mauritian law, foreign tax credits are capped at the Mauritian tax attributable to that income, and any excess credit is forfeited【34†L573-L582】.  
- **Pakistan taxes:**  If Pakistan levies tax on the branch profits (for example, branch profits tax or corporate tax on repatriated profits), those taxes may be credited in Mauritius.  Specifically, the Mauritius–Pakistan DTAA (Article 23) provides that Pakistan tax on UEPL’s Pakistan income can be credited against UEPL’s Mauritius tax on the same income【19†L842-L850】.  In other words, UEPL can offset Pakistani tax paid against its Mauritian liability (subject to the credit cap)【19†L842-L850】【34†L573-L582】.  
- **Iraq taxes:**  There is no Mauritius–Iraq tax treaty. In the absence of a treaty, Mauritius would allow a unilateral foreign tax credit for Iraqi taxes paid (again up to the Mauritian tax on that income)【34†L573-L582】.  This means any Iraqi withholding or branch tax could potentially be credited against Mauritius tax on the branch profit, but only to the extent of the Mauritius tax due on that profit.  
- **80% exemption interplay:**  One important caveat is that if UEPL opts to claim the 80% exemption on the branch profits, those profits are largely exempt from Mauritius tax.  In that case, no foreign tax credit is available on the exempt portion【41†L424-L426】.  In practice, UEPL should choose the most advantageous approach (credit vs. exemption) based on the relative tax burdens in Pakistan/Iraq and Mauritius.

## Treaty Relief (Mauritius–Pakistan; no Iraq DTAA)  
- **Mauritius–Pakistan DTAA:** Article 7 of the Mauritius–Pakistan DTAA confirms that business profits of a Mauritian enterprise are taxable only in Mauritius *unless* it carries on business through a Pakistani permanent establishment【17†L318-L326】.  Since UEPL’s branch in Pakistan qualifies as a PE, Article 7 allows Pakistan to tax the profits of that PE【17†L318-L326】.  Article 23 of the Treaty then requires Mauritius to relieve double taxation by granting a credit for Pakistani tax paid【19†L842-L850】.  In effect, Pakistan has primary taxing rights over the branch profit and Mauritius gives credit for that tax【17†L318-L326】【19†L842-L850】.  
- **Mauritius–Iraq:** No tax treaty exists between Mauritius and Iraq.  Therefore, Iraq has full taxing rights on income sourced there (subject to Iraq’s domestic law), and Mauritius will not have any treaty mechanism to eliminate double tax.  As noted above, Mauritius would apply its unilateral credit provisions for any Iraqi tax, but there is no special treaty relief to reduce the Mauritian tax on the branch profit beyond that.

## Penalties, Interest and Levies  
- **Late‐filing penalty:** Amending a previously filed return is treated as if the return were submitted on the amendment date.  As a result, Mauritius levies a late-filing penalty of MUR 2,000 per month (or part month) for the period of delay, up to a maximum of MUR 20,000【27†L90-L98】.  Thus, if UEPL amends its returns now for prior years, a late-submission penalty will be due for the months past the original due date【27†L90-L98】.  
- **Late payment and interest:**  Any additional tax assessed on the amended return must be paid immediately (with the amendment).  Late payment attracts a penalty of 5% of the tax due and interest at 0.5% per month on the unpaid balance【26†L48-L54】【26†L55-L59】.  For example, if additional Mauritius tax is calculated on the branch profits, a 5% surcharge plus 0.5% monthly interest will apply from the original due date until payment【26†L48-L54】【26†L55-L59】.  
- **Other levies:** There are no separate “fraud” or punitive penalties for a voluntary amendment beyond the above.  UEPL should note that an amended return may trigger a routine review or audit by MRA, but the act of amendment itself does not in itself create a penalty aside from the normal late‐filing/late‐payment charges【27†L90-L98】.

## Proposed Timeline  
- **Week 1:** Execute engagement letter; kick-off meeting or call to confirm scope.  
- **Week 2:** Collection of documentation and branch financials from you (see list below).  
- **Week 3:** Initial analysis and preparation of draft written advice.  
- **Week 4:** Review and finalize our advice; we will provide a written report by the end of Week 4.  

Subject to timely receipt of information, we expect to deliver our formal written advice approximately 3–4 weeks from engagement.

## Fee Estimate  
Based on the above scope, we estimate our professional fees to be in the range of **USD 2,500–3,500** (exclusive of VAT and out-of-pocket expenses).  This is an estimate; the final fee will depend on the actual time spent once we begin work.  We will confirm the fee arrangement once the scope is finalized.

## Required Documentation  
To proceed, we would need the following documents and details:  
- **Mauritius tax filings:** UEPL’s Mauritius Income Tax returns (Form 3F) and computations for the relevant years (the years we will amend), including detailed profit & loss and balance sheet.  
- **Branch financials:** Audited or management accounts of the Pakistan branch and the Iraq branch for each year, showing profits attributable to the branches.  
- **Foreign tax records:** Copies of tax assessments, certificates, or receipts evidencing corporate tax or branch profits tax paid in Pakistan and Iraq. (Include documentation of any withholdings on repatriated profits or dividends.)  
- **Entity structure:** Corporate chart and ownership details of UEPL and its branches, showing how the Pakistan and Iraq branches are operated (e.g. as true branches or subsidiaries).  
- **Branch establishment documents:** Any agreements, registrations or local filings related to the establishment of the Pakistan and Iraq branches (e.g. branch registration certificates).  
- **Prior correspondence:** Any previous tax opinions, rulings or correspondence with Mauritius, Pakistan or Iraqi tax authorities concerning the branch income.  

Providing these documents will allow us to confirm the tax positions and compute any additional tax liability accurately.

We trust this outlines the key points.  Please let us know if you have any questions or if you would like to discuss any aspect in more detail.  We would be happy to arrange a conference call or meeting at your convenience to go over our findings and next steps.

Yours sincerely,

[Your Name]  
Senior Tax Advisor

# Mauritian Tax Implications – Pakistan & Iraq Branch Profits

Dear Walid,

Thank you for your enquiry on the Mauritian tax treatment of branch profits from Pakistan and Iraq.  This involves both Pakistan/Iraq domestic law and any applicable Mauritius treaties or credits.  We have engaged PwC teams in Pakistan, Iraq, and Mauritius to confirm each jurisdiction’s position.  We will provide a formal timeline and fee quote once we have their input.  In the meantime, based on public information, our preliminary analysis is as follows:

## Coordination with Local Experts  
- **Cross-border input:**  We have reached out to our counterparts in Pakistan, Iraq, and Mauritius to clarify the tax rules in each country and confirm the treatment of branch profits and any related taxes.  Their feedback will ensure our advice is fully informed by local practice.  
- **Timeline & fees:**  After receiving their responses, we will issue a formal engagement letter that includes our estimated timeline and fee proposal.

## Preliminary Analysis – Pakistan Branch Profits  
- **Tax rates and branch profit tax:**  Under Pakistani law, a foreign company’s branch is taxed like a domestic company.  The branch’s income is subject to Pakistani corporate tax, and if profits are remitted to the head office, a branch profits tax of 15% applies【18†L373-L381】.  
- **Mauritius tax credit (treaty):**  The Mauritius–Pakistan Double Tax Agreement allows Mauritius to credit taxes paid in Pakistan against the Mauritian tax on the same income【14†L854-L859】.  Accordingly, a Mauritius-resident company would include the branch profits in its Mauritius return (since residents are taxed on worldwide income) and claim credit for Pakistani taxes paid.  In particular:  
  - The Pakistani corporate income tax and any branch profits tax should be creditable in Mauritius, subject to treaty rules【14†L854-L859】.  
  - Mauritius law provides foreign tax relief: foreign taxes paid may be credited against Mauritius tax on the same income【15†L23-L26】【35†L67-L72】.  
- **Comments:**  We will confirm with the Pakistani team whether any special conditions or exclusions apply to the branch profits tax.  At present, our view is that Mauritius should grant full credit for the Pakistani taxes borne on these profits.

## Preliminary Analysis – Iraq Branch Profits  
- **Taxation in Iraq:**  Current information indicates that Iraq treats a foreign branch similarly to a local corporation【20†L371-L374】.  Corporate income tax (at 15%) is imposed on Iraq-source profits of the branch.  We are not aware of a specific branch repatriation tax in Iraq, but we will verify this with our Iraq tax experts.  
- **Mauritius tax credit (domestic law):**  There is no known Mauritius–Iraq DTA in force.  However, under Mauritian domestic law a resident company still pays tax on foreign income and may credit foreign taxes.  Mauritius allows a credit for actual foreign taxes paid on the same income【35†L67-L72】.  Therefore, any Iraqi corporate tax on the branch profits should be creditable in Mauritius, subject to confirmation.  
- **Royalties and other levies:**  If the Iraqi branch pays royalties or other government levies (for example, in oil & gas projects), we will confirm whether these amounts are treated as taxes.  Often, such mandatory payments are considered similar to taxes for credit purposes (see next section).

## Definition of “Tax Paid” (Tax Treaties and Royalties)  
- **Broad definition in treaties:**  Tax treaties like Mauritius–Pakistan generally use a broad concept of “tax paid” for credit purposes.  For example, Article 23 of that treaty states that “tax paid” includes taxes that would have been payable but for certain tax incentives【14†L854-L859】.  This reflects an intent to prevent double taxation even when incentives reduce actual tax.  
- **Royalties to government:**  By analogy, mandatory royalties or payments to the government could be viewed as a form of tax or duty.  In the oil and gas context, the Mauritius tax authority has acknowledged that in-kind payments (e.g. *“Tax Oil”* and royalties) made to the government are effectively government levies.  Technical Release TR226 notes that royalty fees (e.g. 15% of gross revenue) and in-kind corporate tax (paid in oil volumes) are recognized and grossed up as taxes【34†L93-L100】.  This suggests that royalties paid to the Federal Government of Iraq might qualify as “tax paid” for Mauritius credit purposes.  
- **Subject to confirmation:**  We will confirm with our Iraq/Mauritius teams whether Iraqi royalties and levies are treated as taxes.  In principle, if they are mandatory payments to the government, Mauritius would likely allow a credit (especially under a broad treaty definition or domestic credit system).  We will clarify this point in our follow-up advice.

## Historical Tax Positions – Caution  
- **Past deductions vs. depreciation:**  We understand that UEPL may have historically treated certain below-ground installations (e.g. pipelines, wellhead equipment) as immediate expenses rather than capital assets.  Under Mauritian tax law, such capital expenditures generally must be capitalized and depreciated over their useful life.  Writing off these costs immediately is aggressive.  
- **Potential scrutiny:**  If we amend or restate the Mauritius returns to include the overseas branch profits, the Mauritius Revenue Authority will likely review prior year treatments.  We caution that any non-standard deductions could be challenged.  It would be prudent to revisit these positions: proper depreciation (annual allowance) should be taken on below-ground assets, and any write-offs may need to be adjusted.

## Next Steps  
- **Integration of feedback:**  Once we receive the detailed input from Pakistan, Iraq, and Mauritius, we will finalize our analysis.  We expect to provide a comprehensive advisory report taking into account local laws and treaties.  
- **Formal engagement:**  We will issue an engagement letter outlining our services, timeline, and fees.  Only after this will we deliver the final advice.  
- **Interim nature:**  Please note the above points are preliminary, based on initial information.  They should not be relied on as final advice until confirmed by our complete review.

Based on our review of the current contractual arrangements and applicable tax laws, we provide the following analysis and recommendations regarding the withholding tax (WHT) implications of the FSRU charter contract with Excelerate Energy (EEDD, UAE).

---

### 1. **Current Withholding Tax Treatment**

Under the existing time-charter agreement, payments comprising fixed charter hire and operations & maintenance (O&M) fees are treated as royalties, subject to a 12% WHT. This classification is based on:

- **Article 12 of the Pakistan-UAE Double Taxation Treaty (DTT)**, which includes payments for the use of industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment within the definition of royalties.

- **Section 152(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance (ITO), 2001**, mandating WHT on royalties paid to non-residents.

The Authority for Advance Rulings in 2018 affirmed this treatment, classifying FSRU lease payments as royalties under Article 12 of the Pakistan-UAE DTT, thereby triggering the 12% WHT.

---

### 2. **Proposed Contractual Recharacterization**

EEDD has proposed bifurcating the master contract into:

- A pure charter-hire agreement for the FSRU vessel (dry lease), and

- A separate O&M services agreement.

This restructuring aims to reclassify the charter-hire component as a dry lease of machinery, potentially excluding it from the definition of royalties under both domestic law and the DTT. The rationale is that the FSRU functions as a self-operating plant, generating output, and thus may not fall under the "equipment" category envisaged in Article 12.

If successful, this recharacterization could remove the charter-hire payments from the scope of Article 12 and Section 152(1), potentially reducing or eliminating the associated WHT.

---

### 3. **Permanent Establishment (PE) Risk**

Notwithstanding the above, the risk of EEDD being deemed to have a PE in Pakistan remains under both the current and proposed arrangements.

- **Section 2(41) of the ITO** defines a PE to include a place of business through which the business of a person is wholly or partly carried on, encompassing branches, offices, workshops, and other fixed places of business.

- **Article 5 of the Pakistan-UAE DTT** similarly defines a PE and includes provisions for service PEs, where services are furnished in Pakistan for periods aggregating more than 9 months within any 12-month period.

Given the long-term presence of the FSRU in Pakistan and the involvement of EEDD personnel, there is a substantial risk that EEDD could be considered to have a PE in Pakistan.

---

### 4. **Taxation Implications of PE Status**

If EEDD is deemed to have a PE in Pakistan:

- **Article 7 of the Pakistan-UAE DTT** stipulates that only the profits attributable to the PE are taxable in Pakistan.

- **Section 152(2A) of the ITO** requires Engro to withhold tax on payments to the PE at reduced rates (e.g., 3.5%–6%), depending on the nature of the payment.

- EEDD would be subject to tax on net profits attributable to the PE, allowing for deductions of expenses incurred for the purposes of the PE's business, including depreciation on the FSRU and head office expenses, as per **Sections 22 and 24 of the ITO**.

This net taxation approach could result in a lower effective tax rate compared to the current 12% WHT on gross payments.

---

### 5. **Anti-Avoidance Considerations**

**Section 108 of the ITO** empowers the tax authorities to recharacterize transactions between associates to reflect the substance over form, ensuring that transactions are at arm's length. While Engro and EEDD are not associates, the tax authorities may scrutinize the proposed contract split to ensure it is commercially justified and not solely for tax avoidance purposes.

---

### 6. **Recommendations**

- **Proceed with Caution on Contract Recharacterization**: While the proposed split could reduce WHT, it is essential to ensure that the recharacterization is substantiated by the actual conduct of the parties and that the dry lease arrangement is genuine.

- **Prepare for Potential PE Assessment**: Given the PE risk, EEDD should maintain detailed records of expenses related to the FSRU operations in Pakistan to support deductions in the event of net profit taxation.

- **Seek Advance Ruling**: To mitigate uncertainty, consider applying for an advance ruling from the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) on the tax implications of the proposed contractual arrangements.

- **Ensure Arm's Length Pricing**: All inter-company transactions should be conducted at arm's length, with appropriate documentation to support the pricing and terms.

We recommend engaging with tax advisors to navigate the complexities of the proposed arrangements and to ensure compliance with all applicable tax laws and treaties.

Please let us know if you require further assistance or clarification on any of the points discussed above.

Respectfully,

[Your Name]  
Tax Consultant (Engro)

# To: Engro Internal Stakeholders  
**Subject: Withholding Tax Optimization Strategies – Excelerate FSRU Charter Contract**

As discussed, under our current time‐charter contract with Excelerate Energy (EEDD, UAE), payments (fixed charter hire plus O&M) have been treated as “royalties” subject to 12% withholding tax (WHT)【22†L14562-L14569】【44†L472-L474】.  This treatment is driven by the Pak-UAE Double Taxation Treaty (DTT) Article 12 definition of “royalties” (which includes payments for use of industrial, commercial or scientific (ICS) equipment) and Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance (ITO) Section 152(1) (which mandates WHT on royalties to non-residents)【22†L14562-L14569】.  In practice the Authority for Advance Rulings in 2018 concluded that FSRU lease payments are “royalties” under Article 12 Pak–UAE DTT【15†L15-L23】, triggering 12% WHT.  **Thus, the baseline WHT on the single contract is 12% on gross.**  

**Proposed Split Contract and “Dry Lease” Recharacterization.**  EEDD has proposed splitting the master contract into (i) pure charter-hire of the FSRU vessel and (ii) separate O&M charges.  Under this structure, the hire component could be treated as a dry-lease of machinery (no crew or fuel supplied by the lessor).  In our view, **recharacterizing the FSRU hire as rental of equipment (plant & machinery) – rather than let-out of “equipment” under the ICS definition – may fall outside the domestic/treaty definition of royalty【42†L38-L46】.**  In effect, the FBR’s prior characterization of the entire invoice as royalty would be challenged, since the FSRU is arguably a **“machinery”** (plant) that generates output, not merely an **“equipment”** that does nothing by itself【15†L54-L61】【42†L38-L46】.  If successful, this could remove the hire payments from Article 12 (and ITO Section 152(1)) altogether.  In other words, *pure hire payments might no longer qualify as royalties*, potentially reducing WHT.  (For example, under the Pak–UAE DTT a pure dry-lease without associated services might be treated like sale of service or business profit rather than royalty.)

However, **we must emphasize that PE risk remains under any scenario.**  Even if the contract is dry-leased, the FSRU on a long-term charter in Pakistan and operated by EEDD personnel may itself constitute a *fixed place of business*, creating a Permanent Establishment (PE) for EEDD in Pakistan under ITO Section 2(41) and DTT Article 5【50†L229-L237】【31†L1028-L1034】.  Section 2(41) of the ITO defines a PE as “a fixed place of business…through which the business of the person is wholly or partly carried on,” including branches, offices, workshops, warehouses, etc.【50†L229-L237】.  In particular, a vessel on a 15-year charter could be seen as a **continuous fixed base or installation project** in Pakistan, especially if EEDD staff (crew/engineers) are engaged.  (By contrast, if the charter were strictly a “dry lease” with no fixed office or personnel of EEDD in Pakistan, OECD commentary suggests no PE would arise【42†L19-L26】.  But in practice EEDD provides onshore supervisory personnel, so a PE is likely.)

**PE Consequences – Net Profit Taxation.**  If EEDD is treated as having a Pakistani PE (under Article 5 of the DTT and ITO s2(41)), then Article 7 (Business Profits) applies, and Pakistani tax should be computed on *net profits* of that PE【17†L53-L60】【17†L101-L106】.  In practice this means **tax at corporate rates on income after allowable deductions**, not on gross receipts.  The Income Tax Ordinance enshrines this: all **business expenditures** of a PE are deductible in computing profit【17†L101-L106】.  In particular, **capital allowances** for the FSRU (depreciation, amortization) and ordinary business expenses (including head office/administration costs allocable to the PE) can reduce the taxable base【17†L101-L106】.  Section 17(1) of the Ordinance and Part II, Division I of the First Schedule set depreciation rates; for a specialized asset like an FSRU, substantial annual write-offs may be available.  Likewise, reasonable head-office support costs (e.g. management, finance) should qualify as “expenditure incurred for purpose of business” and thus be deductible【17†L101-L106】.  In short, *if a PE is constituted, EEDD’s Pakistani tax liability should be on taxable income (net profit) – not on gross charter hire – which yields a much lower effective tax than final WHT on gross*.  

This approach is grounded in both treaty and domestic law.  Article 7 of the Pak–UAE DTT provides that only profits “attributable to” the PE are taxable in Pakistan.  Domestic law mirrors this: the Ordinance (s2(41) and related provisions) treats a PE like a resident enterprise for branch profits purposes【50†L225-L234】【17†L53-L60】.  Indeed, **FBR practice (Finance Act 2012 amendments)** now explicitly treats branch profits under net taxation.  (Finance Act 2012 inserted s.152(2A) to apply withholding on *branch* payments at nominal rates while the branch itself pays tax at the corporate rate on its profit【50†L192-L200】.)  In our context, it means if EEDD is viewed as having a branch, Engro would withhold minimal 3.5–6% on certain payments, but EEDD would file a normal return on net profit.  Either way, the outcome is taxing EEDD’s bottom-line profit (after deductions), not the 12% of gross we currently pay.  

**Caution – Section 108 (Anti‑Avoidance).**  We must also be mindful of anti-avoidance rules.  Section 108 of the Ordinance authorizes the FBR to disregard or reallocate any inter-company or related-party transaction that is not at arm’s length【25†L9391-L9395】.  While Engro and EEDD are not affiliated, splitting one integrated charter into two contracts purely for tax benefit could attract scrutiny under s.108 and related Rules (transfer pricing rules).  The Division A ruling notes that tax authorities may look through the formal split if it lacks economic substance.  Therefore, any restructuring should be commercially justified (e.g. genuine allocation of vessel hire vs O&M) and documented at arm’s length.  

**Recommendations:**  In light of the above, our clear recommendations are:  

- **Pursue Lease Recharacterization Carefully:** Structuring the charter hire as a **dry lease** of the FSRU (with minimal crew/servicing by EEDD) may remove it from Article 12 “royalties” and reduce WHT.  However, we should not assume royalty status will be entirely avoided – if the arrangement still resembles equipment “use” or includes significant services, the tax authority may maintain royalty classification.  

- **Prepare for PE Assessment:** Regardless of classification, the risk of a PE is high.  We should plan to treat EEDD’s Pakistani operations as a branch for tax purposes.  This means preparing separate accounts for the FSRU business in Pakistan (with depreciation schedules and direct/indirect expenses) so that net profits can be shown.  In the event of a PE determination, Engro’s payments would ideally be characterized as branch receipts, allowing full corporate-style deductions.  

- **Document Allowable Deductions:** To optimize taxation of any PE, document and allocate all relevant deductions – especially (i) **depreciation/amortization** on the FSRU as a fixed asset, (ii) **operational expenses** (fuel, spares, dockage paid by Engro), and (iii) **head office allocations** (overhead, supervisory salaries, etc.).  Under s.17 and s.24 of the Ordinance (and general principles), these are deductible against branch profits【17†L101-L106】.  

- **Compliance with Withholding Rules:** Until a PE is recognized, Engro must comply with ITO s.152.  Currently that means withholding 12% on the invoiced amounts (as royalties)【22†L14562-L14569】.  If we argue for branch status, Engro may in future use the reduced rates of s.152(2A) (3.5%–6%) when paying a Pakistani PE【50†L192-L200】, but we must obtain formal guidance (e.g. FBR opinion).  

- **Legal/Advance Rulings:** Given the complexity, consider seeking an Advance Ruling or formal clarification from FBR on (a) whether a dry-lease split remains non-royalty, and (b) the applicability of PE rules and branch treatment.  Notably, a branch in Pakistan of a non-resident can elect to have business profits taxed on net at 29% (currently)【42†L30-L34】 (with credit for withholding), which may be preferable to withholding on gross at 12%.  

In summary, **while recharacterizing the FSRU charter as a dry lease could materially reduce withholding tax**, we must simultaneously manage the **risk of a permanent establishment**.  If a PE is deemed, the tax base shifts from 12% of gross to the company’s *net taxable income* from the project, after depreciation and other expenses【17†L101-L106】【50†L229-L237】.  This is typically more favorable, but requires diligent accounting and compliance with branch tax rules (ITO Sections 2(41), 108, 152 and the Pak–UAE DTT Articles 5, 7, 12)【50†L229-L237】【17†L101-L106】.  Our strategy should therefore balance WHT savings with the need to document an arm’s-length, bona fide lease arrangement and to be fully prepared for branch taxation.  

Please let us know if you have any questions or would like to discuss next steps. 

Respectfully,  

**[Name]**  
Tax Consultant (Engro)  

**Citations:** Relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Sections 2(41), 108, 152) and Articles 5, 7, 12 of the Pak–UAE Double Tax Treaty, as noted above【50†L229-L237】【25†L9391-L9395】【22†L14562-L14569】【44†L472-L474】【17†L101-L106】.

If EEDD is treated as having a Pakistani PE (under Article 5 of the DTT and ITO s2(41)), then Article 7 (Business Profits) applies, and Pakistani tax should be computed on net profits of that PE. In practice this means tax at corporate rates on income after allowable deductions, not on gross receipts. The Income Tax Ordinance enshrines this: all business expenditures of a PE are deductible in computing profit. In particular, capital allowances for the FSRU (depreciation, amortization) and ordinary business expenses (including head office/administration costs allocable to the PE) can reduce the taxable base. Section 17(1) of the Ordinance and Part II, Division I of the First Schedule set depreciation rates; for a specialized asset like an FSRU, substantial annual write-offs may be available. Likewise, reasonable head-office support costs (e.g. management, finance) should qualify as “expenditure incurred for purpose of business” and thus be deductible. In short, if a PE is constituted, EEDD’s Pakistani tax liability should be on taxable income (net profit) – not on gross charter hire – which yields a much lower effective tax than final WHT on gross.
This approach is grounded in both treaty and domestic law. Article 7 of the Pak–UAE DTT provides that only profits “attributable to” the PE are taxable in Pakistan. Domestic law mirrors this: the Ordinance (s2(41) and related provisions) treats a PE like a resident enterprise for branch profits purposes. Indeed, FBR practice (Finance Act 2012 amendments) now explicitly treats branch profits under net taxation. (Finance Act 2012 inserted s.152(2A) to apply withholding on branch payments at nominal rates while the branch itself pays tax at the corporate rate on its profit.) In our context, it means if EEDD is viewed as having a branch, Engro would withhold minimal 3.5–6% on certain payments, but EEDD would file a normal return on net profit. Either way, the outcome is taxing EEDD’s bottom-line profit (after deductions), not the 12% of gross we currently pay.
Caution – Section 108 (Anti Avoidance). We must also be mindful of anti-avoidance rules. Section 108 of the Ordinance authorizes the FBR to disregard or reallocate any inter-company or related-party transaction that is not at arm’s length. While Engro and EEDD are not affiliated, splitting one integrated charter into two contracts purely for tax benefit could attract scrutiny under s.108 and related Rules (transfer pricing rules). The Division A ruling notes that tax authorities may look through the formal split if it lacks economic substance. Therefore, any restructuring should be commercially justified (e.g. genuine allocation of vessel hire vs O&M) and documented at arm’s length.
Recommendations: In light of the above, our clear recommendations are:
•	Pursue Lease Recharacterization Carefully: Structuring the charter hire as a dry lease of the FSRU (with minimal crew/servicing by EEDD) may remove it from Article 12 “royalties” and reduce WHT. However, we should not assume royalty status will be entirely avoided – if the arrangement still resembles equipment “use” or includes significant services, the tax authority may maintain royalty classification.
•	Prepare for PE Assessment: Regardless of classification, the risk of a PE is high. We should plan to treat EEDD’s Pakistani operations as a branch for tax purposes. This means preparing separate accounts for the FSRU business in Pakistan (with depreciation schedules and direct/indirect expenses) so that net profits can be shown. In the event of a PE determination, Engro’s payments would ideally be characterized as branch receipts, allowing full corporate-style deductions.
•	Document Allowable Deductions: To optimize taxation of any PE, document and allocate all relevant deductions – especially (i) depreciation/amortization on the FSRU as a fixed asset, (ii) operational expenses (fuel, spares, dockage paid by Engro), and (iii) head office allocations (overhead, supervisory salaries, etc.). Under s.17 and s.24 of the Ordinance (and general principles), these are deductible against branch profits.
•	Compliance with Withholding Rules: Until a PE is recognized, Engro must comply with ITO s.152. Currently that means withholding 12% on the invoiced amounts (as royalties). If we argue for branch status, Engro may in future use the reduced rates of s.152(2A) (3.5%–6%) when paying a Pakistani PE, but we must obtain formal guidance (e.g. FBR opinion).
•	Legal/Advance Rulings: Given the complexity, consider seeking an Advance Ruling or formal clarification from FBR on (a) whether a dry-lease split remains non-royalty, and (b) the applicability of PE rules and branch treatment. Notably, a branch in Pakistan of a non-resident can elect to have business profits taxed on net at 29% (currently) (with credit for withholding), which may be preferable to withholding on gross at 12%.
In summary, while recharacterizing the FSRU charter as a dry lease could materially reduce withholding tax, we must simultaneously manage the risk of a permanent establishment. If a PE is deemed, the tax base shifts from 12% of gross to the company’s net taxable income from the project, after depreciation and other expenses. This is typically more favorable, but requires diligent accounting and compliance with branch tax rules (ITO Sections 2(41), 108, 152 and the Pak–UAE DTT Articles 5, 7, 12). Our strategy should therefore balance WHT savings with the need to document an arm’s-length, bona fide lease arrangement and to be fully prepared for branch taxation.
Please let us know if you have any questions or would like to discuss next steps.
Respectfully,

- Inter-agency enforcement coordination

- Restore zero-rating under the Export Facilitation Scheme
- Reintroduce Final Tax Regime for exporters
- Reduce advance tax and provide energy incentives for export industries

---

### 8. **Women, SMEs & Stationery Sector Demands**
- **IWCCI** urged budget allocations and lowering of Rs. 50m revenue threshold for corporate women.
- **SMEs** called for financial support and incentives based on export performance.
- **Stationery industry** demanded immediate withdrawal of taxes promised last year.

---

### 9. **Supreme Court Denies Zero Duty Claim under HS Codes 3402**
The apex court upheld that customs exemptions under SROs are conditional. Importers must meet all pre-requisites, including registration with the Ministry of National Food Security, to qualify for duty exemptions.

---

### 10. **Customs Valuation Efficiency Improves**
The Directorate of Customs Valuation issued **235 rulings in two years**, modernizing outdated benchmarks under Sections 25 and 25A of the Customs Act. This move supports fair trade assessments and boosts import compliance.

Tech firm Galaxefi has introduced **AI-powered Faceless Operations** to digitize cross-border trade. The initiative addresses the estimated **$36 billion loss** from outdated paper-based systems and aims to secure over **3 million jobs**.

- Broadening the tax base
- Curbing political appeasement of trader lobbies
- Implementing wealth registries and audit laws

Here is a detailed, paragraph-style website update based on the contents of the uploaded document, structured under interactive headings to enhance readability and engagement for your website visitors:

---

## 🔒 Restrictions on Non-Filers: Major Clampdown Begins July 2025

Under the **Tax Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024**, adopted by the National Assembly Standing Committee on Finance, strict restrictions will be imposed on non-filers from July 1, 2025. The proposed law eliminates the threshold for immovable property valuation and introduces a broad-based ban on various economic transactions by non-filers. These include the purchase or booking of vehicles above 800cc, acquisition of high-value property, stock market participation, and even opening new bank accounts. Ineligible individuals will also be restricted from transacting in mutual funds and securities. However, certain low-cost vehicles like motorcycles and tractors will remain accessible. These measures, which will be formalized in the Finance Bill 2025–26, aim to enforce tax compliance by integrating real-time data from banking systems into FBR's platforms. The FBR is also expected to demonstrate the upgraded digital systems and apps to ensure seamless implementation.

---

## 🧾 Sales Tax Exemption in Ex-FATA Set to Expire

The **Senate Standing Committee on Finance** has supported the decision not to extend the sales tax exemption for the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) beyond **June 30, 2025**. Businesses in formal sectors, such as steel and edible oil, raised concerns about the competitive disadvantage caused by the continuing tax exemption in ex-FATA. The Karachi Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI) further criticized the misuse of this exemption, citing a fivefold increase in tea imports routed through these areas, allegedly causing annual losses of Rs 30 billion. The business community recommended phasing out the exemption and restoring tax parity across the country.

---

## 📊 FBR’s Mixed Revenue Performance Amid IMF Target Cuts

While the **Federal Board of Revenue (FBR)** recorded a **30% month-on-month growth** in April 2025, it still fell short of its 10-month target by **Rs 831 billion**. Revenue collection in April totaled **Rs 846 billion**, down from the Rs 963 billion target. Although income tax collection surpassed targets by Rs 327 billion, sales tax and customs duties lagged behind due to subdued imports and historically low inflation. Consequently, the IMF revised the FBR’s target for FY25 downward from **Rs 12.91 trillion** to **Rs 12.33 trillion**. Despite improvements in enforcement—particularly in sectors like sugar—the overall tax-to-GDP ratio remains weak. 

---

## ⚖️ Landmark ATIR Judgment on Sealing of Business Premises

In a significant ruling, the **Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR)** Islamabad has declared that sealing a business under **Rule 150ZEO** of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 without due process is unlawful. The tribunal ruled that failure to issue a show cause notice, verify alleged invoices, or adhere to jurisdictional protocols violates principles of natural justice. Importantly, the judgment emphasized that harsh enforcement measures like sealing should only be used proportionately and that alternatives like real-time monitoring under **Section 40B** of the Sales Tax Act should be prioritized. This ruling sets a precedent for protecting business operations from arbitrary and excessive departmental actions.

---

## 🚫 Pakistan’s Rs 750 Billion Annual Loss to Illicit Trade

A joint report by **TRACIT and PRIME Institute** estimates that Pakistan loses **Rs 750 billion annually** due to illicit trade and smuggling, particularly in sectors like tobacco, petroleum, and pharmaceuticals. The report highlighted systemic weaknesses in tax enforcement, customs operations, and border controls. With Pakistan ranking **101 out of 158** on the **Global Illicit Trade Index 2025**, the report calls for structural reforms, including modernization of the **Track and Trace System**, inter-agency collaboration, stricter penalties, and the appointment of a **National Illicit Trade Coordinator** to lead enforcement efforts.

---

## 🛍️ FBR Seals Sowears Retail Outlets for Tax Evasion & Money Laundering Probe

The FBR has taken enforcement action against clothing brand **Sowears**, sealing five retail outlets across Karachi for tax evasion exceeding **Rs 100 million**. Investigations revealed that the brand failed to integrate its Point-of-Sale (POS) system with the FBR since 2018, concealing taxable income. Additionally, the company is suspected of running undeclared business operations in the UAE and USA, using courier shipments and possibly shell companies. FBR suspects the involvement of **money laundering**, and the case underscores FBR’s growing focus on international linkages and financial transparency.

---

## 📉 Chambers Demand Reversal of Anti-Export Measures

Business leaders from various chambers of commerce have urged the government to eliminate anti-export levies and restore the **Final Tax Regime (FTR)** for exporters. The **Export Facilitation Scheme (EFS)** was criticized for liquidity bottlenecks due to the withdrawal of zero-rating and the imposition of advance taxes. Stakeholders also recommended regionally competitive energy pricing, tax rebates, and fast-track refund mechanisms to incentivize export growth. A reduction in advance tax on remittances was also proposed by the Lahore and Gujranwala Chambers, while Sialkot Chamber called for reinstatement of tribunals for small taxpayers to ensure accessible dispute resolution.

---

## 👩‍💼 Women, SMEs and Education Sector Policy Recommendations

Several industry bodies have presented proposals for the 2025–26 budget. The **Islamabad Women’s Chamber of Commerce (IWCCI)** advocated for a dedicated fund to support women-led enterprises and reduction of the **Rs 50 million corporate revenue threshold** for women. **Rawalpindi Chamber** recommended reducing **GST to 15%** to support struggling industries, while the **Stationery Association** reiterated its demand for tax relief on educational materials. Stakeholders emphasized the need to create an inclusive and growth-friendly tax environment, especially for young entrepreneurs and small businesses.

---

## ⚖️ Supreme Court Rejects Zero-Duty Petition on Imports under HS Code 3402

The **Supreme Court of Pakistan** has dismissed a petition by **Surfactant Chemicals Co.** seeking zero percent duty on imports under **HS Codes 3402.1300 and 3402.1190**. The Court held that exemptions under **SRO 565(I)/2006** and its amendments are conditional upon registration with the **Ministry of National Food Security**. Since the petitioner was not registered as a pesticide manufacturer or formulator, it could not claim the exemption. This ruling reiterates that HS code classification alone is insufficient; all procedural conditions under SROs must be fulfilled.

---

## 📦 Customs Valuation Directorate Modernizes Import Assessments

The **Directorate of Customs Valuation** has issued **235 valuation rulings** in the past two fiscal years to modernize Pakistan’s import duty assessment framework. These rulings, governed under **Sections 25 and 25A** of the Customs Act, help reduce tax disputes and promote trade transparency. The overhaul has earned praise from trade bodies and is expected to facilitate fairer, faster, and more consistent import evaluations, especially for frequently disputed items.

---

## 📡 Cross-Border Trade Goes Digital with AI-Powered System

Pakistani tech company **Galaxefi** has launched a fully automated **AI Faceless Operations** platform to overhaul cross-border trade processes. The system utilizes a smart assistant named **galaxbot™**, which handles documentation, customs paperwork, real-time shipment tracking, and alerts—all through voice or chat. Designed to reduce the **$36 billion loss** from outdated trade systems, this innovation promises to streamline compliance and protect nearly **3 million jobs** dependent on international logistics.

---

## 🚚 Demurrage Relief Requested by Transporters Amid Protests

The **Pakistan Goods Transporters Association (PGTA)** has appealed for a waiver of demurrage and late delivery charges imposed during recent 12-day protests in Sindh. With over **50,000 trucks stranded**, the association argued that the delays were caused by public unrest and not the fault of transporters. While the **Motorway Police** and **Excise Department** have shown leniency, the transporters are urging shipping lines and port authorities to offer financial relief for the losses incurred.

---

## 🚂 Railways and ICCI Sign Agreement to Boost Freight Efficiency

In a major public-private collaboration, **Pakistan Railways** has signed an agreement with the **Islamabad Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ICCI)** to outsource the Islamabad Dry Port to the Chamber. This move is expected to enhance logistics efficiency and generate new revenue streams. Minister for Railways also approved a freight corridor between **Karachi and Rawalpindi**, reducing cargo delivery time to under four days. Additional infrastructure and cleanliness initiatives were also announced as part of broader railway reforms.

---

## Supreme Court Upholds Taxpayer’s Right to Separate Notice under Section 111: A Landmark Decision Clarifying Assessment Procedures

In a landmark judgment dated February 1, 2024, the Supreme Court of Pakistan has conclusively held that, for tax years prior to the Finance Act, 2021, the issuance of a **separate notice under Section 111 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** is a legal prerequisite before initiating any assessment amendment under **Section 122(5)** of the Ordinance. The consolidated appeals, led by *Commissioner Inland Revenue v. Millat Tractors Ltd. & Others*, involved various taxpayers and raised a core procedural question—whether tax authorities can amend an assessment based on unexplained income without first completing proceedings under Section 111.

The Court clarified that Section 111 is fundamentally inquisitorial in nature and is designed to give taxpayers an opportunity to explain the source of income, asset, or expenditure before it can be treated as “unexplained” and added to taxable income. This process requires the Commissioner to confront the taxpayer with specific grounds falling under Section 111(1)(a) to (d) through a distinct notice and allow them to present their explanation. If the explanation is unsatisfactory in the opinion of the Commissioner, only then does the information qualify as “definite information” for the purpose of amending an assessment under Section 122(5). Therefore, the amendment of an assessment cannot lawfully proceed under Section 122 without the prior conclusion of proceedings under Section 111.

While the Federal Board of Revenue had contended that a combined notice under Section 122(9) could suffice for both provisions—particularly relying on the Explanation inserted into Section 111 through the Finance Acts of 2021 and 2022—the Court rejected this argument for all tax years preceding 2021. The Court emphasized that although the Explanation was couched in clarificatory language, its substantive effect was to **eliminate the separate right to notice and due process under Section 111**. As such, it altered the taxpayer’s legal position and could not be retrospectively applied. Any law or explanation that affects vested procedural rights—particularly one that compromises principles of fair trial, due process, and the right to be treated in accordance with law under Articles 4 and 10A of the Constitution—must be interpreted to apply only prospectively, unless the legislature clearly indicates otherwise.

The judgment also outlined a nuanced procedural path for future cases. Even where a combined notice under Section 122(9) refers to unexplained income, the taxpayer must first be allowed to respond under the framework of Section 111. Only after the Commissioner forms a written opinion based on this response can such opinion be treated as definite information to support a reassessment under Section 122(5). If the opinion formed under Section 111 differs from the original notice issued under Section 122(9), the department must issue a supplementary show cause notice so the taxpayer can respond meaningfully to the updated grounds. The Supreme Court thus reinforced that procedural safeguards and the right to be heard are not hollow formalities but enforceable legal entitlements.

Importantly, the Court also noted that the purpose of separate Section 111 proceedings is not merely procedural but serves a critical function. It allows taxpayers to voluntarily revise their returns and pay tax before facing penalties under Section 182. By folding Section 111 into Section 122 without proper process, taxpayers would be denied this opportunity, which cannot be justified on constitutional or statutory grounds.

This ruling is significant for both taxpayers and tax authorities. For taxpayers, it affirms their right to due process and offers protection against arbitrary assessments initiated without prior explanation or inquiry. For tax administrators, it serves as a directive to strictly follow statutory procedures when invoking powers under the Ordinance. The judgment also highlights the importance of temporal applicability of tax amendments. Amendments affecting substantive or vested rights must not be applied retrospectively unless explicitly provided.

To conclude, the Supreme Court’s decision establishes a binding precedent that **proceedings under Section 111 must precede and culminate before any reassessment can be initiated under Section 122**. The Explanation inserted through the Finance Acts of 2021 and 2022 cannot override this requirement for earlier tax years. This judgment is not only a reaffirmation of taxpayer rights but also a call for legislative clarity and administrative compliance.

## Supreme Court Clarifies Legal Requirement for Section 111 Notices in Income Tax Proceedings

### Background of the Case

In a pivotal judgment dated February 1, 2024, the Supreme Court of Pakistan, in *Commissioner Inland Revenue v. Millat Tractors Ltd. & Others* (C.P. No. 2447-L/2022 and connected appeals), clarified a fundamental procedural requirement under Pakistan’s income tax regime. The matter involved multiple taxpayers and a recurring issue in tax assessments—whether unexplained income or assets, as addressed under Section 111 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, can directly trigger reassessment proceedings under Section 122 without first issuing a separate notice under Section 111. The tax department had taken the position that once a notice under Section 122(9) is issued, there was no need to separately initiate proceedings under Section 111, especially after the insertion of an Explanation to that effect through Finance Acts 2021 and 2022. However, the Court rejected this approach in cases concerning tax years prior to 2021.

### Legal Issue and Procedural Framework

The core legal issue before the Court was whether a separate notice under Section 111 is a necessary condition precedent for invoking Section 122(5), and whether the Explanation added through Finance Act, 2021—which purportedly removes the requirement for a separate Section 111 notice—could be applied retrospectively. The Court analyzed the legal framework of both provisions and reaffirmed that Section 111 has its own independent legal significance and procedural safeguards. It emphasized that Section 111 is an inquisitorial provision, where the taxpayer must be specifically confronted with the facts and grounds concerning unexplained income or assets, and provided an opportunity to explain the nature and source of such income. Only if the Commissioner is not satisfied with the explanation, the resulting opinion may qualify as “definite information,” forming the basis for reassessment under Section 122(5).

### Requirement of Separate Proceedings under Section 111

The Court unequivocally held that for tax years prior to 2021, the initiation of separate proceedings under Section 111 is mandatory before the issuance of any notice under Section 122(9). Even where a notice under Section 122(9) is issued simultaneously, it cannot be acted upon unless proceedings under Section 111 are first finalized. In other words, the Commissioner must first evaluate the taxpayer’s explanation under Section 111, and if the explanation is deemed unsatisfactory, form a written opinion which constitutes definite information. Only then may the tax authority lawfully proceed under Section 122. This two-step process ensures that the taxpayer’s right to be heard and to respond to specific allegations is not undermined. The judgment emphasized that these safeguards are enshrined in the Constitution under Articles 4 and 10A, which guarantee the right to fair trial and treatment in accordance with law.

### Prospective Application of the Explanation Added to Section 111

As part of its reasoning, the Supreme Court carefully considered the Explanation inserted in Section 111 through the Finance Act, 2021 and amended in 2022. While the Explanation stated that a separate notice under Section 111 is not required if the matter is already addressed in a Section 122(9) notice, the Court ruled that this amendment cannot be applied retrospectively. The Explanation was found to alter the taxpayer’s substantive right to separate proceedings under Section 111, and such a right cannot be taken away without express legislative intent to apply the amendment retrospectively. Accordingly, the Court concluded that for tax years prior to 2021, the Explanation has no legal bearing and the pre-amendment framework requiring a distinct Section 111 notice continues to govern.

### Effect on Tax Administration and Taxpayer Rights

The ruling has significant implications for tax enforcement and compliance procedures. First, it affirms the distinct and sequential nature of proceedings under Section 111 and Section 122. Second, it preserves the taxpayer’s opportunity to voluntarily revise returns under Section 114(6A) to mitigate exposure to penalties under Section 182—an option that would otherwise be lost if Section 111 is skipped. The Court also highlighted that where the Commissioner’s opinion under Section 111 differs materially from the original notice under Section 122(9), a fresh or supplementary show-cause notice must be issued to ensure that the taxpayer is properly informed of the new grounds and given an opportunity to respond. This approach reinforces the principles of procedural fairness and natural justice.

### Guidance for Post-2021 Cases and Reconciliation of Procedures

While the judgment primarily addresses cases up to tax year 2020, it also clarifies the framework going forward. For cases falling under the amended law post-2021, the Explanation now allows a combined notice under Section 122(9) encompassing grounds under Section 111(1). However, even under the new framework, the Commissioner must still conclude the Section 111 component first by forming an opinion. The Section 122 proceedings can only formally begin once that opinion crystallizes into definite information. This interpretation preserves the substantive fairness of the process, even if the notices are procedurally combined. Furthermore, the statutory limitation period introduced for completing proceedings under Section 122(9) will only begin once the opinion under Section 111 is shared with the taxpayer, thereby harmonizing the procedural timelines.

### Conclusion

In sum, the Supreme Court’s ruling is a powerful reaffirmation of taxpayer rights and a critical reminder for the tax authorities to follow the statutory framework in letter and spirit. For tax years prior to 2021, a notice under Section 122(9) without separate and prior proceedings under Section 111 is legally deficient. Even under the amended law, taxpayers must be confronted with the Commissioner’s final opinion under Section 111 before assessment amendments can proceed. This ruling not only provides clarity for practitioners but also reinforces constitutional guarantees of due process and fair trial in the realm of tax law. It will undoubtedly influence how tax audits, unexplained income inquiries, and reassessment procedures are structured in the future.

For taxpayers or corporations who have received notices under Section 122 without being given a chance to explain their position under Section 111, this decision provides a strong legal basis to challenge such proceedings. The tax department argued that a combined notice under Section 122(9) should suffice, especially in light of the Explanation now included in Section 111. However, the Court adopted a stricter interpretation of procedural fairness and legislative intent.

### ⚖️ The Court’s Holding: Due Process Prevails

The Supreme Court held that for tax years **prior to 2021**, a **separate and specific notice under Section 111** must be issued. The Court clarified that:
- Section 111 involves **inquisitorial proceedings** that provide the taxpayer an opportunity to explain the source of unexplained income or assets.
- The Commissioner must form a written **opinion** based on the taxpayer’s explanation (or lack thereof).
- Only after this opinion qualifies as **"definite information"** can it form the basis for reassessment under Section 122(5).

This sequence ensures that the taxpayer is not subjected to arbitrary amendments without being heard, in line with **Articles 4 and 10A of the Constitution**, which guarantee due process and the right to be treated in accordance with law.

---

### 📘 Explanation to Section 111: Prospective Application Only

The Explanation introduced through the Finance Act, 2021 (and substituted in 2022) suggested that a separate notice under Section 111 is not required if the grounds are included in a notice under Section 122(9). However, the Court found that:
- While framed as a clarification, the Explanation **substantively altered taxpayers’ procedural rights**.
- As such, it **cannot apply retrospectively** to tax years before its enactment.
- This view aligns with settled law that **tax statutes operate prospectively** unless expressly stated otherwise.

Thus, taxpayers assessed for tax years up to 2020 continue to enjoy the right to **separate proceedings under Section 111**.

---

### 🔄 Procedural Sequence Reaffirmed

The judgment reiterated the two-step sequence for lawful assessment amendment:
1. **Section 111 proceedings** must be initiated first, with a specific notice issued and the taxpayer’s explanation invited.
2. If the Commissioner concludes that the explanation is unsatisfactory, this constitutes **definite information**, which then allows the department to initiate formal reassessment under **Section 122(5)**, following issuance of a **Section 122(9) notice**.

Even where combined notices are issued (post-2021), the **Section 111 component must be finalized first**. If the Commissioner’s eventual opinion differs from the original 122(9) notice, **a fresh or supplementary notice** must be served to comply with the principles of fair trial.

---

### 🛡 Importance of Taxpayer Safeguards

The ruling protects several substantive taxpayer rights:
- It preserves the opportunity to **revise returns voluntarily** under Section 114(6A) to avoid penalties under Section 182.
- It prevents tax authorities from **short-circuiting due process** by bypassing inquisitorial steps.
- It ensures taxpayers receive **adequate notice and clarity** before facing adverse action.

The Supreme Court highlighted that two distinct and independent proceedings under Sections 111 and 122 **cannot be legally merged** into a single notice, even after the 2021 amendment.

- For tax years up to **2020**, **a separate Section 111 notice is mandatory**.
- For tax years **after 2021**, combined notices may be permissible, but Section 111 proceedings **must still be concluded first**.

In this regard, we shall appear before your good office on the scheduled date of hearing and are prepared to present all relevant supporting documents including invoices, payment records, and bank statements, to substantiate our position.

We respectfully request your good office to take the foregoing into consideration and withdraw the proceedings initiated through the subject Show Cause Notice.

Yours faithfully,  
**[Authorized Representative]**  
On behalf of Shell Pakistan Limited

Based on the contents of the attached *Final Opportunity* notice dated January 31, 2025, and the instructions you provided, here is a refined and professional draft of the response for submission to the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB):

---

**[On Client's Letterhead]**

**Date:** [Insert Date]  
**To:**  
Deputy Commissioner (Unit-21)  
Sindh Revenue Board  
2nd Floor, Shaheen Complex  
M.R. Kiyani Road, Karachi  

**Subject:** Response to Final Opportunity Notice – Observations Regarding Alleged Short Payment of Sindh Sales Tax on Franchise and Technical Services

Dear Sir,

We refer to your final opportunity notice dated January 31, 2025 (Ref: UNIT-21/Shell/2024-25/543574), issued in continuation of earlier notices and reminders, wherein it has been alleged that our client, M/s Shell Pakistan Limited, has short-paid Sindh sales tax (SST) on account of franchise services and other taxable services received from related non-resident parties.

At the outset, we respectfully submit that the basis of your observation appears to be the outstanding trade payables disclosed in the annual audited accounts as of December 31, 2023. It is important to clarify that the mere existence of outstanding liabilities in the financial statements does not imply that the associated services were received or that the related SST was payable as of that date. Every tax period under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 operates independently, and tax liability cannot be determined on presumptive basis or inferred solely from accounting entries. Therefore, the comparison drawn in the notice lacks any legal nexus with the actual timing and incidence of tax liability and is wholly based on assumption, which is inconsistent with both the law and the spirit of the show cause mechanism.

Furthermore, it is the consistent and long-standing practice of our client to discharge Sindh sales tax liability at the time of receipt of invoice for services, in accordance with the applicable Sindh Sales Tax Rules. The payables reflected in the books of account are trading liabilities outstanding as of the balance sheet date and do not automatically correlate with the timing of tax payment, which is contingent upon the receipt of invoice as per Rule 21(2) of the Sindh Sales Tax Rules, 2011. Hence, the assumption of tax short payment without correlating the observation with actual invoices and tax periods is grossly misplaced.

It is also relevant to note that your office is well aware of the client’s regular compliance history with respect to services from Shell Brands International AG. In this regard, from July 2013 to December 2019, the tax department passed orders affirming our client’s SST liability, which was duly discharged by the client. Thereafter, since January 2020, our client has been consistently discharging its SST obligations on these services through its monthly sales tax returns under the reverse charge mechanism. The same practice continues to date, and tax has been appropriately paid upon receipt of invoices for each respective period.

Similarly, in respect of services from Shell International Petroleum Company Limited, our client has adopted the same compliant approach of paying SST upon receipt of invoices, regardless of the timing of commercial settlement of underlying liabilities. Moreover, we draw your attention to the fact that SRB had already issued a separate show cause notice for alleged short payment of SST on franchise services for the tax periods from January 2020 to December 2022. In response, our client duly furnished all supporting documentation to your good office. Upon review, it was established that SST had been paid appropriately across Sindh and other provinces based on revenue allocation, and there was no shortfall.

In view of the foregoing, the current allegation of short payment appears to be entirely unfounded and unsupported by documentary evidence. We therefore request that the subject proceedings be dropped and treated as closed.

Should any additional clarification or documents be required, we remain available to assist and cooperate in good faith.

Thanking you,  
Yours faithfully,  
**For and on behalf of Shell Pakistan Limited**  
[Authorized Representative's Name]  
[Designation]  
[Contact Details]

---
