### 📊 Budget 2025-26: Major Tax Overhaul Targets Agriculture and SEZs  
To meet the ambitious revenue target of Rs. 14.3 trillion for FY2025-26, the government is preparing aggressive tax measures, including doubling the Federal Excise Duty (FED) on fertilizers from 5% to 10% and introducing a 5–10% FED on pesticides. Additionally, income from agriculture will now be taxed at rates up to 45% from January 2025, marking a departure from long-standing exemptions. The budget may also limit the tax-free duration of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) from 10 to 9 years as part of a broader commitment to phase out fiscal incentives, in line with IMF conditions focused on reducing market distortions and improving revenue mobilization.

---

### 🚗 Auto Sector Seeks Relief Amid Budget Talks  
The government has reaffirmed its support for the automotive sector in a pre-budget meeting with leading car manufacturers, including Toyota, Honda, Suzuki, and others. Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Industries, Haroon Akhtar Khan, encouraged automakers to work with the Ministry of Industries and Production to draft proposals addressing their concerns, with a strong emphasis on electric vehicle (EV) promotion. The meeting underscored the administration’s intent to provide long-term policy stability and incentives that could bolster local manufacturing and attract investment in green mobility.

---

### 🪙 FBR Intensifies Crackdown on Gold Trade to Curb Money Laundering  
The FBR has intensified its enforcement actions in the gold trade sector following a 47% increase in gold prices, citing risks of financial crimes and undocumented transactions. Dealers are now required to comply with Anti-Money Laundering (AML) laws, including strict Customer Due Diligence (CDD) and Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) for high-risk clients. Transactions exceeding Rs. 2 million must be reported to the Financial Monitoring Unit (FMU), and gold traders must retain comprehensive transaction records for at least five years. These measures aim to formalize the sector and ensure fair contribution to the national tax base.

---

### ⚖️ PTBA and Traders Slam Presidential Ordinances as “Unconstitutional”  
Strong opposition has emerged from the Pakistan Tax Bar Association (PTBA) and nationwide trader groups against the Tax Amendments Ordinance 2025 and SRO 175, which they claim grant arbitrary powers to the FBR and erode taxpayer rights. The PTBA condemned the mandatory 30% upfront payment for obtaining stay orders, calling it unconstitutional, while traders warned of nationwide protests and civil disobedience unless the “black law” is withdrawn. Business leaders described the ordinance as economically damaging and pledged to initiate a unified “Save the Economy Movement” to resist the new laws.

---

### 🏫 Educational Sector Secures Relief from PoS Notices  
The Federal Tax Ombudsman (FTO) has accepted the appeal filed by the All Pakistan Private Schools Federation against FBR’s move to enforce Point of Sale (PoS) integration through SRO 428(I)/2024. The FTO ordered FBR to suspend notices issued to educational institutions and directed the formation of a high-level committee to review the classification of schools as retailers. Federation leaders warned that imposing PoS requirements on schools—most of which lack basic IT infrastructure—would hurt low-income students, increase dropouts, and violate Article 25A of the Constitution that guarantees free education.

---

### 📉 Record Number of Taxpayer Complaints Filed with FTO  
The month of April 2025 saw a record 7,919 complaints filed against the FBR with the Federal Tax Ombudsman (FTO), indicating a surge in public dissatisfaction with tax administration. These complaints, largely concerning harassment, maladministration, and procedural irregularities, contributed to a total of 14,563 cases filed in the first four months of the year. The exponential rise underscores growing concerns over the taxpayer experience and reflects the urgent need for structural reforms in FBR’s enforcement and compliance practices.

---

### 👨‍⚖️ LHC Penalizes Customs for Coercive Recovery Practices  
In a landmark judgment, the Lahore High Court (LHC) imposed over Rs. 1.1 million in penalties and costs on Customs officials who forced a taxpayer to pay fines beyond what was stipulated in an adjudication order. The Court ruled that goods should have been released provisionally under Section 81 of the Customs Act after securing differential duties, and referred the matter to the Classification Committee for final resolution. The ruling is expected to deter coercive recoveries by Customs and reinforces judicial oversight over revenue authorities.

---

### 🔁 Barter Trade with Iran, Afghanistan Sparks Sanctions Concerns  
The Senate Standing Committee on Commerce has raised serious objections to the Ministry of Commerce’s proposal to permanently exempt barter trade with Iran and Afghanistan from the Electronic Import Form (EIF) requirement. Lawmakers expressed concern that such exemptions could breach U.S. sanctions and further complicate bilateral trade. With over 1,200 barter trucks stranded at the border, the committee demanded urgent resolution through formalized frameworks and criticized the Ministry for its lack of preparedness and delayed submissions. A joint meeting with the Finance Minister, SBP, and Commerce Ministry is being planned to resolve the matter.

---

### 💼 Reward & Rating System (RRS): Legal and Internal Crisis at FBR  
The FBR’s new Reward & Rating System (RRS) is facing backlash from its own officers and legal scrutiny from a Supreme Court advocate. Officers criticized the system as biased and manipulative, with some publicly refusing their bonuses. Complaints allege the system was implemented without legal authorization from the FBR Policy Board, violating Section 20 of the FBR Act. With rewards of up to 24 months’ salary reportedly disbursed, questions are being raised about transparency, misuse of public funds, and favoritism—prompting calls for audits and a full review of the scheme.

---

### 👩‍⚖️ Customs Tribunal Reform: Anti-Corruption Drive Gains Momentum  
In a major move to restore transparency, the Ministry of Law & Justice has appointed new technical members to key benches of the Customs Appellate Tribunal in Lahore and Karachi following corruption allegations. These changes come after intelligence reports exposed irregularities and the sale of judgments, triggering broader reform initiatives. The government has increased judicial allowances and is exploring automation to reduce human discretion. The appointments are seen as part of a larger anti-corruption strategy led by the military and judiciary to uphold rule of law in revenue adjudication processes.

# Income Tax Exemption for Shangla and Chitral Residents (PATA Areas)

## Tax-Exempt Zone Status of Shangla and Chitral  
**Shangla (Swat region) and Chitral** are part of the Provincially Administered Tribal Areas (PATA) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which were historically outside the scope of federal income tax laws【35†L189-L197】. After the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018, these areas formally became “taxable” territories, but **a temporary tax exemption was granted** as part of their merger transition【16†L99-L107】. In practical terms, the **Malakand Division** (which includes Swat/Shangla and Chitral) was treated as a tax-exempt zone for several years. Officials confirmed that *“the Malakand Division and all merged tribal districts have been exempted from taxes till June 2023”*【2†L66-L73】. 

However, this **blanket exemption was time-bound**. The law provided relief up to **30 June 2023**, and a proposed one-year extension to June 2024 was **withdrawn** in the Finance Act 2023【10†L149-L157】. **Bottom line:** *Under current law (2025), Shangla and Chitral **were** classified as tax-exempt zones up to 30-06-2023, but that exemption period has lapsed*. No further extension was enacted【10†L149-L157】, meaning income earned in these areas **after July 1, 2023 is no longer automatically exempt** from income tax.

## Legal Provisions Granting the Exemption  
The income tax exemption for residents of FATA/PATA (including Shangla and Chitral) was explicitly provided in the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** via the Second Schedule. The key provision was **Clause (145A), Part I of the Second Schedule**, introduced by Finance Act 2019. Clause 145A states in effect:

> **“Any income which was not chargeable to tax prior to the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 2018 (XXXVII of 2018) of any individual *domiciled* or company and association of persons *resident* in the Tribal Areas forming part of the Provinces of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan under paragraph (d) of Article 246 of the Constitution, with effect from 1st June 2018 to 30th June 2023 (both days inclusive).”**【37†L267-L272】

In simpler terms, **income of persons belonging to the tribal areas (PATA/FATA)** that were previously outside the tax net became **exempt from income tax for the period 01-06-2018 through 30-06-2023**【37†L267-L272】. This covered Shangla and Chitral since they fall under the *“Tribal Areas forming part of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa”* as per Article 246(d) of the Constitution. 

Additionally, the law provided corresponding relief in tax withholding provisions. For example, **Clause (109A), Part IV of the Second Schedule** (also added in 2019) ensured that withholding tax requirements did not apply to payments to FATA/PATA residents during the exemption period【37†L298-L304】. In essence, the Ordinance and its Second Schedule collectively allowed eligible individuals to *earn income without incurring income tax liability up to the mid-2023 cutoff*. This legal framework was initially implemented via FBR notifications (SRO 887(I)/2018 later replaced by SRO 1213(I)/2018) and then cemented in the Income Tax Ordinance by Parliament【16†L99-L107】【37†L298-L304】.

**Important:** As noted, these provisions **expired on 30 June 2023**. The Finance Bill 2023 had proposed extending the exemption to 2024, but the final Finance Act 2023 **did not include the extension**, effectively ending the tax holiday【10†L149-L157】. Therefore, **no section of the law currently in force extends the income tax exemption beyond 2023** for Shangla, Chitral or other ex-FATA/PATA areas.

## Domicile vs. Place of Duty – Conditions for Exemption  
Under the Ordinance’s language, the **exemption is tied to a person’s status (domicile/residency)** in the specified area, **not strictly to the place where the income is earned**. For **individuals**, the law uses the criterion of being *“domiciled”* in the tribal area【37†L267-L272】. In practice, *domicile* means the individual’s permanent legal residence is in Shangla, Chitral or another exempt district (usually evidenced by a domicile certificate). For **companies or AOPs**, the criterion was being *“resident”* in the tribal area【37†L267-L272】 (intended to mean their principal office or management is based there). 

Notably, the exemption was **not explicitly limited to income arising *within* those areas**. The wording raised questions such as whether a domiciled individual’s income earned outside the area would also be tax-free【37†L285-L293】. The law as written suggests the exemption is **personal (status-based)** rather than strictly geographical. This ambiguity led to debates and even misuse – e.g. some taxpayers with tribal area domicile were claiming tax exemption on nationwide business activities【37†L285-L293】. 

**In summary:** To qualify, an individual had to be **domiciled in Shangla/Chitral** (a non-local merely working there would *not* qualify under the clause). The law did **not require** the person’s job or income source to be physically located in the area – only their domicile status mattered【37†L285-L293】. (The intent, however, was to provide relief to income of people *from and in* those underdeveloped areas, and authorities have been wary of those abusing the clause by having a tribal area domicile on paper while operating elsewhere【37†L285-L293】.) In the scenario you describe – an individual **both domiciled in *and* working in Shangla or Chitral** – that person squarely fit the eligibility for the exemption during the 2018–2023 period. 

## Claiming the Exemption – Documentation & Procedure  
To **claim the income tax exemption**, eligible taxpayers needed to **provide proof of their status** and follow certain procedures:

- **Domicile Certificate:** The individual should obtain an official **domicile certificate of the relevant district** (e.g. Shangla or Chitral) as evidence that they are domiciled in a PATA region. This document is fundamental to establish eligibility under Clause 145A.

- **Tax Exemption Certificate from FBR:** In practice, the Federal Board of Revenue required tribal area taxpayers to **apply for an exemption certificate** (under Section 159 of the Ordinance) to ensure no tax is withheld from their income. The Regional Tax Office (RTO) – Peshawar set up facilitation centers to assist in issuance of these certificates【1†L159-L167】. For example, a Tax Facilitation Centre in Malakand was established specifically *“with the purpose of speedy issuance of ... exemption certificates to local industrialists”*【2†L74-L82】. While that reference was about businesses, **individual salary earners** and others also needed to obtain similar certificates so that employers or banks would not deduct withholding tax on salaries, bank profit, etc., during the exemption period. FBR issued detailed circulars outlining the **procedure for issuance of exemption certificates to FATA/PATA residents** (for instance, **Income Tax Circular No. 09 and 13 of 2021** dealt with mechanisms for exemption on imports and other incomes for FATA/PATA taxpayers)【22†L7-L15】【22†L31-L39】.

- **Other Supporting Documents:** When applying for the FBR exemption certificate or dealing with an employer/bank, one may be asked for additional proofs such as a copy of the Computerized National Identity Card (CNIC) showing a permanent address in the exempt area, a letter from the employer confirming the posting in the tribal area (if applicable), or any other evidence the tax authorities deem necessary. These help confirm that the income recipient is genuinely a resident of the exempt zone. For instance, for industrial import exemptions, FBR required documents like the domicile certificate, local chamber of commerce letter, etc., to issue the relief certificate【34†L0-L6】 (similar principles would apply to personal income exemption claims).

- **Tax Return Filing:** During the exemption period, an eligible person’s income was *exempt* but it was good practice (and sometimes required) to still **file an income tax return** declaring the income and claiming the exemption under the relevant clause. The return would disclose the income but show it as exempt under **Clause 145A of Part I, Second Schedule**. This helps document the claim and ensures transparency. If the income was solely exempt and below the normal taxable threshold, FBR generally did not pursue tax, but filing a return citing the exemption clause was advisable, especially for substantial incomes.

In summary, **to avail the exemption, a Shangla/Chitral resident had to prove their domicile status and obtain an Income Tax exemption certificate from FBR**, which would be presented to any withholding agents (employers, banks, etc.) to prevent tax deduction at source【1†L159-L167】. The taxpayer would retain these documents as evidence in case of any query. The government made the process relatively facilitative – dedicated helpdesks were created to issue the necessary certificates promptly to eligible taxpayers【1†L159-L167】. 

**References:** Official legal provisions and government notifications underpinning the above include Clause 145A, Part I of Second Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001【37†L267-L272】 (inserted via Finance Act 2019), and FBR’s circulars and directives for implementing the exemption in FATA/PATA regions【2†L66-L73】【1†L159-L167】. For further reading, you may refer to the text of Clause 145A (Second Schedule)【37†L267-L272】 and FBR’s public notices about tax exemptions for Malakand Division and erstwhile tribal areas【2†L66-L73】, as well as the Finance Act 2023 updates which clarified the sunset of this exemption【10†L149-L157】. These will provide clarity on the legal scope and the administrative process of the income tax exemption for individuals in Shangla, Chitral and other similar zones.

Income Tax Exemption for Shangla and Chitral Residents (PATA Areas)
Tax-Exempt Zone Status of Shangla and Chitral
Shangla (Swat region) and Chitral are part of the Provincially Administered Tribal Areas (PATA) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which were historically outside the scope of federal income tax laws. After the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018, these areas formally became “taxable” territories, but a temporary tax exemption was granted as part of their merger transition. In practical terms, the Malakand Division (which includes Swat/Shangla and Chitral) was treated as a tax-exempt zone for several years. Officials confirmed that “the Malakand Division and all merged tribal districts have been exempted from taxes till June 2023”.
However, this blanket exemption was time-bound. The law provided relief up to 30 June 2023, and a proposed one-year extension to June 2024 was withdrawn in the Finance Act 2023. Bottom line: Under current law (2025), Shangla and Chitral were classified as tax-exempt zones up to 30-06-2023, but that exemption period has lapsed. No further extension was enacted, meaning income earned in these areas after July 1, 2023 is no longer automatically exempt from income tax.
Legal Provisions Granting the Exemption
The income tax exemption for residents of FATA/PATA (including Shangla and Chitral) was explicitly provided in the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 via the Second Schedule. The key provision was Clause (145A), Part I of the Second Schedule, introduced by Finance Act 2019. Clause 145A states in effect:
“Any income which was not chargeable to tax prior to the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 2018 (XXXVII of 2018) of any individual domiciled or company and association of persons resident in the Tribal Areas forming part of the Provinces of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan under paragraph (d) of Article 246 of the Constitution, with effect from 1st June 2018 to 30th June 2023 (both days inclusive).”
In simpler terms, income of persons belonging to the tribal areas (PATA/FATA) that were previously outside the tax net became exempt from income tax for the period 01-06-2018 through 30-06-2023. This covered Shangla and Chitral since they fall under the “Tribal Areas forming part of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa” as per Article 246(d) of the Constitution.
Additionally, the law provided corresponding relief in tax withholding provisions. For example, Clause (109A), Part IV of the Second Schedule (also added in 2019) ensured that withholding tax requirements did not apply to payments to FATA/PATA residents during the exemption period. In essence, the Ordinance and its Second Schedule collectively allowed eligible individuals to earn income without incurring income tax liability up to the mid-2023 cutoff. This legal framework was initially implemented via FBR notifications (SRO 887(I)/2018 later replaced by SRO 1213(I)/2018) and then cemented in the Income Tax Ordinance by Parliament.
Important: As noted, these provisions expired on 30 June 2023. The Finance Bill 2023 had proposed extending the exemption to 2024, but the final Finance Act 2023 did not include the extension, effectively ending the tax holiday. Therefore, no section of the law currently in force extends the income tax exemption beyond 2023 for Shangla, Chitral or other ex-FATA/PATA areas.
Domicile vs. Place of Duty – Conditions for Exemption
Under the Ordinance’s language, the exemption is tied to a person’s status (domicile/residency) in the specified area, not strictly to the place where the income is earned. For individuals, the law uses the criterion of being “domiciled” in the tribal area. In practice, domicile means the individual’s permanent legal residence is in Shangla, Chitral or another exempt district (usually evidenced by a domicile certificate). For companies or AOPs, the criterion was being “resident” in the tribal area (intended to mean their principal office or management is based there).
Notably, the exemption was not explicitly limited to income arising within those areas. The wording raised questions such as whether a domiciled individual’s income earned outside the area would also be tax-free. The law as written suggests the exemption is personal (status-based) rather than strictly geographical. This ambiguity led to debates and even misuse – e.g. some taxpayers with tribal area domicile were claiming tax exemption on nationwide business activities.
In summary: To qualify, an individual had to be domiciled in Shangla/Chitral (a non-local merely working there would not qualify under the clause). To claim the income tax exemption, eligible taxpayers needed to provide proof of their status and follow certain procedures:
•	Domicile Certificate: The individual should obtain an official domicile certificate of the relevant district (e.g. Shangla or Chitral) as evidence that they are domiciled in a PATA region. This document is fundamental to establish eligibility under Clause 145A.
•	Tax Exemption Certificate from FBR: In practice, the Federal Board of Revenue required tribal area taxpayers to apply for an exemption certificate (under Section 159 of the Ordinance) to ensure no tax is withheld from their income. The Regional Tax Office (RTO) – Peshawar set up facilitation centers to assist in issuance of these certificates. For example, a Tax Facilitation Centre in Malakand was established specifically “with the purpose of speedy issuance of ... exemption certificates to local industrialists”. While that reference was about businesses, individual salary earners and others also needed to obtain similar certificates so that employers or banks would not deduct withholding tax on salaries, bank profit, etc., during the exemption period. FBR issued detailed circulars outlining the procedure for issuance of exemption certificates to FATA/PATA residents (for instance, Income Tax Circular No. 09 and 13 of 2021 dealt with mechanisms for exemption on imports and other incomes for FATA/PATA taxpayers).
•	Other Supporting Documents: When applying for the FBR exemption certificate or dealing with an employer/bank, one may be asked for additional proofs such as a copy of the Computerized National Identity Card (CNIC) showing a permanent address in the exempt area, a letter from the employer confirming the posting in the tribal area (if applicable), or any other evidence the tax authorities deem necessary. These help confirm that the income recipient is genuinely a resident of the exempt zone. For instance, for industrial import exemptions, FBR required documents like the domicile certificate, local chamber of commerce letter, etc., to issue the relief certificate (similar principles would apply to personal income exemption claims).
•	Tax Return Filing: During the exemption period, an eligible person’s income was exempt but it was good practice (and sometimes required) to still file an income tax return declaring the income and claiming the exemption under the relevant clause. The return would disclose the income but show it as exempt under Clause 145A of Part I, Second Schedule. This helps document the claim and ensures transparency. If the income was solely exempt and below the normal taxable threshold, FBR generally did not pursue tax, but filing a return citing the exemption clause was advisable, especially for substantial incomes.
In summary, to avail the exemption, a Shangla/Chitral resident had to prove their domicile status and obtain an Income Tax exemption certificate from FBR, which would be presented to any withholding agents (employers, banks, etc.) to prevent tax deduction at source. The taxpayer would retain these documents as evidence in case of any query. The government made the process relatively facilitative – dedicated helpdesks were created to issue the necessary certificates promptly to eligible taxpayers.

**Subject:** Sindh Sales Tax on Royalty Payments to PQA – Advisory

Dear FAP Team,

Thank you for reaching out with your queries regarding the applicability of Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on the royalty payments made to Port Qasim Authority (PQA). We understand that these questions arise in light of recent developments, including the dismissal of your constitutional petition by the Sindh High Court and the need to consider voluntary compliance with any SST obligations. Below, we address each of your concerns in detail, referencing the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“SSTSA 2011”), relevant schedules, and the information from the provided documents.

## Applicable SST Rate on Royalty/Franchise Services  
Under the SSTSA 2011, payments characterized as “royalty” for use of PQA’s property/rights are viewed as consideration for **franchise services** (tariff heading 9823.0000) under the law. The Second Schedule of SSTSA 2011 explicitly includes “franchise services either on the giving or receiving end, including royalties or similar financial benefits arising out of intellectual property rights or other factors of business goodwill”【18†L2016-L2023】. In practical terms, this means the royalty fee to PQA falls within the ambit of taxable services in Sindh. 

**Standard vs. Reduced Tax Rate:** The general statutory **rate of SST on franchise/royalty services is 13%**, which is the standard rate for services in Sindh. However, Sindh has prescribed a special **reduced rate of 10%** (ten percent) **without any input tax adjustment allowed** for franchise services【19†L2619-L2627】. In other words, by default, SST on franchise/royalty fees is charged at 10% with no input tax credit entitlement to the service recipient. Taxpayers do have the *option* to pay the full standard rate (13%) on such services under a special procedure, in order to claim input tax adjustments【11†L1-L4】. This optional regime is intended to align with the fact that Federal Excise Duty on franchise fees was historically 10%, while allowing those who prefer to claim input tax to pay at the normal rate【19†L2619-L2627】【11†L1-L4】. 

In summary, **the applicable SST rate on the royalty paid to PQA is 10% (under tariff heading 9823.0000) if no input credit is to be claimed, or 13% if FAP/PQA opts to treat it under the normal regime with input tax credit.** We advise confirming with PQA/SRB under which regime the tax is being (or will be) paid so that the correct rate is applied consistent with your business needs.

## Input Tax Credit on SST Paid to PQA  
Your next questions concern the availability of **input tax credit** to FAP for any SST paid on these royalties, including for past periods:

- **Claiming Input Tax Credit if SST is Paid Now:** Yes, **FAP can claim input tax credit** for SST paid on the royalty payments **provided certain conditions are met.** Crucially, to be eligible for input adjustment, the tax must be charged at the standard rate and supported by a proper tax invoice from the service provider (PQA). If the royalty is taxed under the **concessionary 10% rate**, the Sindh tariff explicitly disallows any input tax adjustment to the recipient【19†L2619-L2627】. This means that if PQA/FAP utilize the 10% reduced rate for franchise services, FAP **would not be able to claim input credit** for that SST – the tax would simply become a cost. Conversely, if arrangements are made to pay SST at the full 13% rate (under the special procedure election), the SST paid can be treated like any normal input tax (subject to the usual documentation and declaration requirements) and offset against FAP’s SST output liability. In short, **input credit is only available if the tax is paid at the standard rate and all invoicing requirements are satisfied**, not under the reduced-rate/no-credit scheme【19†L2619-L2627】【11†L1-L4】.

- **Input Tax for Previous Years’ Royalty Payments:** Claiming input tax credit for SST now paid on **prior years**’ royalty payments is more complex. The SST law generally requires that input tax be claimed in the tax period in which the tax invoice is issued (or within a limited time thereafter), and it mandates possession of a valid **sales tax invoice** meeting all requirements of the SST Act/Rules. In practical terms, this means PQA would need to **declare those past royalty charges as taxable services in its SST returns for the relevant periods and issue valid SST invoices to FAP dated for those periods**. Only then would FAP have legally valid documentation to claim input tax. If PQA did not charge or report SST on those royalties at the time, retrospective adjustment is challenging. 

  Provincial tax statutes do not typically allow open-ended retrospective credit; there are likely time-bar limitations (for example, in many cases input tax must be claimed within the same financial year or within a prescribed number of months of the invoice date). Since the royalty payments from July 2011 onward were historically not invoiced with SST, simply paying the tax now (in 2025) for past years may not automatically entitle FAP to input adjustments for those past periods. **In essence, input tax credit for previously unpaid periods is not guaranteed and would require corrective compliance steps by PQA.** PQA would have to **amend past returns or otherwise account for those past services now**, and SRB’s permission may be needed to allow FAP to claim input for such backdated periods. We recommend discussing a mechanism with PQA and SRB – for example, whether PQA can issue a consolidated tax invoice or credit note/reference for past periods’ royalties upon payment of the tax – but be aware that **the SST Act’s constraints may effectively bar input claims for very old periods**. At the very least, FAP should obtain and retain documentation from PQA for any tax paid on past royalties (e.g. a letter or invoice referencing the period and amount of SST) and seek specific guidance from SRB on claiming such input. (Notably, in your constitutional petition one grievance was the **“denial of input adjustment on the tax charged at a rate lower than the statutory rate”**, which underscores that under the law as it stands, no input is allowed on the reduced rate【3†L161-L168】.)

## Sindh High Court Dismissal – Legal Implications and Appeal Options  
As you noted, the Sindh High Court has **dismissed the constitutional petition** that FAP (and other petitioners) had filed in 2018 challenging the levy of SST on these royalty payments. The dismissal, we understand, was on grounds of **maintainability**, meaning the court did not entertain the petition on its merits. According to PQA’s recent correspondence, both petitions related to sales tax on royalty have indeed been dismissed by the High Court【21†L21-L29】. 

The immediate legal implication of this dismissal is that **no relief has been granted to FAP by the High Court**, and the **status quo legal position – that the royalty payments are subject to SST under the SSTSA 2011 – remains in force**. The High Court’s decision on maintainability typically suggests that the court found an alternate remedy was available or that the constitutional challenge was not the appropriate course at that stage. In practical terms, this means SRB’s demands for SST on the royalty are not judicially restrained, and PQA (as the service provider) is obligated to collect and deposit the SST going forward【21†L64-L72】. PQA’s April 2025 letter to FAP reinforces this, stating that *“as per orders of the Sindh Revenue Board currently holding the field, sales tax is applicable on royalty which PQA is obliged to collect and deposit”*【21†L64-L72】. 

**Can the matter be appealed to the Supreme Court?** Yes. FAP does have the option to challenge the High Court’s dismissal before the **Supreme Court of Pakistan**. Since the High Court did not adjudicate the substantive issues (e.g. whether the royalty truly constitutes a taxable service or whether the SST Act provisions are unconstitutional as applied), FAP could file a petition for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court may then review whether the High Court was correct in refusing to hear the case and possibly address the constitutional and legal questions involved. It is important to note, however, that an appeal on a dismissal for maintainability can be an uphill task – the Supreme Court will consider if there was a significant question of law or lack of alternate remedy justifying its intervention. FAP’s arguments would likely emphasize the constitutional points (such as the vires of Entry 9823.0000 and Section 2(46) of SSTSA 2011, and the bar of Article 165 of the Constitution regarding taxing a federal instrumentality) which remained unaddressed【2†L78-L86】【21†L64-L72】. If the Supreme Court grants leave, it could potentially overturn the High Court’s decision and/or remand for a hearing on merits. 

In deciding whether to pursue an appeal, FAP should weigh the prospects of success and the time involved. **Meanwhile, since no stay is in place, compliance with the SST law (or obtaining interim relief through the appellate forums under the SST Act, if available) is advisable to avoid accumulation of further liabilities**. Engaging with the tax authorities through the statutory appeal process (e.g. appeal to the Commissioner Appeals or the Appellate Tribunal on any assessment orders that may be issued by SRB) is another avenue that can be pursued in parallel. We can assist in evaluating the merits of a Supreme Court appeal and represent FAP if you choose to proceed.

## Voluntary Discharge of SST Liability – Tariff Heading and Rate Considerations  
Given the High Court outcome, FAP may consider **voluntarily discharging the SST liability** on past and ongoing royalty payments to mitigate exposure to penalties or further litigation. In doing so, it is critical to carefully choose the **appropriate tariff heading and tax rate** under which payments are made/declared, to ensure legal consistency with FAP’s position and to optimize tax credit outcomes.

**Avoiding “Franchise Services” Classification (9823.0000):** We strongly advise caution in classifying these royalty payments under the `9823.0000 – Franchise Services` heading when making voluntary payments. During litigation, FAP’s stance was that the **arrangement with PQA is not a franchise and involves no service element** – for instance, the petition argued that *“mere description of any payment as royalty does not make it royalty or franchise as in substance it is not relatable to any service,”* and that permission to use land/facility is not the same as a taxable service【2†L62-L70】. If FAP were now to start reporting the payments as “franchise services” in order to pay SST, it would **contradict the earlier position** and could be viewed as an implicit admission that those payments are indeed taxable franchise fees. This could not only undermine any pending legal challenge (e.g. an appeal to Supreme Court) but also represent a shift in stance that might be used against FAP in proceedings. 

Moreover, payments under the franchise services heading are, by default, subject to the **reduced 10% rate with no input adjustment**【19†L2619-L2627】. While the 10% rate may seem financially beneficial at first glance (being lower than 13%), using it means FAP would **forfeit the ability to claim input tax credit** on that tax. In effect, the tax paid would become a final cost. Given that FAP as a terminal operator likely charges SST on its own services (output tax) and could otherwise utilize the input credit, foregoing that credit could increase the net tax cost. Additionally, opting for the concessionary rate after having contended that such a regime (with no input) was arbitrary and not applicable may appear inconsistent. The petition filed by FAP even challenged the legality of denying input adjustment at a lower rate【3†L161-L168】, so voluntarily choosing that very regime could weaken FAP’s credibility in any forum.

**Recommendation – Select the Appropriate Tariff Heading:** We recommend that any voluntary payment of SST on past or ongoing royalties be done **under protest and with a classification that least prejudices FAP’s legal position.** One approach is to coordinate with PQA and SRB to determine if there is an alternative, more appropriate service category (tariff heading) under which these payments can be reported. For instance, the nature of the payment is akin to a license fee or operating right granted by PQA (a port authority). If there is a category for “port and terminal operator services” or similar (as SST laws have evolved, some rules now specifically list port/terminal operations as taxable services), it might be worth exploring whether PQA’s charges could fall under that instead. However, if SRB’s stance (as evidenced by their notices and PQA’s directives) is firmly that this is a franchise service, FAP may have limited flexibility. In that case, if you proceed to pay, it may be wiser to **elect the standard rate of 13%** on this service and explicitly reserve your legal stance. Paying at 13% would allow FAP to claim input tax (again, subject to invoice requirements) and demonstrates compliance **without conceding the characterization issue**, since you could note that payment is being made in view of the outstanding orders but not as an acceptance that the levy was correctly characterized. We suggest writing to SRB (or noting in the payment covering letter) that the payment is being made **under protest/without prejudice** to FAP’s legal rights, and that the classification is as directed by SRB/PQA. This creates a record that FAP has not abandoned its legal position even as it complies. 

In summary, **do not simply start using the 9823.0000 “Franchise Services” category at 10% in your SST returns without careful thought.** Instead, decide on the classification and rate in consultation with counsel (and ideally with guidance from SRB) to strike a balance between cost efficiency and legal consistency. We can assist in drafting a letter to SRB/PQA to clarify the basis of any voluntary tax payment so as to protect FAP’s interests.

## Requirements for Input Tax Credit Eligibility  
If and when FAP pays SST on the royalty (whether for past periods or going forward), to actually **claim the input tax credit** against your output SST liabilities, the following requirements must be satisfied under the SST law:

- **PQA Must Charge and Declare the Tax:** PQA, as the service provider of the “royalty/franchise service,” must **declare this service and the SST charged in its monthly SST returns**. Essentially, PQA needs to be a registered person with Sindh Revenue Board (if not already) and treat the royalty fees as taxable receipts in the period they are paid. The recent PQA letter indicates PQA is aware of this obligation and is in fact pressing FAP to pay so that PQA can deposit the tax【21†L64-L72】. PQA even advised that if FAP opts to deposit the tax directly with SRB, FAP should inform PQA of the periods and amounts so PQA can adjust that liability in its records and defend against any future demands【21†L45-L53】. This shows that PQA intends to account for the tax one way or another. From FAP’s perspective, it is important that PQA does reflect the tax in its filings; otherwise, SRB’s system will not show tax output against which your input can be matched, raising the risk of input disallowance in audit. 

- **Valid SST Invoice from PQA:** FAP must obtain a **valid sales tax invoice** issued by PQA for the service. The invoice should meet all requirements of the SSTSA 2011 and the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Rules (e.g. it should contain PQA’s SST registration number, invoice number/date, description of service (royalty/license fee), the value of the service, SST amount charged, etc.). Under Section 26 of SSTSA 2011 and related rules, a registered service provider is required to issue an invoice for each taxable service provided. This document is the primary evidence for FAP’s input tax claim. We recommend that when FAP pays any SST amount to PQA (or even if directly to SRB on PQA’s behalf), **ensure that PQA issues an invoice or at least a written acknowledgement referencing an invoice number for that SST**. Without a proper invoice, FAP’s input claim could be denied by SRB on procedural grounds.

- **Tax Deposit and Invoice Timing:** The input tax is claimable in the tax period in which the invoice is issued (or the tax is paid), in line with the return filing. For ongoing royalties, this simply means each time PQA invoices the monthly/quarterly royalty with SST, FAP can claim the input in that same month/quarter’s SST return. For the backlog of past years, if PQA issues invoices now (dated today) for past period royalties, FAP may end up claiming all that input in the current period’s return (unless special arrangements are made). We reiterate that SRB may scrutinize such large input claims, so all documentation should be in order. It might even be prudent to seek **prior approval or an official ruling from SRB** on how to handle the past period input credits, to avoid any future disallowance.

In essence, **input tax credit is contingent on PQA’s compliance and proper documentation**. FAP should coordinate very closely with PQA to make sure that as you discharge the SST liability, PQA simultaneously fulfills its role by issuing invoices and reporting the tax. If PQA fails to do so, FAP’s remedy (input claim) could be jeopardized.

To summarize our advice: the royalty is considered a taxable service in Sindh (franchise services) at a 10% default SST rate (no input allowed) or 13% standard (with input), FAP can claim input tax if the proper route is taken (13% with invoices), claiming old period inputs may be difficult but should be pursued carefully, the High Court’s dismissal means the tax is payable (subject to any appeal you may file), and any voluntary compliance should be handled in a manner that safeguards FAP’s legal stance (avoid outright concession by using the franchise category at reduced rate) while meeting the statutory requirements for invoicing and reporting so that input credits can be availed.

We can also help with strategizing a potential appeal to the Supreme Court or navigating discussions with SRB/PQA.

Dear Mr. Zuhair,

 

With reference to your recent discussion with Mr. Mazhar regarding the above subject, please note the following:

 

In April 2018, we received a letter from the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) directing us to pay Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on royalty payments, categorized under Tariff heading 9823.0000 Franchise services. This letter was also issued to other terminal operators at Port Qasim Authority (PQA). Copies of both documents are enclosed for your reference.

 

Accordingly, we, along with other operators, filed a constitutional petition in the Sindh High Court and obtained a stay order. Copies are enclosed for your reference.

 

Last week, we received a letter from PQA requesting payment of SST at 10% on royalty amounts. A copy of the letter is attached.

 

As per our Implementation Agreement (IA) with PQA, FAP calculates and pays royalty in accordance with the agreed formula, exclusive of SST. Furthermore, PQA has never issued any invoice for royalty as a taxable service.

 

In light of the above, we seek your advice on the following points:

 

What is the applicable SST rate on royalty/Franchise services?
If SST is paid, can FAP claim input tax credit?
Can we claimed input tax for SST to be paid for previous years?
 

 

We look forward to your guidance on the above.

**Subject: Advisory on SST Applicability on Royalty Payments to PQA and Input Tax Adjustment Options**

Dear [Client Name],

Thank you for your email and for sharing the background documents relating to the applicability of Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on royalty payments made to Port Qasim Authority (PQA). Based on the facts shared, the recent letter received from PQA, and our review of the applicable provisions under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SSTSA 2011), we provide the following guidance:

---

### 1. **Legal Recourse: Possibility of Filing Appeal Before Supreme Court of Pakistan**

It is pertinent to highlight that the constitutional petition filed before the Sindh High Court in 2018, jointly by FAP and other terminal operators, was dismissed on the ground of maintainability and **not on the merits of the case**. This means that the Hon’ble Court did not adjudicate the substantive legal issues, such as whether the royalty payments fall within the scope of taxable “franchise services” under the SST law or whether such levy violates constitutional protections (e.g. Article 165 of the Constitution regarding taxation of a federal instrumentality).

Given this, FAP retains the legal right to consider filing a **Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA)** before the Supreme Court of Pakistan. The petition may seek a review of the High Court's dismissal and request a remand for adjudication on legal grounds. If the Supreme Court is satisfied that important constitutional and legal questions remain unanswered, it may grant leave and hear the matter. We recommend conducting a feasibility assessment and preparing the petition, should you wish to pursue this course.

---

### 2. **Taxability and Input Adjustment: Implication of Reduced Rate under Franchise Services**

As noted, SRB has taken the position that royalty payments to PQA fall under tariff heading **9823.0000 – Franchise Services**, subject to a **concessionary SST rate of 10%**, applicable where both the service provider and recipient are **resident persons**.

It is important to note that:
- This 10% rate is a **reduced rate** under a special regime;
- Under this regime, **no input tax adjustment is allowed** to the recipient;
- This renders the SST paid as a **non-creditable cost** to FAP.

Given that both PQA and FAP are resident entities, this restriction will apply to all royalty payments treated as franchise services. If this path is followed, FAP will not be able to claim input tax credit, resulting in a direct increase in the cost base. Moreover, this classification may undermine FAP’s earlier stance taken in the constitutional petition that the royalty does not qualify as a franchise service.

---

### 3. **Tariff Classification Strategy: Explore Neutral Tariff Heading under Standard Rate**

To safeguard legal consistency and to preserve the possibility of input tax adjustment, we recommend **re-evaluating the tariff heading** under which SST is to be discharged. It may be more appropriate to explore:
- Tariff headings relating to **contractual services**, **licensing arrangements**, or **port/terminal operations**, depending on the nature of the IA;
- Categories taxed at the **standard SST rate (currently 13%)**, which allow for input tax adjustment.

By discharging SST under a neutral heading taxed at the standard rate, FAP can avoid the restrictions of the reduced rate regime and also retain the ability to offset this tax against its output liability. This strategy would also be consistent with your previously asserted legal position.

We are available to assist in conducting a classification review of the Implementation Agreement and to determine the most appropriate tariff heading.

---

### 4. **Claiming Input Tax Credit: Coordination Required with PQA**

To successfully claim input tax credit on SST paid to PQA—whether for current or historical royalty payments—it is critical that the following conditions are fulfilled:

- **Declaration of Output Tax by PQA:** PQA must declare the SST liability in its **monthly sales tax return** corresponding to the royalty payments received. This is a statutory precondition for FAP to claim input tax.
  
- **Issuance of Valid Sales Tax Invoice:** A valid SST invoice must be issued by PQA in accordance with **Section 26 of SSTSA 2011** and associated rules. This invoice must include PQA’s registration number, the nature and value of the service, SST amount, and the relevant tax period.

Without these two components—declaration in SRB’s return by the supplier and issuance of a compliant invoice—FAP’s input claim will not be accepted by SRB, even if the tax has been paid.

We therefore recommend that FAP **formally engage with PQA** to:
- Confirm that SST on royalty will be declared in their next sales tax return;
- Request issuance of proper SST invoices aligned with each tax period; and
- Coordinate on classification and documentation to ensure compliance and input eligibility.

---

### 5. **Input Tax for Previous Years: Legal and Procedural Challenges**

With respect to input tax on royalty payments related to **prior tax periods**, it is important to understand that:
- The SST rules typically **limit the period** within which input tax can be claimed (e.g. same tax year or within six months of the invoice date);
- Retroactive claim is generally not permitted unless **PQA retrospectively declares the tax**, issues valid invoices, and potentially seeks SRB’s condonation;
- Input tax for older periods may be **subject to rejection** unless supported by proper documentation and SRB approval.

Therefore, if SST is to be paid now for historical royalty, we recommend that FAP seek confirmation from PQA that they will:
- Declare such SST for the respective periods (even if now reported in consolidated form);
- Issue invoices referencing the specific historical periods.

We would also suggest **approaching SRB for guidance** or pre-approval on how such input tax for prior years may be treated in current period returns, to avoid post-filing disputes.

---

### 6. **Suggested Way Forward**

In view of the above, we recommend the following action plan:

1. **Legal Evaluation:** Consider filing a CPLA before the Supreme Court on the High Court’s dismissal for maintainability;
2. **Tariff Reassessment:** Avoid voluntary payment under the franchise services heading at 10%, and explore neutral headings with 13% rate;
3. **Coordination with PQA:** Request PQA to declare SST in upcoming return and issue compliant SST invoices;
4. **Documentation for Input Tax:** Maintain complete documentary trail, including cover letters or statements clarifying that any payments are made under protest or without prejudice to legal position;
5. **Engagement with SRB:** Initiate discussions with SRB regarding claimability of input tax for prior years, if required.

---

Please let us know if you would like us to assist in preparing a communication for PQA or initiate discussions with SRB. We remain at your disposal to assist with all next steps, including litigation support and advisory on tariff classification.

Warm regards,  
**Zuhair Minhas**  
_Tax Advisor_  
**Tax Way**

Dear FAP Team,
Thank you for reaching out with your queries regarding the applicability of Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on the royalty payments made to Port Qasim Authority (PQA). We understand that these questions arise in light of recent developments, including the dismissal of your constitutional petition by the Sindh High Court and the need to consider voluntary compliance with any SST obligations. Below, we address each of your concerns in detail, referencing the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“SSTSA 2011”), relevant schedules, and the information from the provided documents.
At the outset, we would like to inform you that the general statutory rate of SST on services is 15% for services in Sindh. Nevertheless, Sindh has prescribed a special reduced rate of 10% (ten percent) without any input tax adjustment allowed for franchise services in case of resident person. In other words, by default, SST on franchise/royalty fees is charged at 10% with no input tax credit entitlement to the service recipient. Taxpayers do have the option to pay the full standard rate (15%) on such services under a special procedure, in order to claim input tax adjustments. 
Input Tax Credit on SST Paid to PQA
Your next questions concern the availability of input tax credit to FAP for any SST paid on these royalties, including for past periods:
•	Claiming Input Tax Credit if SST is Paid Now: Yes, FAP can claim input tax credit for SST paid on the royalty payments provided certain conditions are met. Crucially, to be eligible for input adjustment, the tax must be charged at the standard rate and supported by a proper tax invoice from the service provider (PQA). If the royalty is taxed under the concessionary 10% rate, the Sindh tariff explicitly disallows any input tax adjustment to the recipient. This means that if PQA/FAP utilize the 10% reduced rate for franchise services, FAP would not be able to claim input credit for that SST – the tax would simply become a cost. Conversely, if arrangements are made to pay SST at the full 13% rate (under the special procedure election), the SST paid can be treated like any normal input tax (subject to the usual documentation and declaration requirements) and offset against FAP’s SST output liability. In short, input credit is only available if the tax is paid at the standard rate and all invoicing requirements are satisfied, not under the reduced-rate/no-credit scheme.
•	Input Tax for Previous Years’ Royalty Payments: Claiming input tax credit for SST now paid on prior years’ royalty payments is more complex. The SST law generally requires that input tax be claimed in the tax period in which the tax invoice is issued (or within a limited time thereafter), and it mandates possession of a valid sales tax invoice meeting all requirements of the SST Act/Rules. In practical terms, this means PQA would need to declare those past royalty charges as taxable services in its SST returns for the relevant periods and issue valid SST invoices to FAP dated for those periods. Only then would FAP have legally valid documentation to claim input tax. If PQA did not charge or report SST on those royalties at the time, retrospective adjustment is challenging.
Provincial tax statutes do not typically allow open-ended retrospective credit; there are likely time-bar limitations (for example, in many cases input tax must be claimed within the same financial year or within a prescribed number of months of the invoice date). Since the royalty payments from July 2011 onward were historically not invoiced with SST, simply paying the tax now (in 2025) for past years may not automatically entitle FAP to input adjustments for those past periods. In essence, input tax credit for previously unpaid periods is not guaranteed and would require corrective compliance steps by PQA. PQA would have to amend past returns or otherwise account for those past services now, and SRB’s permission may be needed to allow FAP to claim input for such backdated periods. We recommend discussing a mechanism with PQA and SRB – for example, whether PQA can issue a consolidated tax invoice or credit note/reference for past periods’ royalties upon payment of the tax – but be aware that the SST Act’s constraints may effectively bar input claims for very old periods. At the very least, FAP should obtain and retain documentation from PQA for any tax paid on past royalties (e.g. a letter or invoice referencing the period and amount of SST) and seek specific guidance from SRB on claiming such input. (Notably, in your constitutional petition one grievance was the “denial of input adjustment on the tax charged at a rate lower than the statutory rate”, which underscores that under the law as it stands, no input is allowed on the reduced rate.)
Sindh High Court Dismissal – Legal Implications and Appeal Options
As you noted, the Sindh High Court has dismissed the constitutional petition that FAP (and other petitioners) had filed in 2018 challenging the levy of SST on these royalty payments. The dismissal, we understand, was on grounds of maintainability, meaning the court did not entertain the petition on its merits. According to PQA’s recent correspondence, both petitions related to sales tax on royalty have indeed been dismissed by the High Court.
The immediate legal implication of this dismissal is that no relief has been granted to FAP by the High Court, and the status quo legal position – that the royalty payments are subject to SST under the SSTSA 2011 – remains in force. The High Court’s decision on maintainability typically suggests that the court found an alternate remedy was available or that the constitutional challenge was not the appropriate course at that stage. In practical terms, this means SRB’s demands for SST on the royalty are not judicially restrained, and PQA (as the service provider) is obligated to collect and deposit the SST going forward. PQA’s April 2025 letter to FAP reinforces this, stating that “as per orders of the Sindh Revenue Board currently holding the field, sales tax is applicable on royalty which PQA is obliged to collect and deposit”.
Can the matter be appealed to the Supreme Court? Yes. FAP does have the option to challenge the High Court’s dismissal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Since the High Court did not adjudicate the substantive issues (e.g. whether the royalty truly constitutes a taxable service or whether the SST Act provisions are unconstitutional as applied), FAP could file a petition for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court may then review whether the High Court was correct in refusing to hear the case and possibly address the constitutional and legal questions involved. It is important to note, however, that an appeal on a dismissal for maintainability can be an uphill task – the Supreme Court will consider if there was a significant question of law or lack of alternate remedy justifying its intervention. FAP’s arguments would likely emphasize the constitutional points (such as the vires of Entry 9823.0000 and Section 2(46) of SSTSA 2011, and the bar of Article 165 of the Constitution regarding taxing a federal instrumentality) which remained unaddressed. If the Supreme Court grants leave, it could potentially overturn the High Court’s decision and/or remand for a hearing on merits.
In deciding whether to pursue an appeal, FAP should weigh the prospects of success and the time involved. Meanwhile, since no stay is in place, compliance with the SST law (or obtaining interim relief through the appellate forums under the SST Act, if available) is advisable to avoid accumulation of further liabilities. Engaging with the tax authorities through the statutory appeal process (e.g. appeal to the Commissioner Appeals or the Appellate Tribunal on any assessment orders that may be issued by SRB) is another avenue that can be pursued in parallel. We can assist in evaluating the merits of a Supreme Court appeal and represent FAP if you choose to proceed.
Voluntary Discharge of SST Liability – Tariff Heading and Rate Considerations
Given the High Court outcome, FAP may consider voluntarily discharging the SST liability on past and ongoing royalty payments to mitigate exposure to penalties or further litigation. In doing so, it is critical to carefully choose the appropriate tariff heading and tax rate under which payments are made/declared, to ensure legal consistency with FAP’s position and to optimize tax credit outcomes.
Avoiding “Franchise Services” Classification (9823.0000): We strongly advise caution in classifying these royalty payments under the 9823.0000 – Franchise Services heading when making voluntary payments. During litigation, FAP’s stance was that the arrangement with PQA is not a franchise and involves no service element – for instance, the petition argued that “mere description of any payment as royalty does not make it royalty or franchise as in substance it is not relatable to any service,” and that permission to use land/facility is not the same as a taxable service. If FAP were now to start reporting the payments as “franchise services” in order to pay SST, it would contradict the earlier position and could be viewed as an implicit admission that those payments are indeed taxable franchise fees. This could not only undermine any pending legal challenge (e.g. an appeal to Supreme Court) but also represent a shift in stance that might be used against FAP in proceedings.
Moreover, payments under the franchise services heading are, by default, subject to the reduced 10% rate with no input adjustment. While the 10% rate may seem financially beneficial at first glance (being lower than 13%), using it means FAP would forfeit the ability to claim input tax credit on that tax. In effect, the tax paid would become a final cost. Given that FAP as a terminal operator likely charges SST on its own services (output tax) and could otherwise utilize the input credit, foregoing that credit could increase the net tax cost. Additionally, opting for the concessionary rate after having contended that such a regime (with no input) was arbitrary and not applicable may appear inconsistent. The petition filed by FAP even challenged the legality of denying input adjustment at a lower rate, so voluntarily choosing that very regime could weaken FAP’s credibility in any forum.
Recommendation – Select the Appropriate Tariff Heading: We recommend that any voluntary payment of SST on past or ongoing royalties be done under protest and with a classification that least prejudices FAP’s legal position. One approach is to coordinate with PQA and SRB to determine if there is an alternative, more appropriate service category (tariff heading) under which these payments can be reported. For instance, the nature of the payment is akin to a license fee or operating right granted by PQA (a port authority). If there is a category for “port and terminal operator services” or similar (as SST laws have evolved, some rules now specifically list port/terminal operations as taxable services), it might be worth exploring whether PQA’s charges could fall under that instead. However, if SRB’s stance (as evidenced by their notices and PQA’s directives) is firmly that this is a franchise service, FAP may have limited flexibility. In that case, if you proceed to pay, it may be wiser to elect the standard rate of 13% on this service and explicitly reserve your legal stance. Paying at 13% would allow FAP to claim input tax (again, subject to invoice requirements) and demonstrates compliance without conceding the characterization issue, since you could note that payment is being made in view of the outstanding orders but not as an acceptance that the levy was correctly characterized. We suggest writing to SRB (or noting in the payment covering letter) that the payment is being made under protest/without prejudice to FAP’s legal rights, and that the classification is as directed by SRB/PQA. This creates a record that FAP has not abandoned its legal position even as it complies.
In summary, do not simply start using the 9823.0000 “Franchise Services” category at 10% in your SST returns without careful thought. Instead, decide on the classification and rate in consultation with counsel (and ideally with guidance from SRB) to strike a balance between cost efficiency and legal consistency. We can assist in drafting a letter to SRB/PQA to clarify the basis of any voluntary tax payment so as to protect FAP’s interests.
Requirements for Input Tax Credit Eligibility
If and when FAP pays SST on the royalty (whether for past periods or going forward), to actually claim the input tax credit against your output SST liabilities, the following requirements must be satisfied under the SST law:
•	PQA Must Charge and Declare the Tax: PQA, as the service provider of the “royalty/franchise service,” must declare this service and the SST charged in its monthly SST returns. Essentially, PQA needs to be a registered person with Sindh Revenue Board (if not already) and treat the royalty fees as taxable receipts in the period they are paid. The recent PQA letter indicates PQA is aware of this obligation and is in fact pressing FAP to pay so that PQA can deposit the tax. PQA even advised that if FAP opts to deposit the tax directly with SRB, FAP should inform PQA of the periods and amounts so PQA can adjust that liability in its records and defend against any future demands. This shows that PQA intends to account for the tax one way or another. From FAP’s perspective, it is important that PQA does reflect the tax in its filings; otherwise, SRB’s system will not show tax output against which your input can be matched, raising the risk of input disallowance in audit.
•	Valid SST Invoice from PQA: FAP must obtain a valid sales tax invoice issued by PQA for the service. The invoice should meet all requirements of the SSTSA 2011 and the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Rules (e.g. it should contain PQA’s SST registration number, invoice number/date, description of service (royalty/license fee), the value of the service, SST amount charged, etc.). Under Section 26 of SSTSA 2011 and related rules, a registered service provider is required to issue an invoice for each taxable service provided. This document is the primary evidence for FAP’s input tax claim. We recommend that when FAP pays any SST amount to PQA (or even if directly to SRB on PQA’s behalf), ensure that PQA issues an invoice or at least a written acknowledgement referencing an invoice number for that SST. Without a proper invoice, FAP’s input claim could be denied by SRB on procedural grounds.
•	Tax Deposit and Invoice Timing: The input tax is claimable in the tax period in which the invoice is issued (or the tax is paid), in line with the return filing. For ongoing royalties, this simply means each time PQA invoices the monthly/quarterly royalty with SST, FAP can claim the input in that same month/quarter’s SST return. For the backlog of past years, if PQA issues invoices now (dated today) for past period royalties, FAP may end up claiming all that input in the current period’s return (unless special arrangements are made). We reiterate that SRB may scrutinize such large input claims, so all documentation should be in order. It might even be prudent to seek prior approval or an official ruling from SRB on how to handle the past period input credits, to avoid any future disallowance.
In essence, input tax credit is contingent on PQA’s compliance and proper documentation. FAP should coordinate very closely with PQA to make sure that as you discharge the SST liability, PQA simultaneously fulfills its role by issuing invoices and reporting the tax. If PQA fails to do so, FAP’s remedy (input claim) could be jeopardized.
________________________________________
Closing Remarks: We trust that the above addresses your queries regarding the SST on royalty payments to PQA. To summarize our advice: the royalty is considered a taxable service in Sindh (franchise services) at a 10% default SST rate (no input allowed) or 13% standard (with input), FAP can claim input tax if the proper route is taken (13% with invoices), claiming old period inputs may be difficult but should be pursued carefully, the High Court’s dismissal means the tax is payable (subject to any appeal you may file), and any voluntary compliance should be handled in a manner that safeguards FAP’s legal stance (avoid outright concession by using the franchise category at reduced rate) while meeting the statutory requirements for invoicing and reporting so that input credits can be availed.
Please treat this as a formal client advisory. If you need further clarification on any point or assistance with the compliance and documentation steps, do not hesitate to contact us. We can also help with strategizing a potential appeal to the Supreme Court or navigating discussions with SRB/PQA.
Thank you for your attention, and we hope this provides a clear path forward on this matter.
Sincerely,
[Your Name]
[Your Position]
[Your Firm]

Dear [Client Name],

Thank you for your email and for sharing the relevant documentation.

We understand that the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB), through its letter dated April 2018, directed terminal operators at Port Qasim Authority (PQA), including FAP, to discharge Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on royalty payments under tariff heading 9823.0000 (Franchise services). As a result, you, along with other operators, challenged the matter through a constitutional petition before the Sindh High Court, where an interim stay was obtained. However, we further note that the said petition has since been dismissed on the ground of maintainability, without adjudication on the legal merits.

In view of the recent communication from PQA requesting payment of SST at the rate of 10% on royalty payments, we address your specific queries below:

### 1. **Applicable Rate of SST on Royalty/Franchise Services**

As per SRB’s interpretation reflected in its 2018 correspondence, royalty payments made under agreements such as the Implementation Agreement (IA) are treated as consideration for "franchise services" under tariff heading 9823.0000, which is currently subject to SST at the **standard rate of 13%** (previously 10%).

While SRB’s interpretation may be debatable, especially in cases where no brand rights or business models are licensed, any voluntary discharge of SST at this stage must align with a legally supportable tariff heading. In our view, classifying royalty under “franchise services” may contradict your earlier position taken before the High Court, where you denied the existence of a franchising relationship. Therefore, discharging SST under the franchise tariff heading could amount to a tacit admission, weakening your legal position.

Instead, it is advisable to reassess whether any alternative, neutral tariff heading may apply, such as “contractual or licensing services” (tariff 9810.0000) if the arrangement fits, subject to a careful review of the IA. However, this requires a detailed legal assessment.

### 2. **Eligibility to Claim Input Tax Adjustment**

Under Section 16 of the Act read with Rule 22 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Rules, 2011, input tax is generally admissible if the following conditions are met:

- The corresponding output tax is duly declared and paid;
- A **valid sales tax invoice** is issued by the service provider (in this case, PQA);
- The service provider **declares the output tax in their SST return** for the relevant tax periods.

In your case, since PQA has historically not issued any SST invoice and has not declared the royalty as a taxable service in their monthly returns, the input tax claim by FAP would not fulfill the conditions required under the law. Therefore, unless PQA declares SST liability in their sales tax returns and issues a valid SST invoice, FAP will **not be eligible to claim input tax adjustment**.

We strongly recommend formally requesting PQA to issue SST-compliant invoices and ensure return filings for any future or past tax periods where SST is being charged.

### 3. **Input Tax Claim for Prior Periods**

As per Rule 22(2) of the Rules, input tax relating to prior tax periods can be claimed **within six months** of the relevant tax period, unless an exception under Section 47 (e.g., condonation or waiver by SRB) applies. If FAP intends to claim input tax for earlier periods beyond the limitation period, it must seek SRB’s approval for condonation, which may be considered in cases where delay was not deliberate and was due to circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control.

That said, as discussed above, without a valid SST invoice and return declaration from PQA, the input tax claim would remain inadmissible regardless of time limitations.

---

### Additional Legal Strategy Consideration

Since the High Court dismissed the petition on grounds of maintainability, and not on legal merits, the possibility of challenging the matter before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan may still be explored—particularly if a question of public importance or interpretation of taxing statutes is involved. We suggest seeking a formal legal opinion from your constitutional counsel to assess the viability of filing a **civil petition for leave to appeal (CPLA)** before the Supreme Court.

---
