**Dear Sir,**

**K-Electric Limited – Tax Year 2022 – Notice for Payment of Super Tax on High Earning Persons under Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**  

We refer to your notice (IRIS barcode No. 100000236897926) dated April 10, 2025, requiring our client to pay super tax of Rs. 1,027,977,626 under Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“Ordinance”) for Tax Year 2022. At the outset, we thank you for granting an extension for compliance until April 29, 2025. We now submit our reply on behalf of K-Electric Limited, addressing each point raised in the notice. 

## Applicability of Section 4C from Tax Year 2023 Onwards  
It is respectfully submitted that the levy of super tax under Section 4C of the Ordinance (introduced through the Finance Act, 2022) **does not apply retrospectively to Tax Year 2022, but only from Tax Year 2023 onwards.** This position has been conclusively settled by superior courts across Pakistan. Most notably, the Hon’ble Islamabad High Court (“IHC”), in its detailed judgment dated June 30, 2023 in **Writ Petition No. 4027 of 2022** (M/s Fauji Fertilizer Co. Ltd. v. Federation of Pakistan) and other connected cases, **categorically held that applying Section 4C retroactively to Tax Year 2022 violates the doctrine of past and closed transactions and infringes vested rights of taxpayers**【24†L57-L65】【24†L63-L68】. The Court emphasized that a taxpayer’s right to retain earnings from a concluded period is fundamental and cannot be curtailed by a later law unless the legislature explicitly makes the law retroactive【24†L59-L66】. Since Section 4C was enacted on July 1, 2022 (after Tax Year 2022 had already ended on June 30, 2022), the IHC ruled that any attempt to levy super tax for Tax Year 2022 is **ultra vires** (beyond lawful authority) and void【24†L61-L68】. The IHC thus **confined Section 4C’s operation to Tax Year 2023 and onwards**【24†L63-L68】【9†L53-L61】.

Similarly, the Hon’ble Sindh High Court (“SHC”), in **Constitutional Petition No. D-5842 of 2022** (*Shell Pakistan Ltd. & others v. Federation of Pakistan & others*), decided along with a batch of connected petitions, unequivocally held that **super tax under Section 4C shall be read as applicable only from Tax Year 2023 onward**【24†L72-L80】【21†L1662-L1670】. The SHC observed that applying Section 4C to income years that had already closed before its enactment would amount to an impermissible retroactive taxation without clear legislative intent, violating principles of legal certainty and fairness【24†L73-L81】【21†L1662-L1670】. In its short order announced on December 22, 2022 (reasons recorded January 13, 2023), the SHC **declared**: 

> “Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 is read to reflect that the levy shall be applicable from the tax year 2023.”【21†L1662-L1670】

*(Emphasis added.)* 

Importantly, the above IHC and SHC judgments—addressing the validity and timing of Section 4C—operate **in rem** on the law itself and are not limited to the petitioning taxpayers. In other words, these court decisions settle the interpretation of Section 4C generally, barring its retrospective enforcement for **any** taxpayer for Tax Year 2022. Accordingly, your office is bound by these pronouncements. It is respectfully requested that **no super tax demand be raised for Tax Year 2022**, as Section 4C was not legally in force for that year. Any attempt by your good office to impose super tax on our client for 2022 would be contrary to the explicit rulings of the Hon’ble High Courts and therefore without lawful authority【26†L93-L100】【26†L95-L102】. 

## Sindh High Court’s Turnover Ruling – No Impact on Clause 102A Exemption  
The audit notice heavily relied on a recent Sindh High Court judgment pertaining to **Section 113 (minimum tax on turnover)** in our client’s own case. With respect, that reliance is misplaced. The cited SHC decision dealt **only with the narrow question of whether tariff adjustment subsidies are part of “turnover” for purposes of minimum tax under Section 113**【23†L157-L165】. In that judgment (on Income Tax Reference Applications decided in 2024), the SHC answered that **the subsidy/tariff adjustment received by K-Electric from the Government is to be included in turnover for Section 113**【23†L157-L165】. **Critically, however, the SHC’s turnover ruling did not address Clause 102A or the tax exemption for income representing a subsidy**, nor did it disturb that exemption in any way【26†L109-L118】. The court was not asked to decide, and did not decide, the availability of the Clause (102A), Part I of the Second Schedule exemption for government subsidies; it focused solely on the mechanics of minimum tax calculation. 

Clause 102A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance unambiguously **exempts from tax any income that represents a subsidy granted by the Federal Government for implementing its orders**【5†L598-L607】. This provision squarely covers the tariff differential subsidy received by our client from the Government, and it **remains valid law**. The SHC’s decision on Section 113 turnover treatment does **not** override or negate Clause 102A’s exemption – it simply means that even exempt income was considered part of “turnover” for the limited purpose of computing minimum tax. There was no finding in that case that the subsidy ceased to be exempt income, and indeed **the long-standing exemption for such subsidy continues to apply**【26†L109-L117】. We respectfully submit that denying the Clause 102A exemption in K-Electric’s Tax Year 2022 assessment by invoking the SHC’s turnover judgment is a legal error. The department’s own consistent practice in prior years confirms this: in multiple earlier assessments (e.g. Tax Years 2016, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021), the **tariff subsidy was accepted as exempt under Clause 102A** during proceedings under Section 122(5A) of the Ordinance【26†L112-L120】. It is thus patently incorrect and without precedent to disallow the subsidy exemption in Tax Year 2022. The recent SHC ruling simply did not pertain to the exemption, so any reliance on it to deny Clause 102A relief is **misplaced**【26†L113-L120】. We respectfully request that the lawful exemption under Clause 102A be upheld in our client’s case, as it has been in the past. 

## Section 4C Computation after Losses and Depreciation (IHC Fauji Fertilizer Case)  
Without prejudice to the above points, **even if** (for the sake of argument) Section 4C were considered applicable to Tax Year 2022, our client’s super tax base would still be **zero** after proper adjustments. This is because K-Electric had substantial brought-forward **tax losses and unabsorbed depreciation allowances** available in 2022, which fully eliminate any positive income. The Hon’ble Islamabad High Court in the **Fauji Fertilizer case (WP No. 4027/2022)** explicitly held that Section 4C must be “**read down**” to allow taxpayers the deduction of **all brought-forward business losses and depreciation/amortization** in computing income for super tax【9†L51-L54】. The IHC found that the law could not constitutionally exclude prior years’ losses and allowances from the definition of “income” – indeed, any attempt to do so was declared **unconstitutional**【15†L77-L80】. In line with that authoritative interpretation, **our client is entitled to offset its entire brought-forward losses and depreciation against any income** before any super tax is calculated.

In the present case, K-Electric’s tax return for 2022 declared a **taxable loss of approximately Rs. 161 billion**, reflecting accumulated losses and depreciation from prior years【27†L231-L239】. The subsequent amended assessment (dated Oct 31, 2024) erroneously disallowed the subsidy exemption (as discussed above), thereby converting the loss into a taxable income of Rs. 25.699 billion【27†L231-L239】. However, once the correct legal position is applied – i.e. the subsidy remains exempt and **all brought-forward losses/allowances are deducted** – the **adjusted income for Section 4C purposes becomes nil**【26†L131-L139】【26†L137-L142】. In other words, even on the amended figures, the entire Rs. 25.699 billion income would be wiped out by the available brought-forward losses and unabsorbed depreciation, leaving **no taxable surplus** on which any 4C super tax could be levied. Thus, under a proper computation consistent with the IHC’s judgment in *Fauji Fertilizer* and the Income Tax Ordinance’s normal principles, **our client’s super tax liability for 2022 comes to zero**【26†L135-L142】. 

## Non-Consideration of Refunds and Tax Credits  
We further submit that the amended order for 2022 contains apparent errors which, when corrected, also eliminate any remaining tax demand. In particular, **valid refund orders under Section 170(4) of the Ordinance (aggregating Rs. 1,823,806,394)** were not given effect in the assessment. These refunds had been duly sanctioned in our client’s case and were available for adjustment, yet the order erroneously omitted them【26†L154-L162】【26†L156-L160】. Additionally, there was a **short allowance of tax credit for withholding taxes**: only Rs. 192,652 was credited instead of the correct amount of Rs. 26,763,264, leaving a shortfall of Rs. 26,570,612【26†L155-L162】. Our client has already moved a rectification application under Section 221 of the Ordinance (vide letter No. DT-3212 dated February 14, 2025) pointing out these mistakes. Copies of the Section 170(4) refund orders are enclosed again for your ready reference. Once these legitimate adjustments for refunds and withheld tax credits are made, the taxable income and any resultant tax liability for Tax Year 2022 would be **reduced to nil**【26†L156-L162】. In fact, incorporating the refunds alone would offset any notional super tax demand. We trust that your office will take note of these verifiable errors and ensure the correct refund adjustments are accounted for, obviating any unjust demand. 

## Conclusion and Request for Withdrawal of Super Tax Demand  
In view of the foregoing submissions, it is evident that **no super tax under Section 4C is payable by K-Electric for Tax Year 2022**. The binding judgments of the Hon’ble High Courts have clarified that Section 4C was **not applicable for TY 2022** (only from 2023 onward)【24†L53-L61】【21†L1662-L1670】. Moreover, the amended assessment’s departure from the Clause 102A subsidy exemption is untenable in law and contrary to past practice. Even on a without-prejudice basis, after allowing rightful losses, depreciation, and due refunds/credits, there remains **no taxable income** to subject to super tax. We therefore **respectfully request that the impugned super tax demand be withdrawn in its entirety**. Kindly revise the assessment accordingly and confirm that no demand under Section 4C will be enforced for Tax Year 2022. This will bring the matter to a just resolution in line with the law and the honorable courts’ decisions. 

We appreciate your attention to this submission. Please do not hesitate to contact us if any further information or clarification is required. 

Yours faithfully,  

**For K-Electric Limited** (Through Authorized Representatives)

Great. I will prepare a formal reply to the Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue on behalf of K-Electric Limited in response to the 4C Super Tax notice for Tax Year 2022. This reply will address all five points raised in the notice.

In particular:
- For Points I and III, I will provide a legal rebuttal based on the argument that the Sindh High Court and Islamabad High Court rulings on Section 4C apply in rem (universally), not in personam (individually).
- For Point II, I will reinforce the previous arguments that the Sindh High Court judgment regarding tariff adjustment for minimum tax under Section 113 has no bearing on the exemption under Clause 102A.
- For Point IV, I will confirm that the refund orders under Section 170(4) are already available with the tax office but will note that they are also enclosed for reference.

Below is a refined and expanded section that specifically addresses why the judgments of the **Sindh High Court** and **Islamabad High Court** on the applicability of Section 4C are **judgments in rem**, not **in personam**, and therefore binding beyond the petitioners, including on the tax department in the case of K-Electric:

---

### Legal Nature of High Court Judgments on Section 4C: *Judgments in Rem, Not in Personam*

With reference to points (i) and (iii) of your notice, your office has raised an objection suggesting that our reliance on the judgments of the **Hon’ble Sindh High Court** and **Hon’ble Islamabad High Court** regarding the prospective applicability of Section 4C is misconceived unless our client was a petitioner in those cases. With due respect, this assertion mischaracterizes the **binding effect and scope** of the said judgments, both of which were rendered **in rem**, and not merely **in personam**.

A **judgment in rem** is one that **settles the law itself**—it adjudicates on the validity, interpretation, or applicability of a statutory provision and is **binding on all persons**, not just the parties before the court. In contrast, a **judgment in personam** binds only the parties to the litigation on matters specific to their private rights or obligations.

In this context, the **judgments of both High Courts are clearly in rem** for the following reasons:

1. **Statutory Interpretation of Section 4C as a Matter of General Law**:  
   Both courts were called upon to **interpret the temporal scope and constitutional validity** of Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001—specifically, whether it could be applied to Tax Year 2022 despite being introduced through the Finance Act, 2022, effective from July 1, 2022. This is not a question of factual dispute between individual taxpayers and the tax department; rather, it is a **pure question of law affecting all similarly situated taxpayers**, including our client.

2. **Sindh High Court – CP No. D-5842 of 2022 (Shell Pakistan Ltd. and others v. Federation of Pakistan & others)**:  
   In this batch of constitutional petitions, the SHC examined whether Section 4C had **retrospective applicability to TY 2022**. The SHC held unequivocally:
   > “Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 is read to reflect that the levy shall be applicable from the tax year 2023.”  
   The judgment did not hinge on any fact specific to Shell Pakistan or any other petitioner. Rather, it declared **what the law is** and how it is to be **interpreted uniformly**. As such, it constitutes a **declaration of law under Article 189/201 of the Constitution**, and **binds all authorities in the province**, including your good office, as well as the FBR.

3. **Islamabad High Court – Writ Petition No. 4027 of 2022 (Fauji Fertilizer Co. Ltd. v. Federation of Pakistan)**:  
   Similarly, the IHC judgment examined the constitutionality and enforceability of Section 4C with reference to the **doctrine of past and closed transactions, legal certainty, and legitimate expectation**. The court declared that retrospective application to TY 2022 would be **ultra vires and void**. Again, this was a **principled judicial determination of the scope of a statutory provision**, not a case-specific relief. Such judgments inherently **bind the tax department as to the legal position** on the applicability of the statute.

4. **Precedent and Departmental Practice Recognizing In Rem Character**:  
   Historically, tax authorities have themselves acknowledged the in rem character of constitutional and statutory interpretation judgments. For example, when courts have struck down particular SROs or statutory provisions (e.g., certain minimum tax levies or retrospective amendments), the FBR has **issued circulars accepting the binding nature of such judgments** on all similarly situated taxpayers, without requiring that each taxpayer file their own writ petition.

5. **Principle of Judicial Discipline and Avoidance of Multiplicity of Litigation**:  
   The Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan has repeatedly held that **when a High Court has declared a statutory provision to have a particular meaning**, subordinate authorities **must not take a contrary view** in other cases (see: *Collector of Customs v. Karamat Enterprises*, PLD 2006 SC 293). Attempting to enforce Section 4C for TY 2022 on our client—when two constitutional courts have declared it **inapplicable to that year**—is contrary to judicial discipline and opens the door to unnecessary and avoidable litigation.

6. **Article 189 and 201 of the Constitution** – Binding Precedents:  
   While Article 189 makes Supreme Court judgments binding, **Article 201 of the Constitution of Pakistan** expressly provides:
   > “Subject to Article 189, any decision of a High Court shall, to the extent that it decides a question of law or is based upon or enunciates a principle of law, be binding on all courts subordinate to it.”  
   Thus, both the SHC and IHC decisions on the **interpretation of Section 4C** are binding on the tax authorities operating under their territorial jurisdiction, and persuasive across Pakistan. Your office, being located in Karachi, falls directly within the jurisdiction of the Hon’ble Sindh High Court.

---

**Conclusion on This Issue**  
In view of the above, the objection that our client must have been a named petitioner to benefit from these judgments is legally untenable. Both judgments constitute **binding declarations of law**, not merely private reliefs. Accordingly, your good office is **legally obliged to follow the interpretation laid down by the Sindh High Court and Islamabad High Court**, and **cannot enforce Section 4C for TY 2022** against K-Electric or any other taxpayer similarly situated.

We request that this position be duly appreciated, and the super tax demand under Section 4C for Tax Year 2022 be **withdrawn in full**.
